title: WebMCP Portfolio Kit
pitch: An evidence-first WebMCP portfolio kit: agents inspect published work, identify gaps, and prepare human-reviewed next steps.
about_excerpt: An evidence-first WebMCP portfolio kit: agents inspect published work, identify gaps, and prepare human-reviewed next steps. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I'm a freelance WordPress/WooCommerce and Shopify developer, and I already had a portfolio site built for an earlier dev.to Gemini hackathon. What stuck with me from that event wasn't the winning entries — it was one unranked submission: an MCP-enabled portfolio where an agent could actually query someone's CV instead of just reading it. It never won anything, but it was the only project I actually remembered months later. The WebMCP Challenge was the excuse to finally build that properly — and to fix what I think was the real gap in that original idea: answering "what are his skills" is a parlor trick. Answering "does he actually fit this job, and where are the gaps" is what a technical buyer actually needs. What it does WebMCP Portfolio Starter Kit exposes 8 WebMCP tools on a normal-looking portfolio site. An agent — acting for a recruiter, a CTO, whoever — can hand it a real brief and get back a transparent requirement → evidence → gap map: evidence found, or no direct evidence, stated plainly. It's never a forced "95% match" score. From there the agent can compare engagement options (migration / optimization / audit / advisory), save a session-only discovery brief, and prepare a contact request. A human reviews the draft; the core kit never sends a message. It's also a starter kit, not just a personal site: config, content, and code are cleanly separated, so anyone can fork it, drop in their own skills and projects, and deploy their own copy to Vercel with one click and zero required environment variables. How we built it I extended my existing Vite/React portfolio rather than starting from scratch, restructuring it into config/ (the fork surface), content/ (skills, case studies, engagement options), and generic src/lib/ tool code that never hardcodes a name. All 8 tools use the WebMCP Imperative API with explicit input schemas. Evidence tools are read-only; the remaining tools only update the visible page or create an unsent, reviewable draft. The core kit needs no backend. The one optional exception is a /setup Profile Bootstrapper that uses Vercel AI Gateway to help a forker draft their profile.json from raw material — off by default behind an explicit env var, output validated against a strict schema, and prompted to treat source text as data, never as instructions. Testing wasn't just manual clicking: validate-content checks the profile data against a schema, test:forkability runs the matching logic against a completely unrelated fixture persona, and a production run of the official webmcp-evals suite passed all eight tools against the live deployment. Challenges we ran into The hard trade-off was breadth versus coherence. I kept all eight tools, but prioritised their shared evidence model, clear side-effect boundaries, and production testing over extra visual polish and stretch features. Avoiding a false-precision "fit score" was a real design problem, not just a copy choice — early versions of the matching tool risked implying certainty the underlying logic didn't have. I settled on a plain requirement/evidence/gap map with an explicit disclaimer field on every response instead. And I didn't want "forkable" to just be a claim in a README. Proving it meant building an actual unrelated test persona and a smoke test, not just asserting the code was generic. Accomplishments that we're proud of The forkability test genuinely passes against a persona with nothing to do with cloud infrastructure — it surfaces a real skill match, a real project match, and an honestly stated unmatched requirement, for a profile that shares nothing with mine. Zero required environment variables to deploy the core kit — fork, edit two JSON files, click deploy. The optional AI-assisted drafting path is off by default and explicitly designed against prompt injection in its own source material, not just in theory. And map_requirements_to_evidence stating a gap plainly, instead of forcing a match — that's the single behavior the whole project is really about. Existing-work disclosure The visual portfolio and its self-authored project history existed before the challenge. During the submission period, I meaningfully extended it with eight WebMCP tools and schemas, the requirement-to-evidence interface, source-labelled outputs, the reusable config/content/code split, the Bootstrapper, and automated validation and evaluation. The public repository’s dated September 2–3 commits document that WebMCP-specific work. What we learned That a "never overclaim" constraint has to be enforced in the code itself, not just promised in a README — stating a gap instead of forcing a match, and never wiring up an auto-send path for the contact tool. That deterministic, auditable matching is a legitimate design choice against a generative one, not just a corner cut when you're short on time — every match traces back to real data instead of a model's guess. And that two small automated tests, plus one production evals run, are worth more than an evening of manual clicking when there's no time left to re-verify everything by hand before a deadline. What's next for WebMCP Portfolio Starter Kit Support importing authorised structured exports or pasted profile material — for example from a PeoplePerHour export — into profile.json , instead of a one-time manual copy. Semantic, embedding-based matching via Vercel AI Gateway as an option — making the matching smarter while keeping every match's underlying evidence fully auditable, not replacing it with a black box. And more real forks, to prove this out beyond the one alternate-persona fixture. title: Remy
pitch: Remy lets AI agents take real actions without taking control away from users. Safe work runs automatically, risky actions wait for approval, and every change gets a receipt and recovery path.
about_excerpt: Remy lets AI agents take real actions without taking control away from users. Safe work runs automatically, risky actions wait for approval, and every change gets a receipt and recovery path. Like Comment Story Updates Homepage Agent Activity Inspiration AI agents are becoming capable of changing real application state, but the current trust model feels broken. Users either approve every small action, making the agent slow and irritating, or grant broad autonomy and inspect the damage afterwards. Remy explores a middle ground: let reversible work happen automatically, pause consequential actions for explicit approval, and give users a clear record of what happened and a way back when possible. What it does Remy is a protocol-neutral action layer for applications that allow AI agents to take real actions. Developers define an action once, including what it changes, its risk, and how it can be recovered. Remy then provides: Runtime validation and action previews Developer policies and user-selected autonomy Explicit approval for consequential actions Human-readable receipts and diffs Append-only action history Exact undo, compensation, or an honest irreversible state The demo is a fictional headphone shop using WebMCP. An agent can add headphones, select delivery, and apply a discount automatically. Placing the order spends money, so Remy pauses and presents the exact item, price, address, and payment method for the user to approve. How we built it Remy’s core is a TypeScript action engine that does not depend on React or WebMCP. Every semantic action passes through the same validation, preview, policy, execution, receipt, and recovery pipeline. A WebMCP adapter exposes those actions as page-scoped tools. The shop’s normal interface and its WebMCP tools use the same underlying engine, keeping policy enforcement beside the application’s business logic. The demo uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Zod, Tailwind CSS, Motion, and Vitest. State and receipts are persisted locally for the challenge demonstrator. I also built an alpha initializer that scaffolds Remy into a Next.js application. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was making approval a real enforcement boundary rather than an instruction in a prompt. If an agent is merely told to wait, it may continue through another interaction path. The restriction therefore has to be enforced where the final state change occurs. Approval is also asynchronous, while agent tool calls may be short-lived. Remy represents approval as pending application state and revalidates the authoritative data before execution. Recovery introduced another challenge. Some changes can be undone exactly, some require a new compensating action, and others are genuinely irreversible. Remy needed to represent each case honestly without pretending that every action has an undo button. Accomplishments that we're proud of The working demo shows useful autonomy rather than simply approving or blocking everything. Reversible shopping actions can execute automatically, while the irreversible purchase stops for explicit approval. An agent cannot grant itself greater autonomy. Every attempt produces a readable receipt, duplicate effects are prevented with idempotency keys, stale approvals are invalidated, and reversals remain linked to the original action instead of erasing history. The same semantic action definitions power the normal website, the WebMCP tools, the policy engine, receipts, and recovery. What we learned Action history by itself is only observability. A receipt written after an unsafe mutation cannot protect the user. The action layer must make its decision before execution and remain on the path to the real state change. We also learned that reversibility is a useful basis for autonomy. Users should not need to approve harmless work that can be safely reversed, but consequential or irreversible actions deserve a clear checkpoint. Finally, WebMCP works well as an adapter, but the underlying action contract should remain protocol-neutral so the same guarantees can follow an action across different agent environments. What's next for Remy The next steps are publishing the core SDK and initializer, adding MCP and agent SDK adapters, and moving histories from local storage to a durable hosted journal. Future versions could add authenticated agent identity, approval routing, shared policies, monitoring, alerts, signed receipts, and evidence exports while allowing applications to keep their own interface and business logic. title: Fentanyl Watch
pitch: Track fentanyl drugs throughout the United States.
about_excerpt: Track fentanyl drugs throughout the United States. Like Comment Story Updates dashboard Inspiration The fentanyl overdose crisis killed more Americans last year than car crashes, yet the public data behind it is scattered across CDC provisional files, DEA press releases, and hundreds of local news stories. We built Fentanyl Watch to pull that picture into one place — a 3D map of 56 metro hotspots, each with a sourced profile. Click on a city for the full disclosed information. But a visualization can only answer the questions its designer anticipated. WebMCP changes that: if the page exposes its data and its camera as tools, an AI agent can answer any question — and then show you the answer on the map. That felt like the right test of what human-agent collaboration on the web should look like. What it does Fentanyl Watch renders 56 overdose hotspots on an extruded, Albers-projected 3D map of the lower 48. Column height encodes annual overdose deaths; column color encodes deaths per 100,000 residents. A toggleable second layer plots 32 major fentanyl seizures from 2025–26 and the 7 southwest border corridors with their share of national seizures. Every hotspot carries a sourced profile: statistics with their exact geographic and year basis, trend, seizure activity, and dated news events with source URLs. The page registers 10 WebMCP tools via document.modelContext.registerTool. Seven are read tools — list, fetch, and compare hotspot profiles, national summary and CDC timeline, seizures, border corridors, and a get_data_caveats tool that hands the agent the dataset's honest limitations before it quotes a number. Three are control tools that move what the human sees: focus_hotspot flies the 3D camera to a city and opens its profile drawer, set_seizure_layer toggles the seizure layer, and reset_view returns to the full-country frame. Ask an agent "which metro has the worst per-capita overdose rate?" and it doesn't just answer — it flies you there. How we built it The visualization is Three.js + Vite, with d3-geo and topojson-client projecting a Census TopoJSON into an extruded landmass — no framework, no runtime dependencies beyond those. The dataset was compiled from CDC WONDER and provisional VSRR data, DEA press releases and the National Drug Threat Assessment, state and county health departments, and news reporting, then normalized through a build pipeline into one JSON file. The WebMCP layer is a single module that builds tool descriptors with JSON Schemas and async execute handlers, then registers them against document.modelContext (with a fallback to the older navigator.modelContext draft, and a graceful no-op that stages the tools on window.__webmcpTools for console testing in browsers without the API). Read tools carry readOnlyHint annotations. Control tools call the exact same functions the UI buttons call — we refactored the seizure toggle so the agent and the human drive one shared code path, and the button state can never drift from what the agent did. Challenges we ran into A moving spec. WebMCP documentation still shows several API shapes — navigator.modelContext vs. document.modelContext, provideContext vs. registerTool, string returns vs. MCP-style content arrays. We read the current W3C explainer and Chrome's implementation docs side by side and wrote a small adapter that registers correctly against whichever surface the browser exposes. Overdose figures vary in geographic basis (city vs. county) and time basis (calendar year vs. rolling 12-month provisional windows), and provisional counts get revised. Rather than flattening this into a fake-uniform dataset, every profile labels its own basis, hotspots without a published rate say so instead of getting an invented number — and we exposed all of it to agents as a first-class get_data_caveats tool. Agent-driving a WebGL scene. Most WebMCP demos manipulate DOM. Our control tools have to fly a camera through a Three.js scene, compute framing around HUD panels, and open drawers — so tool handlers had to hook into the animation system, not just flip state. Accomplishments that we're proud of A tool surface with real depth: 10 tools spanning data query, comparison, and visual control — not a single bolted-on demo tool. The human-agent loop actually closes: the agent's answer and the human's screen stay in sync, because focus_hotspot shows you what the agent is talking about. A dataset that tells agents the truth about itself. get_data_caveats means an agent quoting our numbers can also quote their limitations. Every figure in all 56 profiles traces to a named source with a URL. What we learned Designing tools for agents is a different discipline from designing UI for humans. Descriptions are prompts: the difference between an agent using compare_hotspots well or ignoring it lives entirely in one sentence of description text. Read/write separation matters — readOnlyHint annotations let an agent explore freely while being deliberate about tools that move the user's view. And the most valuable tool wasn't a data query at all: it was giving the agent the dataset's caveats, because an agent that can explain a number's basis is more trustworthy than one that just recites it. What's next for Fentanyl Watch Live data refresh — automate the CDC VSRR and DEA ingestion pipeline so the map tracks each provisional release. Richer agent tools — timeline queries per hotspot, region-level aggregation, and a find_sources tool that returns citations for any claim on screen. Declarative WebMCP — annotate the search and filter UI with the declarative API as it stabilizes. Beyond fentanyl — the architecture (sourced hotspot profiles + agent tool surface over a 3D map) generalizes to any geographic crisis dataset: xylazine spread, HIV outbreaks, disaster response. title: CircuitForge
pitch: CircuitForge is a browser-based digital logic simulator where AI agents and humans build, test, and debug circuits together in real time using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: CircuitForge is a browser-based digital logic simulator where AI agents and humans build, test, and debug circuits together in real time using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates 1 CircuitForge in action. Inspiration I built CircuitForge because I was struggling in my digital circuits class. Building combinational logic by hand or using clunky desktop simulators is frustrating, and one tiny wiring error can take hours to track down. I wanted to use modern AI to help design and debug my circuits, but standard AI assistants completely break when faced with visual canvas tools. They rely on screenshots and pixel coordinates, which fails miserably when pins are a few pixels wide and wires overlap. Instead of forcing AI to squint at a canvas and guess where to click, I wanted to give it direct, semantic access to the underlying mathematical graph of the circuit. What It Does CircuitForge is a browser-based digital logic studio where humans and AI agents collaborate on the exact same circuit in real time. For Humans: A clean visual canvas to place gates, route wires, and build computers from scratch. For AI Agents: A WebMCP control plane with 19 native tools to inspect, build, and verify circuits without ever "seeing" a single pixel. Key features include: Modular Synthesis: Agents can build subcircuits (like an OR gate made of NANDs), test them, and package them into reusable custom ICs. Automated Verification: Instead of guessing if an LED is on, agents run a full truth-table verification that systematically tests every input combination. Signal Tracing: Tools to trace signals upstream/downstream and find floating inputs. Shared Viewport: Agents can pan and zoom the camera so the human and AI are always looking at the same part of the board. How We Built It We built CircuitForge as a 4-tier web app bridging modern web standards with a compiled WebAssembly simulation engine: Simulation Core: A modernized, browser-safe version of Sebastian Lague's Digital Logic Sim, running in Unity WebGL/WASM. C# Semantic Bridge: A custom command dispatcher that executes typed graph mutations (adding gates, toggling pins) directly on the C# netlist. TypeScript WebMCP Host: A Vite frontend that registers our tools into the browser's document.modelContext with strict Zod schemas. Dual-Agent Support: Built-in browser WebMCP (for ChatGPT/Chrome) and a standalone WebSocket relay so external CLI agents (like Claude Code or Codex) can control the canvas too. Challenges We Ran Into The Opaque Canvas: WebGL renders straight to the GPU, so there are no DOM nodes for gates or wires. Automation tools just see a blank <canvas> . We solved this by serializing the internal C# graph into clean, typed JSON snapshots that the AI can read directly. Async JS vs. Single-Threaded WASM: JS is async, but Unity WebGL runs single-threaded. Blocking the main thread froze the browser. We built a custom async request map with UUIDs so JS could fire a tool call, yield to the event loop, and wait for C# to resolve the Promise via a .jslib extern. Timing and Physics Bugs: When agents packaged subcircuits, long chip names would clip through the pins. We had to write an auto-sizer algorithm. We also had to fix race conditions during truth-table verification by forcing the simulation to "settle" for a few physics cycles before reading the outputs. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of True Agentic Control: We built a system where AI can design complex logic purely through code and semantic tools, completely bypassing the hallucinations of computer vision and OCR. Autonomous Hierarchical Design: It was awesome to watch the AI take a prompt like "build a 3-input OR gate using only NANDs", wire it up, verify the truth table, package it as a custom chip, and then immediately use that new chip to build a majority function. Works Everywhere: Whether you're using an in-browser agent or an external CLI tool like Claude Code, it interacts with the live canvas seamlessly. What We Learned Canvas apps can be agent-native: You don't need to sacrifice rich WebGL graphics to support AI agents. You just need to expose the underlying data model via WebMCP. State tracking matters: Adding monotonic revision numbers to every tool call completely fixed race conditions between the human clicking and the AI placing components. Digital logic is perfect for AI: Because boolean logic has strict, unambiguous mathematical rules, it's an incredible benchmark for testing an AI's ability to reason and self-correct. What's Next for CircuitForge Full CPU Architectures: Moving beyond basic gates to build full 8-bit CPUs with registers, decoders, and RAM. Interactive Tutor Mode: An AI tutor that generates circuits with subtle bugs (like floating inputs or race hazards) and helps students debug them step-by-step. HDL Support: Adding tools to compile Verilog/VHDL directly into interactive CircuitForge schematics. title: QuePlan × WebMCP — a real insurance comparator, agent-ready
pitch: 13 WebMCP tools turn Latin America's health-insurance comparator into a shared workspace for people and AI agents: real pricing engine, explained recommendations, the human keeps the click.
about_excerpt: 13 WebMCP tools turn Latin America's health-insurance comparator into a shared workspace for people and AI agents: real pricing engine, explained recommendations, the human keeps the click. Like 8 Comment Story Updates Production: the real www.queplan.cl comparator with the same 13 tools registered natively (?webmcp=1) comparar_seguros: head-to-head comparison opened by the agent, the human sees exactly what it reasons about recomendar_seguros: an explained top 3 opens on screen as a podium, with per-attribute winners 13 tools registered on Chrome's native WebMCP API (document.modelContext), polyfill as fallback setear_perfil + aplicar_filtros_comparador: one sentence becomes a family profile and checked filters; the panel narrates preparar_solicitud: the agent scrolls and highlights Contratar. It cannot click it; the person does input_invalido: a typed error instead of a broken page. Nothing changed, the agent knows why Inspiration We run QuePlan, a health-insurance comparator that has been live in Chile for ten years and later in Peru and Colombia. About 4.5 million people used it in the last twelve months, and more than 165,000 policies contracted through it are active today. For months we had been watching AI agents try to use our site. They do fine on a blog and badly on a comparator, because there is no price to read: every price depends on who is asking (age, sex, dependants, Fonasa or Isapre) and our engine calculates it per family. An agent scraping our HTML picks up the "from" price and confidently gives people the wrong number. So the question for the challenge was simple: what if the page told the agent what it can do, and did the work itself? What it does Our comparator now exposes 13 WebMCP tools. A person opens the page in ChatGPT's in-app browser (or Chrome with WebMCP on) and just talks: "I'm 34, two kids of 5 and 8, complementary or catastrophic plans under 120,000 pesos". The agent sets the profile and applies the filters, and the page moves exactly as if the person had clicked through the forms. From there it can ask for an explained top three (we return structured reasons and open the podium on screen), compare two plans head to head, open a detail sheet, page forward, and produce a link that restores the whole state so the family can look at it together later. One decision we made early: the agent never contracts anything. The last tool, preparar_solicitud , scrolls to the plan and highlights the Contratar button. That click, and everything after it, stays with the person. Health insurance is a consequential decision and we wanted the boundary to be visible in the UI, not buried in a disclaimer. There is also a small panel on the right that narrates every tool call in plain Spanish and lights up the part of the page that changed. It started as a debugging aid and became the thing testers liked most: you can see what the agent is doing to your screen. How we built it The production app is Angular. Registering tools was the easy part; getting them to run inside ChatGPT's browser was not. zone.js patches Promise and the native WebMCP API only accepts real ones, so at first ChatGPT registered one tool out of thirteen. We wrote a "native boundary" wrapper that hands the browser V8-real promises (via Zone.__symbol__('Promise') ), keeps descriptors structured-clone safe and returns errors in band. After that: 13/13. Every tool has an inputSchema with enums, an outputSchema with structuredContent , readOnlyHint / untrustedContentHint annotations, and one shared set of outcomes: ok , timeout , error_backend , input_invalido , sin_cambios , limite_excedido , circuito_abierto . We added that after catching the agent telling a user "filters applied" while the backend was still thinking. A slow answer is not a success. We could not ask judges to poke at a production site full of real insurers, so we also built an open replica: same 13 tools, same contracts (a test checks they match production verbatim), synthetic plans with made-up insurers, MIT license, 63 tests. That is the live URL. The production integration is linked as well for anyone who wants the real thing, in Spanish. Challenges we ran into Our own agent testing gave us the scare of the week. One session fired 586 identical quote requests in 70 seconds, twelve per second, because each re-quote cancelled the previous one in the browser but not on the server. An agent can hurt your backend without meaning to. The layer now de-duplicates in-flight requests, rate-limits per tool, detects duplicate retries and opens a circuit breaker after consecutive backend failures. The agent gets a clear error with how long to wait instead of a timeout. Other things that bit us: ChatGPT's runtime clones the registerTool options bag, so passing an AbortSignal silently broke registration; ids that came back as strings in one environment and integers in another; and a profile helper that "invented" a dependant's sex when the agent only gave the age. Fixing that last one mattered to us. The agent should ask, not guess. Accomplishments that we're proud of It works in every runtime we could get our hands on: ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome's native API, and Claude through a local MCP relay, with an end-to-end harness that runs all 13 tools. The layer is live in the real comparator, not only in the demo. It was a team effort in Santiago: product, engineering and QA all had a hand in it, with review rounds on every PR. We used AI coding agents for implementation and, separately, for adversarial review, and the second model kept finding things the first one missed. What we learned WebMCP turned out to be less about exposing functions and more about deciding what the human should still see and still do. Most of our time went into contracts, errors and on-screen feedback, not into the tool bodies. And "agent-safe by default" (dedup, limits, breakers) belongs inside the layer, not in a later hardening sprint. What's next Roll the same tools out to queplan.pe and queseguro.co (the layer is already parameterised by country), add needs-based recommendation ("I have a chronic condition, what should I look at?"), and measure the agent channel like any other: tool calls, quotes, requests, policies. Prior work The comparator and an older 7-tool prototype predate the challenge. The six new tools, the contract system, the native boundary, the guards, the activity panel and the public demo were built during it. PRIOR_WORK.md in the repo has the dated commits. Links Live demo (synthetic data, no login): https://queplan.github.io/queplan-webmcp/ Public repo (MIT): https://github.com/QuePlan/queplan-webmcp Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e99_6OGt1BM Production integration (QuePlan Chile; Chrome 149+ with the WebMCP flag, or ChatGPT's in-app browser): https://www.queplan.cl/Comparar/Seguros-de-Salud?webmcp=1 Built With angular.js chatgpt chrome express.js github google-cloud-run mcp-b-polyfill model-context-protocol node.js postgresql rxjs typescript vite webmcp zone.js Try it out queplan.github.io github.com www.queplan.cl github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by José Oropeza Matías Stäger Koller Axel Aaron Quezada Mario Hoare Like 8 8 people like this: Share this project: Updates Matías Stäger Koller started this project — Sep 03, 2026 02:13 PM EDT

title: Airlock: Agent-Native Data Workspace
pitch: AI analysis for file you can't upload. In-browser DuckDB plus WebMCP tools, every change staged for your approval, with a signed receipt of what the agent saw.
about_excerpt: AI analysis for file you can't upload. In-browser DuckDB plus WebMCP tools, every change staged for your approval, with a signed receipt of what the agent saw. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every team has a spreadsheet nobody is allowed to paste into ChatGPT: compensation, customer lists, finances under NDA. Yet people paste anyway — roughly 11% of ChatGPT pastes contain confidential information, a fifth of breaches now involve shadow AI, and AI chats have been ruled discoverable in court. We wanted the analysis without the upload: AI help with data that physically cannot leave the room. What it does Airlock is a data workspace in a single browser tab. Your file is read locally and queried with in-browser DuckDB-WASM — nothing uploads, ever. An AI agent works on it through WebMCP tools the page exposes: 8 read tools that run immediately and are logged, and 12 staged actions where every change (filters, derived columns, charts, flags, reports, redaction, export) appears as a visible diff that nothing applies until you press Approve. An activity ledger records every call with exact rows disclosed. A signed attestation receipt — hashes and counts, never values — verifies offline at /verify.html . God mode runs a Qwen model fully on-device via WebGPU for genuine airplane-mode analysis, or bring your own endpoint key, which never leaves tab memory. It also imports PDF, DOCX and images OCR'd on-device into queryable tables. How we built it React 18 + Vite + TypeScript + Tailwind, npm workspaces. The reusable core is packages/webmcp-staged — a zero-dependency propose→review→commit primitive spanning WebMCP, OpenAI tool-calling and plain MCP transports. DuckDB-WASM, pdf.js, Tesseract and the model weights are all self-hosted same-origin; an egress monitor wrapping fetch/XHR/beacon/WebSocket proves zero bytes leave, live, in the top bar. 530+ tests, npm audit clean, Netlify deploy with COOP/COEP, WASM MIME types and origin-trial support. Challenges we ran into Honesty was harder than engineering: "data never leaves the browser" is false the moment a cloud agent reads query results, so cloud mode states plainly that slices travel (and counts them) while the fully-local loop makes the strong claim literally true. Small models were the second fight — 1.5B-parameter callers loop, invert comparisons and stuff GROUP BY into filter boxes — answered with schema-tolerant tools, corrective errors, repeat guards and a fail-fast circuit breaker. Third was host discovery: WebMCP gates on origin isolation and trial enrollment, which took real header and deploy work. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete loop the camera can verify: offline analysis with Seal at zero, every mutation human-gated, a signed receipt that verifies offline, and an agent surface ChatGPT, a local model, your own endpoint, or the built-in console can all drive unchanged. Plus a reusable MIT primitive any WebMCP app can adopt for the same propose→approve→commit safety. What we learned Agent UX is approval UX — the review queue, not the chat, is where trust happens. A privacy claim the code can't back is worse than no claim at all. And tiny on-device models are usable agents if the tool surface is tight enough to hold them. What's next for Airlock: Agent-Native Data Workspace Depth over breadth: the pay-equity workflow first (EU Pay Transparency deadlines make the receipt a requirement, not a nicety), then adjacent regulated-data reviews. On the tech side: richer provenance-linked reports, local folder and localhost-database sources, and a second independent implementation of the staged-authority protocol so the receipt becomes an interoperable standard, not a single-app artifact. title: Commonplace
pitch: A blog and reading platform that adapts to you. Using WebMCP, browser agents reshape layout, colors, and drafts around how you write and read.
about_excerpt: A blog and reading platform that adapts to you. Using WebMCP, browser agents reshape layout, colors, and drafts around how you write and read. Like Comment Story Updates OLED pitch-black feed with headers, hero, quote, and agent rail hidden via user settings. Personalization studio drawer for adjusting layout density, measure, type scales, and surfaces. Realtime voice guide in dark emerald monospace connecting spoken intent to WebMCP actions. Distraction-free reading view on warm paper with generative artwork and local save actions. In-page WebMCP tool inspector displaying schemas and live execution for all 44 tools. Adaptive desk in night mode with live WebMCP telemetry and quick palette switching. Publishing composer with structured fields exposed directly to browser agents. Public profile rendered in editorial serif typography and dark emerald forest slate. Commonplace Commonplace is a blog and reading platform prototype that adapts to you. Using WebMCP, browser agents reshape layout, colors, and drafts around how you write and read. Inspiration For as long as I can remember, the very first thing I do when opening any new piece of software is dive straight into settings. I inspect every toggle, theme picker, and slider to bend the tool to how I think. Google built Material Expressive for a reason. I spend hours tuning browser extensions and user scripts because default interfaces never quite fit. The web has spent thirty years treating consumers as passive recipients of frozen pixels. A product team in another time zone decides your column width, font scale, and color scheme, and you are expected to conform to it. In the AI era, that model makes no sense. We now have the capability to make software listen and adapt. I wanted to build a corner of the web that I could reshape in real time to what matters to me right now. What it does Commonplace is a personal blog and reading platform where the interface adapts to how you read, write and feel. Instead of hiding controls inside nested preference menus, Commonplace turns its entire runtime into an action contract for browser agents via WebMCP: You can tell the agent you feel tired, and it instantly softens contrast, drops into night mode, and narrows the reading measure. You can ask the agent to hide sidebars, rearrange homepage blocks, or surface your saved queue without touching settings. The agent searches topics, queries your reading list, and edits active drafts beside you in the composer without taking over your screen. Through OpenAI Realtime WebRTC mapped to the exact same WebMCP tools, you can talk to the desk to dictate thoughts or re-theme the workspace hands-free. How I built it Commonplace is built as a local-first application using React 19, TypeScript, Bun, and Vite, with styling powered by Tailwind CSS v4 and dynamic CSS custom properties. The platform registers 44 distinct tools on document.modelContext using @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill . Every tool includes strict JSON schemas, descriptions, and operational hints like readOnlyHint and idempotentHint . Tools are registered under their canonical dot names and parallel underscore aliases so ChatGPT browser agents can call them without validation failures. The styling system maps 13 semantic OKLCH tokens directly to CSS variables, allowing runtime palette and typography adjustments with zero layout jank. The app links document.modelContext , window.modelContext , and navigator.modelContext so host environments that attach to any of the three discover all capabilities. All post data, drafts, and theme overrides live in browser localStorage , removing all sign-up friction for judges. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making the UI look coherent and intentional given the sheer amount of live customization built into it. When you allow an agent to adjust corner radii, swap between sans-serif and editorial serifs and manipulate color scales dynamically, layout can quickly become messy. Engineering a design system that holds its balance and typography rhythm while every dial remains turnable was technically demanding. I also ran into browser environment edge cases and platform nuances. Ensuring that WebMCP implementation works properly across all supported platforms was the primary challenge, as it's the first thing you have to get right if you want to deliver the rest of the experience. Accomplishments that I'm proud of It clicked when the experience I craved for years finally matched the one I built. I opened the browser, spoke to the space, and watched the page translate my intent and mood into the exact visual setup I needed, right there, with no delay. The experience is as seamless as it should be, and I think it's the first time when the paradigm shift can finally happen as scale, for all. What I learned Rigid rules will soon be a thing of the past in consumer software. Building Commonplace proved that WebMCP fundamentally changes the relationship between people and software. When websites expose typed tool contracts instead of forcing agents to scrape fragile CSS selectors, software becomes truly flexible and accessible. What's next for Commonplace Commonplace represents a design philosophy I intend to carry into every product I build. Beyond this hackathon, I want to explore multi-device agent synchronization, peer-to-peer reading networks, and richer declarative forms so that adaptive software becomes the standard way people experience the web moving forward. pitch: A maze game where an AI agent can inspect, solve, and actually play the game through WebMCP tools
about_excerpt:

 Inspiration 

 We wanted to explore how AI Agent can do more than just give instructions it can interact with a real web application and complete a task . 

 We chose a maze because it provides a simple and visual way to demonstrate this idea. By combining WebMCP with Amazon Bedrock , the AI Agent can understand the maze, find a valid path, make the moves, and verify that the player has reached the exit. 

 Our goal was to turn a simple maze game into an AI-interactive web application . 

 What It Does 

 Maze Escape is a browser-based maze game that can be played manually by a user or automatically by an AI Agent . 

 The AI Agent can interact with the live game using WebMCP tools . It can: 

 
 View the current maze and game state 
 Check the player's position 
 Check available moves 
 Find the shortest valid path using BFS 
 Execute the solution through the game 
 Verify whether the maze has been successfully completed 
 

 The project uses Amazon Bedrock for AI reasoning and WebMCP for interaction with the game. 

 In simple terms: 

 
 * You can play the maze yourself or ask the AI Agent to find the shortest path and actually solve it. * 
 

 How we built it 

 We built Maze Escape as a browser-based game using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript , with a Node.js backend and Netlify Functions for the AI integration. 

 1. Maze Game 

 The frontend manages the maze, player movement, timer, move counter, and game status. Users can navigate the maze manually using the available controls. 

 2. WebMCP Integration 

 We exposed the game's important functions as WebMCP tools , allowing a compatible AI Agent to interact directly with the running game. 

 The main tools include: 

 
 get_maze_state 
 get_player_state 
 get_available_moves 
 move_player 
 restart_game 
 get_game_status 
 find_solution 
 execute_solution 
 

 3. Maze Solving 

 We implemented Breadth-First Search (BFS) to find a shortest valid path from the player's current position to the exit. 

 This keeps pathfinding deterministic and reliable instead of asking the AI Agent to calculate every movement itself. 

 4. AI Agent 

 We integrated Amazon Bedrock using the Converse API. The AI Agent receives the user's request and can decide which WebMCP tools to use to inspect, solve, and verify the game. 

 5. Backend and Security 

 The Bedrock integration runs through a Netlify Serverless Function . AWS credentials are stored as environment variables and are never placed in the browser or frontend code. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Building Maze Escape involved solving a few important technical challenges: 

 
 * Connecting AI Agents with the live game: * We needed the AI Agent to access the actual maze state and perform actions, so we exposed the game's functionality through WebMCP tools. 
 Reliable maze solving: ** Instead of relying on the AI Agent to calculate every move, we implemented **BFS to consistently find a shortest valid path. 
 * Efficient tool execution: * Calling move_player for every step could require many tool calls. We added execute_solution to execute the complete path more efficiently. 
 * Amazon Bedrock integration: * Connecting the AI Agent to Bedrock required a server-side integration through a Netlify Function while keeping AWS credentials secure. 
 * Deployment and configuration: * We had to correctly configure Netlify environment variables, the Bedrock model identifier, and the serverless API so the AI Agent worked in the deployed application. 
 

 These challenges helped us build a more reliable connection between AI reasoning, WebMCP tools, and real-time web application actions . 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud of turning a simple maze game into a working AI-interactive web application . 

 Our key accomplishments are: 

 
 🤖 Built an AI Agents that can understand and interact with the live maze . 
 🌐 Integrated WebMCP tools for structured interaction with the game. 
 🧠 Implemented BFS to reliably find a shortest valid path. 
 ⚡ Added execute_solution to complete the maze efficiently with fewer tool calls. 
 ☁️ Integrated Amazon Bedrock for AI reasoning. 
 🔐 Kept AWS credentials securely on the server-side using Netlify Functions . 
 🚀 Successfully deployed the application as a live web app. 
 

 Most importantly, the AI Agent does not just explain how to solve the maze it can actually perform the actions and verify that the maze has been completed . 

 What we learned 

 Building Maze Escape helped us understand how AI Agents can interact with real web applications instead of only generating text. 

 We learned how to: 

 
 🌐 Use WebMCP to expose website functionality as structured tools for AI Agents. 
 🤖 Build an AI workflow where the Agents can understand, act, and verify . 
 🧠 Use BFS to find a reliable shortest path through a maze. 
 🔗 Combine AI reasoning with deterministic algorithms for better reliability. 
 ☁️ Integrate Amazon Bedrock using the Converse API. 
 ⚡ Use Netlify Functions to connect the web application with cloud AI services. 
 🔐 Keep AWS credentials secure by keeping them on the server side. 
 🛠️ Design tools that are simple and clear enough for an AI Agents to use effectively. 
 🚀 Deploy and configure an AI-powered web application for real-world use. 
 

 The biggest lesson we learned is that AI becomes more useful when it can interact with applications through well-defined tools and take real actions , rather than only explaining what should be done. 

 What's next for Maze Escape Game 

 We plan to extend Maze Escape from a single maze experience into a more capable AI-interactive application. 

 Our future plans include: 

 
 🧩 More maze levels and difficulty modes with larger and more complex mazes. 
 🎲 Procedurally generated mazes for a new challenge every time. 
 🤖 Smarter AI interactions with more WebMCP tools and improved agent workflows. 
 📊 AI performance tracking to compare solving time, moves, and efficiency. 
 👤 AI vs. Human mode to compare how quickly the AI Agent and players can solve the same maze. 
 🎨 Better visualizations showing how the AI Agent finds and follows a path. 
 🔌 Multiple AI model support so different models can be tested with the same WebMCP tools. 
 🌐 More real-world AI tasks beyond maze solving, using the same idea of giving AI Agents structured access to web applications. 
 

 Our long-term goal is to explore how WebMCP can make web applications more useful and interactive for AI Agents , allowing them to understand a task, use application tools, take actions, and verify the result.

title: Remnic Canvas
pitch: A visible memory page for you and every AI agent. Agents recall, propose, correct, and forget through native WebMCP tools while you approve every change.
about_excerpt: A visible memory page for you and every AI agent. Agents recall, propose, correct, and forget through native WebMCP tools while you approve every change. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents forget. Start a new conversation and you often start from zero. The memory that does exist is usually hidden inside one vendor's system. You cannot inspect it, fix it, move it, or decide exactly what gets saved. I build Remnic , an open source memory store for AI agents. The WebMCP Challenge made me ask a different question: what if the web page itself became the shared memory between a person and any browser agent? What it does Remnic Canvas is one live page where you and an agent share the same memory. The page exposes five native WebMCP tools: recall_memories searches approved memories and highlights the matching cards. remember proposes a new memory and waits for the person to approve, edit, or reject it. correct_memory replaces a stale fact while keeping its visible history. forget_memory asks for explicit confirmation before removing a memory. load_context gives the agent a focused set of approved memories for its next task. The approval step is part of the tool call. The agent proposes the words. The person can rewrite them. The edited text returns to the agent as the tool result. If a person does not answer before the agent's tool deadline, the tool returns pending while the card stays actionable on the page. Shared spaces let another browser or agent use the same memory later. Every memory exports as a plain markdown file with YAML frontmatter. You can read it, edit it, track it in Git, or add it to Remnic. Why WebMCP This interaction needs the tool and the interface to share one live page. A backend MCP server cannot show a pending card inside the page and wait for a human edit. Screen scraping cannot guarantee that the page's approval rules were followed. WebMCP lets the agent use the same code paths as the visible interface. The browser discovers a small set of structured tools. The person sees each action happen and keeps control of every write. How I built it The app uses React, TypeScript, Vite, IndexedDB, MiniSearch, and the WebMCP imperative API. A MemoryStore interface supports browser-local memory and shared spaces. Shared spaces sync through a Cloudflare Worker and Workers KV. The site is deployed on Cloudflare Pages and stays within the free tier. The UI uses warm paper cards on a dark canvas. Teal marks agent actions. Amber marks human decisions. The activity rail records each tool call and approval. Corrections keep their lineage. Forgotten cards dissolve. Export and import use Remnic's markdown format. Chrome requires WebMCP pages to be origin isolated, so the deployment sends Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and a tools=(self) permissions policy. I tested the production page in Chrome 151 with enable-webmcp-testing . Chrome's official WebMCP Model Context Tool Inspector discovered all five tools, returned a structured recall result, and completed a real remember call through human approval. Challenges The hardest part was making human approval work inside a tool call without leaving the agent runtime hanging. The first design waited for 120 seconds. The final design returns a valid pending result after 55 seconds while leaving the card open for a later decision. Browser support also required careful testing. My first ChatGPT tests opened links in the default external browser instead of ChatGPT's built-in browser. I corrected the setting and repeated the test on the right surface. Site Tools were not enabled for my ChatGPT account, so I completed native testing through the contest's other official path: Chrome 151 with the WebMCP flag and Inspector extension. The video created a different challenge. A technical demo was not enough. I rebuilt it around the problem people feel, added captions and motion, showed the native Chrome Inspector result, zoomed into the human edit, and proved that export produces readable markdown rather than another black box. What I learned WebMCP is most useful when an agent action needs to stay visible, editable, and under human control. The strongest tool is not always the most autonomous one. Sometimes the important result is a clean handoff between the agent and the person. I also learned that open memory is a natural WebMCP use case. The page can keep the human interface, expose a narrow tool contract, and let different agents share context without giving one AI vendor permanent control of that context. What was built during the challenge Remnic is an existing open source project and is used only as an external format and optional destination. Remnic Canvas is a new standalone app and public repository created during the challenge window. All Canvas code, the five WebMCP tools, approval flow, browser store, shared-space Worker, visual design, tests, deployment, video, and submission assets were built during the challenge. title: Investigation Canvas
pitch: Investigation Canvas turns messy data into a shared, visual investigation where humans spot what matters and AI agents test it with auditable WebMCP tools
about_excerpt: Investigation Canvas turns messy data into a shared, visual investigation where humans spot what matters and AI agents test it with auditable WebMCP tools Like Comment Story Updates About the project Inspiration Most AI data tools force people into one of two interfaces: a chat window that hides the underlying evidence, or a dashboard that an agent can only understand by scraping text, pixels, and DOM elements. Real investigations work differently. A human notices an unusual cluster, questions an assumption, or recognizes missing context. An agent can search hundreds of records, compare cohorts, inspect documents, and track several explanations simultaneously. We built Investigation Canvas around one idea: the human and the agent should work on the same visible investigation—not exchange disconnected summaries. What it does Investigation Canvas is a visual reasoning workspace for exploring datasets, evidence, relationships, hypotheses, findings, and possible causes. Humans can: Filter, search, and visually select records Explore linked scatter plots, timelines, tables, and relationship graphs Inspect evidence and its trust level Challenge the agent with contradictory examples Arrange findings and evidence on a spatial canvas Review every action through an auditable provenance trail Through WebMCP, an external agent receives 48 structured tools operating on the same workspace. It can query records, compare cohorts, rank distinguishing features, find correlations and outliers, inspect evidence, navigate relationships, create competing hypotheses, search for counterevidence, record findings, build causal links, save views, and branch an investigation. Every agent action changes the visible workspace. The human can inspect, rearrange, question, or reject the result. The project includes three complete example investigations: A checkout conversion regression with two independent causes An ML model-quality regression involving preprocessing and optimizer behavior A suspicious transaction network with explicit evidence-trust boundaries Why WebMCP A scatter plot may be immediately meaningful to a person but opaque to an agent. Investigation Canvas already knows which records each point represents, which cohort is selected, how evidence relates to a hypothesis, and which actions changed the investigation. WebMCP exposes those semantics directly instead of making the agent reverse-engineer the rendered interface. This creates shared attention . A human can select an unexpected group of records and ask the agent to investigate exactly that selection. The agent can focus a source, create a hypothesis, or place a finding on the canvas, and the human immediately sees the result. WebMCP turns agent reasoning into inspectable product actions. How we built it Investigation Canvas is a dependency-light static web application built with JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. A deterministic state store drives both the visual interface and the WebMCP tool implementations. Human interactions and agent actions therefore operate on the same investigation state rather than separate copies. The page registers its tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Read-only tools are marked accordingly, while tools returning third-party evidence identify that output as untrusted. Mutating tools use the same state operations as the visible interface, making their effects observable across selections, filters, evidence, hypotheses, findings, canvas artifacts, branches, and provenance. We also implemented: CSV, JSON, JSONL, and NDJSON imports Public JSON API snapshots Schema inference Investigation export and restoration Browser-local persistence Undo and redo Saved analysis views Restorable investigation branches Web-worker processing for larger local datasets Three deterministic example datasets The Do example experience lets a judge choose an investigation, understand its mission, load an isolated workspace, and copy a prompt for an external WebMCP agent. It never fakes an agent conversation or silently runs a scripted simulation. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was making agent activity understandable. Our early demo concepts moved too quickly, displayed too much information, and blurred the distinction between a real external agent and a scripted presentation. We replaced that approach with a clear handoff: choose a dataset, understand the mission, copy a prompt, connect through WebMCP, and watch durable actions appear in the shared workspace. We also had to preserve spatial context. Selecting a record or focusing evidence should not unexpectedly reset the canvas or camera. Data-state changes and view-state changes were separated so human exploration remains stable while the agent works. Finally, evidence is not automatically truth. The suspicious-transaction scenario contains both verified internal material and untrusted external claims. Investigation Canvas makes this distinction explicit instead of allowing an agent to treat every document as authoritative. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most powerful when a website already possesses rich domain semantics. Structured tools make agents more reliable, but the larger benefit is collaboration: agent actions become visible and reviewable instead of disappearing inside a chat response. We also learned that a serious investigation tool must make disagreement easy. Competing hypotheses, contradictory evidence, falsification questions, human-selected counterexamples, and provenance are not optional additions. They are what keep fast agent analysis accountable. What’s next Next, we would add authenticated streaming data connectors, server-side processing for very large datasets, real-time multi-user investigations, and exportable investigation reports. The central interaction would remain unchanged: humans direct attention and exercise judgment, while agents perform structured analysis through visible, auditable tools. The saved version is also available in SUBMISSION.md . title: ArcadeOps Relay
pitch: Browser intent becomes a bounded mission, a human decision, and cryptographically verified delivery.
about_excerpt: Browser intent becomes a bounded mission, a human decision, and cryptographically verified delivery. Like Comment Story Updates The verified end state: four evidence checks pass and the accepted delivery receives a valid Ed25519 certificate. One shared Project Aurora workspace: browser agent, bounded worker, human authority, and evidence in the same state. Browser intent to verified delivery WebMCP mission control from browser intent to verified delivery. Inspiration Browser agents can understand the page in front of a person, while worker agents can execute substantial tasks. What was missing was the operational layer between them: a shared place to turn intent into a mission, keep work moving, bring in human judgment at the right moment, and carry trustworthy context through to delivery. We built ArcadeOps Relay as that mission control layer. What it does Relay gives a browser agent seven intent-level WebMCP tools on a live Project Aurora workspace. The agent inspects the objective and constraints, drafts a bounded mission, delegates a persisted internal worker, and follows authoritative progress. ArcadeOps coordinates the handoffs and surfaces one strategic release choice when human judgment adds value. The person sees the consequences and evidence in the same workspace, chooses whether to stage or postpone, and the exact run resumes with its context intact. The worker produces the release-readiness artifacts, ArcadeOps evaluates four required evidence checks, and a hash-bound Ed25519 certificate proves the accepted delivery. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets the browser agent use the current page, scoped judge session, project, and human-visible state without DOM guessing or a separately installed MCP connector. Relay registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Tools appear only on the challenge page, use strict schemas, avoid duplicate registration, and disappear on navigation. Human-agent collaboration The human, browser agent, and worker share one authoritative workspace. The browser agent turns visible project context into a mission; the worker executes; ArcadeOps preserves progress, cost, decisions, and evidence; and the human guides the strategic moments. Together they can delegate real bounded work, resume safely after a decision, and prove delivery without losing context or letting an agent approve itself. How it was built Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Zod, native imperative WebMCP, server-side SQLite transactions, signed HMAC authority handles, canonical SHA-256 evidence packs, and Ed25519 certificates. Playwright covers desktop, dark theme, mobile, accessibility, isolation, tool lifecycle, and the complete visible workflow. Vitest covers state transitions and adversarial security cases. The app runs as a non-root Docker container behind TLS. The judge worker is intentionally deterministic. It performs real persisted state transitions and creates real hashed artifacts over synthetic Project Aurora data, but has no network, provider, production, email, calendar, financial, deployment, or destructive capability. Challenges Making WebMCP registration survive React Strict Mode without duplicate tools. Keeping server authorization authoritative while exposing useful browser intent. Binding decisions, resumes, and acceptance to exact signed targets and versions. Making retries safe under duplicate and concurrent calls. Distinguishing worker completion from evaluated evidence and accepted delivery. Providing a credential-free public demo without exposing production data or private source. Accomplishments Seven native, page-scoped intent tools. One genuine browser-agent → persisted worker → human decision → evidence → certificate loop. Zero approval bypasses and zero duplicate mutations in the reproducible five-run evaluation set. Signed, expiring, session-scoped handles and exact evidence-hash acceptance. A public, synthetic, resettable judge experience with no paid model calls. Automated unit, integration, browser, accessibility, evaluation, build, dependency, and secret checks. What was new for the challenge ArcadeOps existed before August 25, 2026 as a private agent operations platform with mission, approval, evidence, and certificate concepts. The challenge work is the self-contained WebMCP adapter; seven mission tools; Project Aurora judge workspace; live browser-agent/worker collaboration; deterministic challenge runtime; challenge policy; session isolation; authority and evidence binding; WebMCP evaluations; public deployment package; documentation; video; and submission materials. The private ArcadeOps repository and unrelated proprietary components are not published. What we learned The best browser tools describe product intent, not page mechanics. Shared state matters more than another chat transcript. A model response is not delivery truth. Human authority becomes usable when the page explains both the blocked action and the consequences, while signed handles let the agent safely continue afterward. What's next The same pattern can govern broader agent-native operations: richer workers, organization policies, external evidence attestations, and portable certificates—while preserving scoped authority, explicit human decisions, and honest cost and completion truth. Judge data All demo data is synthetic. No credentials are required. title: Wishopai Pocket Merchant
pitch: From three phone captures to a ready-to-sell business—with an AI agent and the merchant in control.
about_excerpt: From three phone captures to a ready-to-sell business—with an AI agent and the merchant in control. Like Comment Story Updates Mobile-first capture inbox: one request turns three phone captures into a catalog, storefront, and point of sale. Inspiration Small merchants rarely run their business from a quiet desk. They work from a phone, between customers, deliveries, and family responsibilities. Existing commerce software asks them to learn separate systems for catalog, storefront, point of sale, inventory, and reporting. We wanted the interface to adapt to the merchant instead. WebMCP makes that possible without hiding the business behind a chat window. The merchant and the agent work on the same live page. The agent gets structured, purpose-built actions; the merchant keeps the visual context, approval, and ability to undo. What it does Pocket Merchant starts with three lightweight phone captures. An AI agent can: inspect the current business state and capture inbox; turn those captures into a structured product catalog; generate a synchronized mobile storefront preview; configure a point of sale that shares the same inventory; validate launch readiness and explain blockers; prepare a token-bound launch plan for human approval; publish only after explicit confirmation; record a sandbox sale and update stock everywhere; and undo the last mutable action. The regular interface mirrors the agent actions, so the product remains useful in browsers without WebMCP and the merchant can take over at any moment. How we built it The app is a dependency-free, mobile-first web application. Its business actions are shared by the human interface, an automated guided preview, and ten top-level WebMCP tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . The tool layer uses narrow JSON Schemas, clear read/write annotations, input validation, bounded values, and structured verification results. Catalog, storefront, POS, activity, sales, and inventory all use one live state model. The demo persists only in local browser storage and connects to no production commerce system. Publishing uses a deliberate two-step protocol. prepare_launch_approval validates the complete workspace and returns an exact review summary plus a short-lived token. confirm_demo_launch accepts only that token and the literal confirmation PUBLISH . This makes the safety boundary both machine-readable and visible in the UI. How WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent would have to infer controls by looking at the page and clicking through a multi-step commerce interface. Pocket Merchant gives the agent semantic business operations while preserving the page as the shared source of truth. The strongest moment is not a single tool call. It is the closed loop: capture → structured catalog → visual preview → readiness validation → human approval → sale → synchronized stock → undo Each tool changes or verifies the same state the merchant sees. Closing the page removes the tools; reopening it restores the isolated demo state on that device. Challenges we ran into Designing tools that were powerful enough to complete a business goal but narrow enough to be safe and predictable. Separating preparation from consequential execution without making the workflow feel slow. Keeping the experience genuinely mobile-first while making the shared state obvious on a desktop judging environment. Creating a useful fallback interface without duplicating business logic or turning the project into a scripted mockup. Accomplishments that we are proud of Ten working WebMCP tools, all backed by the same actions as the visible interface. A complete merchant journey instead of an isolated search or cart proof of concept. Explicit human approval with a time-limited, state-bound review token. Shared inventory demonstrated by an actual sandbox sale and receipt. A visible audit trail and one-step undo for every mutable demo action. Responsive operation from a narrow phone viewport through a wide desktop workspace. What we learned The biggest opportunity in agentic commerce is not removing the interface. It is making the interface and the agent collaborate. Merchants trust automation more when they can see the state, understand the pending change, approve the important step, and recover from mistakes. We also learned that a good WebMCP tool is a product decision, not only a technical wrapper. Tool boundaries determine how well the agent plans, how clearly the user understands the result, and how safely the system can act. What's next Connect the shared action layer to permission-scoped Wishopai test tenants. Accept real phone photos and voice notes while preserving merchant review. Add locale-aware taxes, currencies, and receipt rules. Bring the same operations to Wishopai's remote MCP integration so merchants can work both inside the live page and from a general chat. Add multi-user approvals and richer audit exports for growing teams. title: Verbe
pitch: Verbe is a macOS layer powered by Gemini. Say what you want in 3 words, voice or text, and it happens instantly on your screen. OS is the interface. No copy-paste. Just intent. Screen is the context.
about_excerpt:
Verbe is a macOS layer powered by Gemini. Say what you want in 3 words, voice or text, and it happens instantly on your screen. OS is the interface. No copy-paste. Just intent. Screen is the context.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Verbe - Intelligence Amplification for macOS 

 Inspiration 

 Two observations collided: 

 1. The friction problem is real. A New York Times study found that 25% of ChatGPT usage is just translation and typo fixes. Micro-tasks. But for a micro-task, the workflow is broken: open a tab, copy text, paste into chat, wait, copy result, switch back, paste. That's 7 steps for a 2-second task. Most people just... don't bother. 

 2. The AI landscape has a gap. On one side, chatbots - you go to them, you wait, you copy-paste back. It's a detour. On the other side, autonomous agents - they work without you, you discover results later. It's delegation. Neither felt right for how we actually work: fast, contextual, in control. 

 We wanted something different. Not an app you open. Not a bot you talk to. A layer - always there, always ready, always instant. 

 The term "Intelligence Amplification" was coined by Douglas Engelbart in 1962. He imagined technology that extends human capability rather than replacing it. 

 Sixty years later, that vision is still being actively debated in product choices. Much of the current momentum is pushing toward autonomous agents - systems designed to act on behalf of users, outside their immediate flow. Tools like OpenClaw , Claude CoWork , and OpenAI Frontier frame AI as a delegated collaborator: you hand off work, and check back later. Powerful, but fundamentally asynchronous and detached from the moment of action. 

 At the same time, a different signal is emerging. Recently, the Chrome Built-in AI team at Google presented WebMCP , a set of early preview APIs that let websites expose explicit, real-time actions to AI systems. Instead of agents guessing how to operate an interface, sites can declaratively define what can be done - while the user is present, in the browser, inside the workflow. 

 In parallel, AG-UI explores a similar direction: standardizing how AI systems and user interfaces communicate in real time, at the interaction layer. Not backend orchestration, not long-running delegation - but AI operating directly alongside the human, responding to what's on screen, in context. 

 Together, these signals point to a clear tension in the landscape: delegation versus amplification . AI that works instead of you - versus AI that works with you, at the moment work is happening. 

 Verbe takes a clear stance. Not an agent you send away, but the ambition to be the intelligence layer that stays with you - instant, contextual, and under your control - extending human capability exactly where attention and decisions already live. Bring this augmentation down to the operating-system level, unifying context across apps into a single, user-centric layer, for real-time assistance and instant feedback by amplifying the human at work, rather than replacing them. 

 

 What it does 

 Verbe is an intelligence layer that sits on top of macOS. It works in any app - Mail, Slack, Figma, Chrome, Notion, WhatsApp, VS Code - with the same two gestures: 

 
 Cmd+Opt → Text input (use shortcut or type what you want) 
 Fn → Voice command (say what you want) 
 Fn+Shift → Live conversation (conversation with Gemini) 
 

 The result appears as an overlay , a floating panel right where you're working. You decide what to do with it: insert, copy, or dismiss. 

 Core Features 

 Screen as Context 
When activated, Gemini sees what you select - or your entire screen if no text is selected. No need to explain, copy, or describe. Looking at an email? Say "reply yes but suggest Thursday." Looking at a chart? Say "why is this dropping." Looking at code? Say "what's wrong here." Gemini's vision capability turns your screen into the prompt. 

 Recipes 
Repeatable intentions. A recipe is a transformation template you save and reuse. "Professional" rewrites any text formally. "First Principles" analyzes any design through fundamental needs. "Explain Like Mom" simplifies anything. Same recipe, different content, always adapted. Create new recipes by just describing what you want in natural language. 

 Zero-Friction Ergonomics 
Every interaction is designed to minimize hand movement and cognitive load. Cmd+Opt is a hold-and-release gesture - hold to show the radial menu, move your mouse to pick a recipe, release to dismiss. No clicking through menus, no switching windows. The overlay appears at your cursor so your eyes stay where they are. The entire flow - from intent to result - happens without leaving your current app or lifting your hands off the keyboard. 

 Streaming Responses 
Gemini 3 Flash Preview streams results token by token directly into the overlay. You start reading before the response is complete. No spinner, no waiting for a full answer - the output builds in front of you in real time. When feedback is instant, you stay in flow. When it's slow, your brain moves on. 

 Image Generation 
Some recipes generate images instead of text. Describe what you need - a diagram, a mockup, an illustration - and Gemini produces it directly in the overlay. No need to open a separate tool or bounce between apps. 

 Voice Command 
Hold Fn to give a one-shot voice instruction. Verbe records while you hold, then sends the audio to Gemini when you release - like a walkie-talkie. "Translate this to Spanish." "Summarize this page." Quick, hands-free, no typing required. 

 Voice Live Mode 
Hold Fn + Shift for a bidirectional conversation with Gemini. Brainstorm, debug, think out loud. Interrupt anytime - you're always in control. The AI doesn't monologue; it collaborates. Audio streams both ways in real time. 

 Non-Intrusive Overlay 
The overlay floats above your work as a transparent panel that never steals focus. You can keep typing in your app while the response streams in. macOS 26 Liquid Glass gives it a native, non-obtrusive feel. Insert the result, copy it, or dismiss it - your workflow is never hijacked. 

 How we built it 

 Architecture 
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ macOS App │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Hotkey Listener │ Accessibility API │
│ (Cmd+Opt / Fn) │ (selected text, app) │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Screen Capture (Vision) │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Context Builder │
│ (app name + selection + screen + intent) │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Gemini 3 Flash API │
│ (multimodal: text + vision + audio) │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Overlay Renderer │
│ (NSPanel, .accessory level, no focus) │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
 
 Swift + AppKit for the native macOS experience. The overlay system uses NSPanel with .accessory window level - it floats above apps without stealing focus. This is crucial: Verbe should never interrupt your work. 

 Accessibility API captures selected text and identifies the active application before the overlay appears. This ordering is critical - once our app activates, the source app loses its selection. 

 Screen Capture sends the visible screen to Gemini when no text is selected. This enables vision-based queries: "analyze this design," "what's wrong here," "explain this chart." 

 Gemini 3 Flash handles all AI processing with streaming responses. Multimodal input (text + image + audio) goes in, streamed response comes out. Speed depends on the model, but streaming means you start reading immediately. 

 Live Audio Streaming for Voice Live mode uses Gemini's real-time API. The conversation is truly bidirectional - you can interrupt, redirect, or end at any moment. 

 The Overlay System 

 The overlay is the heart of Verbe. Design constraints: 

 
 Never steal focus - you should be able to keep typing in your app 
 Appear at cursor - minimal eye movement 
 Actionable - Insert, Copy, or dismiss with one click 
 Dismissable - release the hotkey or click outside 
 

 The overlay uses macOS 26's Liquid Glass aesthetic - semi-transparent, blurred background, fully native feel. Getting an NSPanel to float above all apps, accept keyboard input, yet never steal focus from the underlying application was the hardest UI challenge of the project. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 1. Focus management is hard. 
macOS really wants windows to steal focus. Making an overlay that appears, accepts clicks, but doesn't take focus from the underlying app required deep diving into NSPanel behavior, window levels, and activati

title: uk.gov Radar
pitch: Your agent reads everything the UK government published this month. You make the calls.
about_excerpt: Your agent reads everything the UK government published this month. You make the calls. Like Comment Story Updates The agent filled the profile. It stays blue until you keep it. A suggestion, its reason, the next step, and your note, on one card. Dropped, with a reason the agent reads before it suggests again. The weekly brief. Every claim links to its source page. One page, two hands. The founder and the agent point at the same row. I run Hyperdrift, a small AI studio in the UK. Every month the government publishes the grant, the consultation or the tender that could change a founder's quarter. Every month I miss it, because it's buried under sixty documents I don't have time to read. So I built a radar. It reads gov.uk, UKRI and Parliament for me. Useful, but not enough: a list of what changed still needs someone who knows my company to say which lines matter. WebMCP was the missing link. Open the radar in a browser that has an agent, and the page hands the agent its controls. It fills my profile from what it already knows about me. It works the list on my screen: filters move, cards light up, every suggestion comes with a reason and a date. Then I tell it something the website will never hear: my NHS partner has gone and I've got six weeks. The list re-ranks in front of me. I drop one, I say why, and it reads my reason before it speaks again. The site keeps the data. My agent keeps my context. I keep the last word. A plug-in on a server can't do that. Try it: radar.hyperdrift.io/explore, in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP on. Three prompts wait at the top of the page. Under the hood: seven tools on document.modelContext, one of them registered only once a shortlist exists; every tool calls the same functions the buttons call.
