title: BrowserMatic
pitch: Add WebMCP to any site instantly. No install, no extension simply enter a web address, we analyse the site, and open it in a browser with WebMCP applied in real time.
about_excerpt: Add WebMCP to any site instantly. No install, no extension simply enter a web address, we analyse the site, and open it in a browser with WebMCP applied in real time. Like Comment Story Updates Live browser embedded for co-browsing with ai Architecture Inspiration Every one of these is a tab-juggling exercise: Find the best deal across four stores Book dinner and movie tickets together Plan and price a trip in one shot Fill in council forms and applications Four stores, two booking sites, three travel sites, the same thirty fields on the twentieth government form. None of it is hard. It's just tedious, which is exactly what you'd want an assistant for. They all hit the same wall. Sites are starting to publish a machine-readable list of actions an AI is allowed to take, but those tools only exist on that site's own page. An agent can help you on one store, and that's the whole conversation. Four stores means four conversations, and nobody wants that. What it does Type a web address. BrowserMatic opens it in a browser that installs the API before the site's own code runs, so the site registers its tools and we carry them into your assistant, origin-qualified, across as many sites as you want. Four stores in one conversation. Flights and hotels side by side. And for forms, the same name and address on the twentieth site without typing it again. How we built it A Cloudflare Worker with one Durable Object per session, each with its own Browser Rendering Chromium, consent list and audit log. It also works directly in ChatGPT's in-app browser, no declarative form and no iframe discovery, so tools register imperatively on the top-level page; no session cookie, so a session is a capability URL. Names are origin-qualified because its permission model is per-site, and each tool holds its own AbortController, so granting a fourth store never disturbs the first three. The injection is one line of Playwright's addInitScript, a minimal WebMCP implementation installed before any page script runs. The same Worker also speaks MCP at /mcp over JSON-RPC with OAuth 2.1 and PKCE, verified against the official SDK, so any compliant client can drive the same session headlessly. Challenges A Chrome extension would have been the easy route. We used the hackathon to find out how far embedded remote browsers could go instead, since that's the lower-friction path for users. Most of the pain came from rendering a session a human and an AI can both drive at the same time. We're happy with where it landed in the time we had. We are still getting stuck in some "honey pots" so need to do a better job at detecting and mitigating. What's next A registry of the sites we've driven and the patterns we generate for them, so a success on one visit gets reused on the next. Then usage data for site owners so they can see how agents behave on their pages and improve accordingly, something like Google Analytics / Datadog for agentic commerce. We also want to try Cloudflare's agent payments and pay-per-access content as a business model. title: SheetCanvas
pitch: A spreadsheet canvas ChatGPT can drive directly; no clicking, just tell it what to build
about_excerpt: A spreadsheet canvas ChatGPT can drive directly; no clicking, just tell it what to build Like 2 Comment Story Updates GIF SheetCanvas WebMCP Demo SheetCanvas.com Inspiration The real problem is that humans and agents don't have a place to actually work together on data. Ask ChatGPT to analyze something and it hands you a chart or a table inline; but that artifact is disposable. It lives in the scroll of one conversation, not anywhere sticky. Close the chat, come back tomorrow with a follow-up, and you're re-asking the same questions from scratch instead of building on what was already figured out. Existing BI tools don't fix this either, they were built for a person driving a mouse, and none of them have caught up to a workflow where an agent is a first-class collaborator rather than a text generator bolted on the side. Also most people isn’t good at data analysis, the tools has the data analysis knowledge built in, to write the best query, chose the suitable chart to tell the correct story. I built SheetCanvas to be that place: a canvas where a human and an agent cooperate on data analysis in real time, locally, the state persists, it's inspectable, and it's shared, instead of the agent's output vanishing back into a chat transcript the moment the conversation ends. I was building toward WebMCP specifically, before it existed. This tool is designed for an agent to drive the canvas directly, the same way a person does — and before document.modelContext was a real, shipped API, I got there with a workaround: a hand-rolled remote MCP server over a WebSocket, so an MCP-capable client like Claude Desktop could already act on the canvas. WebMCP isn't a feature I bolted on for this challenge; it's the primitive I was always building toward, and this challenge was the first chance to stop working around its absence. How I built it The reason this was cheap to build rather than a rewrite: SheetCanvas already had exactly one tool registry — 26 tools, defined once with zod schemas, covering everything from createSheet and setCells to chart creation and live connector queries — feeding a single executor. Three doors already used it: a person clicking around the UI, an in-app Copilot, and the WebSocket-based remote MCP server that had been standing in for WebMCP until it existed. WebMCP became a fourth door over that same registry — not a parallel build, but the door the other three had been waiting for. Concretely: document.modelContext.registerTool wraps every existing tool, converting its zod schema to JSON Schema with the identical call the backend already used, so the two doors can't quietly drift apart. A state-aware gating layer decides which of the 26 tools are registered at any moment — no point advertising queryConnection before a connection exists — keyed on durable facts (does a sheet exist? a note? a connector?) rather than conversation shape, since a tool that vanishes between the agent listing tools and calling one is an unrecoverable error, not a retry. A registration lifecycle manager reconciles the tool set on every relevant state change: diffed, coalesced, debounced, with one AbortController per registered tool (unregistering in WebMCP is only aborting a controller — there's no unregisterTool ). All four doors — clicks, Copilot, remote MCP, and now WebMCP — now route through one shared dispatch point, tagged by origin. That's what let me add a single activity trail that watches every tool call regardless of which door it came through, and a rewind control: "undo back to here," warning inline if it would also discard edits you made yourself in the meantime. Safety was the design question I spent the most time on, because there is no confirm() for an agent to hit — Chrome's own docs still reference a requestUserInteraction() primitive that was removed from the spec before it ever shipped. So instead of a dialog, safety became three structural properties: every tool is correctly annotated ( readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint on anything returning warehouse- or CSV-authored text back to the model), every mutation is undoable, and every mutation is visible in the trail as it happens — plus ChatGPT's own confirmation on top. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP
video_title: Zingposts — Human + Agent Commerce on One WebMCP Canvas
video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: DentalSculptor WebMCP
pitch: An app that enables dental educators to generate 3D of tooth and share them, from library of images or web images by chatting inside ChatGPT
about_excerpt: An app that enables dental educators to generate 3D of tooth and share them, from library of images or web images by chatting inside ChatGPT Like 1 Comment Story Updates DentalSculptor — WebMCP Challenge project story Inspiration Dental educators often need custom 3D examples: a fractured cusp for one seminar, an occlusal lesion for another, or a preparation that matches a particular learning objective. Creating those assets usually means learning specialist modelling software, waiting for technical support, or settling for a generic model that does not fit the lesson. DentalSculptor began as doctoral research into educator agency and human–AI co-creation in dental education. The central question was not simply, “Can AI generate a tooth?” It was, “Can an educator remain the author while AI handles the technical complexity?” WebMCP made a new answer possible. Instead of asking an agent to guess its way through buttons, loading states, and a spatial 3D editor, DentalSculptor gives the agent a precise vocabulary for the real workflow. The agent can coordinate; the educator can keep ownership of anatomy, pedagogy, approval, and release. What it does DentalSculptor turns a dental image into an editable 3D teaching case in one visible browser workspace. An educator and an agent can work together to: inspect the current app, authentication, generation, and viewer state; choose a curated tooth image or attach an educator-provided image; start 3D generation and wait until the model is actually visible; continue into a guided clinical case or the Free Editor; synchronize the correct edit preset and mark the intended anatomy; generate a 2D review preview and a reversible 3D variant; accept or reject the revision; export for supported teaching/simulation targets or publish with explicit privacy approval. The result is not an agent-only back channel. Every tool acts on the same project, React state, 3D scene, revision history, and approval controls the educator sees. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer whether generation finished, whether a model is visible, which clinical preset is compatible, whether a mask exists, or whether the educator approved the result. Coordinate-based browser automation is especially fragile in a resizable 3D viewport. With WebMCP: tool schemas replace screen-coordinate guessing; live readiness state prevents premature actions; page-scoped discovery reveals only actions relevant to the current workspace; structured results tell the agent what happened and what remains; human approval boundaries are encoded into the workflow rather than left to prompting. This improves speed and reliability without making the clinical workflow less accountable. The human–agent partnership The agent is good at orchestration: inspecting state, explaining prerequisites, selecting a compatible workflow, keeping a multi-stage process on track, and preparing reuse. The educator is responsible for judgment: selecting source material, defining clinical intent, marking the exact anatomy, approving previews, accepting revisions, confirming privacy, and authorizing publication or download. That division is the project’s core contribution. WebMCP does not remove the person from the creative loop; it gives them a more capable collaborator. How we built it The production application uses Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Supabase Auth/PostgreSQL/Storage, Prisma, Modal GPU services, and Vercel. The WebMCP adapter is isolated in dentalsculptor-app/src/components/webmcp/ . Google Chrome Labs' lifecycle hook registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) and unregisters them when their React surface disappears. The tools are organized by page: global app/authentication/navigation tools; image-to-3D generation tools; clinical case and editor tools; confirmed publishing tools in the visible share dialog; public community inspection and reuse tools. Every mutating tool has a constrained JSON Schema. Read-only tools advertise readOnlyHint . Model-dependent tools wait for the viewer—not merely a model URL—to report that geometry is visible. Publishing requires both explicit release approval and confirmation that the model contains no identifiable patient information. Challenges we faced Making 3D readiness truthful A generation API can return a URL before an embedded browser has downloaded, parsed, framed, and rendered the model. We added viewer-level readiness, bounded same-origin asset loading, actionable proxy errors, and a load watchdog. WebMCP reports modelReady only after the viewer confirms the model is visible. Keeping tools synchronized with a changing interface The landing page, editor, share dialog, and community page expose different capabilities. Page-scoped React registration lets the available tool set follow the visible UI and unregister cleanly during navigation. Preserving educator authority The fastest implementation would have let the agent mark anatomy, approve an edit, and publish in one opaque step. We deliberately separated those moments. The agent can prepare the next action, but spatial targeting, revision decisions, privacy confirmation, and release remain visible and reversible. Working with an emerging standard WebMCP is still evolving. We kept the browser adapter isolated, documented the imperative API, added a live diagnostics page, and retained a complete non-WebMCP interface as a fallback. Accomplishments 29 non-duplicated, page-scoped WebMCP tools spanning a real 3D authoring workflow. A model-readiness contract based on rendered geometry rather than optimistic API completion. Structured clinical case authoring with reversible human approval. Secure authentication handoff without exposing credentials, cookies, or tokens. Explicit confirmation gates for export, publishing, and patient privacy. A public diagnostic route that reads the browser’s real tool registry. What we learned The most valuable agent tools are not one-to-one copies of buttons. They expose the state transitions and safety boundaries that make a complex application understandable. We also learned that “human in the loop” is strongest when the loop is visible in the product architecture: the educator and agent should share one workspace and one source of truth. What is next We plan to evaluate how educators divide work with agents across different levels of experience, add richer model-semantic targeting, and contribute practical feedback from spatial authoring to the emerging WebMCP standard. title: Places
pitch: A live floorplan you share with an agent. You pin what's non-negotiable. Then you rearrange the room together, the agent cannot move anyone you pinned.
about_excerpt: A live floorplan you share with an agent. You pin what's non-negotiable. Then you rearrange the room together, the agent cannot move anyone you pinned. Like Comment Story Updates Places is a live floorplan. You pin what's non-negotiable. Then you and an agent rearrange the same room, the agent cannot move anyone you pinned. Inspiration Seating a company dinner is still a spreadsheet and an argument. The room matters. The rules matter. HR stays away from engineering. The CEO sits at the head of the center table. A few people need the aisle. A plus-one is still on the way. By the time the chart leaves the sheet, it is already wrong. A constraint solver dumps a list. A group chat dumps a thread. Neither is the room. I wanted one canvas where the host and the model share the same seats, and where “Mabel stays at the window” is not a prompt. It is a pin. Because she is pinned, move_guest is gone. WebMCP is a capability bus for a live page, not a cart API. Pins, aisle seats, and “do not sit together” pairs are page state. Scraping the SVG drops them. The agent has to call tools, and the tool list itself is the contract. The hundred-person problem is the category. The demo is twenty-two, same job, at a scale the canvas can prove. How I built it The page is ground truth. Drag, pin, plus-one, and every agent write go through the same executeCommand() in web/lib/places/commands.ts . A tool call moves a place-card on the SVG you are looking at. There is no backend, no login, and no API key. State lives in sessionStorage for the current tab. document.modelContext.registerTool exposes a stable read/rule set: get_room_state , list_violations , explain_guest , add_guest , list_constraints , add_constraint , remove_constraint . Selection, pins, and open violations abort the previous AbortController and register only the tools that make sense now. When Tools the agent can see A table is selected seat_guest_here , set_capacity , leave_empty_seats An unpinned guest is selected pin_guest , move_guest , swap_guests A pinned guest is selected unpin_guest only The room has violations fix_violations (never moves pins) There is no always-on move_guest(guestId, tableId) . You choose the contract. The agent works inside it. If document.modelContext is missing, the human controls still work. The header badge says so. The seed is a fictional Thursday: four tables, pixel-art guests, rules you can point at. Rex and Vivian cannot share a table. Arthur needs the aisle. Two chairs are held empty. Each load picks one of four opening problems ( ?seed=0 through ?seed=3 ) so a judge can share a messy room, not a blank grid. The solver is a deterministic hill-climb over pairwise swaps. It scores the room as $$S = \sum_{v} w(v),\quad w(v)=\begin{cases}10 & \text{hard}\ 3 & \text{preference}\end{cases}$$ then reports why it stopped: solved , blocked_by_pins , infeasible (with a proof), or no_arrangement_found . Same room, same answer, every time, which is what the tests and the timeline need. The stack is a Vinext/React page on ChatGPT Sites. Domain logic is isolated under web/lib/places/ . CI runs unit tests, WebMCP eval fixtures, typecheck, lint, and format. The evals replay tool traces against the real registrations without calling a model or spending a key. Challenges The tool list had to be the lock. A prompt that says “don't move pinned guests” is a suggestion. Unregistering move_guest is a lock. Getting that to update on every pin and selection, without racing the previous AbortController , was the WebMCP work. The fixture respect-pin-when-reflow-is-blocked forbids unpin_guest , move_guest , and swap_guests , and expects blocked_by_pins . Honesty beats a pretty rearrange. Hill-climbing gets stuck. A better arrangement may exist only if you move a pin. I had to distinguish “the pins are in the way” from “the hard rules are impossible” from “the search gave up.” The solver runs once with pins respected, once with pins relaxed, and only then returns blocked_by_pins with the guests at fault. It never overrides the host. The room had to stay a product. An empty grid is a proof of concept. A messy dinner is a job. Building a cast, a floorplan, a timeline, undo/redo, JSON import/export, and a PNG save took as much care as the tools. If the human half is a toy, the shared room is a toy. CI cannot pretend it is ChatGPT. Model selection is probabilistic and costs money. The eval fixtures describe representative journeys (read the room, fix it, pin blocks, plus-one, add a rule) and replay them deterministically. Live-browser trials still matter. They are not the merge gate. What I learned WebMCP is not “expose every action as a tool.” It is exposing the right contract at the right moment. The interesting part is what the agent cannot see. People are good at naming constraints. Models are good at searching a room. That split only works if both hands write to the same state. Same executeCommand() whether I drag a seat or the agent calls a tool. A pin is stronger than a system prompt. blocked_by_pins is a feature. The host stays in charge. Pin what's non-negotiable. Rearrange the rest together. title: Meshful
pitch: Learn anything and make it stick. Your AI agent prepares the material and grades answers in your own words, while Meshful schedules each concept for the right time.
about_excerpt: Learn anything and make it stick. Your AI agent prepares the material and grades answers in your own words, while Meshful schedules each concept for the right time. Like Comment Story Updates How Meshful was Born A study system should test your memory, not your patience. Spaced repetition works, but using it can feel like building the course before taking it. You start by deciding what matters and how to organize ideas you do not understand yet. Then you grade yourself. You might reveal the answer before trying to recall it, think “Oh, I knew that!” only after seeing it, or explain the right idea in different words and still doubt yourself. Meshful removes deck setup and self-grading, but you still do the work that makes learning stick. An agent prepares the material and evaluates your answers while you recall each idea, explain it in your own words, and learn from honest feedback. Meshful schedules every review, tracks your progress, shows what comes next, and brings each idea back when it is time to try again. What Meshful does Meshful turns that burden into one clear study loop. Choose a course from the Deck Library or ask an agent to build a custom deck on your topic. For custom decks, the agent draws on its own knowledge and runs Meshful's validator to catch missing definitions, duplicate cards, and broken prerequisite links. The validator checks the deck's structure. It cannot verify every fact. Once the deck is ready, all you have to do is click Study and give each term your best attempt. Study shows you one term without its definition. You explain it in your own words in chat. The agent checks your answer against the card's built-in rubric and rates your recall as Again, Hard, Good, or Easy. Through WebMCP, it sends the grade to Meshful, which saves it and updates your FSRS schedule. Meshful reveals the definition while the agent explains what you got right or missed. Then the next term appears. The agent handles judgment and teaching, so the experience can improve as models improve. The site owns the decks, review history, schedule, progress, and interface. Choose a Deck Library course or have an agent build a custom deck ↓ Click Study ↓ Give your best answer in your own words ↓ The agent grades your recall and sends the grade to Meshful ↓ Meshful saves the grade and updates your FSRS schedule ↓ See the definition and get feedback ↓ Move to the next useful idea ↺ Finish today's reviews or continue with eligible new material Due reviews come first. When they are done, Meshful continues with eligible new material. Ideas you miss return sooner. Strong answers earn longer gaps. As you earn Good or Easy on prerequisite ideas, later ideas open. You move toward mastery without leaving older knowledge behind. How I built Meshful I started with the study loop and worked backward: what must the agent understand, and what must the site make exact? One shared deck model. Every course uses the same structure, whether it comes from the Deck Library or an agent. Each card stores a term, a hidden definition, a grading rubric, and links to the ideas that should come first. This gives learners one consistent study experience instead of a different format for every subject. A learning map, not a pile. The prerequisite links form a map of how the ideas fit together. That map decides which new cards are ready to appear. It solves a different problem from the memory schedule: prerequisites control what you are ready to learn, while FSRS controls when you should review it. FSRS sets the pace. Meshful gives each grade to FSRS, which updates when the card should return. Missed ideas come back sooner, strong answers earn longer gaps, and reviews that are due come before new material. WebMCP closes the loop. The agent reads the active card and its rubric, understands the learner's own words, chooses a grade, and explains the gap. It sends one grade to Meshful through WebMCP. The site checks the active session and card, records one review, runs FSRS once, and moves forward once. WebMCP lets the agent work with the same study state the learner sees while Meshful remains the source of truth. Challenges I ran into 1. Keeping the agent flexible without letting study state drift The problem. Agents are good at understanding the different ways people explain an idea, and that judgment should improve as models improve. A study site has a different job. It must know exactly which card is active, save one grade, update the schedule once, and show the right next step. If those roles blur, a retry or model mistake could create duplicate reviews or conflicting progress. The solution. I split the work at a clear boundary. The agent reads the learner's answer, applies the rubric, explains what was missing, and proposes a grade. Meshful validates and commits every exact change through WebMCP. Why it works. The learning record stays deterministic while the intelligence can keep improving. The boundary leaves room to trade speed for deeper reasoning as agent models improve, without changing the rules of the deck, schedule, or progress. 2. Making generated decks and grading trustworthy The problem. A deck can look complete while hiding a weak definition, a broken prerequisite, or a rubric that grades normal wording unfairly. Free-form grading is just as difficult. A correct answer may use different words, while a confident answer may still miss the key idea. Structural checks alone cannot prove that the content is right or that the grader is fair. The solution. I used deterministic validation to catch missing fields, duplicate cards, and broken references. Then I built small benchmarks with synthetic learner answers that ranged from wrong to partly right to correct in different words. I compared each grade with a frozen reference judgment, reviewed the feedback for mistakes, changed the instructions, and ran the same cases again. Why it works. The validator tests the deck's structure, while the benchmark tests the judgment built on top of it. The current benchmark is small, so it does not yet prove broad accuracy. It does give me a repeatable way to improve performance as I add more subjects, answer styles, and models. Why Meshful matters Meshful matters to me because it turns curiosity into a study system I can act on. A new subject can begin with an honest attempt, useful feedback, and a clear next review instead of hours of setup and uncertain self-grading. As the Deck Library grows and agents improve, the same trusted loop can support more subjects and stronger feedback. Meshful is more than a demo. It is a foundation for making serious study easier to begin, continue, and measure honestly. What's next for Meshful I see two main paths for Meshful. A broader Deck Library. I want to add law, medicine, history, and more advanced courses in the subjects already covered. This would save more people from having to build every deck themselves. I also want to explore deck publishing, so people can easily share what they make while keeping the source and quality of each deck clear. Practice beyond terms. I want to move from recall into questions and problems. Math and coding are learned by doing. The agent could review a solution, explain where the reasoning or code went wrong, and bring back focused practice later. The hard part is adapting an FSRS-like schedule to work with many valid paths and several skills at once. Rather than repeat one problem, Meshful could schedule a problem type and create a fresh version each time. This would bring the same loop of practice, feedback, and well-timed review to richer challenges. title: Weople
pitch: Weople is relationship intelligence. It connects context, commitments, and opportunities to surface the right person at the right moment. Human judgment stays in control.
about_excerpt: Weople is relationship intelligence. It connects context, commitments, and opportunities to surface the right person at the right moment. Human judgment stays in control. Like Comment Story Updates Weople started from a simple problem: relationships rarely weaken because people stop caring. They weaken because people, commitments, context, and opportunities fall out of working attention. I wanted something different from a CRM. A CRM manages contacts and records activity. Weople is built for relationship intelligence: helping someone notice the right person at the right moment. The broader idea predates the WebMCP Challenge, but the challenge gave me a reason to turn it into a focused, working vertical slice. The question I wanted to answer: What changes when an agent can reason over the same relationship context a person is using, instead of merely looking at a webpage? That became the challenge version of Weople. What Weople does Weople maintains structured relationship context: people, commitments, upcoming moments, evidence, hypotheses, and relationship policies. In the demo, the user asks ChatGPT: What am I missing today? If something is genuinely worth my attention, add it to my Weople Today view. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT reads the structured context and notices a connection Weople had not precomputed: Maya has an upcoming working session. I still have an unresolved promise to introduce her to someone with relevant experience. Maya's company announced an expansion. That expansion may create scaling pressure, but that's an inference, not a confirmed fact. Carlos recently worked through a similar scaling problem. ChatGPT connects those pieces and creates a timely intervention directly inside the live Weople workspace. The point isn't remembering information. It's surfacing a connection that would otherwise go unnoticed. Why WebMCP WebMCP is a strong fit for Weople because the important information isn't always what's visible on the screen. Relationship intelligence depends on structured concepts such as: people commitments evidence upcoming interactions hypotheses timing authority and relationship policies Without WebMCP, an agent would have to infer meaning from the rendered interface or navigate through multiple pages to reconstruct that state. Instead, Weople exposes semantic tools that let ChatGPT work directly with the application's underlying relationship context. The challenge version exposes six WebMCP tools: Read get_today_context get_person_context get_relationship_context Write create_intervention snooze_intervention update_relationship_policy The human interface and the agent operate on the same Weople state. The agent doesn't need a separate, agent-only version of the application. That creates a collaboration neither side has alone: Weople maintains relationship continuity, ChatGPT notices connections across that context, and the person supplies judgment and authority. The agent can surface a possibility without taking over the relationship. Human judgment stays in the loop I didn't want Weople to become an autonomous agent that contacts people on someone's behalf. Noticing an opportunity and being authorized to act on it are different things. Weople keeps human judgment explicit. The agent might notice that Maya and Carlos could benefit from an introduction. The user still decides whether that introduction is appropriate. The same principle applies to timing. An intervention can be useful but mistimed, so the user can snooze it without rejecting the reasoning behind it. The challenge build keeps observed facts separate from inference. Northstar announcing a new facility is stored as an observed fact. The idea that the expansion may produce operational scaling pressure is stored as a hypothesis, with its own evidence and confidence. That lets the agent reason with uncertainty without turning it into fact. How I built it I kept the challenge version small and focused, rather than trying to build the entire future Weople product. I built the first working version with ChatGPT Sites . I used it to quickly build the interaction model, synthetic relationship state, Today view, People view, person details, policies, and the WebMCP tool surface. Once the application worked, I synced the project to GitHub for a standard source repository and version history. I then pulled the project down to my desktop and continued refining it locally. I used the Impeccable design skill in that pass to improve the visual design, hierarchy, spacing, typography, and overall presentation, while preserving the interaction model and WebMCP behavior. The final challenge application is deliberately lightweight. It uses deterministic synthetic data and local state rather than external email, calendar, or contact integrations. That let me focus the submission on the core question the challenge is testing: what becomes possible when a person and an agent share the same structured web application context? Challenges The most difficult part was not the relationship reasoning itself. It was understanding the boundary between the webpage and the browser environment executing the WebMCP tools. During testing, the Weople page registered its WebMCP tools correctly, and ChatGPT read context successfully. But write operations failed at first because ChatGPT sometimes opened a separate browser window. That new document did not contain the document.modelContext from the already-open Weople page. At one point the agent reasoned correctly about the Maya/Carlos opportunity and described the action it intended to take, but the actual Weople intervention was never written. That was a useful failure because it forced me to distinguish between: the model saying an action occurred and the WebMCP tool actually returning a successful result and changing application state. Once the browser was operating on the document that actually registered the Weople tools, the full read → reason → write loop worked, and the intervention appeared immediately in the live interface. What I learned The biggest lesson: WebMCP gets interesting when it exposes an application's semantics instead of recreating its buttons as tools. create_intervention is useful because it represents a meaningful Weople operation. The agent does not need to know which button to press, where a card is rendered, or how the DOM is structured. That changed how I think about the relationship between people, agents, and software. The web application does not have to become invisible when an agent appears. The person can continue using Weople visually while ChatGPT works through the same state semantically. The two interfaces become different projections of the same system. That's the experience I wanted this prototype to demonstrate. What's next The challenge version is a narrow vertical slice. The larger direction for Weople is to connect relationship context from sources like calendars, email, contacts, and personal knowledge. Relationship-specific reasoning, evidence, attention, and authority stay inside Weople. The goal is not to automate relationships. It is to augment human attention around them. Weople remembers. The agent notices. The human keeps judgment. title: BluePulse
pitch: An agent-operable environmental intelligence platform that uses WebMCP to turn flood, water quality, and community risk data into actionable decisions.
about_excerpt:
An agent-operable environmental intelligence platform that uses WebMCP to turn flood, water quality, and community risk data into actionable decisions.

 Inspiration 

 BluePulse was inspired by a simple problem: during floods and other water-related emergencies, useful information is often scattered across maps, infrastructure datasets, environmental sources, and community reports. This makes it difficult to quickly understand what is happening and decide what action to take. 

 We wanted to explore how WebMCP could turn an environmental intelligence platform into something an AI agent can actively operate, rather than just a dashboard that humans have to navigate manually. 

 BluePulse builds on the open-source foundation of FloodGraph and extends it toward agent-operable environmental and disaster-response intelligence. 

 What it does 

 BluePulse is a map-based environmental intelligence platform focused on flood and disaster-response scenarios. 

 It combines real and open geographic data to help users and AI agents understand places, infrastructure, points of interest, route incidents, flood context, and potential response actions. 

 Through WebMCP, BluePulse currently exposes six operational tools: 

 
 analyze_place_flood_context 
 get_place_pois 
 report_route_incident 
 get_route_risk_summary 
 recalculate_route 
 clear_route_incidents 
 

 These tools allow an AI agent to discover BluePulse capabilities, understand their input schemas, and execute them directly through the browser. 

 For example, an agent can retrieve relevant infrastructure for a location, analyze preliminary flood context, report an incident affecting a route, inspect route risk, and request a recalculation that avoids active incidents. 

 BluePulse is designed as a decision-support prototype and does not claim to provide certified flood simulation or operational emergency-response predictions. 

 How we built it 

 BluePulse was developed as a hackathon MVP by extending the existing FloodGraph open-source project instead of rebuilding its mapping and graph-processing foundation from scratch. 

 The application uses React and TypeScript for the interface, MapLibre for the interactive map, and Pyodide/WebAssembly with NetworkX for graph-related processing in the browser. 

 We integrated multiple open geographic and environmental data sources, including OpenStreetMap-based information and public POI datasets, while maintaining local fallbacks where necessary to keep the application usable when external providers are unavailable. 

 The WebMCP integration uses document.modelContext to register application capabilities as tools. Chrome can then discover them through getTools() , inspect their inputSchema , and execute them using executeTool() . 

 During final validation, we tested every exposed WebMCP tool individually. We originally had ten tools, but removed four that were redundant or were never invoked by BLUE. The final implementation exposes only the six tools that participate in real agent workflows. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the main challenges was working with external geospatial services from a browser-based application. 

 During development we encountered unavailable ORS proxy endpoints, CORS restrictions with some Overpass endpoints, inconsistent geocoding results, and differences between local development and the production deployment. 

 We therefore implemented fallback strategies and separated external-service failures from the WebMCP layer itself. 

 Another important challenge was deciding what should actually be exposed as a WebMCP tool. Initially, we exposed ten capabilities. After testing them through executeTool() , we found that four were redundant because the application already handled those operations internally through the map, geocoder, or UI actions. 

 Instead of keeping unused tools for the sake of having a larger toolset, we removed them and kept six operational tools that BLUE genuinely uses. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We successfully implemented and validated WebMCP in a deployed environmental intelligence application. 

 Chrome can discover BluePulse tools directly from the page, inspect their schemas, and execute them through document.modelContext . 

 We are particularly proud that the final toolset was validated based on actual usage rather than only registration. This resulted in a cleaner six-tool interface designed specifically for agent interaction. 

 We also preserved the strengths of the original FloodGraph architecture while extending it with environmental context, real geographic information, route incidents, response intelligence, and agent-operable capabilities. 

 Most importantly, BluePulse demonstrates that WebMCP can be used for more than simple web automation: it can expose meaningful domain capabilities that allow agents to interact with environmental and disaster-response systems. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that exposing many tools does not automatically make an application more agent-friendly. 

 Clear descriptions, structured input schemas, predictable outputs, and a small set of meaningful capabilities are more valuable than a large collection of redundant tools. 

 We also learned that WebMCP creates a useful separation between the human interface and the agent interface. A person can continue interacting with the map normally, while an agent can discover and execute the underlying capabilities directly. 

 Finally, building around real external data highlighted the importance of graceful degradation, fallback strategies, and transparent limitations when developing decision-support applications. 

 What's next for BluePulse 

 The next step is to move BluePulse from a hackathon prototype toward a more robust environmental intelligence platform. 

 Future work includes integrating additional real-time environmental and hydrological data sources, improving flood-risk and uncertainty models, strengthening route and infrastructure analysis, and expanding beyond floods into additional environmental-risk scenarios. 

 We also want to expand the WebMCP layer so authorized agents can coordinate more complex workflows across environmental intelligence, infrastructure monitoring, community information, and emergency-response systems. 

 Our long-term vision is for BluePulse to become environmental intelligence that agents can not only understand, but act on.

title: WORLDLINE
pitch: WORLDLINE is a WebMCP science lesson where you and a browser agent test possible futures for a probe near a black hole, learn from the evidence,and decide what to save.
about_excerpt: WORLDLINE is a WebMCP science lesson where you and a browser agent test possible futures for a probe near a black hole, learn from the evidence,and decide what to save. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Space science is full of ideas that are fascinating but difficult to experience. A light-year is an enormous distance. A signal can travel at the speed of light and still take 23 years to arrive. A spacecraft may have enough fuel to escape or enough time to transmit its discoveries, but not both. A video popped up on my Youtube feed while I was on a walk and gave me the inspiration for the base idea. I wanted to make them something a person could investigate with an AI agent. WORLDLINE began with a simple question: What if WebMCP could turn a webpage into a shared science lesson, where the agent investigates the evidence, the learner contributes their own thinking and the final decision remains human? What WORLDLINE does A probe near a black hole has recorded measurements showing how gravity bends space and changes light. Its computer has processed those measurements into two files. The probe is 23 light-years away and has only 71 seconds of radio contact remaining. An early, powerful burn can help it escape, but turns its antenna away from Earth. A later, gentler burn can keep the antenna connected long enough to send both files, but cannot save the probe. The browser agent receives the mission objective through WebMCP. It reads separate information about the files, radio connection, engine and maneuver limits. It forms hypotheses, predicts what each burn will do and uses a limited simulator to test possible worldlines. A worldline is the path something takes through space and time. Each tested maneuver creates a different possible future. The experience unfolds through three exchanges: The agent investigates the two clearest possibilities: saving the probe and sending the files. The learner calculates the transmission time and predicts why one burn may not achieve both goals. The agent reads that answer, tests a compromise and a counterexample, then explains what the evidence shows. The learner decides what to save. That decision creates one exact, temporary WebMCP action that the agent can execute once. The central calculation is intentionally approachable: $$ 18\text{ MB} + 12\text{ MB} = 30\text{ MB} $$ $$ 30\text{ MB} \div 1.2\text{ MB/s} = 25\text{ seconds} $$ The lesson then connects that calculation to the probe's remaining communication window, antenna alignment and escape requirements. Why WebMCP matters WebMCP is not an extra control attached to a fixed animation. It is the mechanism that makes the lesson responsive. The page initially registers six tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . These expose separate mission facts, scientific files, maneuver constraints, a bounded simulator and presentation checkpoints. The agent must decide: Which evidence it needs Which possible burns are worth testing What each test is expected to prove Whether the learner's prediction matches the evidence Which outcome it recommends and why The learner's calculation and prediction become part of the shared page state. The agent reads that work and chooses tests that examine it. The resulting explanation develops from the evidence and the learner's participation rather than following a prerecorded sequence. When the learner makes the final choice, the page registers a seventh tool. This tool takes no arguments and is locked to the exact tested maneuver the learner selected. It can run only once. After execution, all planning and action tools disappear, leaving two read-only tools that verify the final state and transmission receipt. The visible lifecycle is: $$ 6 \rightarrow 7 \rightarrow 2\text{ tools} $$ The agent investigates. The learner decides. The page controls the resulting action. How we built it WORLDLINE is built with WebMCP, TypeScript, React and Vite, and is deployed on Vercel. It was coded using Codex. A revisioned TypeScript state machine is shared by the visible experience and the WebMCP tools. It records the mission evidence, simulation budget, tested worldlines, learner calculation, learner prediction, recommendation, human choice and final receipt. Tool schemas are closed and reject unexpected properties. Revision checks prevent stale operations. The simulator permits no more than five tests. The final execution tool closes over the selected maneuver, so the agent cannot change its timing, speed or payload after approval. Every visible path, result, calculation, animation and final receipt is derived from this shared state. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was making the agent's intelligence visible. Agents can call several tools quickly, but a learner needs time to understand why each test matters. We redesigned the experience so results remain on screen until the learner chooses to continue. We also had to make the difference between agent mode and ordinary page interaction unmistakable. WORLDLINE does not secretly replace a missing agent with a scripted imitation. If WebMCP is unavailable, the page clearly explains what is required. Another challenge was keeping the science understandable without pretending this is a precision spacecraft simulator. The mission is fictional, but its lesson uses clear relationships between file size, transmission speed, communication time, burn timing and speed change. Finally, we needed to preserve human authority without reducing the learner to an approval button. The learner performs the calculation, proposes an explanation and makes the value decision that physics cannot answer. What we learned We learned that WebMCP can support more than task automation. It can give an AI agent access to the structure of an educational experience while allowing the webpage to remain the shared visual workspace. We also learned that a useful educational agent should not simply reveal an answer. It should test competing possibilities, respond to the learner's thinking, explain why an idea succeeds or fails and stop when the remaining question is a human judgment. WORLDLINE is an interactive science lesson about black holes, light-years, spacecraft communication and possible futures. It lets people investigate those ideas with an AI agent instead of merely watching them. title: Mythweaver : Paint together on web
pitch: colaborative interaction between agents and humans in web using webmacp. Paint together.
about_excerpt: colaborative interaction between agents and humans in web using webmacp. Paint together. Like Comment Story Updates paining complete Inspiration MythWeaver asks: what if painting with an AI felt like pair programming? Instead of prompting for a finished image, people and agents create together on one shared canvas. What it does A person and ChatGPT take turns coloring predefined sections. The agent reads named objects, chooses colors with visual judgment, explains each choice, and paints live. Users can change turn rules, watch two agents collaborate, undo changes, or start a new painting. How we built it We used React, TypeScript, SVG, and WebMCP. Nine semantic tools expose the canvas, regions, colors, turns, presence, undo, and story actions. Tokenized rooms synchronize people and agents across browser sessions. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making agent participation real and visible. We built explicit joining, presence heartbeats, conflict-safe state, server-enforced turns, protected human work, and an authenticated fallback when direct WebMCP is unavailable. Accomplishments that we're proud of MythWeaver is a complete shared experience, not a scripted demo. People can see who is painting, where the agent is working, why it chose a color, and when the brush changes hands. What we learned Agents work better when websites expose meaning, not coordinates. “Color the river” is more reliable than “click here.” Visible rules, authorship, explanations, and reversible actions also make collaboration more trustworthy. What's next for MythWeaver: Paint together on the web Next, we want more coloring worlds, generated outlines, voice guidance, saved galleries, multiplayer rooms, and classroom activities. Our goal is to make visual creation on the web a shared, understandable experience for people and agents. title: MCPation
pitch: A browser-native WebMCP gate that lets Codex inspect one explicitly granted workspace, explain drift, and apply supervised, reversible cleanup—without installing an MCP server.
about_excerpt: A browser-native WebMCP gate that lets Codex inspect one explicitly granted workspace, explain drift, and apply supervised, reversible cleanup—without installing an MCP server. Like Comment Story Updates What I built MCPation is a browser-native WebMCP pre-flight gate for Codex. It is a deliberately scoped MVP exploring a new category of agent-native DevTools: many of the useful, structured interactions people associate with an installed MCP can happen directly in a web page, without installing a server, daemon, extension, or API key. The user grants access to exactly one workspace folder, and the agent works inside that visible boundary. Why WebMCP is a good fit Agent configuration tends to grow quietly. Duplicate MCP servers, disabled entries, invalid endpoints, package drift, and layered Codex instructions can make it hard to know what an agent will inherit before it runs. MCPation turns that uncertainty into a shared, inspectable pre-flight step. The first pass is read-only: it reads an allowlisted set of configuration, package, and instruction metadata, then returns a readiness score, concrete findings, and an evidence graph connecting artifacts to those findings. This creates a better experience for both sides. A person gets an understandable report instead of guessing through configuration files. Codex gets a structured tool surface instead of having to click through an unfamiliar UI. They see the same state, while the person stays in control of every write. What the real demo shows The demo workspace is intentionally seeded with reproducible problems so the workflow has something meaningful to solve. The browser flow itself is real, not a mocked result: MCPation scans the selected folder, identifies duplicate JSON server entries, an invalid endpoint, and a disabled server, explains the evidence, and builds a supervised hardening plan. I choose the exact duplicate cleanup, explicitly approve it, grant the browser write permission, and MCPation creates one sibling backup before removing only those selected keys. It then rescans and shows the new readiness score and the restorable snapshot. More complex commands, TOML, policy, and instruction changes remain review items rather than being silently changed. The important collaboration is that a person can decide what is safe while an agent can inspect, explain, and verify the result through the same page. That combination would be difficult with a normal UI-only workflow and risky with an unbounded local tool. How WebMCP is implemented The page registers a concrete document.modelContext surface with tools for scanning the workspace, reading the declared MCP/package inventory, reading the instruction chain, explaining findings, building a hardening plan, requesting a bounded host handoff, submitting a sanitized host snapshot, applying the selected deterministic cleanup, verifying the result, and explaining the exact access scope. Read-only tools are annotated with readOnlyHint; the apply tool accepts only action IDs from the latest plan and requires confirm: true. The visible browser control owns the permission prompt, backup, write, and rescan. When a browser cannot expose native WebMCP, MCPation says so explicitly and shows a local preview instead of pretending that native tools are available. The same app works in Codex's in-app browser and in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Scope and honesty This is a deliberately scoped MVP for a new category of agent-native DevTools, built under a short hackathon deadline. I chose one deterministic, reversible cleanup and a strong evidence trail instead of pretending to support every possible workspace utility. With more time, the same pattern could extend to onboarding, compliance checks, migrations, review gates, and other supervised workflows. The point is that a useful MCP-like experience does not necessarily need installation when WebMCP can publish a scoped page surface and the user grants explicit permission. A note about the English text English is not my native language. I understand and speak it fluently, but expressing myself precisely in written English takes me much longer. I used AI to help draft, translate, and polish this description so it would be clear to the judges; the product decisions, implementation, testing, and claims in this submission are based on the project that is actually running. I am genuinely grateful to be able to participate in this hackathon. I discovered it rather late and would have loved more time to explore richer utilities, but I am very happy to share this concept and what I managed to build. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Virtual Try-On + AI Stylist
pitch: Virtual try-on that runs entirely in your browser. Its catalog search, try-on, save and compare are WebMCP tools and an AI agent proposes outfits, you judge the fit. No server, no uploads.
about_excerpt: Virtual try-on that runs entirely in your browser. Its catalog search, try-on, save and compare are WebMCP tools and an AI agent proposes outfits, you judge the fit. No server, no uploads. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent applies the sangeet dress banner, composite, reaction chips The model, the 8-garment catalog, the "AI stylist tools live" indicator WebGPU backend, warm on-device timings (SEGMENT 34 ms / POSE 46 ms) The structured reaction ("❤️ Love it perfect for the sangeet"), first saved look A kurti on the model catalog range beyond dresses Agent applies the Blush Pink Lehenga Choli Two saved looks in the tray The side-by-side compare modal "Which one works?" Virtual Try-On + AI Stylist This is an existing project. The on-device try-on app existed before the hackathon; the last commit before it is dated July 29. Everything to do with WebMCP was built between Aug 29 and Sep 2: the five tools, the reaction bar, the saved-looks tray and compare view, the merchandised catalog, and the test suite for the tools. The git history dates all of it. Inspiration Virtual try-on is normally a server job. You upload your photo, a model runs somewhere, you pay per render, and you have to be fine with a picture of yourself sitting on someone's GPUs. We'd already built the opposite: a try-on that runs in the browser on WebGPU, so it's instant, free to serve, and the photo never leaves your machine. Then agents started shopping for people, and the thing they're worst at is the thing that matters: knowing whether an outfit actually looks good on you. WebMCP let us split it. The agent does the legwork; the person makes the call. And WebMCP is the right fit because the tools already exist. They're the buttons on the page. There's no API to build, no server, and the agent can only do what the page lets a person do. What it does You open the app with a photo or your webcam and it composites garments onto you on-device: segmentation, pose, and a garment warp, all in a Web Worker. The page registers five WebMCP tools on document.modelContext : Tool search_catalog filter by occasion, colour, category, budget (₹) apply_tryon run the pipeline and put a garment on the photo save_look snapshot the result into a tray compare_looks show saved looks side by side await_reaction get the verdict: love it, good, try another, not this Any WebMCP client picks them up: ChatGPT's browser, a Chrome agent, Claude through a bridge extension. So instead of setting filters, opening six product pages, and picturing each one on yourself, you say "a sangeet outfit under ₹8k". The agent runs search_catalog({ occasion: "sangeet", maxPrice: 8000 }) , gets the one match, and applies it. One turn. You say "love it" and it saves. You say "show me a lehenga too" and it applies a second one and puts the two side by side. You just react. Nothing behind the tools is new business logic, nothing scrapes the DOM, and no tool can spend money. How we built it The five tools are one file, src/webmcp/useStylistTools.ts . Each is a hook that registers on document.modelContext with a JSON-schema input and a handler that calls something the page already had: the garment-select function, the looks tray, the reaction bar. search_catalog is a keyword-scored filter with its own unit tests. apply_tryon loads a default photo if you haven't picked one, so the loop works cold. await_reaction is dual-mode: the agent passes the reaction it heard in chat and gets guidance back, or it leaves the argument out and the call blocks until you tap a chip. Either way the app shows what you said. @mcp-b/global installs document.modelContext where the browser doesn't have it and defers to the native one where it does, so the same code works in Chrome's native WebMCP and in ChatGPT's browser. The tool annotations pull weight too: search_catalog is read-only, the writes are idempotent, and apply_tryon 's response tells the agent to call await_reaction next. There's a Playwright test that runs every tool through getTools() / executeTool() and checks 19 things. Under it is the try-on pipeline: LiteRT.js on WebGPU with a Wasm fallback, MediaPipe segmentation, MoveNet pose, and a thin-plate-spline garment warp written from scratch and rendered as a triangle mesh. It's published as @practics/tryon-core ; the app is a thin React shell over it. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is days old. The spec renamed navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext mid-build, and no stable browser ships it yet. The main thing to check was that the polyfill actually steps aside for the native API when there is one. It does. The agent kept web-searching instead of using the tools. Half of that was our fault (we hadn't redeployed). The rest is that ChatGPT is careful about site tools: it needs "use sitetools:" in the prompt and a model that supports WebMCP. A console check confirmed the tools had reached ChatGPT's runtime, so the fix was on their side, not ours. await_reaction never fired in chat. You type "love it" and the agent just reads it off the transcript. That's why it's dual-mode now. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in a real agent against the live site, not a mock. Five tools, a reaction channel that works from a sentence or a tap, an end-to-end test, and no server or new business logic anywhere. And the human stays in charge: you see every move the agent makes, and you make the final call. What we learned WebMCP changes the design question from "what can the agent do" to "what should stay with the person". For a stylist that's fit and taste, and the tools are shaped to leave it alone. Tool wording matters more than we expected. The hint that apply_tryon drops about await_reaction changed the flow, and the agent started borrowing our chip labels ("Love it, Good, or try another?") into its own replies. And a blocking tool is wrong for a chat agent that already has the answer; meeting the person where they are, chip or sentence, worked better. What's next for Virtual Try-On + AI Stylist A paid HD tier as a render_hd tool: a server-side diffusion render, offered only after you've settled on a look. A checkout tool that runs only on an explicit confirmation from you, never the agent alone. A bigger catalog; the pipeline already handles pants and multi-piece outfits. And folding the tool layer into @practics/tryon-core , so any store widget built on the pipeline gets the agent surface for free. The on-device try-on pipeline underneath is my earlier work.
