title: ShowMe
pitch: Where did they hide that setting? Your agent lights up where to click next, on your own screen. No help article, no guessing, no handing over your account. Next time you won't need to ask.
about_excerpt: Where did they hide that setting? Your agent lights up where to click next, on your own screen. No help article, no guessing, no handing over your account. Next time you won't need to ask. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I'm bad at finding things in apps. Not proud of it, but it's true. Some real ones: Auth0. I needed to change one setting for a login flow and spent way too long clicking around the dashboard before I found it. The docs said "go to Settings". There are a lot of places called Settings. Jira. New team, new board, and a few days in I'm running standup from it in front of everyone, trying to find where you change an issue type or add a column while people wait. Datadog. When I was learning it I couldn't find where to filter logs properly, and later I struggled to find where the RUM integrations live. And that's me, with a technical background. I can only imagine how the websites regular people use every day make people from other backgrounds struggle. These all have the same problem. The answer exists, someone wrote it down, and it still doesn't help, because it's not on your screen. The AI answer to this is "let the agent do it for you". Agents are great, I use them all day. But that answer has two problems. You didn't learn anything, so next month you'll ask again. And the site now has to trust a robot with your login settings or your money. And sometimes you just can't hand it off. You're presenting. You're running standup. You're the one who's supposed to know where it is. Nobody wants to say "hold on, let me ask the agent" in front of the room. So I didn't want an agent that does it for me. I wanted one that points at my screen and says "there", waits for me to click, and next time I don't need it. That's ShowMe. What it does You open a site in a browser that has WebMCP, and you ask your agent something like "how do I turn on international transfers?" Then this happens: The site gives the agent a map of its own interface. Every screen, every menu, every button, with a sentence about each one. The agent works out the path and hands the whole thing to the page in one call. The page lights up the first thing you need to click, with a short message. You click it. The next one lights up. And so on. You don't wait for the model between steps. It's not involved between steps. Click the wrong thing and the page tells the agent, which re-plans. Say "just do it for me" and the site decides. Opening a menu, fine. Pressing Confirm on a transfer, no. The agent tells you why. When you're done, the agent tells you the path in one line so you remember it. I made two sites to show it. Neither has any guide code in it, just the attributes. PeruBank is a fake bank. The switch for international transfers is four levels deep, and the final Confirm is a button I never want an agent pressing. Meridian is a fake team tracker. Board settings behind one three-dots menu, project settings behind another, a type icon nobody realises is a button. Basically the board I struggled with. Who it's for: anyone in an app with hundreds of settings, like developer dashboards and admin consoles. People who should never hand an agent their account, like my parents and their bank. And anyone learning a tool in front of other people. Why WebMCP To show someone where something is, you need three things, and only the page has them: A map of the interface that's actually true right now. A way to wait for a real click and know it happened. A say in what the agent is allowed to do. A screen-reading agent guesses at all three. You could maybe get the map from an accessibility tree. You can't get the other two. WebMCP gives the site one standard way to hand all three to whatever agent the person is using. That's why this works now and didn't before. How I built it One JavaScript file, one stylesheet, no build step. Both sites use the same two files. The site marks its elements: data-guide is the id. data-guide-desc is a sentence about it, written like you'd explain it to a new colleague. data-guide-delegable means an agent may do this step for you. Leave it off and it's yours. data-guide-danger means it can't be undone. Never delegated. data-screen , data-panel , data-dialog , data-menu group things so the agent knows what has to be open first. The map is rebuilt from the live page every time it's asked for, so anything rendered later is in it too. Whether something is open is read from what's actually visible on screen. Five tools, all registered through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_ui_map and get_current_view . Read-only. Flagged untrustedContentHint because they echo text people typed. run_walkthrough . The long one. Takes the whole path, paces you through it on the page, listens for the AbortSignal , and comes back with what you did and where you are now. If it's taking a while it returns in_progress after 40 seconds and the agent calls again. do_step_for_person . Reads the policy from the markup. Refuses anything not marked delegable. end_walkthrough . Only exists while a guide is running. Registered with an AbortController , so when the guide ends the tool disappears and toolchange fires. A Playwright test drives both sites through getTools and executeTool , with Google's polyfill injected so it runs on plain Chrome. Each site also has an Agent activity panel. It shows which bits of the API have actually been used this session, plus a transcript of every call and every click. I added it because the agent's own call log is just two lines, and everything interesting happens inside one of them. Challenges I ran into The first version did one spotlight per tool call. In ChatGPT's browser every round trip was 10 to 20 seconds, so you'd click and then sit there. Handing the whole path to the page in one call fixed that. Then I hit tool timeouts, which is where in_progress came from. Knowing what the person actually did. Clicks are easy. Text fields need Enter or a pause. Checkboxes fire change, not click, if you hit the label. "Clicked somewhere else" needed a listener on the whole document that ignores the overlay, the label around a checkbox, and the panel button. Things that aren't visible yet. If the agent asks for something inside a closed menu, the page has to say what to open first, in a sentence the agent can act on. Annotations. Not every browser accepts every one, so registration retries without the rejected one and the panel says which. The map is big. About 20K characters on the bank, 40K on the tracker. It works, but it's most of the minute the first answer takes. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The first time it worked end to end in ChatGPT's browser. I asked how to turn on international transfers, the profile menu lit up, I clicked, Settings lit up, I clicked, and it kept going all the way to Confirm without me waiting once. Seven steps, planned once. The version before that had a spinner between every click, so that was the moment I knew the design was right. The bank saying no. I asked the agent to press Confirm for me, and instead of doing it, it came back with PeruBank's own words: this is irreversible and an agent never does it. The agent didn't decide that. I didn't put it in a prompt. It's one attribute on one button, and the tool reads it. That's the part I'd show a bank. Getting the wrong click right. I clicked somewhere else on purpose, and instead of the guide silently breaking, the agent got back exactly what I'd clicked, said so, and re-planned from where I actually was. It took a while to teach the page the difference between "clicked the thing", "clicked the label around the thing", "clicked the panel", and "wandered off". A tool that appears and disappears. end_walkthrough only exists while a guide is running. Open Site tools mid-guide and it's there. Finish, and it's gone. Small, but it means the agent's own tool list tells it what state the page is in, and the browser fires toolchange to say so. The whole thing is one file and one stylesheet, and both demo sites run the exact same two. Nothing in PeruBank or Meridian knows about the guide except the attributes. And the one I actually care about. After the guide, I turned the setting back off myself. No agent, no help article. Profile menu, Settings, Transfer limits, Advanced. Four clicks. That's what it was for. What I learned The biggest one: keep the model out of the loop between steps. My first version asked the agent after every click, and every answer took 10 to 20 seconds. Once the agent planned once and the page did the pacing, the whole thing went from painful to instant. The agent is good at reading a map and planning. The page is good at waiting for a click. Let each do its job. Writing the sentence for each element is the real work. It's the same work as writing a help article, one line per button, written for a colleague. The difference is these lines show up on the person's screen at the moment they need them, instead of in a doc nobody finds. U

title: Zatom
pitch: AI-native chemical modeling applications (WebMCP native)
about_excerpt: AI-native chemical modeling applications (WebMCP native) Like 1 Comment Story Updates COVERS A B What If an Agent Could Look at the Same Atom You Are Looking At? Inspiration We started with a slightly annoying observation. LLMs are becoming very good at operating software. They can call tools. They can edit files. They can write code. They can chain dozens of actions together. But put an agent inside a scientific 3D modeling environment and ask: “Move the molecule to that site.” …and suddenly “that” becomes the hardest word in the sentence. Humans do not think about molecular structures as lists of Cartesian coordinates. We look at a surface and say: “this atom” “the site on the right” “the layer underneath” “rotate it toward that oxygen” “not there — the other bridge site” Scientific modeling is deeply spatial, visual, and interactive. Language models, on the other hand, are usually handed something like: Atom 148: O 3.422 7.183 12.901 Atom 149: H 3.981 7.652 13.441 ... Technically correct. Also technically miserable. So we started asking a different question: What if the 3D viewport itself became a shared workspace between a human and an agent? That question became this project. What We Built We built WebMCP support for a scientific modeling environment covering molecular and condensed-matter structures. The goal is not simply to expose every GUI button as a tool. That would be useful, but it would still leave the agent fundamentally blind. Instead, we treat WebMCP as a bridge between three things: scientific structure → agent reasoning → human attention The agent can inspect the model, reason about its local environment, manipulate geometry, and — importantly — control what the human is looking at. That last part turned out to be surprisingly important. If the agent proposes an adsorption site, it should not respond with: “Use atoms 102, 117 and 118.” It should move the camera there. Highlight the atoms. Mark the candidate site. Then ask: “This one?” If the user says: “No, the one on the right.” the agent should be able to continue from the shared visual context. That is the interaction we wanted. Not human or agent modeling. Human with agent modeling. Shared Spatial Attention The concept we kept coming back to while building the project was something we now call shared spatial attention . An agent needs more than a scene dump. It needs ways to answer questions such as: What structure is currently visible? What has the user selected? Which atoms are nearby? Which direction is the surface normal? Which atoms belong to the top layer? Where are plausible adsorption sites? What did I just highlight? What does “the one beside it” refer to? What changed after my previous operation? And the agent also needs to influence the viewport: observe ↓ understand ↓ focus ↓ propose ↓ human confirms ↓ act ↓ observe again ↓ verify That loop is the core of the project. A successful MCP call does not necessarily mean the task succeeded. The resulting scientific structure still has to make sense. A Tiny Example That Contains the Whole Idea One of our favorite demos is intentionally simple: “Help me adsorb a water molecule on this surface. Ask me before important decisions.” The agent first inspects the surface. It identifies candidate sites. It focuses the viewport on one of them. The user rejects it: “Not this one. The one on the right.” The agent shifts focus to another candidate. The user confirms. The agent places H₂O using the oxygen as an anchor. Then the user says: “Point one hydrogen toward that oxygen.” The nearby oxygen is highlighted. The water molecule rotates. The geometry is checked again. No atom IDs. No coordinates. No copy-pasting between a chat window and a modeling program. Just shared context. For us, that interaction captures the entire project better than a hundred tool definitions could. How We Built It The modeling application already understands scientific objects: atoms, bonds, molecules, periodic cells, surfaces, selections, transformations, local neighborhoods, and camera state. WebMCP becomes the layer through which those concepts can be exposed to an agent in a structured and controllable way. Rather than giving the model the entire universe every time, we try to make spatial reasoning progressive . For a large system, the agent should be able to go from: entire system → structural region → local neighborhood → selected atoms → target site This matters because a user may be working with hundreds or thousands of atoms while only caring about three of them. The agent should not need a 20,000-line coordinate dump just to rotate one functional group. We also designed operations around reversibility and verification. Scientific modeling involves experimentation: “Try this.” “No, undo that.” “Actually, the previous orientation was better.” That means an agent needs to be able to make tentative edits, inspect the result, detect obvious geometric problems, undo them, and try again. In other words: scientific software should support agent curiosity without turning agent curiosity into structural chaos. The Hard Part Was Not Tool Calling The easiest part was exposing actions. Move atom. Rotate molecule. Create structure. Select object. Measure distance. The harder problem was grounding . What does “this” mean? What does “behind” mean in a rotatable 3D scene? Does “right” mean screen-right, crystallographic direction, or a neighboring adsorption site? What happens when the camera moves halfway through the conversation? How much structure should be sent to the agent? When should the agent act autonomously, and when should it visually ask for confirmation? These questions made us realize that agent-native scientific software needs more than APIs. It needs a language for attention, ambiguity, and shared state . That was probably the most important thing we learned while building this project. What We Learned We originally thought the important question would be: “How many modeling functions can WebMCP expose?” We ended up believing the better question is: “How little internal software machinery does the user need to think about?” If the user has to know atom IDs, coordinate systems, internal object handles, and tool names to collaborate with the agent, then we have merely moved the command line into a chat box. The interesting interface appears when users can communicate at the level they naturally think: “Put it here.” “Rotate this bond.” “Show me another possible site.” “Why did you choose this one?” And the agent can answer not only with words, but by changing the shared visual world . That feels much closer to collaboration. Why WebMCP WebMCP gave us a useful way to think about the boundary between the application and the agent. The application remains responsible for being a serious scientific modeling environment. The model remains responsible for reasoning, interpretation, and planning. WebMCP connects the two. We do not want the agent to replace the modeling application. We do not want the modeling application to pretend to be an AI. We want both sides to expose what they are good at. The result is something that feels less like: “AI controlling software.” and more like: “two participants working inside the same scientific workspace.” What's Next This project currently focuses on giving agents better access to scientific 3D structure and human visual context. But the same idea extends much further. A future agent could move naturally between: molecular construction, crystal defects, surfaces, interfaces, reaction structures, simulation setup, analysis, and eventually computational workflows. The long-term goal is not a giant prompt that builds everything automatically. Scientific work is too exploratory for that. Instead, we are interested in something more practical: an agent that can stand beside you while you work. It can inspect. It can suggest. It can point. It can manipulate. It can verify. And when neither side is completely sure, it can simply ask: “This one?” That may sound like a tiny interaction. For 3D scientific software, we think it is a pretty big deal. title: Jhola - a trip finder whose slow searches you can stop
pitch: A trip finder with real, slow fare searches and a Cancel button that actually cancels - timers clear, nothing lands after, and the agent knows exactly what it never saw.
about_excerpt: A trip finder with real, slow fare searches and a Cancel button that actually cancels - timers clear, nothing lands after, and the agent knows exactly what it never saw. Like Comment Story Updates The trip finder: destinations, budget, and dates Tool console: get_brief tool called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: long-running tools accept execute(args, {signal}) and are genuinely abortable - a cancelled search stops mid-flight, not just in the UI. Inspiration "Somewhere warm under ₹40,000 for four days from Bengaluru" is a complete brief to a friend and an impossible query to a travel site, which wants a destination first, then makes you wait through a slow search per place - with no way to say "that's enough, I've seen what I need." What it does Jhola exposes catalogue, fare search, stay availability, and hold as tools. The agent runs one slow search across twelve destinations while results land one card at a time; the moment the traveller has seen enough, they press Cancel and the search stops honestly - timers cleared, nothing lands afterward, the agent told exactly what was found and what was never searched. A cancelled search returns a first-class partial report, never an error. Booking is irreversible, so there's no book tool at all - Book is a human-only button; holding is reversible, so hold_itinerary is a tool. How we built it execute(args, { signal }) , honoured all the way through: search_fares and check_stays advance through staged timers that obey the AbortSignal Chrome hands every tool call. One AbortController per call, shared by all four ways a call can end - the in-flight strip's own Cancel, the tool console's Cancel, the cancel_call tool, or the caller's own signal - and the activity log always says which one fired. Challenges we ran into Building runtime fallbacks for when Chrome's real cancellation bridge has gaps: if a Cancel click doesn't visibly end the in-flight record within 250ms, the console aborts the call directly and says so; if executeTool() 's own promise doesn't resolve with the string the call actually produced, the console reads it off the call's own record instead - both proven against a simulated broken bridge, not just the happy path. And, like its sibling apps, a self-abort race in hold_itinerary 's dynamic registration, found and fixed with the same deferred-abort pattern. Accomplishments that we're proud of A cancel that is actually honest - a stopped search names exactly what it never searched, instead of pretending it finished or silently discarding the question. What we learned Real cancellation UX needs a fallback story, not just a happy-path signal - a judge's browser, a flaky bridge, or a headless test environment can all diverge from the ideal case, and the app has to stay honest in every one. What's next A price-drop watch tool that re-checks a held itinerary's fare periodically and surfaces it only if it's dropped, without the traveller having to ask again. How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Jhola - a trip finder whose slow searches you can stop Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Tablemap (dynamic tool registration), Signoff (a tool that only exists once a human approves it), Paperwork (structurally human-only fields), Shortlist (a tool schema generated live from the catalog), Almari (quarantined untrusted content), Dhwani (declarative, no-JavaScript tools). title: Grant Scout
pitch: An AI agent that finds real funding for solo, non-incorporated founders - live SerpApi search, Gemini reasoning, every claim cited.
about_excerpt:
An AI agent that finds real funding for solo, non-incorporated founders - live SerpApi search, Gemini reasoning, every claim cited.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it does 

 Grant Scout helps solo, non-incorporated founders find funding programs they can actually apply for. Ask a plain-language question - "grants for a non-incorporated solo founder building an AI agent product in the US" - and Grant Scout runs a live Google Search through SerpApi, or - for clearly US federal questions - a live search against grants.gov's own public Search API for real opportunity data (real opportunity number, agency, close date, and a real grants.gov detail-page link). Gemini reviews only the real returned results and explains which programs plausibly don't require a legal entity, citing the real source URL for every claim. Nothing is fabricated: if a program doesn't appear in a real search result, it never makes the list. 

 We built this because it's a real problem for our own team. ArkNet Digital is a real, currently non-incorporated solo-founder operation, and finding non-dilutive funding that doesn't assume you already have an LLC or C-corp is a genuine, unsolved friction point. Grant Scout is the tool we wished existed. 

 Discovery → Eligibility → Readiness: the agent workflow 

 Every question runs through three stages, visible in the UI, not just in raw JSON: 

 Discovery agent - runs the live SerpApi or grants.gov search and returns real results, each linked to its original publisher page (tracking-redirect links are filtered out, so every citation is the actual destination URL, not a redirect).
Eligibility agent - Gemini reviews only the real returned snippets and groups the answer into what's likely open to you as an individual versus what likely requires incorporation or is unclear - always tied to a cited source, never a guess.
Readiness agent - every source gets an evidence-strength label (primary registry vs. search discovery) and an eligibility-signal flag (present vs. not visible in returned evidence), plus a concrete next action ("open the cited source and verify applicant type, geography, deadline, and exclusions"). This is evidence quality, not an eligibility verdict - a search snippet can never prove you qualify, only tell you what's worth checking next. 

 When the search comes back empty or a signal simply isn't visible in what was returned, Grant Scout says so explicitly instead of inventing an eligibility conclusion. This tool surfaces real, verifiable leads - it never promises funding. 

 Why this could be a real business, not just a demo 

 The addressable user isn't hypothetical - solo/indie AI builders are one of the fastest-growing segments on platforms like Devpost, Product Hunt, and Indie Hackers, and nearly all of them face the same non-incorporated-founder funding gap this tool was built to close. The workaround today is manually reading eligibility fine print across dozens of grant pages, or giving up and assuming "grants are for companies" - a real, specific, and currently unsolved piece of friction, not a nice-to-have. 

 Path to a real product, honestly scoped for where this is today: 

 This hackathon build is a working prototype, not a monetized product yet - that's the honest state.
The natural monetization shape is subscription (continuous monitoring + alerts when a founder's specific eligibility profile matches a newly posted program) rather than pay-per-search, since the recurring value is in not having to re-search every few weeks.
Distribution is realistic without paid acquisition: indie-builder communities (Indie Hackers, Product Hunt launches, X/Twitter's build-in-public crowd, Devpost itself) are exactly where non-incorporated solo founders already look for this kind of tool, and word-of-mouth in that community is dense.
Defensibility isn't the search itself - it's the eligibility-reasoning layer (grants.gov + SerpApi results filtered specifically for "no entity required") that a generic search or ChatGPT session won't give a founder without real digging.
Kill criterion we'd actually apply: if a small cohort of real non-incorporated founders don't return to re-run a search within a few weeks of first use, the recurring-value thesis is wrong and this stays a one-off tool, not a company. 

 How it works 

 Agent: Built on Google's Agent Development Kit (google-adk), running a single Agent with two live-grounding tools - tool_search_funding_programs and tool_search_grants_gov.
Live grounding: tool_search_funding_programs calls SerpApi's Google Search API ( https://serpapi.com/search ) at request time; tool_search_grants_gov calls grants.gov's own public Search API ( https://api.grants.gov/v1/api/search2 , no API key required) for real US federal opportunities. Which tool runs is decided deterministically before the agent is even built, based on whether the question signals US federal funding (mentions "federal", "grants.gov", SBIR/STTR, a specific federal agency) - never left to model judgment, since testing found the model didn't reliably choose the more precise source on its own.
Reasoning: the agent (gemini-flash-lite-latest via the free Gemini Developer API) reviews the real results returned by whichever tool ran, flagging which ones plausibly fit a non-incorporated applicant and which likely require a registered entity - always citing its source.
Backend: the same agent code runs inside a Vercel Python serverless function (frontend/api/chat.py), avoiding a Python framework preset so it coexists with the Next.js frontend in one deployment.
Frontend: Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, Tailwind CSS v4 - a trustworthy, financial-adjacent design (navy-to-emerald gradient, Inter type). 

 SerpApi + grants.gov integration 

 Neither is a decorative add-on - together they're the entire grounding layer. Every single answer the agent gives is the direct result of a live request made in that request, to whichever source is the more authoritative fit for the question. There is no fallback to the model's own training data; if the chosen tool returns no usable results, the other tool is tried once as a fallback, and if both come up empty the agent says so rather than guessing. 

 Try it live 

 https://grant-scout-jayblast.vercel.app - ask it a real funding question and watch the Discovery → Eligibility → Readiness workflow run in front of you, with cited sources and evidence labels underneath the answer. 

 GitHub repo 

 https://github.com/jayblast-spec/grant-scout - MIT licensed, README has local run instructions.

title: GridBrief TR
pitch: An agent-ready bilingual workspace that turns public EPİAŞ Transparency Platform 2.0 data into explainable market, portfolio, and planning decisions through native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: An agent-ready bilingual workspace that turns public EPİAŞ Transparency Platform 2.0 data into explainable market, portfolio, and planning decisions through native WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Türkiye's electricity-market teams must reconcile prices, system conditions, generation, consumption, and planning data before making a shift decision. Today that work often spans operator pages, spreadsheets, and chat. Each team rebuilds the same context, while the most important questions — which source, which timestamp, which scope, and how complete is the data — are easy to lose. GridBrief TR reimagines the public EPİAŞ Transparency Platform 2.0 as a bilingual, agent-ready decision workspace. It keeps the familiar market information architecture, but makes provenance, freshness, coverage, and missing data first-class product features. What it does GridBrief TR combines: a real-data market overview; the searchable Transparency 2.0 electricity catalogue; public organization and power-plant discovery; production and consumption planning views; English and Turkish interfaces; and a native WebMCP tool surface shared by the human user and browser agents. The production walkthrough uses a completed historical day and visibly shows EPİAŞ provenance, retrieval time, scope, coverage, and warnings. Examples include market price and imbalance context, 24/24 planning coverage, the public PURE ENERGY organization view and linked UEVÇB records, and an ACARSOY plant view that honestly leaves unavailable actual generation as null. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the interaction layer, not a chatbot bolted onto a dashboard. GridBrief registers eight structured tools on document.modelContext: set_analysis_scope get_market_snapshot find_market_entities compare_plan_actual stress_test_position draft_shift_brief search_transparency_datasets get_transparency_dataset A compatible browser discovers these tools and calls the descriptor returned by getTools() with schema-bounded arguments. Successful calls update the same visible workspace used by the participant, so the agent and human share the selected date, hour window, results, warnings, and sources. Our native Chrome 152 verification discovered all eight tools. It also executed search_transparency_datasets through document.modelContext and visibly synchronized the selected catalogue item. That is separate from the real-data production evidence: during the recorded native verification run, an upstream EPİAŞ live read timed out, so the harness failed closed, recorded the failure, and skipped downstream sensitivity and brief actions. It never substituted a synthetic observation. Example agent workflow A trading agent can retrieve price and imbalance context. An operations agent can inspect generation evidence and publication coverage. A planning agent can compare KGÜP, KUDÜP, EAK, load-plan, and actual series only at valid data levels. A portfolio-risk agent can apply a transparent local sensitivity after the live price reference passes validation. A management agent can turn the sourced evidence, risks, and proposed checks into an editable shift brief. These are role-specific uses of one WebMCP contract, demonstrated by a deterministic sample agent workflow in the repository. GridBrief does not claim that the runner itself is an LLM. It exposes no market-order, trading-account, message-sending, or upstream mutation tool. How we built it The application uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Vercel. A server-only EPİAŞ gateway obtains and caches the short-lived ticket-granting token without returning or logging credentials. Responses carry provider, retrieval time, scope, quality, coverage, and warnings. Partial data preserves nulls; live errors fail closed. The browser layer registers imperative WebMCP definitions for the lifetime of the workspace. A Node/CDP verification harness launches Chrome with WebMCP enabled, checks unique tool discovery, executes native descriptors, and writes bounded sanitized evidence and screenshots. The harness accepts no username, password, token, cookie, or authorization-header argument. Challenges and learnings The hardest part was preserving market-data integrity while making the experience useful to agents. EPİAŞ reports have different scopes and publication schedules; organization filters do not turn system-level actuals into organization data; and upstream availability can change during a demo. We therefore made data level explicit, preserved missing hours, withheld full-day deviation when coverage is not comparable, and separated catalogue availability from successful observation retrieval. We also learned that the current experimental Chrome implementation requires the descriptor returned by getTools() and JSON-stringified arguments. Testing that real boundary exposed issues a mock panel would have hidden, including duplicate registration risks, inclusive-versus-exclusive hour semantics, and upstream timeout handling. What's next Next steps are formal review of EPİAŞ report semantics and terms, organization-level audit retention, role controls, shared rate limiting, richer data-quality tests, and approved connections to internal portfolio systems. We will preserve the no-execution boundary unless a separately governed product is designed and authorized. Links Live English workspace: https://gridbrief-tr.vercel.app/en Turkish workspace: https://gridbrief-tr.vercel.app/tr Source code: https://github.com/haakanergun/gridbrief-tr Demo video: https://youtu.be/5dGW_ocNZJw Disclosure GridBrief TR is an independent prototype and is not affiliated with or endorsed by EPİAŞ. It provides decision support only and does not place trades or provide financial advice. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: DraftSmith powered by Excalidraw
pitch: An Excalidraw fork that declares eight tools on document.modelContext. Any agent - ours, ChatGPT, or one that's never heard of it, discovers the vocabulary and edits the live canvas. No screenshots!!
about_excerpt: An Excalidraw fork that declares eight tools on document.modelContext. Any agent - ours, ChatGPT, or one that's never heard of it, discovers the vocabulary and edits the live canvas. No screenshots!! Like Comment Story Updates Title End Draftsmith (powered by Excalidraw) Live: https://nice-field-0f080db0f.7.azurestaticapps.net Inspiration Every architecture conversation we've had starts on a whiteboard and ends with someone taking a photo of it. If you actually want to keep the diagram, somebody has to sit down and redraw it, and that's the point where you stop thinking about the system and start nudging boxes around to fit one extra service in. We'd already tried the usual escapes. Mermaid and similar tools hand you a rendered picture; change one word and the layout reshuffles under you, and you can't just grab a box and move it. Image models produce something diagram-shaped that can't be edited at all. Agents that drive a canvas by clicking are guessing coordinates off screenshots, and the results look like it. Two things made us think this was worth a weekend. The first is that Excalidraw already stores the right thing. A scene is real data: elements, and arrows that stay bound to the shapes they connect. If an agent could write that scene directly, you'd get a diagram you can keep working in instead of a picture of one. The second is WebMCP. Normally the backend owns the tool list and one bespoke agent loop calls it. WebMCP flips that around: the page declares what it can do, and any agent the browser trusts can discover and call those tools. We wanted to see whether that actually holds up on something hard, and a canvas is about as hard as it gets - it's stateful, it's spatial, and it's basically opaque to an agent that can only click. Somewhere in there we also decided that a diagram handed over with no commentary isn't much use. So the agent should be able to explain what it drew, not just draw it. What it does Draftsmith is Excalidraw with an agent living inside it. Describe a system, get a diagram. "Draw a 3-tier architecture with a load balancer, two app servers and a database" comes back laid out in one turn: ranked into tiers, ordered to reduce arrow crossings, with long arrows routed around whatever sits between their endpoints. Arrows use Excalidraw's native binding, so they snap to shape edges and follow the boxes when you drag them. Nothing about it is an export - you can keep editing by hand, or keep asking. Talk to it while it draws. Voice mode runs hands-free over a single socket. It listens continuously, answers out loud, asks follow-up questions when your request is vague, and pushes back if the design looks off. You can talk over it to cut it off. When a question needs actual thought ("40M events a day, Postgres is melting - shard, CQRS, or a queue?") it says "let me think about that for a second" out loud and hands that one turn to a stronger model, rather than running the whole conversation slowly for the handful of turns that need it. Point at things. Select shapes on the canvas and they show up as pills above the composer, the same way you'd select code before asking your editor about it. "Make this blue" restyles that box and nothing else. "Connect these" binds them in the order listed. No guessing from labels. Ask to be taught. "Walk me through this" starts a spoken walkthrough with a Tutor cursor tracing the canvas, moving to each element as it's explained and panning off-screen ones into view. The finished lesson goes into the chat history, so a follow-up like "why is there a load balancer?" already has it as context. Teaching is a tool rather than a UI mode, which means "draw a 3-tier architecture and then explain it to me" draws it, binds it and teaches it in a single turn. The canvas is a WebMCP tool provider. Eight tools ( get_scene , create_diagram , add_shape , add_text , bind_arrow , set_style , remove_element , teach_diagram ) are declared to the browser, so an agent that knows nothing about our code can still drive the canvas. The panel header shows WebMCP · native · 8 tools or · shim · , and clicking the badge opens the live manifest. That was partly so we could debug it without devtools, and partly so a demo can't quietly imply native support it doesn't have. How we built it It's a fork of Excalidraw with the agent added, but we didn't vendor upstream. setup.sh clones a pinned Excalidraw commit and copies our files in. The repo stays at roughly the 6k lines that are actually ours, and our diff stays readable. The browser owns the tool definitions. app/ai-agent/webmcp/descriptors.ts is the only source of truth for the tool surface, and it lives in the browser because that's where WebMCP expects it - the page is the provider, so the declarations belong next to the code that runs them. The backend gets the list with every request. It carries its own copy, but that's a clearly labelled fallback for clients too old to send one. Our own agents are WebMCP clients. The sidebar and the voice agent both go through callTool exactly like a third party would. This was deliberate. If we'd registered the tools and then kept calling the canvas directly, the published path would have been exercised by nobody and would have rotted within days. As it stands, if the WebMCP surface breaks, the product breaks with it, and we find out immediately. The model does semantics, code does geometry. create_diagram takes an entire graph, and app/ai-agent/layout.ts runs a layered (Sugiyama) pipeline over it: break cycles, assign layers, insert dummy nodes so a long edge reserves a corridor in each layer it crosses, order within layers to cut crossings, then assign coordinates. Those dummy corridors turn into real bend points on the arrow, and since Excalidraw keeps bend points on a bound arrow, the routing survives without losing the bindings. Spatial invariants live in the tool layer. add_shape finds a non-overlapping position before it creates anything, searching outward on a grid, and reports back where the box actually ended up. Colour is assigned per layer instead of per box, so a tier comes out consistent without the model having to think about it. House style - rounded corners, hachure fill, label colour matched to the border - is set in code, so it holds regardless of what the model asks for. Voice is one socket, speech to speech. Mic audio goes up; spoken audio and tool calls come back down, over the Azure OpenAI Realtime API. One model hears audio and replies with both audio and function calls on the same stream, so there's no STT → LLM → TTS chain to keep in sync. The server proxies the socket instead of minting a client token. That keeps the key out of the browser, and because only the server sends session.update , a tampered client can't swap the instructions or widen the tool list. It can talk and listen, and that's it. The lesson is data, not prose. The scene goes to the backend, which runs a teaching prompt with one forced tool call that returns { intro, segments: [{ elementIds, narration }], closing } . Since every chunk of narration names the elements it's about, the frontend can point the cursor at exactly those elements for exactly as long as that chunk is playing. We treat the output as untrusted: schema-checked, then every element id verified against the real scene, with invented ids dropped and a lesson about nothing real rejected outright. Narration uses the browser's own speechSynthesis , so it needs no key and no audio leaves the machine. The tracing cursor isn't custom drawing either - "Tutor" is a synthetic entry in Excalidraw's collaborators map, the same code that renders a teammate's pointer, so it pans and zooms with the scene for free. No server-side session state. Each POST /api/chat is one model turn. It returns either final text or the tool calls to run; the browser runs them against the live editor and posts again. The server is a pure function of the history it's given, so it restarts cleanly, scales without stickiness, and holds the only copy of the credentials. Azure OpenAI and Anthropic sit behind one interface and are selectable per request. It's deployed as two halves on Azure, because they need different things. The editor is a static bundle on Static Web Apps. The backend has to hold a WebSocket open for the length of a voice session, which rules out serverless. Challenges we ran into Arrows went straight through the boxes. The bindings were fine - correct element ids on both ends - but the geometry wasn't, and it took a while to see why. Excalidraw derives an arrow's fixedPoint from the endpoint you seed it with: [(px - box.x) / box.width, …] . Seed an arrow centre to centre and you've recorded [0.5, 0.5] , which literally means "anchor at the centre of this shape." Seeding between the two outlines gives you bottom-centre and top-centre instead. While fixing that we hit a second one: Excalidraw computes default points as element.width || 100 , so a perfectly vertical arrow h

title: Traces
pitch: An AI agent can read your code but not your page, so it guesses why the button is dead. Traces gives it 17 WebMCP tools to search inside a recording, and to ask a human what it cannot see.
about_excerpt: An AI agent can read your code but not your page, so it guesses why the button is dead. Traces gives it 17 WebMCP tools to search inside a recording, and to ask a human what it cannot see. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Six words of bug report and a 45-second recording. Seventeen WebMCP tools are live in the header; there is no server behind this page. Every step has an author. The activity feed shows the agent bisecting to 28.049s in 17 probes, then seeking the human's playhead there. The agent stops and says it cannot see: it asks a human to look at 28.0s and pick an answer. The tool call blocks until someone does. Ranked hypotheses, best first. Each cites recorded evidence you can click: a 200 with 0 items at 11.6s, an empty select at 28.0s. Lower-ranked cards are kept, not hidden. A card with no evidence is rejected by the page, so confidence is never just the model's word. A drafted bug report, waiting on a human. All nine reproduction steps are checked against the event stream: zero unverified. Root cause with timestamps, not prose: 200 with 0 items, empty select, failed postcode check, rage-click. The human approves or rejects. Inspiration While building Xurel I hit a login form that would not submit. The email was valid, the password was valid, both fields were exactly what the standard asks for — and the button still did nothing. So I did what everyone does now: I handed it to an AI agent. It read the code, guessed, was wrong, guessed again. It could see the source. It could not see the page . Every guess cost tokens and told us nothing about the one thing that mattered — what state the form was actually in at the instant the button refused. We fixed it in the end by hand, by looking. Every engineer gets the six-word version of that bug from someone else: "checkout is broken, please fix it." No steps, no browser, no timestamp. It is the same problem one step removed — the state that would explain it is already gone by the time anyone reads the report. Which is why the demo app here ships with a pay button that stays grey. The state that explains a dead button exists for one instant, in one browser, and nowhere else. The DOM at 28.157 seconds is not stored data — it is the result of a computation : replaying thousands of mutation events up to that instant. No backend can return it. Only a live replay engine can, and only while it is running. That makes the tab running the replay the only place in the world where "at what millisecond did the province dropdown become empty?" can be answered. WebMCP is the primitive that opens that tab to an agent. Debugging Xurel, I did not know it existed. What it does Traces loads an rrweb recording in the browser and registers 17 WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . In the demo, a human drops six words into the task queue and an agent investigates: read_network — one request at 11,599 ms succeeded, 200 OK , and came back array, 0 items . A request that fails is easy to find. This one didn't fail. bisect — the agent sends a predicate and the page runs a binary search across the replay timeline: 10 probes, 36 ms, ±250 ms , landing on 28,157 ms . The playhead visibly jumps ten times while it runs, so a human watches the agent's search as motion rather than as a log line. read_dom_at — 1,845 characters of HTML arrive as 16 lines, 557 characters , and one of them is the entire bug: select#province[name=province] [empty options: 0] . ask_human_visual — the agent stops. It cannot see the screen, it says so, and it asks a human to look. The human drags the playhead to the moment and picks an answer, which comes back as structured data rather than prose: { choice: "looked normal but empty", markedTimestamp: 28157 } . propose_hypotheses — four ranked explanations, top one at 0.55 confidence, each citing evidence the human can click to highlight on the timeline. The human promotes one. propose_report — a bug report whose nine reproduction steps were each checked against the real recorded event stream. Zero unverified. The human approves it. Six words in. A root cause with timestamped evidence out. The human is the eyes. The agent is the reasoner. That is the exact inverse of an agent taking a screenshot and guessing. Why WebMCP, and not an API The answer does not exist until the page computes it. read_dom_at(28157) is not a lookup. The page has to replay the mutation stream to that instant and rebuild the DOM. A server holding the same recording file cannot answer without becoming a replay engine itself. bisect does not fetch — it programs the page. The agent hands over an algorithm to run over time, and the page runs it ten probes deep. There is no request/response shape for that, and no amount of clicking or DOM-scraping produces it either. A human can be a tool. execute() returns a Promise, so a tool is allowed to simply not resolve . That turns a person into something the agent calls when it reaches the edge of its own perception. An HTTP API cannot block on a human who is looking at your screen. The side effect is on human attention. seek moves the playhead; annotate leaves a marker a person sees. The agent isn't reading state — it is pointing at evidence and saying look here . That only works because the tool provider and the user interface are the same page. Nothing has to leave the machine. A recording is a full reconstruction of a page and everyone on it. With WebMCP it stays in the tab, and the agent receives only the small compressed slices it explicitly asks for. The constraint that made the design better WebMCP tool results are a content array, and today "text" is the only specified type — "image" is still an open question. We could not send a screenshot if we wanted to. Designing around that produced the two things we are proudest of: An agent-legible DOM representation with a hard budget of 60 lines and 1,200 characters , enforced by a test rather than by good intentions. Interactive and state-bearing nodes only, attributes from a whitelist, text truncated, layout wrappers discarded. It gives an agent things a screenshot never could: it can read aria-invalid , count option elements that were never rendered, and tell a genuinely disabled button from a merely grey one. ask_human_visual , for questions that honestly require eyes. Did this dropdown look broken, or normal but empty? No amount of DOM state answers that. A screenshot would have been the lazy answer and a worse one — thousands of tokens per call, and the agent still guessing at state it cannot read off pixels. How we built it Next.js and TypeScript, rrweb for record and replay, zustand for state, Tailwind for a dense instrument UI. No backend. Recordings are static JSON; replay, binary search, DOM compression and report validation all happen in the tab. lib/replay , lib/dom and lib/bisect are pure functions with no React, no store, and no knowledge that WebMCP exists — which is why the search algorithm and the DOM compressor have real tests. 309 tests pass. Three suites ( compress-dom , bisect , evaluatePredicate ) were written first as specifications and stayed red until the implementations satisfied them. Security was a design constraint, not a closing paragraph, because the premise of this challenge is handing a language model influence over a live page: Nothing from the model is executed. Predicates are a closed set of seven structured shapes — never a string, never eval , never new Function . A test greps the source and fails the build if either appears, so it cannot regress quietly under deadline pressure. Every response has a size budget , because a tool returning 800 KB has silently denied service to every later call in the conversation. Personal data is minimised at the recorder , not at the reader: maskAllInputs is mandatory, values are truncated to 20 characters when a tool reads one, and network bodies are summarised ( array, 0 items ) rather than forwarded. Every recording in the repo is synthetic , produced by bugbait/ — our own deliberately broken checkout, which ships alongside so anyone can make their own. Challenges we ran into The UI was the part we underestimated. The first version of Traces was genuinely bad to look at, and fixing it took more passes than any single feature. What finally worked was turning taste into constraints the build enforces: a type scale with a 13px floor for anything a person has to read — a compressed 1080p frame turns 10px body copy into grey texture — and a radius scale that stops at 6px, replaced rather than extended, so rounded-lg does not resolve and "no oversized rounded cards" is a build error instead of a line in a document. It is still not a beautiful app. It is a legible one, which for an instrument is the part that matters. bisect was too fast to see. Ten probes is about 36 ms of machine work — zero frames, invisible. We animate the probe trace on the timeline for the human's benefit and display the real elapsedMs next to it, rather than pretending the search was sl

title: CareWeave
pitch: CareWeave gives older and disabled people one calm place to coordinate daily care with loved ones and WebMCP agents, reducing complexity while protecting independence, privacy, and human control.
about_excerpt: CareWeave gives older and disabled people one calm place to coordinate daily care with loved ones and WebMCP agents, reducing complexity while protecting independence, privacy, and human control. Like Comment Story Updates Summary Careweave - Functionality Careweave - Overview Inspiration An appointment reminder arrives by email. The journey depends on the weather. A carer is visiting that morning. A son can help, but should not need access to private messages. None of these facts is difficult on its own. Keeping them aligned is. For many older and disabled people, daily life is spread across inboxes, calendars, maps, notes, and several people's memories. A small uncertainty can become a missed appointment, a wasted journey, an empty fridge, or another phone call asking someone else to check. The result is not just inconvenience. It is time, energy, confidence, and independence gradually lost to administration. Most planning tools assume that someone can scan a crowded calendar, remember where each detail lives, notice every change, and recover when information conflicts. Those assumptions become barriers for people managing fatigue, pain, reduced mobility, sensory loss, memory changes, or recovery. Support can also come with a hidden trade. To receive help, a person is often expected to hand over more privacy or control than the task requires. CareWeave began with a belief that independence does not mean doing everything alone. It means deciding how help happens. We wanted to build one calm place where a person, the people they trust, and an agent could work from the same understanding. The technology should carry the complexity. The person should keep the authority. What it does CareWeave turns the scattered work of daily care into one accessible dayboard. It brings together appointments, care visits, food, shopping, reminders, travel, weather, and important messages, then answers three human questions: What is happening today? Is there anything I need to decide or prepare? Can you help me deal with it safely? Instead of a dense monthly calendar, CareWeave begins with a clear day. It shows what matters now, what needs attention, and whether the pace feels calm or rushed. Large controls, readable text, high contrast, written alternatives to speech, and generous touch targets reduce the effort needed to use it. WebMCP makes CareWeave a genuinely shared workspace. A compatible agent can understand structured household information instead of guessing from pixels. It can explain the day, check the surrounding week, focus the visible board on an appointment, calculate when to leave, and open the route on the same screen the person is viewing. The clearest example is a clinic appointment. A person can ask: What matters today, and is tomorrow rushed? CareWeave returns confirmed plans, preparation, travel, and unresolved attention items. The person can then ask: Show me tomorrow and the route to Dr Patel. The dayboard moves to tomorrow and displays the route with a safe departure time. The conversation and the interface stay in sync. If the day feels too demanding, the person can ask: Prepare a request to move the appointment to a calm morning. CareWeave finds suitable options and prepares the exact recipient, subject, and message. It presents an expiring review plan before anything progresses. The original appointment remains confirmed until the clinic verifies a new time. A suggestion is not a draft, a draft is not a sent request, and a request is not a confirmation. Trusted supporters have a deliberately limited view. They can offer practical help without reading private messages, medical notes, or detailed care records. The person receiving support can accept, decline, undo, or revoke access. The agent handles coordination. The person keeps the decision. How we built it CareWeave is an installable SvelteKit progressive web app built with Svelte 5, TypeScript, and Vite. We started with the domain model rather than the interface. Confirmed commitments, untrusted attention items, reminders, support offers, data freshness, and action plans are separate objects. This prevents proposed actions from being mistaken for real outcomes. The application registers 32 imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . They cover understanding the day, checking pace, finding options, changing shared visual focus, showing routes, managing reminders, offering support, reviewing mailbox information, preparing actions, and applying verified confirmations. All tool inputs are validated again when they run. Read-only, untrusted-content, and consequential annotations expose the relevant safety boundaries to compatible agents. State revisions prevent an old action plan from being approved after the household information changes. If tool registration fails, CareWeave rolls back the attempted set instead of claiming a partial connection is ready. The touch interface, voice experience, and WebMCP tools call the same domain functions. There is one state for the person and the agent, not separate implementations that can quietly disagree. We used Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for routes, Open-Meteo for privacy-conscious forecasts, browser speech features, and an optional OpenAI Realtime voice path. An optional server-side Gmail connection reads bounded previews and creates drafts, but it cannot send email. The challenge experience uses deterministic fictional data stored on the device. It needs no account, credentials, API key, or private information. Unit tests, Playwright interaction and accessibility tests, and a browser-based WebMCP evaluation cover the core workflows. The production-host smoke run completed all 10 expected tool steps across six journeys. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making the interface tell the truth about real world state. In ordinary software, "requested," "drafted," and "confirmed" can blur together. In care coordination, that ambiguity matters. Someone could leave at the wrong time or believe help is arranged when it is not. We created an explicit appointment lifecycle and made every consequential action pass through a frozen, expiring review plan. We also had to find the right boundary for agency. A single powerful tool would have been easier to demonstrate, but harder for a person to understand or interrupt. We chose narrow tools that can be inspected, combined, and stopped at meaningful human decision points. The next challenge was keeping a broad care story visually calm. Every extra status, button, and warning adds cognitive work. We reduced density, enlarged targets, revealed details progressively, tested tablet and phone layouts, and kept spoken information available as text. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that WebMCP changes the actual CareWeave experience. The agent does not merely describe the page. It understands structured care context, reasons across it, and brings the person to the same date, appointment, or route being discussed. We built an end-to-end appointment workflow that remains truthful at every step. CareWeave can interpret an attention item, assess the week, find calmer options, prepare the exact clinic request, show it for review, and record the result without silently changing the confirmed appointment. We are equally proud of the social model. Supporters can be useful without becoming supervisors. Privacy is limited by purpose, help can be revoked, and the person at the centre retains the final say. The working build exposes 32 validated WebMCP tools, shares domain logic across touch and agent interactions, protects changes with revisions, and passed all 10 steps in our production-host smoke evaluation. It also supports large text, high contrast, keyboard navigation, reduced motion, and responsive tablet and phone layouts. What we learned We learned that autonomy is not a permission checkbox. It is the visible difference between offering help and taking over. We also learned that truthful state is part of accessibility. People should not need technical knowledge to know whether an appointment has changed, a message has been sent, or a relative has accepted a task. Structured tools help an agent understand a website. Shared visual focus helps a person understand the agent. CareWeave needs both. If the answer remains only in chat, the person still has to find the appointment, route, or reminder afterwards. Finally, calmness has to be engineered. Every new capability carries a cognitive cost. The best interface is not the one that shows everything. It is the one that helps someone answer the next question with the least effort. What's next for CareWeave The next step is to develop CareWeave with the people it is intended to support. We want to test the core experience with older and disabled people, unpaid family supporters, and professional carers, then adapt it to their language, routines, and access needs. Before CareWeave handles real household or care

title: Genga Studio
pitch: An anime studio in a browser tab. Give an agent a paragraph and it writes the script, draws the key frames, animates, voices, scores, and cuts a film. Collaborate in the browser and guide your vision.
about_excerpt: An anime studio in a browser tab. Give an agent a paragraph and it writes the script, draws the key frames, animates, voices, scores, and cuts a film. Collaborate in the browser and guide your vision. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In July I set out to make a short anime film with generated frames, on my own hardware. The pipeline grew the way pipelines do. An image model for key frames. A motion model for the few seconds that had to move. A script that froze the tail of a clip when the model drifted, another that chained a second clip off the last good frame, another that composited a moving cel over a painted plate. A dashboard that could cut the film. By the end of the month I had 97 shots, 567 takes, and a four-minute animatic of act one. Then I turned that pipeline into an application I could host, because I wanted the same control over every future film and I wanted it to run on hosted models instead of a GPU on my laptop. Cutroom, as it was called then, became a FastAPI server and a React studio: projects, a film editor, a shot page with a compose console and a generate console, a comp editor for cels, a timeline, a jobs queue, a settings page for backends. Every decision I had ever made became a toggle, a drawer, or a field. That is where it stalled. I had built a tool with a billion toggles and drawers. I could not remember where we put half of them. Pro-level control over every aspect of production turned out to mean a Photoshop-sized surface that only its author could navigate, and the author was losing track too. The revelation came from hearing about the WebMCP challenge. WebMCP lets a page register its own actions as tools on document.modelContext , and an agent running in the browser can call them. So the studio doesn't need fewer toggles, it just needs to publish them! An agent that can read the tool list can find the drawer I forgot, fill the console I never open, and press the button I would have pressed, while I watch it happen on screen and learn my own app back. Control stays total. The navigation cost goes to zero. That is what makes a video production tool a fantastic use case for WebMCP. It has to offer everything, because a film needs pro-level control over every part of production. Yet the person using it usually does not know which control they want, and does not want to become an expert in the tool to get the benefit of that control. Publishing the controls as tools resolves both halves at once: the studio keeps every knob, and the agent turns them. What it does Genga Studio is a cutting room for AI-generated limited animation, the way anime has always been made on a budget: key frames as the anchor point, holds and cels and cuts from the studio. Every action in the studio is also a WebMCP tool, 52 of them at submission: list the film, generate stills, restyle a take, set a keeper, plan a motion budget across shots, animate a cel, voice a line, score a bed, set a timeline source, cut the film, screen the result. An agent in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag sees the same studio you do and drives the same buttons. The hosted demo made a two-minute short, "Two Claudes," inspired by an NPR story about the two chatbots wired to talk to each other until they broke out of the loop. Fifteen shots, each animated for its full length from its keeper frame, fifteen voice lines, a piano bed, cut and re-cut after every motion pass. The takes on screen cost $2.80 in API calls. How we built it The plan came first: a frozen contract for tools (names, input schemas, a shared ActionContext , page anchors so a tool can wait for the console it needs), then the pages exposed their actions through a registry, then the tools were written against that registry. Parallel Claude agents built and tested the tool layer while I reviewed and drove the result. A Playwright driver launches system Chrome with the WebMCP feature enabled and executes tools through the browser's own document.modelContext , so the same script that tests the tools is the one an agent effectively runs. Hosting was its own small project. The director runs on OpenRouter. Stills come from a Gemini image model through OpenRouter, motion from Seedance or Wan on fal, voices from ElevenLabs. Backends are toggled by API key, the demo is invite-only, and a spend cap stops things from going wild just in case. Challenges we ran into The agent found every weakness in the studio's defaults. It chose the free instant test backend over the paid ones until that lane was removed from the hosted build. It asked for five-second clips and got three seconds, because seconds turned into frames on one model profile and back into seconds on another. It animated from the keeper when I had selected a different still, which is now an explicit source on the motion tool. The film fought back too. One motion model refused a crowd plate on content grounds, so refusals now come back with a reason and a fallback model. Another flashed a night scene into daylight. The registry now says which model drifts how, and the guidance says to switch models rather than re-prompt the same one. And on the last night the 454 MB volume filled up, so cuts failed inside ffmpeg with no space left, and the cut button did nothing. Disk usage now shows in the system panel and an admin purge keeps the newest cuts and clips. What we learned Tool descriptions are the user interface. A one-line description decides whether an agent uses a feature or walks past it, and a result that names the next step does more for the agent than a longer description would. Guidance has to be progressive: the note about photo-real drift belongs in the motion plan's result, not in the feature list an agent reads on arrival. And the thing I wanted from the start turned out to be true. Watching an agent work the studio taught me where my own features were, so if I want to grab the wheel and drive, I've been watching an expert this whole time, and learned from the best. What's next Character reference LoRAs for identity across shots to enable longer-running films, a motion budget that plans a whole act, and the studio driven end to end from a single paragraph of script. Better evaluation and guidance between available image, motion, and audio models. Superior visibility, implementation, and usage of the anime-specific animation tricks that let limited motion generation carry plenty of narrative moemntum. title: AutoFlow Web Agent
pitch: An intelligent web automation agent powered by WebMCP that bridges human intent and browser execution to automate complex, repetitive workflows effortlessly.
about_excerpt:
An intelligent web automation agent powered by WebMCP that bridges human intent and browser execution to automate complex, repetitive workflows effortlessly.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 2 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 As an automation and RPA lead, I see firsthand how much time corporate users and developers waste on repetitive web tasks, data entry, and navigating fragmented portals. With the introduction of OpenAI's WebMCP, we have a groundbreaking opportunity to shift from rigid scripts to fluid, agent-driven web automation. We wanted to build a bridge where human intent and browser execution meet seamlessly. 

 What it does 

 AutoFlow Web Agent is an intelligent browser assistant powered by WebMCP. It allows users and AI agents to interact, execute workflows, and perform automated actions directly within the web application. By registering native tools through WebMCP, the AI can understand page structures and execute tasks like automated data processing and form handling on command. 

 How we built it 

 We built the application using modern web technologies for a clean UI and integrated WebMCP via JavaScript APIs: 

 
 Registered tools using document.modelContext.registerTool to expose core browser automation functions. 
 Structured the execution layer to handle input schemas safely and reliably. 
 Deployed a lightweight, responsive interface optimized for AI agent integration. 
 

 Challenges we faced 

 The main challenge was designing a robust schema for the WebMCP tool registration to ensure the AI could reliably parse input parameters and trigger the correct execution functions without failing on edge cases. 

 What we learned 

 We discovered how powerful native browser-context tool use can be. It eliminates the need for heavy, brittle external browser extensions by letting the web page itself expose its capabilities directly to AI models.
