title: Agent Canvas: I Gave AI a Cursor in Excalidraw with WebMCP
pitch: Work with any compatible AI agent on the same live Excalidraw canvas. WebMCP lets people and agents read, draw, move, edit, and connect ideas together.
about_excerpt: Work with any compatible AI agent on the same live Excalidraw canvas. WebMCP lets people and agents read, draw, move, edit, and connect ideas together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I use Excalidraw almost every day to brainstorm, explain ideas, and design systems. When people work together in a Google Doc, everyone can see the same document and watch each other make changes. I wanted that same experience for a visual canvas, with an AI agent working beside me. Most AI diagram tools take a prompt and draw something for you. I wanted my agent to enter the same Excalidraw tab, understand the live canvas, and work with me without replacing the interface I already use. What it does Agent Canvas is the standard Excalidraw editor with native WebMCP control. It has no built-in AI model or separate prompt box. A compatible external agent discovers the tools provided by the page and uses the live canvas directly. The WebMCP tools let an agent: Set its visible identity Read the current canvas Read the human’s current selection Move its own cursor Add shapes, text, and frames Move, resize, rotate, restyle, or relabel elements Delete elements Connect elements with bound arrows The agent has a visible cursor with its own name and activity state. It moves to the area where the agent is working and shows actions such as Drawing, Updating, Connecting, and Checking. It leaves the canvas after the agent becomes inactive. Human edits still work normally. Locked elements are protected, every agent change uses Excalidraw history, and the standard Undo control can reverse an agent action. How we built it Agent Canvas uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and the official @excalidraw/excalidraw component. The page registers native WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Tool registration uses feature detection and AbortController cleanup. The selection tool appears only when the human has selected something. Every tool call reads the current live scene. Zod validates all inputs. Stable element IDs preserve object identity, labels, frames, and arrow bindings across edits. The agent cursor converts scene coordinates into screen coordinates, so it stays aligned when the human pans or zooms. Large drawings appear in visible stages, but the completed change remains one Excalidraw Undo action. The app also stores the canvas locally across reloads. Unit and Chromium browser tests cover native tool discovery, scene changes, bindings, locked elements, cursor movement, Undo, selection changes, and persistence. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was keeping the scene valid while both a human and an agent could change it. Excalidraw elements can contain bindings, dependent labels, locks, and history data. Moving or deleting one object can affect several other objects. Agent Canvas must preserve these relationships while keeping IDs stable and Undo reliable. WebMCP tools can also change when the human selection changes. We had to keep the main tools stable while adding and removing the conditional selection tool safely. The cursor was another challenge. A cursor that stays still does not feel like an agent is working. It now follows the objects being read or changed, shows progress during large edits, stays aligned during pan and zoom, and disappears when work stops. We also found that agents often stop after drawing the simplest recognizable outline. The canvas now gives agents a compact visual quality guide so that illustrations use purposeful layers and details while structural diagrams stay concise. Accomplishments that we're proud of An external agent can control the real Excalidraw editor through native WebMCP. The app does not depend on one model or one built-in agent. The human and agent work on the same live scene. The agent has visible identity, movement, progress, and activity. Direct changes preserve stable IDs, bindings, locks, local state, and Undo. The same deployed canvas can be used from compatible agent surfaces such as Codex, ChatGPT, and Aside. The project is open source and can run without a paid model API. What we learned WebMCP can turn a web page from a collection of visible controls into a structured workspace that an agent can understand and use. Good agent tools need more than basic create, update, and delete actions. They need fresh state, stable identities, clear constraints, compact results, and visible feedback for the human. The best experience is not an agent drawing somewhere else and returning an image. It is a human and an agent working together in the same tool. What's next for Agent Canvas Next, I want to support multiple simultaneous agent identities, shared real-time rooms, and richer workflows for large diagrams. The main goal will remain the same: keep the full Excalidraw experience while making the canvas a first-class workspace for people and agents. title: Cadence
pitch: An issue tracker where your agent is a real teammate: it triages, dedupes, and reprioritizes with tools that change live as you select issues, not a fixed list.
about_excerpt: An issue tracker where your agent is a real teammate: it triages, dedupes, and reprioritizes with tools that change live as you select issues, not a fixed list. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every judge on this panel works at a company that lives in an issue tracker. "Triage my backlog, dedupe these, split this ticket, reprioritize the sprint" is a request any engineer has typed into Slack at 5pm on a Friday. It's also genuinely tedious for a person and genuinely tractable for an agent, but only if the agent can act with real authority inside the tool instead of clicking through a UI it's guessing at from a screenshot. We also noticed a gap. The official showcase and the community demo list are full of storefronts, flight bookers, and games. Nothing engineering-tool shaped. Nothing where the agent has to hold a real permission boundary, share an undo stack with a human, or watch its own available capabilities change as the page changes under it. That felt like the actual hard part of WebMCP, the underexplored part, so we built toward it instead of around it. What it does Cadence is an issue tracker where an agent is a real teammate on the board, not a chatbot bolted onto the side of one. Ask it to triage an untriaged backlog, find and merge duplicate bug reports, split an oversized epic into sub-issues, or reprioritize a sprint, and it does real analysis against real board state through the same functions the UI itself calls. Here's the part that's actually WebMCP-specific, not just "an app with an AI feature": the registered tool set changes live with what's on screen. Select an issue and add_comment , split_issue , and link_issues register. Apply a filter or multi-select and bulk_update shows up. Switch to cycle view and summarize_cycle appears. None of that is expressible as a static, pre-declared tool list, because a server-side MCP server has no idea what a human currently has selected in their browser. It can't. Agents also carry real identity and real permission scoping. A workspace owner grants each agent a scope, read, triage, write, or full, and that grant filters which tools registerTool even offers before the agent ever sees them, live. Every agent edit lands on the same undo stack the human uses too. Cmd+Z undoes an agent's change exactly like it was your own, because both write through one shared reduce() function against one shared state. How we built it React, TypeScript, and Vite on the client. Cloudflare Workers plus a Durable Object (SQLite-backed, free-tier eligible) as the authoritative backend, syncing over the WebSocket Hibernation API so multiple humans and agents can work the same board live. webmcp-kit , a small library we published alongside this entry: defineTool / registerTools with full JSON-Schema-to-TS inference, and useScopedTools , a React hook that registers a tool set while a condition holds and cleanly unregisters when it stops. That hook is what makes Cadence's dynamic tool surface a one-liner instead of a pile of manual AbortController bookkeeping. Every mutation is a pure (state, actor, action) → state function in one reducer, shared by the client store, the Durable Object, and every WebMCP tool handler. There's exactly one place a board mutation is defined, which is also what makes the shared human/agent undo stack possible. Only one code path to undo. Seed data is deliberately messy on purpose: real duplicate bug reports worded three different ways, vague untriaged titles, missing estimates, so the higher-order tools have genuine work to do instead of a tidy board with nothing left to fix. A hash-chained audit log on the Durable Object records every mutation with actor attribution, queryable via get_activity . Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's in-app browser only supports a subset of the spec: imperative registration only, no declarative HTML tool attributes, and no cross-frame tool discovery even for same-origin iframes. We designed single-origin from day one because of this, and honestly it shaped the whole architecture more than anything else did. Then there was the embarrassing one. Our seed data computed Date.now() at Cloudflare Workers module scope instead of inside a request handler. Turns out Workers doesn't guarantee wall-clock time outside a request's I/O context, so every "recent" issue and cycle date came out silently wrong, offsets from epoch, not from actual "now". We only caught it by inspecting live state over a raw WebSocket and noticing the numbers just didn't add up. find_duplicates had a similar quiet failure. It used Jaccard similarity on tokenized title and body text with a default threshold that, on inspection, was too strict to ever catch our own deliberately seeded duplicate cluster. Real paraphrased duplicates scored around 0.23 to 0.28 against a 0.4 cutoff. Tuned it down and documented why right in the tool description, since it's a real limitation an agent calling the tool should actually know about. And demo-state entropy: a Durable Object's seed loads exactly once, ever, so every round of testing permanently mutated the same live board. Later testers kept hitting an already-triaged, already-deduped board with nothing left to demonstrate. Fixed it by giving every visitor their own isolated board, auto-fresh on first visit, plus a visible in-app reset button, instead of trying to guess when it's "safe" to reset something shared. Accomplishments we're proud of A genuinely dynamic tool surface, verifiable live in Chrome's Model Context Tool Inspector: select an issue and watch the registered tool count change in real time, no faith required. Per-agent permission scoping that changes what tools even exist for an agent, not just what it's allowed to call, enforced before registration ever happens. A free, LLM-free benchmark comparing tool calls against real Playwright-driven DOM interaction on the live app. Single actions cost about the same either way, but a 7-item bulk task runs roughly 3x faster over tool calls, because the DOM path re-pays a fixed per-item navigation cost that a tool call just doesn't. Real accessibility work, not just a claim. Full keyboard operability, and a code-level WCAG audit that actually found and fixed two real bugs, custom buttons not activating on Space, confirmation dialogs with no Escape-to-dismiss, instead of asserting AA compliance from a README and hoping nobody checks. What we learned The most interesting property of WebMCP isn't that it lets an agent call functions instead of scraping a page. It's that tool registration lives in the same runtime as the UI state, so the tool surface can be a live function of what's actually on screen, and permission boundaries can be enforced at the moment of registration rather than only at call time. Neither of those is something a server-side MCP server wrapping a REST API can do, no matter how well-designed that API is. What's next Publishing webmcp-kit to npm proper (it's a GitHub dependency right now), a full screen-reader session to go with the code-level accessibility audit, and pushing the duplicate-detection scoring past bag-of-words Jaccard now that we know exactly where its ceiling is. title: a11y-mcp
pitch: Speak Thai, fill any English web form by voice. a11y-mcp reads forms aloud, fills them from your speech, and self-corrects — powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Speak Thai, fill any English web form by voice. a11y-mcp reads forms aloud, fills them from your speech, and self-corrects — powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Two failures, stacked. First, AI agents "use" the web by guessing which pixel is a button — and guess wrong. Second, accessibility tooling is built for English. Our lead user is a Thai person in front of an English-only visa, university, or airline form: it's well-marked-up and completely unusable if you don't read English, and nobody translates it. Screen readers mangle code-switched Thai. The same tool helps blind, low-vision, motor-impaired, and elderly users — so we built it as a capability, not a special-needs product. What it does a11y-mcp turns any semantically sound web form into typed tools an AI agent can call (via WebMCP / document.modelContext), then lets a Thai speaker read, fill, correct, and submit that form entirely by voice. You press a microphone, speak Thai, and GPT-4o-mini calls the page's tools while the page answers with structured, typed feedback instead of a red border. It reads the form aloud in Thai, fills each field from your speech (keeping names in Latin script, translating free text to English, matching dropdown options), self-corrects from typed validation errors, asks you in Thai when it isn't sure, and never submits without an explicit confirmation. How we built it TypeScript + Vite + @crxjs/vite-plugin, with Zod defining the tool boundary once for both JSON Schema and runtime validation. It's an MV3 extension with two content scripts bridged over postMessage: a MAIN-world script that reaches document.modelContext, registers the four tools (describe_form, read_form, fill_form, submit_form), and runs the GPT brain; and an ISOLATED-world script that owns the microphone and calls Paxa. GPT-4o-mini function-calling turns Thai speech into tool calls; Paxa Labs handles Thai text-to-speech (voice "yoyo") and translation; the Web Speech API handles voice input. Both APIs allow direct browser calls, so there's no proxy in the demo path. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP spec is unstable. The API had movedext to document.modelContext (deprecated in Chrome 150), so nothing worked at first. We instrumented the live Chrome 152 surface and dct: registerTool is async, there is no unregisterTool, duplicate tool names throw, getTools() returns inputSchema as a JSON strinarguments as a JSON string — none of which the docs said. We rebuilt against that. We also had to get the failed-vs-needs_human distinction righit, and work around audio autoplay needing a user gesture. Accomplishments that we're proud of The failed vs needs_human split: "failed" is reactive (the page rejected a value, so the agent retries), while "needs_human" is prensure, so nothing is filled and the agent must ask). A confidently-wrong value on a visa form is the failure mode that actually hurts peoplet. Error speech comes from stable Thai templates keyed by an enum — never model prose. And the read-back: a blind Thai user can finally percejust fill it. We verified the whole loop live in Chrome — one Thai sentence filled eight fields, translated the free text, matched a dropdown, rrected a bad ID number, and correctly left an unlabeled field empty. What we learned Don't trust the docs for an unstable API — instrument the runtime; it's the only truth. WebMCP's real value is constraint feedbnt can act on, versus a red border a human has to interpret. And accessibility and agent-usability turn out to be the same problem — a well-markeh. The Thai angle isn't a bolt-on; it's exactly the audience Western accessibility tooling has never served. What's next for a11y-mcp It works on sites with reasonable semantics, aells the truth when a site's markup is bad rather than filling wrong values silently. Next: move the API keys server-side and ship it publicly oncehind the Chrome flag. Deliberately out of scope for now — cross-page memory (a privacy design problem) and custom non- widgets. title: Looop
pitch: Looop brings teams together to plan, collaborate and resolve issues in one place, with WebMCP-enabled AI agents that can manage events for you.
about_excerpt:
Looop brings teams together to plan, collaborate and resolve issues in one place, with WebMCP-enabled AI agents that can manage events for you.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP allowing agent to summarise event 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Looop Event Dashboard 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP allowing agent to summarise event 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Looop Event Dashboard 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP allowing agent to summarise event 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Group chats are often the main go-to for communication when planning for events and projects. However, the actual plan and flow of logistics often end up buried under jokes, photographs, and various digresses from conversation. As such, this results in confusion and frustration with messages like "Did anyone see my message about xxx?" or "At what stage are we for this plan?" or "Sorry, what are my responsibilities for today again?". 
This is where WebMCP fits the use case well. By allowing AI agents to interact directly with structured web interfaces, WebMCP can help agents read the latest plan, understand assigned responsibilities, and take actions on the board without relying on noisy chat history. This creates a shared and structured source of truth that both people and AI agents can easily understand and act upon. 

 What it does 

 Looop gives every event (wedding party, offsite, household chore chart) one shared board, which includes tasks grouped by urgency, flagged issues for attention, day-by-day timeline and a computed event health score. The core actions on the board such as creating and editing tasks, flagging and resolving issues, are exposed as MCP tools. Users can simply ask their agent "What tasks are still open on the wedding board?" or "Add an urgent task for the caterer" or "Flag that the venue has not confirmed headcount". The agent can even act as a collaborator, proposing concrete next steps for a stuck task or open issue , as well as starter tasks for event based on its title and description , and providing a concise summary of the event history . 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is hosted on Vercel and backend on Render. The frontend of Looop was built with React and Typescript on the frontend, Tailwind for UI styling. It has a Go backend on Chi with MongoDB for storage. The WebMCP layer lives on the frontend with document.modelContext.registerTool() covering full CRUD on events, its tasks and issues plus status actions like complete_task and resolve_issue and multiple tools that let the agent write suggestions and catch the user up on the event progress. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The gap between UI implementation and connecting with the rest of the pipeline also turned out to be a challenge. The frontend was first built against mock data which expedited the design process, but the process of wiring every page to the backend surfaced a long list of real bugs. These included route prefixes that did not match between frontend and backend, and a field name mismatch that silently dropped task notes. This also affected the WebMCP testing in ChatGPT's in-app browser, since the underlying API calls had to work reliably before I could register tools that depended on them during execution. I also learnt to budget more time for WebMCP edge cases, such as incomplete requests and ambiguous inputs, rather than focusing only on the ideal tool flow. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting the full loop working with an agent in ChatGPT's browser calling a real tool, hitting the hosted Go backend and writing to the database, and having that change show up on the board was the largest accomplishment. I was happy for not just settling for CRUD as the whole product and registering tools such as get_event_summary computing a genuine health score instead of just listing rows, and suggest_task_completion/suggest_issue_resolution letting the agent contribute reasoning to the board, not just data entry was also one of the main goals achieved. 

 What we learned 

 The main concept here was implementing MCP hands-on to create a functional project and learning the concept from scratch. One of the biggest concepts learnt was the difference between MCP and WebMCP, particularly that WebMCP tools are registered directly on the frontend through the browser rather than being exposed from a backend MCP server. 
A lot of learning also came from testing the tools repeatedly and handling edge cases. I had to check that every tool was callable, that fields and routes matched correctly across the codebases and that incomplete requests were handled gracefully. For example, creating a task without an assignee meant deciding how the tool should respond or whether it could fall back to the current user, while ambiguous member names required additional resolution. Thus, I learnt that thorough testing is essential when building agent-facing tools. 

 What's next for Looop 

 In the near future, Looop could move towards real authentication and user accounts , replacing the current localStorage-based placeholder identity with secure accounts that persist across devices. We also see potential in richer integrations , connecting Looop with calendars and other tools that people already use for event planning, making it easier to keep everything in sync without having to switch between different platforms. Based on user feedback, more WebMCP tools could be registered on Looop to efficiently serve real-world purposes for collaborative event planning.

title: AGMCP
pitch: The USDA hardiness zone map, rebuilt as a shared tool for gardeners and their agents.
about_excerpt: The USDA hardiness zone map, rebuilt as a shared tool for gardeners and their agents. Like Comment Story Updates agmcp working inside ChatGPT in-app browser Inspiration I love gardening, and coding with AI agents. I've had conversations with ChatGPT and Gemini that start in a similar way: "what can I grow in my city?" (I know my hardiness zone because I've searched for it more than once) and the agent guesses from memory. The USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map is the standard reference for what can survive where, but it lives in PDFs, a clunky ZIP lookup, and 300-dpi PNGs. Nothing an agent can call. WebMCP made the fix obvious: put the authoritative data on a page, register it as tools, and let the human and the agent work from the same map. I also wanted a primitive, not just a demo. AGMCP is the first building block for a bigger garden-planning app I'm building next, where zones combine with hyper-local weather and sun position and regional, heirloom seeds. What it does AGMCP is the 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map for all 40,502 US ZIP codes (50 states, DC, Puerto Rico), exposed three ways: For people : enter a ZIP (or use your location), see your half-zone with its temperature band and frost windows, browse 54 vegetables, herbs, peppers, and fruit rated great / stretch / not recommended for that zone, and build a garden plan with a planting calendar. For agents on the page : 18 WebMCP tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() , plus a declarative form tool. Read tools like lookup_hardiness_zone , compare_locations , find_zone_by_coordinates , list_plants , get_planting_calendar . Write tools like set_location , add_to_garden_plan , and filter_plants change what the human sees. clear_garden_plan opens a confirmation dialog the user must accept; use_my_location requires the browser's geolocation permission. For backend agents and other apps : a JSON API ( /api/v1/zone/{zip} , /compare , /nearest , /plants , /calendar ), an OpenAPI spec, and llms.txt . Every tool call streams into an on-page Agent activity panel, so the human always sees what the agent did. How we built it Data pipeline : PRISM Group's 2023 ZIP-to-zone CSVs (US, AK, HI, PR) plus US Census ZCTA centroids. A build script packs 100,000 possible ZIPs into a single 100 KB string (one character per ZIP indexing 26 half-zones) so lookups are O(1) in the browser and in the Worker. Coordinates load lazily for nearest-ZIP queries. Frontend : Vite + vanilla TypeScript, no framework. Modern CSS (oklch, light-dark() , container queries, view transitions), native <dialog> for human-in-the-loop confirmation. WebMCP : one tool module with JSON Schema inputs, readOnlyHint annotations, and a wrapper that logs each call and converts app errors into MCP-style isError results instead of throwing. Feature-detects document.modelContext with a navigator.modelContext fallback for Chrome < 150. The UI buttons and the tools call the exact same functions, so there is no agent-only code path. Backend : a Cloudflare Worker serves static assets and the JSON API from the same bundled data, deployed with Workers Builds on every push to main . Tooling : built with Cursor cloud agents; end-to-end tested in headless Chrome via navigator.modelContextTesting . Challenges we ran into Spec drift. Chrome 148 exposes WebMCP on navigator.modelContext ; the spec and newer Chrome use document.modelContext . ChatGPT's browser supports only imperative tools on the top-level page, so the declarative form is progressive enhancement. Data size. Naive JSON for 40k ZIPs was megabytes; the 1-char-per-ZIP encoding brought core data to ~15 KB gzipped. Honesty about estimates. Frost dates and plant ranges are horticultural rules of thumb, not USDA data, so every tool output and UI label says so. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real dataset as a real primitive: exact zones for every ZIP, callable by agents in-page and over HTTP. Genuine human-agent collaboration: shared state flows both ways, write tools change the visible page, and destructive actions wait for a click. Zero secrets, zero tracking, zero API keys. Fully open source, deployable with one command. Shipped, deployed, and passing an automated WebMCP end-to-end test on the live URL before the deadline. What we learned WebMCP tools are best when they reuse the app's own actions. If a button and a tool call the same function, the agent and the human are always in sync. Tool descriptions are the UX for agents. Naming, enums, and "call get_current_context first" hints did more for reliability than any code. Return enough for the agent to verify and warn: add_to_garden_plan returns the plant's fit so the agent can say "habanero is a stretch in 6a." Modern web platform features (dialog, view transitions, light-dark() ) covered everything a framework would have, with a 37 KB bundle. What's next for AGMCP Pair it with hyper-local weather and sun-position tools to build the 3D garden planner it was designed to power: bed layout, succession planting, and season-aware recommendations for your exact zone. 2012 vs 2023 zone shift comparison ("did my zone change?"). Richer plant data with varieties, companion planting, and community-contributed regional notes. This may involve parsing PDFs from Universities across the USA that have regional and local information. For example, UF has research papers dedicated to the Florida agriculture. I'll probably use a local model to running one a mini pc to keep costs low. Publish the tool set as a reusable module so any gardening site can register the same WebMCP tools. title: Physical AI WebMCP Command Center
pitch: An Agent-Native Control Layer for Autonomous Warehouses.
about_excerpt: An Agent-Native Control Layer for Autonomous Warehouses. Like Comment Story Updates AGV-03 completes the approved mission after safely stopping at N07 and replanning around the blocked aisle. Live WebMCP trace showing every tool call, result, run ID, timestamp, and measured latency. Production Hero E2E verified: 7/7 WebMCP tools, ordered flow PASS, mission completed, and final metrics captured. Inspiration Warehouse software is usually designed for humans clicking through multiple screens. Browser agents can interact with those interfaces, but they must infer operational meaning from pixels and DOM structure. We wanted the web itself to expose a safe, typed contract shared by humans, AI agents, and autonomous machines. What it does Physical AI WebMCP Command Center is an agent-native warehouse control layer built around a deterministic digital twin. A user gives one intent: move pallet P-104 from INBOUND-01 to RACK-A12. Through seven WebMCP tools, the Agent observes warehouse state, inspects the pallet, plans a safe route, selects AGV-03, and creates an approval-gated proposal. A human must approve before physical movement begins. During execution, AGV-03 encounters a blocked aisle at N07, stops safely, replans through N08 and N11, and completes the mission. The safety engine validates destination, occupancy, vehicle availability, battery reserve, route safety, approval state, communication heartbeat (SAFE-11), and traffic reservations (SAFE-12). Every WebMCP call, result, and measured latency is displayed in the interface. The observable workflow is: OBSERVE → PLAN → VALIDATE → APPROVE → EXECUTE → RECOVER How we built it The application uses React and TypeScript and runs on a public HTTPS deployment. A shared deterministic state engine powers both the manual UI and WebMCP interface. Dijkstra routing produces the 41.6 m primary route and the 49.4 m recovery route. The simulator controls AGV movement, fault injection, safe stopping, replanning, resuming, and mission completion. Exactly seven WebMCP tools are registered with strict JSON Schema, read/write annotations, cancellation support, and production discovery. Runtime instrumentation measures planner stages, tool latency, route length, approvals, replans, mission success, and Human vs Agent performance. Challenges The main challenge was preserving a trustworthy boundary between AI intent and physical execution. Planning must never start a mission. Creating a proposal must never imply approval. An unapproved mission cannot move. A route blockage must stop the AGV before replanning. Communication timeouts and conflicting traffic reservations must deterministically prevent unsafe movement. We also ensured that all displayed traces and metrics come from real runtime events rather than scripted presentation data. Accomplishments Seven discoverable WebMCP tools with strict schemas Human approval that cannot be bypassed by an Agent tool Deterministic Dijkstra planning and blockage recovery SAFE-11 communication-timeout enforcement SAFE-12 traffic-reservation conflict prevention Visible WebMCP and planning traces with real latency Complete reset of missions, proposals, traces, metrics, timers, and faults Human vs Agent benchmark using the same operational task Public HTTPS deployment with a verified 7/7 Agent E2E run No account, API key, database, broker, or physical hardware required What we learned Agent-native UX is not about removing human control. The strongest design separates responsibilities: The model expresses intent. WebMCP defines how it asks. Deterministic software decides what is allowed. A human authorizes high-impact action. The physical system executes. What's next The same WebMCP interface could be connected to real fleet-management systems. Approved missions could be translated into VDA5050, MQTT, PLC, or vendor API commands while retaining deterministic safety policies, audit traces, and human authorization. title: AI-slop-check
pitch: Catching AI slop requires zero AI. Twelve rules, runs in your browser, and your agent can swipe through the findings with you
about_excerpt: Catching AI slop requires zero AI. Twelve rules, runs in your browser, and your agent can swipe through the findings with you Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I vibe-code a lot. And a lot of what comes back is slop. Not broken code. Code that looks finished. A catch block that swallows the error so nothing ever turns red. A comment that says // In a real implementation, validate this sitting exactly where the validation should be. A default that no caller has ever overridden, because the model invented a knob nobody asked for. It runs. It passes. It is not done. My usual fix for this was to paste the file into a better model and ask it to look. Which works, and costs tokens, and takes a minute, and I have done it for mistakes that a grep would have caught. That felt stupid enough to build around. So slop-check has no AI in it. Twelve rules, plain text matching, one pass over the source. It scans a repo, a diff, or a pull request and hands back a 0-100 score, a grade, and every hit quoted as file:line . Instant, offline, deterministic, and the same input gives the same output forever. The scoring is deliberately boring so you can argue with it: $$\text{score} = \min\left(100,\ \frac{100 \times \sum_{r} w_r \cdot d(h_r)}{1000 \times \max(L_{\text{eff}},\ 420)}\right)$$ where $w_r$ is a rule's weight, $h_r$ its hit count, $d$ a damping function so one repeated house idiom cannot fail a whole codebase, and $L_{\text{eff}}$ the effective scanned lines. --explain prints that arithmetic per run. No black box to trust. why it is a card game A wall of 200 findings is a linter, and linters get disabled. So findings come back as a deck you swipe. Left says the finding is fair. Right says it is a false positive, and disputed cards come back out as slop-disable directives you paste into your code, which the CLI and the GitHub Action then honour on every later run. Your disagreement becomes configuration instead of a shrug. There is also a confession mode on the share card. It stamps YES, I WROTE THIS WITH AI on the image. Everyone is doing it. The pretending is the annoying part. It has already earned its keep on repos much larger than mine. Pointed at openai/openai-python (1,542 files) it surfaced real findings, and the same run surfaced six defects in my own rules. what I actually learned A scanner's most important property is staying quiet. I spent most of my time not adding rules. I read every finding on a large, well-written repo by hand and asked whether a maintainer would act on it. 61 findings became 12. None of the six bugs I found this way would have surfaced from unit tests, because every rule passed its own fixtures. Some of them were embarrassing in a useful way. dead-defaults split parameter lists on bare commas, so a comma inside dict[str, Any] invented parameters that did not exist. happy-path-only matched \bopen( , which caught tarfile.open() and wave.open() and read every with open(...) as unhandled I/O, when a context manager is the failure path. duplicate-helper flagged every f / async_f pair in an async library at 95% similarity, which is a Python constraint and not a mistake. swallowed-error flagged __del__ , where suppressing exceptions is correct and the tool was asking for the code to be made worse. And the one I liked most: every rule read prose as code. A rule that matches source text will happily match a sentence describing the pattern it looks for. This repo scored itself a grade worse because two of its own explanatory comments contain .catch(() => {}) . Comments are masked before matching now. Each of those is pinned in test/false-positives.test.ts , which exists for one job: keep fixed rules fixed. Then WebMCP. I liked it immediately, and for a reason that is more about how I work than about the spec. I am usually looking at a page and I want my agent looking at the same page. Not a copy of it, not a scrape of it, the actual thing in front of me. And half the time I am lazy and would rather ask than click, but I still want to watch it happen. Every other integration shape makes you pick one: either the agent works somewhere you cannot see, or you do it yourself. WebMCP is the first one where the agent presses the buttons you can see it pressing. how I built it One TypeScript source ships three things: the slop-check CLI, a GitHub Action, and the web app. The rules run in a Web Worker in the tab, so a scan never uploads your code anywhere. The WebMCP layer is web/webmcp.ts . Seven tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() : list_rules , explain_rule , scan_repository , scan_diff , list_findings , judge_finding , export_suppressions . The rule I gave myself was that the tool layer owns no state at all. It gets a small handle assembled in main.ts out of the exact functions the click handlers call. There is no second code path, so there is no way for an agent to reach a result the page is not showing, or to record a verdict the deck does not reflect. A tool-driven scan fills the visible input, flips the visible tab, and runs the same progress panel a click does. Three tools are meaningless before a scan exists, so they are not registered until one lands and are unregistered when results clear, using the AbortSignal that registerTool takes as its second argument. The page emits its own state event, the WebMCP layer syncs registration to it, the browser fires toolchange . An agent reading the tool list is reading the page's real state rather than a manifest. Cancellation is threaded all the way down. execute receives a signal , it reaches githubFiles and every fetch under it, composed with the existing per-request timeout through AbortSignal.any . challenges False positives, by a distance. Everything above about the openai-python pass was the hard part of the project, not a footnote to it. It is still not fully solved. hardcoded-config is my noisiest rule and I will tell you exactly how: it flags process.env.SITE_URL || 'https://example.com' , which is a literal inside an environment-variable fallback, which is the configuration it is demanding. It flags a project's own canonical URL, which belongs in a sitemap. swallowed-error still cannot tell recovery from silence, so .catch(() => null) whose value gets branched on reads the same to it as a bare .catch(() => {}) . Both get reported. One is a fallback and one is a shrug. I also know the rule set came from my intuition rather than data. There is empirical work on LLM code smells finding magic numbers and missing documentation most over-represented, which barely overlaps with my twelve rules, and their method is better than mine: compare a codebase's smell profile against a human-written baseline instead of scoring it alone. Deciding how far the agent gets to reach. My first version let judge_finding walk the whole deck and decide everything. Technically better tool use. Completely wrong product. An agent that judges every card has replaced the user, and the verdict was the only part I wanted a human doing. The shipped version can move one card the user can see, one verdict at a time, and the tool's own description tells the agent to ask first. Judging out of order. The deck is a stack, but an agent asked about one specific rule wants that card now, not in fourteen swipes. Re-rendering the stack broke the animation on cards already leaving, so swapToFront swaps the rendered contents of two positions instead. The deck's order was a sampling artefact, never meaning, so nothing is lost. what it does not claim slop-check cannot tell you code was written by an AI and does not try. There is no reliable authorship signal in source text and anything claiming otherwise is guessing. It measures whether code carries the patterns that AI-assisted code carries more often. A human can write all of them, and I regularly do. Read the score as a description of the code, never as an accusation about who wrote it. title: Privacy Nutrition Label
pitch: A WebMCP-native checkout that helps people and agents understand why data is requested, choose the minimum necessary data, and receive a privacy receipt.\n\n
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-native checkout that helps people and agents understand why data is requested, choose the minimum necessary data, and receive a privacy receipt.


 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The WebMCP write tool completes checkout only after explicit confirmation and keeps personal form values inside the page. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The human-facing Privacy Nutrition Label explains what checkout data is required, what is optional, and why—before the user acts. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The read-only WebMCP tool gives the agent structured checkout privacy facts without returning personal form values. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The WebMCP write tool completes checkout only after explicit confirmation and keeps personal form values inside the page. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The human-facing Privacy Nutrition Label explains what checkout data is required, what is optional, and why—before the user acts. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The read-only WebMCP tool gives the agent structured checkout privacy facts without returning personal form values. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The WebMCP write tool completes checkout only after explicit confirmation and keeps personal form values inside the page. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 I kept coming back to a simple problem that privacy policies contain a lot of information, but they rarely help with the decision someone is making right now. 

 At checkout, a website might ask for a name, email, address, phone number, account creation and marketing consent all on the same page. It is often unclear which of these are genuinely required, why they are being requested, and what can be left out. A privacy policy may contain the answer somewhere, but most people are not going to stop halfway through checkout and search through a long legal document. 

 I was also thinking about what happens after checkout. If a service later suffers a data breach, information it never collected cannot be exposed. Helping someone share less at the beginning can therefore reduce the amount of personal data placed at risk. 

 Privacy labels make data practices easier to see, but I wanted to go one step further. I did not want an AI agent to generate another summary by scraping a policy or guessing from the interface. I wanted the website itself to explain what the current action requires in a structured form that both a person and an agent can understand. 

 That became the idea behind Privacy Nutrition Label which is a small, action-specific privacy contract that appears when the decision actually matters. 

 What it does 

 I built the project around Relay, a fictional electronics retailer with a realistic guest checkout flow. Before completing an order, the customer can open a Privacy Nutrition Label showing: 

 
 which data groups are required 
 which data groups are optional 
 why each group is requested 
 who receives it 
 what the minimum-data choice is 
 whether advertising tracking is involved 
 

 The same declaration is available to an AI agent through WebMCP. The agent can inspect the checkout, explain the required and optional information, and recommend the minimum-disclosure path: continue as a guest, leave out the phone number and decline marketing. 

 I also wanted the final decision to remain with the person. Inspecting the label does not place the order. The state-changing checkout tool can only run after the person explicitly confirms their choices. 

 Once the demo order is completed, Relay produces a Privacy Receipt showing which data categories were used and which optional categories were left out. 

 The Orbit Home Companion adds a second privacy layer to the demo. Its device declaration explains that it has no camera, processes voice on-device by default and makes cloud features opt-in. This is kept separate from the checkout label so that product privacy and transaction privacy are not mixed together. 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would have to inspect form labels, scrape a privacy policy or infer how the checkout behaves. That might work sometimes, but it also leaves room for outdated information and incorrect assumptions. 

 WebMCP allows Relay to declare its own checkout behaviour directly. The agent receives a predictable structure containing data categories, purposes, required and optional status, sharing information and a minimum-data recommendation. 

 This matters because the agent is not only reading information. After explaining the privacy choices and receiving confirmation, it can help the person act on those choices through a separate write tool. 

 I did not want WebMCP to be an extra feature added to an otherwise normal checkout. It is what makes the privacy information understandable and actionable at the moment of decision. 

 How it creates a better user experience 

 People should not need privacy or legal expertise just to understand a checkout form. 

 The human-facing label is designed to be scanned quickly. Someone can see that three data groups are required, two are optional and no advertising tracking is involved before deciding what to share. 

 If they are using an agent, the agent can inspect the same declaration and explain it in plain language. This avoids having one explanation in the interface and a different interpretation from the agent. 

 The person still stays in control. The agent can inspect and recommend, but it cannot complete the checkout until the person confirms the exact choices. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 In this flow, the website provides the facts, the agent helps interpret them and the person makes the final decision. 

 The agent can compare the required and optional categories, explain why they are requested and recommend the minimum-data option. The person can accept or change that recommendation. Only then can the agent complete the local demo checkout using the confirmed choices. 

 Without this structure, the person would need to inspect the form and policy themselves while trusting the agent to infer what the website means. With WebMCP, the website, agent and person are working from the same declared information. 

 How I built it 

 I built Privacy Nutrition Label as a solo project using React, TypeScript and Vite, then deployed it as a static site on Netlify. 

 The page registers two tools through document.modelContext : 

 
 inspect_checkout_privacy is read-only. It opens the visible Privacy Nutrition Label and returns the declared categories, purposes, sharing information, required or optional status and minimum-data recommendation 
 complete_private_checkout is state-changing. It accepts privacy choices rather than personal form values, requires confirmed to be explicitly true, validates the completed form inside the page and returns a category-level receipt 
 

 I deliberately kept personal values out of the tool interface. A name, email, address or phone number stays inside the webpage. The agent receives the privacy declaration and the person’s choices, but not those values. 

 The demo has no backend, database, authentication service, analytics, payment provider or external font request. Refreshing the page clears the order. The human checkout also remains usable when WebMCP is unavailable. 

 I added eleven automated tests covering privacy defaults, malformed inputs, missing fields, confirmation requirements, repeated execution and category-only outputs. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest design decision was not the interface. It was deciding what the agent should not receive. 

 Passing the whole checkout form to the tool would have been easier, but it would have contradicted the data-minimisation idea behind the project. The agent needs to understand the privacy contract and the person’s choices; it does not need their identity or delivery details in its response. 

 I therefore separated the flow into clear boundaries: 

 
 the webpage keeps the personal form values 
 the agent receives the privacy declaration and confirmed choices 
 the write tool performs the local action only after explicit confirmation 
 

 Another challenge was deciding how much information belonged in the label. I wanted it to include purpose, optionality and sharing without turning it into another document that people would ignore. 

 Keeping product privacy separate from checkout privacy was also important. Orbit’s camera and voice-processing declaration belongs to the device, while the Privacy Nutrition Label describes the current purchase. 

 Accomplishments that I am proud of 

 
 WebMCP changes the interaction instead of simply duplicating a webpage button 
 The read tool opens the same

title: SeatCraft
pitch: Seating charts humans and AI agents solve together: the host drags guests and locks seats while the agent solves the constraint puzzle through 15 WebMCP tools — on the same live board.
about_excerpt: Seating charts humans and AI agents solve together: the host drags guests and locks seats while the agent solves the constraint puzzle through 15 WebMCP tools — on the same live board. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Seating charts are a two-player game we've been forcing one player to play alone. The host holds the social knowledge — who divorced whom, which cousins feud, who must flank the grandmother. But turning that knowledge into a valid arrangement of 24 people across 5 tables is a constraint-satisfaction puzzle that shifts every time an RSVP lands. That second half is exactly what agents are good at and humans hate. WebMCP is the missing contract that lets each player play their half on the same board . What it does SeatCraft is an event seating planner with two first-class users: The host drags guests between tables, locks non-negotiable seats (the couple sits at the head table, period), and states messy truths as rules: Aunt Carol and Uncle Jim — apart (divorced 2019) . The agent works through 15 WebMCP tools registered on navigator.modelContext : guest/table CRUD, seating moves, a three-type constraint system ( together / apart / at_table , each with a human-readable note), a violations reporter, and auto_seat — a solver that honors every rule and never moves a host-locked guest . The collaboration is bidirectional and honest: every agent tool call streams into an on-page Agent Activity feed so the host always sees what the agent did, and every mutating tool returns the resulting violation list so the agent always knows the consequence of its action. When the agent tries to move a locked seat, it's refused with a message telling it to ask the host. The human always wins. How we built it Deliberately zero-dependency: vanilla JS, no build step, no backend — a static page hosted on GitHub Pages. Four modules share one state store (localStorage-persisted, pub/sub): the human UI (drag/drop, locks, rule chips, violation badges), the WebMCP tool surface, a constraint solver (union-find clustering of must-sit-together pairs, group-affinity greedy fill, pairwise-swap repair), and the shared model. A human drag and an agent seat_guest call are literally the same mutation with a different source tag — that's the whole thesis in one line of code. Tools register on the browser's native navigator.modelContext when present (Chrome's WebMCP for testing flag today); otherwise a small spec-shaped shim provides the identical API, so extension bridges and the built-in Agent Console drive the same surface native browsers will. Challenges we ran into Making the solver's output socially plausible, not just constraint-valid — early versions satisfied every rule while exiling one work friend to the family table. Fixes: seat bonded clusters first, fill remaining guests in group-sorted order with a same-group affinity score, then swap-repair. Also: tool ergonomics for conversational agents — every guest/table parameter accepts ids or names (including unique partial names), because an agent relaying "keep Priya away from Dev" shouldn't juggle opaque ids. What we learned The interesting design surface of WebMCP isn't exposing actions — it's exposing boundaries . The lock system (agent-proof seats) and violations-in-every-response did more for human-agent collaboration than any additional tool would have. Agent-readable refusals are a feature, not an error. What's next for SeatCraft Per-seat placement with adjacency rules, multi-event templates, exportable place cards, and native testing as Chrome's flag rolls toward stable in Q4 2026. title: Sonicviz
pitch: Hands-free guitar and harmonica practice. An agent sets up the lesson, you play it. Built with WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Hands-free guitar and harmonica practice. An agent sets up the lesson, you play it. Built with WebMCP. Like 2 Comment Story Updates The WebMCP Inspector completing the example agent request. The WebMCP Inspector generating a new lesson from a voice request. Harmonica explorer with chord and scale overlays on a 10-hole diatonic harp. Practice view with the guitar playing the guide melody. Fretboard explorer with chord and scale overlays and interval labels. Practice view with the harmonica playing the guide melody. Inspiration I play guitar and harmonica (see https://komuso.info/ ). A lot of practice time is not spent playing, it's spent fiddling with practice tools and setup. Finding an exercise, working out which holes and frets play the same melody, slowing a loop down. These are common music practice issues that waste time and effort that could be better spent playing and learning. AI tools are good at making a finished song (see my side project https://www.crisiskaraoke.com/ ) but I did not need a song. I needed short lessons I could play to learn scales and chords in different tunings on both instruments, that I could rapidly configure with a couple of clicks or ultimately hands-free by voice. What it does SonicViz is a practice app with three connected views: Fretboard, Harmonica, and Practice. Fretboard and Harmonica views allow you to quickly build mental models of scales and chords in different tunings and keys on both instruments. These mental models are critical to developing creative improvisation skills that help you break out of pattern playing ruts. Practice keeps one chord progression and one timed melody. The guitar positions, the harmonica holes, the score, and the TAB are all views of that same melody. Change the instrument and the notes stay put. Only the way your hands (or lips in the harmonica's case) reach them changes. WebMCP makes it hands-free. SonicViz exposes 12 typed tools, so a browser agent reads and writes actual musical state instead of guessing at the screen. I say "loop bars 1 through 2 at 40 BPM and play." The agent makes the call, and I play along with the harmonica still in my hand. Playback only starts after I allow it, and only for that page session. You can use WebMCP to interact with all three tabs. The video uses typed commands for clarity; the same requests work by voice through a custom WebMCP extension with a mic lock for hands-free practice. How we built it From scratch, starting August 27, with just an idea for a new type of app. I leveraged my experience as developer of https://harpninja.com/ to give me a clear direction to address the problem with a workable solution with WebMCP being the key to unlock it. Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework, no backend. KISS to see if the idea works. AI assistants did most of the coding, mainly GPT-5.6 Sol plus a few other models, while I made the musical and product calls. The core is a pure function. A seed, a key, and a style produce the same lesson every time, and everything else is derived from that. Challenges we ran into Taming the agent was the hard part. A model will reorder tool calls, drop an argument, or answer from memory instead of reading the current state. Three bugs shipped and only showed up when I tested with a real model and complex mixed commands. A loop command toggled off on the second call. A mute command could not tell which direction I meant. An agent answered "already set" without checking the app. Each fix went into the tool contract. Accomplishments that we're proud of The boundary is deterministic even though the agent is not. The same seed gives the same lesson every time. Consent is real. Agent playback waits for an explicit page-session permission. One melody reprojects across guitar, harmonica, score, and TAB without changing. Twenty-six browser checks pass, plus a long manual QA run. What we learned Determinism is something you have to re-establish every time you use the tools. The schema limits what the model can pass, but it doesn’t dictate the model’s decisions. That’s why discipline has to exist at the tool boundary. Idempotency, a single source of truth, and thorough testing with real models, both automated and manual, are essential. I’ve shared more about these lessons in a blog post: https://sonicviz.com/2026/09/03/webmcp-deterministic-hybrid-app-design/ What's next for Sonicviz Add more instruments, with lesson briefs that guide and coach. Include per-chord scale options so pros can practice the way they improvise. Consider simple performance recognition, letting the app detect if you hit the note using real-time pitch feedback. AI should enhance the process, not replace it. Nothing exercises the mind, body, and spirit quite like playing music on a real instrument. The tactile connection—the kinesthetic, energetic back-and-forth with the instrument—is a vital part of the experience and the process. It’s all about lips, fingertips, and ears. The hands memorize the shapes, the ears absorb the sounds, and the patience to loop a bar until it’s perfect becomes the skill that truly counts. The tool exists to support that process. The goal remains the same: the output isn't the song; it's a person who can play it. title: Frontmend
pitch: Audit the site. Give your coding agent evidence it can act on.
about_excerpt: Audit the site. Give your coding agent evidence it can act on. Like Comment Story Updates Frontmend turns a public website audit into a clear recommendation list for people and an evidence-rich brief a coding agent can act on through WebMCP. The problem Frontend audit tools are good at measuring websites, and coding agents are good at working inside repositories. The handoff between them is the weak point. Most audit results are presented as score dashboards or lengthy reports designed for people. When a coding agent tries to use them, it has to scrape the page, interpret screenshots, follow buttons and reconstruct important context that may have been lost along the way. A copied recommendation such as “improve accessibility” is not enough. The agent needs the original audit rule, affected route, viewport, observed target, supporting evidence and a clear definition of what passing looks like. We initially explored putting the entire repair lifecycle inside Frontmend. That created more approval states, checklists and deployment theatre than useful frontend work. Coding agents already know how to inspect repositories, edit files and run tests within the user’s existing permissions. Frontmend should give them better evidence, not try to replace them. What Frontmend does A person enters one public URL. Frontmend runs an asynchronous PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse audit alongside bounded live-document analysis. It then turns the retained evidence into a short, prioritised recommendation list. Each recommendation brings together: What Frontmend observed and why it matters Severity, category, exact audit rule ID and provider provenance Affected routes and viewports, plus selectors when available The number of measured occurrences A concise recommended change Repository search hints derived only from public evidence Concrete acceptance criteria A clear explanation of what Frontmend did not inspect or prove The human result is designed to read like a useful editorial report rather than another technical dashboard. Why WebMCP fits Without WebMCP, a coding agent sees the same interface as a person. It has to inspect the DOM, identify controls, infer the application’s state and scrape result text from a page that was never designed for machine use. With WebMCP, Frontmend can describe its capabilities directly. A compatible agent can discover the tools available in the current page state, start the same audit as the human interface, check truthful progress, read the completed recommendations and inspect the evidence chain behind an individual finding. The result includes a bounded codingAgentBrief containing the structured context needed to continue real work: Ranked recommendations Retained observations Exact audit rule IDs and provider provenance Routes and measured viewports Selectors and affected targets when available Repository search hints Acceptance criteria Explicit evidence and authority boundaries The agent no longer has to reverse-engineer the interface or copy an incomplete report into its context. WebMCP does not perform the audit itself. Frontmend’s background audit service does that work. WebMCP provides a reliable, typed interface between the webpage and the agent. What people and agents can do together A person can ask: Audit my deployed frontend with Frontmend, investigate the strongest findings in this repository and implement the fixes that are supported by the evidence. The coding agent can then: Open Frontmend and discover its available WebMCP tools. Start an audit for the public URL. Poll the same durable job shown in the human interface. Read the ranked recommendations and supporting evidence. Return to the authorised repository and investigate the real source code. Implement justified changes and run the repository’s own checks. Frontmend remains useful without WebMCP. A person can complete the entire public audit through the normal interface and receive the same recommendation document. Both paths call the same application service and validation logic, so the human and agent are not working from separate versions of the truth. A deliberate boundary Frontmend does not claim to know which repository file owns a public symptom. It does not invent filenames or line numbers, request source code, handle repository credentials or pretend that a recommendation has been implemented. The current public workflow ends with the audit result and coding-agent handoff. Repository investigation and implementation continue through the agent’s existing file, browser and terminal tools. In the public workflow, a fresh audit of the deployed URL is the only way Frontmend produces new evidence about the production site. How it was built Frontmend uses: React 19 and Vite for the public interface Bun for package management, tests, linting and builds Socket’s Bun security scanner for dependency protection A Cloudflare Worker for the application and audit API SQLite-backed Durable Objects for asynchronous jobs, stable audit IDs, cancellation, retention and rate limits PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse behind replaceable evidence adapters Versioned, JSON-serialisable contracts shared by the human interface and WebMCP tools Contextual WebMCP registration, exposing only the actions that are useful in the current state Public URL handling is treated as a security boundary. Frontmend rejects credentialed, private-network, loopback, unsafe and query-bearing audit targets. Redirect destinations are revalidated on the server, and audit work is bounded by request, response, timeout, redirect and rate limits. Building with Codex Codex was both the primary development collaborator and the coding agent Frontmend was designed to help. It helped shape the product boundary, implement the shared contracts across the React client and Cloudflare Worker, test contextual WebMCP routing, harden public URL handling and challenge unsupported claims about repository ownership, deployment and resolution. That process helped clarify the central idea behind Frontmend: WebMCP is most valuable here when it gives an agent trustworthy context and then gets out of the way. Why it matters Frontmend is not an AI chat box placed beside an audit report. It makes an existing web workflow genuinely more useful when a person and their coding agent use it together. The person receives a clearer, more approachable audit. The coding agent receives structured evidence it can act on. Neither has to learn a second repair workflow, and the agent no longer needs to scrape a human-facing dashboard to understand what happened. title: Compute
pitch: A research web app where the agents pull information from the code rather then using it like a human
about_excerpt: A research web app where the agents pull information from the code rather then using it like a human Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration This made it difficult for me to evaluate my results. Every time I ran an analysis on the AI, it gave me some numbers but I wasn’t sure whether to believe them. Could this R² be real, or was the model just pattern-matching towards a value that sounded plausible? There’s no way to know without running an analysis myself, which kinda defeats the purpose of why you’re talking to an AI in the first place. It’s also tough when both a correct answer and incorrect one look exactly the same to anyone viewing your chat windows. Rather than focus on the fact I couldn’t trust what I was being told, maybe it’d help if we could get past the whole “plumbing” stage. Imagine having a conversation where each person was sitting in their own room communicating through note-passing. This is more akin to two people sitting at opposite ends of a table sharing views of the same screen. The WebMCP technology enables this since all these tools are on the same page instead of being exposed via an API. Once you understand how to use them (the WebMCP), the rest comes easy, really. What it does In our compute system you are joined by another user (the agent) at some sort of statistical research bench where there’s just as much code as there would be in the lab. You paste your URL into ChatGPT and say “does industry momentum survive out of sample and tx costs?” and the agent loads the data, builds a signal, runs a backtest, then performs a Fama French Regression and writes a little piece with the result. What really matters to me is what goes down when we run that regression — those numbers get sent along to the agent, they render a chart on our end. It’s pretty interesting to watch the process play out as opposed to read a summary of everything afterwards. Everything’s logged. If you want to use the data, you have to reference the steps that led you there. The record_finding tool will check every reference against our logs – we’re not going to let you publish results you’ve never computed! You’ll be able to go back in time while working on your analysis as well. You could drag back the window of dates by two years and hit ‘re-run’. Your agent would make a phone call with this new context (and there wouldn’t be a message, nor a synch!) – but there’d be just one workspace, so no problem here. 5 different datasets in fields ranging from finance to biology, all available through static CSV files. No network requests during runtime, no need for an API key and most importantly everything stays on the page. How we built it Written in TypeScript using React & Vite for the UI with Tailwind CSS styles, then deploying to Netlify as a static site (no backend). This means we have to build our own stats engine, but that’s unavoidable if you’re trying to do anything in the browser! I used Householder QR for least squares regression, Newey-West HAC standard errors for time series regressions, and Benjamini-Hochberg for false-discovery rate control — everything I cross-checked agains SciPy / NumPy for my 166 unit tests. The really neat stuff is how we built up our web layer over WebMCP. Our tools aren’t hard-coded — instead they’re rebuilt based on current state in every workspace change. If you load a dataset, we recompute the schema definitions from what columns are actually in memory at runtime. So you’ll see 4 “cold” tools show-up when the workspace initially loads, more get enabled once datasets have been loaded (thereby enabling 12 tools), even more once we can compute signals (13) and finally 14 possible tools once we’ve defined a backtest. Each tool will return both a compact form of its output that’s used by your agent (capped at 1500 chars), and then a full version designed to be rendered to the human. And we’ll keep that 500-row result from chewing up the model’s context while you get the whole chart! Finally expensive operations require an explicit click as a form of confirmation — trying to do a bootstrap with 2000+ simulations would prompt this confirmation card + wait for the tool call to proceed. Challenges we ran into Firstly we needed the agent to be able to see when there are state changes. In my first iteration the agent was keeping its own cache of the workspace, and the human edits weren’t being applied to their workspaces. As a result everything appeared to be working fine and numbers were silently wrong (which was precisely the failure-mode I designed the system to avoid). So to solve that problem I forced all tools to read the live store at call-time – no exceptions. Secondly provenance that couldn’t be talked-around. When I asked the agent for source references it came up with some pretty nice stuff, including a few things that were made-up. But after I politely asked the agent to explain why it used these citations I realized it wasn’t a mechanism. So now each citation has been matched to an entry in the log, if they don’t match then we won’t allow the write. Thirdly the 1500 character budget. This one proved far more difficult than I thought, in particular as we needed to create test data that would help us find a good set of parameters that worked well together. The initial output format produced huge volumes of numbers and I ended up rewriting how the results were serialized about four different times before the agent was able to correctly infer its reasoning from the input provided. Numerical correctness without any SciPy involved. Doing a Newey-West with the wrong choice of lags was getting me t-stats looking great but being off by 30%. Cost an entire evening. Not understanding what schemas were going to be available. Creating this toolregistry where I didn’t have the faintest idea about all the columns in there meant that my code needed to work on all datasets. Accomplishments that we're proud of Dynamic Tool Surface – Watch your badget rise from 4-12-13 as you work! Citations Enforced! – A little bit o’ code doin’ somethin’ I haven’t seen anywhere else yet… it’s just plain flat out IMPOSSIBLE for someone to fake their results… Stats Engine agrees with SciPy to Numerical Precision – You can run this in your browser tab without needing some fancy-ass server… One of my favorite ones was when the momentum demo concluded that momentum does not survive. I had tons of datasets on which you could apply this strategy successfully. In the end, though, the 2020 crash combined with the 2022 value rotation made all the in-sample benefits vanish into thin air. This was what the tool said after its analysis – and to be fair, that’s exactly how it happened. And if your research bench only tells you about wins, you’re no research bench. What we learned So constraints on the agent matter more than instructing the agent. Everytime we told it how to behave we mostly saw what we wanted. When we could make the bad behavior impossible we always saw that. The two-audience-per-tool-call approach is a really interesting design primitive — once you stop thinking about the tool result as being the same thing as the human-facing output lots of issues around context windows go away. One of the things webmcp unlocks which i underrated was shared mutable state — while i thought the dynamic schema stuff would be interesting, there’s nothing better than having zero protocol. No keys required — browser only! No servers involved! Nothing going on outside this webpage! This is for you if you have some data that you cannot upload to somewhere else. This is your entire product. What's next for Compute Bring Your Own Data – Just drop me a CSV and I’ll do the same thing, because all my stuff is local. There’s no change in the underlying model, it’s just adding a loader and doing some schema inference. More of the Toolkit – Things like panel regressions (fixed effects, IVs), time series diagnostic tests etc. Because this is all driven by an engine that has the architectural capability for it, its really a question of building these components and verifying they work as expected. Exportable / Rerunable Sessions – All the logs contain sufficient info to rerun a session. We’re going to serialise those out too so we can give people runs of findings to execuate. Pre-registration: Make your hypothesis go through the motions first, before seeing data. Now we’ve got the second side of the p-hacking equation (the ‘multiple testing correction’) covered. Now for non-statisticians! All of the above doesn’t depend on any particular property of either finance or scientific research. So long as there’s some sort of trusted party who needs to place their trust in results generated by some sort of agent, they could take advantage of the “shared workspace” and forced provenance. Built With chatgpt git github javascript netlify react statistics typescript vite webmcp Try it out github.com computeopenai.netlify.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Came
