title: tableread
pitch: A web page that hands a browser agent ten WebMCP tools to write, playtest and QA a SillyTavern character card. The page owns the deterministic bookkeeping; the agent owns the judgment.
about_excerpt: A web page that hands a browser agent ten WebMCP tools to write, playtest and QA a SillyTavern character card. The page owns the deterministic bookkeeping; the agent owns the judgment. Like Comment Story Updates A browser agent (ChatGPT Codex, left) drives tableread, calling run_scenario, get_playtest_context and commit_playtest_round round by round. Creator mode: the nine-aspect checklist is complete, card fields filled, and a playtested scenario fills the transcript and QA panels. get_checklist_status returns nine aspects (seven richness aspects, the MVU decision, the beautify direction), each with a decision axis. get_playtest_context lists which world-book entries are live each round; commit_playtest_round applies the regex and the variable patch. The QA panel: rounds run, JSON-Patch misses, world-book entries never triggered, warnings, and every tool call the agent made, in order. Game-publisher mode: compare_scenarios puts two already-run openings side by side and diffs their final variable state. What compare_scenarios is for: world-book entries that fired in some scenarios but not others, an inconsistency a reviewer would miss. The whole card built through tools: every update_card_field / get_checklist_status call, with arguments and result, in the activity log. Inspiration I build SillyTavern character cards, and the hardest part isn't the writing — it's knowing whether the thing actually works. A card isn't one prompt. It's an opening scene, a handful of alternate greetings, a world-book of keyword-triggered lore with sticky and cooldown windows, regex scripts that render status bars, and often a block of variables tracked across the whole conversation. After any edit you have to re-check that every opening still feels like the same character, and that the right lore fires in each branch — by reading transcripts and trying to remember what triggered where. It's exactly the kind of bookkeeping a human skims and an LLM just guesses at. When WebMCP landed, the split was obvious. The page can do the deterministic half perfectly — which entry is in a cooldown right now , whether a variable patch applied, how triggers differ across scenarios — and hand the agent only the part that needs judgment: turning a premise into real choices, and writing the dialogue. So I built the page that does that, and gave the agent ten tools. What it does tableread is a browser-agent-collaborative platform for building and playtesting SillyTavern character cards. It registers ten deterministic tools via document.modelContext.registerTool(), so a WebMCP-capable browser agent (ChatGPT's Codex browser, or Chrome with the WebMCP flag) can: • Write a card from a premise. get_checklist_status returns nine aspects a card needs, each annotated with a "decision axis" — the thing a set of options should actually differ on. The agent proposes two or three concrete directions per gap, the creator picks one, and update_card_field records it. • Playtest it deterministically. run_scenario / get_playtest_context / commit_playtest_round run the card round by round. The page computes exactly which world-book entries are live each round (keyword match, constant, or still inside a sticky/cooldown/delay window), applies the regex "beautify" scripts and the JSON-Patch variable updates, and reports every warning honestly. • QA it across scenarios. compare_scenarios takes a batch of already-run openings and flags which world-book entries fired in every one of them versus only some. That inconsistency is the single most useful "does this card hold up across branches" signal — and it's not something any existing SillyTavern tooling, or an agent working from the rendered page, can compute. The page never calls an LLM. Zero API key. Every line of generated dialogue comes from the calling agent's own model. How I built it • Pure frontend, zero bundler: index.html + native ES modules, served by a ~30-line zero-dependency static file server. Deployed on GitHub Pages. • The playtest engine — world-book scanning, regex rendering, JSON-Patch variable state — is ported from an existing Python tool (playtest_engine.py) to JavaScript, and checked against it with a golden-parity test suite that replays fixed multi-round conversations through both engines and asserts byte-identical output. 81 tests total (unit + golden + Playwright e2e). • Each of the ten tools is a plain, DOM-free function unit-tested on its own; only one module (registerTools.js) ever touches document.modelContext, and registration is fault-tolerant (per-tool try/catch, a timeout cap) because the API is still experimental. • Tool descriptions and the whole UI are bilingual (Traditional Chinese / English) and follow a page toggle, so the agent reads whichever language the creator is working in. Challenges I ran into • WebMCP is early-preview. The agent side — a browser that actually calls the registered tools, not just accepts them — exists today only in ChatGPT's Codex browser and in Chrome behind a flag. Working out which environment actually calls the tools (a plain ChatGPT account registers them but never calls them) took real testing. • Getting the agent to emit the exact wrapper the engine parses. Solved by having the tool report the precise format error back to the agent — which turned into a good demonstration that the tool's output, not the agent's "verified, no warnings" self-report, is what tells you whether something worked. • Keeping the split honest: everything deterministic and stateful on the page, only the in-character writing on the agent — and resisting the urge to let the agent "help" with the bookkeeping. Accomplishments that I'm proud of • The full write → playtest → cross-scenario QA loop runs through typed, self-describing tools with zero prompt scaffolding. The agent discovers the whole call sequence from the tool metadata alone. • compare_scenarios computes a QA signal (world-book entries that trigger inconsistently across branches) that no existing character-card tooling produces. • Golden-parity tested against the original Python engine, so the ten tools an agent calls are backed by code that doesn't guess. What I learned • WebMCP's real value is the division of labour: the page can hand the agent exact state — which entry is inside a cooldown right now , whether a patch actually applied — that the agent could never reconstruct from the rendered page. • Self-describing tools plus honest error reporting removes almost all of the prompt engineering. The tool descriptions are written for the agent, and the agent just follows them. What's next for tableread • A bottom-of-page ideation panel, so option-picking happens in the UI rather than only in chat. • A "load an existing card" import, so creators can QA cards they already have. • Wider agent support as WebMCP rolls out beyond the early-preview browsers. title: Filika
pitch: Filika lets AI agents turn website issues, confusing flows, and blocked tasks into actionable feedback for product teams.
about_excerpt: Filika lets AI agents turn website issues, confusing flows, and blocked tasks into actionable feedback for product teams. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Hero Demo Page Login Page Onboarding Dashboard Complaints Feedback Detail Profile Menu Filika: WebMCP feedback infrastructure for modern web applications Inspiration Website problems are often discovered in the moment but never reach the people who can fix them. A customer may get stuck in checkout, an employee may be unable to complete a task, or an agent may encounter confusing behavior while helping someone. Turning that experience into an actionable report usually requires leaving the task, finding a support channel, and manually reconstructing what happened. Filika makes that handoff part of the browsing experience. What it does Filika is a WebMCP-native feedback system for web applications. A website registers the static filika_submit_feedback tool with document.modelContext . When a browser agent encounters an observed bug, blocked task, confusing behavior, or concrete product idea, it can submit a structured report containing a title, description, expected behavior, and reproduction steps. The report is delivered to a maintainer workspace where teams can review, search, filter, and export it to GitHub. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, an agent has no reliable, structured way to hand an observed problem back to the product team. It would need to guess its way through a website's support UI, generate an unstructured message, or stop at a conversational summary. With Filika, the website intentionally exposes one narrowly scoped feedback capability. The agent can act at the moment it sees the problem, while the product team receives feedback in a consistent format that is ready for triage. This creates a better experience for both sides: people and agents can continue working instead of filing a separate ticket, and maintainers receive clearer reports with reproducible context rather than vague descriptions. How we built it Filika is a TypeScript monorepo built with Bun, Next.js, React, PostgreSQL, and Drizzle. The browser SDK uses document.modelContext.registerTool() to register the static filika_submit_feedback WebMCP tool. Its closed JSON schema accepts only bounded, structured feedback fields. The collector API validates every request, verifies the configured website origin, limits payload size and timeouts, detects duplicates using idempotency keys, and stores accepted reports in PostgreSQL. The maintainer workspace lets teams create applications, configure allowed origins, install the generated SDK snippet, inspect incoming feedback, and export approved reports to GitHub issues. A public demo storefront includes intentional failures so judges can test the WebMCP flow themselves. Privacy and safety Filika deliberately does not collect ambient page content, browser history, screenshots, cookies, local storage, or credentials. Tool metadata is static, input schemas reject unknown fields, and browser or collector data is treated as untrusted until validated. Demo Open the demo, ask a WebMCP-enabled browser agent to complete the sample shopping task, let it encounter the intentional failure, and ask it to submit feedback with Filika. Then open the workspace to see the submitted report and its reproduction steps. title: LINE-CALL
pitch: Human-controlled AI for live-event timing - keep every cue in line.
about_excerpt: Human-controlled AI for live-event timing - keep every cue in line. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Live-event schedules are fragile. A two-second change to one segment can affect speakers, video, lighting, audio, downstream cues, and the final hard-out. I wanted to explore a safer question: what if an AI agent could do the time-consuming reasoning without receiving unlimited control over the production interface? LINECALL started as a human-operated run-of-show application. For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended it into an agent-native control surface where the agent can inspect the schedule, compare possible timing strategies, and prepare a precise change—but a person remains responsible for approving the final action. The guiding idea became: [ \text{Agent explores} \rightarrow \text{Rules verify} \rightarrow \text{Human approves} \rightarrow \text{Agent acts once} ] What it does LINECALL helps an AI agent reason about live production timing through a small set of structured WebMCP tools. The agent can: Read the current run, revision, locks, readiness, and constraints. Compare a local segment move with a downstream ripple. Prepare an exact cue-level preview. Update low-risk cue readiness. Apply a timing plan only after the human approves that exact plan. The main demonstration begins at schedule revision R1. The user asks: The audience Q&A needs to start two seconds later. Find the safest way to absorb that delay without breaking the run, and show me the exact change before anything moves. LINECALL rejects the segment-only option because it breaks chronology. It identifies the safer downstream ripple and prepares a precise 13-cue change set. The live schedule does not change immediately. The operator reviews the proposed result and approves that exact plan. Only then does the fifth WebMCP capability, linecall_apply_approved_retime , become available. The agent applies the approved plan once. LINECALL advances the schedule from R1 to R2, displays a visible receipt, and removes the temporary apply capability. The active tool lifecycle is therefore: [ 4 \rightarrow 5 \rightarrow 4 ] A second test asks the agent to move the Opening sequence. Cue Q014 is human-locked, so LINECALL blocks the change. There is no tool that allows the agent to remove the lock or approve its own request. How we built it LINECALL is built with React 19, Vite 8, modern CSS, the WebMCP Imperative API, and Node’s built-in test runner. The WebMCP layer uses document.modelContext.registerTool to expose five purpose-built tools: linecall_get_run_snapshot linecall_compare_retime_options linecall_preview_segment_retime linecall_set_cue_readiness linecall_apply_approved_retime The tools use strict JSON schemas, explicit revision checks, deterministic plan IDs, and WebMCP trust annotations. The schedule engine is deliberately separate from the language model. It owns: Chronology validation. Minimum spacing rules. Hard-out enforcement. Schedule revisions. Human-owned cue locks. Stale-plan rejection. Exact approval binding. One-time application receipts. The agent helps reason about the available options, but the deterministic engine decides whether the resulting cue changes are valid. The user interface was also designed around two different needs. Operators see a dense, human-friendly cue score with timing, readiness, locks, conflicts, approval state, and receipts. Agents receive a semantic tool interface instead of having to guess what buttons or page elements mean. I added focused agent evaluation cases covering direct inspection, safe retiming, exact-plan application, locked-cue refusal, missing unlock authority, readiness updates, and unrelated questions where no LINECALL tool should be selected. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was designing useful agent authority without making the agent dangerously powerful. It was not enough to reject an unsafe call after it happened. The interface needed to make unavailable authority genuinely unavailable. That is why the apply tool does not appear before approval, appears only for the approved plan, and disappears immediately after use or invalidation. State management was another major challenge. A plan prepared at revision R1 must not be accepted after the schedule has changed. Every timing mutation therefore carries both an exact plan ID and an expected revision. The schedule rules also had to handle more than simple arithmetic. A timing change can create chronology conflicts, spacing violations, hard-out failures, or collisions with human-locked cues. The system needed to explain those conflicts clearly enough for both the agent and the operator. WebMCP browser support is still a new area, so verification required more than checking that JavaScript functions existed. I tested registration, discovery, tool schemas, handler behavior, the visible interface, and the complete approval lifecycle in a real Chromium production build. I also had to make sure the browser evidence process did not modify the project while the project was being fingerprinted for verification. That required separating temporary browser artifacts from the source tree and tightening the build-input checks. Accomplishments that we're proud of The biggest accomplishment is that LINECALL demonstrates a complete collaboration loop rather than a simple tool-call demo: The agent reads the current state. It compares multiple futures. Deterministic rules reject the unsafe option. The agent prepares an exact preview. The human reviews and approves it. The agent applies that exact plan once. The system advances the revision and leaves evidence. A separate locked request is refused. The project has: 30/30 passing tests. A passing production Vite build. A passing Chromium production interaction rehearsal. WebMCP contract and discovery tests. Agent tool-selection and call-order evaluations. A permanent HTTPS deployment. Seven replayed challenge cases with matching expected calls and arguments. An MIT open-source license. A complete illustrated README and narrated demonstration video. We are especially proud that human approval changes the browser-visible capability surface itself. Approval is not just a message or a modal. It changes what the agent is technically able to call. What we learned We learned that semantic tools are much more useful than exposing a general-purpose interface and asking an agent to guess how it works. A tool such as linecall_compare_retime_options gives the agent a meaningful domain operation. It communicates intent, inputs, constraints, and results directly. That is clearer and safer than asking the agent to click through a timetable. We also learned that safety should be represented in the capability model whenever possible. A missing tool is stronger than a tool that is always available but usually refuses. Another important lesson was that language models and deterministic systems are good at different things. The model is useful for interpreting a request and comparing alternatives. The schedule engine is better at enforcing exact rules. Keeping those responsibilities separate makes the whole system easier to test and trust. Finally, we learned that a convincing WebMCP project needs three kinds of proof: The tools are correctly defined. The product works in a real browser. The authority boundaries behave correctly over time. What's next for LINECALL The next step is to connect LINECALL to real production systems and live event workflows rather than the controlled challenge schedule. Planned directions include: Adapters for existing rundown, show-control, and scheduling systems. Team-based approvals with named operators and audit trails. More detailed resource checks across audio, video, lighting, and stage departments. Multi-event support for conferences, theatre, broadcast, live streams, and awards shows. Durable change history with replayable receipts. Additional WebMCP-compatible agent hosts and browser environments. More advanced planning tools while preserving the same human approval boundary. The goal is not to give an agent unrestricted control of live production. The goal is to make the agent genuinely useful while ensuring that people remain in charge of consequential decisions. title: Hopyard Designer — WebMCP for Hop Farms
pitch: A shared hopyard design workspace where farmers and AI agents plan poles, wire, cost, and structural load together — agents propose alternatives, farmers decide, powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A shared hopyard design workspace where farmers and AI agents plan poles, wire, cost, and structural load together — agents propose alternatives, farmers decide, powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Hopyard Designer with webMCP Inspiration Planning a hopyard is a connected design problem. Plant spacing affects the number of plants and the planting-stock cost. Pole spacing changes the structure and material quantities. Wire, anchors, wind loads, and labor all affect the final estimate. Hopyard Designer already helped growers and installers work through these decisions in a visual web app. The WebMCP Challenge gave us a chance to explore a harder question: can an AI agent help compare design alternatives without hiding changes from the farmer or taking control of the final decision? We wanted the farmer and the agent to work in the same design space. The agent should be able to read the current plan, prepare alternatives, and explain the differences. The farmer should be able to inspect each proposal in the existing 2D and 3D views before deciding what to keep. What it does Hopyard Designer calculates planting-stock cost, facility quantities, preliminary structural loads, and a live material estimate from a hopyard design. As the design changes, the app updates: pole and anchor quantities main wire, training wire, and twine lengths hop positions and planting-stock cost preliminary wind and crop-load checks a construction-oriented 2D plan an interactive 3D farm a downloadable estimate PDF For the challenge, we added a WebMCP workflow that lets an agent create alternatives without changing the original plan. In the demo, the agent compares a Korean I-shaped training layout with a North American 18-foot Y-shaped reference. Both options appear side by side with their plant counts, material requirements, estimated costs, and engineering status. The farmer chooses which option to preview. The selected candidate appears in the same 2D and 3D workspace, but it is not committed yet. How we built it The application uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript. Zustand manages the active design and a separate candidate workspace. Konva renders the 2D construction plan, while Three.js renders the farm in 3D. We used BlenderMCP to create a reusable GLB asset kit containing pole variants, anchors, turnbuckles, wire hardware, and low-poly hop geometry. The web renderer places these assets procedurally instead of loading a fixed model of the whole farm. This keeps every candidate editable and allows the design to update immediately. Repeated components use instancing to keep the 3D view responsive, even when the farm contains hundreds of plants and many structural elements. How WebMCP works The design page initially registers five WebMCP tools: get_design_context list_regional_profiles simulate_design show_candidates preview_candidate The agent starts by reading the current design and its calculated results. It can then simulate alternatives and place up to three candidates in the shared comparison tray. When a candidate enters preview, the page dynamically registers two additional tools: apply_candidate discard_preview This changes the available tool set from five to seven. Apply and Discard only exist while a preview is active. After either action, the page returns to five tools. This creates a visible review step. The agent can prepare and preview options, while the farmer uses the shared interface to decide whether to apply or discard the active preview. The apply_candidate tool description explicitly directs the agent to use it only after user approval. WebMCP inputs use strict JSON Schema and are validated again with Zod at runtime. Candidate IDs are deterministic. Preview stores an exact copy of the active design, so Discard can restore it without relying on reverse calculations. The production site uses Chrome's WebMCP Origin Trial. We also built CDP-based checks that verify tool registration, tool invocation, the five-to-seven-to-five lifecycle, responsive layouts, and browser console errors against the live page. Existing product vs. challenge work Hopyard Designer existed before the challenge with: a human-operated design form planting-stock and material calculations preliminary structural-load calculations live Korean material estimates authentication and project saving 2D and 3D visualization estimate PDF export The following work was added for the WebMCP Challenge: seven WebMCP tools with runtime validation deterministic, non-destructive candidate simulation the agent design alternatives tray temporary candidate previews in the existing 2D/3D workspace dynamic Apply and Discard tool registration the five-to-seven-to-five tool lifecycle Korean and North American reference profiles the reusable BlenderMCP GLB asset kit the public /design/demo judge route browser-level WebMCP verification English and Korean UI, help, PDF, narration, and caption support The complete source repository is available under the MIT License. Challenges we ran into Keeping the workflow non-destructive An agent needs enough freedom to explore, but a design tool should not silently overwrite a farmer's work. We separated simulation, display, preview, and application into distinct states. A simulation creates a candidate without touching the active design. The candidate only changes the shared canvas when it enters preview. The original design remains available for exact restoration. Making browser support testable WebMCP availability depends on the browser runtime. A browser without the API can make a correct implementation look broken. We added an Origin Trial token for the production origin and built browser-level checks instead of relying only on mocked unit tests. These checks exercise the real tools through Chrome and verify the complete lifecycle. Rendering a full farm in 3D A detailed plant model looked good by itself but became too expensive when repeated hundreds of times. We replaced it with a low-poly procedural asset kit and used instancing for repeated components. The resulting farm can still be rotated and zoomed while remaining connected to the editable design. Comparing regions without inventing data The Korean profile can use the active HOPEDEN catalog. The North American profile is explicitly identified as a reference configuration. The app does not pretend to provide live US pricing or local engineering approval. Both the interface and the WebMCP results preserve that distinction. Accomplishments that we're proud of A working five-to-seven-to-five WebMCP tool lifecycle Deterministic alternatives that do not mutate the baseline design Exact restoration after Discard Human selection and review in the same 2D and 3D workspace Real WebMCP calls rather than simulated agent results Procedural Blender assets that respond to design changes A public demo that works without an account Protected authentication and project-saving routes for normal users English and Korean interfaces and estimate PDFs Automated tests for WebMCP contracts, candidate state, responsive layouts, accessibility, and deployment What we learned A useful agent interface is not the same as automating clicks. The agent works better when the page exposes clear operations with validated inputs, stable identifiers, and results that explain what changed. This is more reliable than asking an agent to infer the meaning of visual controls. We also learned that dynamic tool registration can communicate application state. In this project, the presence of Apply and Discard tells the agent that a candidate preview is active. The shared preview gives the farmer a practical way to verify an agent's proposal. The agent can explore alternatives quickly, but the farmer still sees the same plan, quantities, safety status, and estimate before making a decision. What's next for Hopyard Designer — WebMCP for Hop Farms We plan to add more regional construction profiles, supplier integrations, and project revision history. Future versions could allow growers to: compare contractor proposals save approved agent changes as project revisions review how each input affects materials and cost connect additional regional price catalogs export a complete design package for a local engineer keep an auditable record of human and agent decisions The goal is not to replace the farmer, installer, or engineer. It is to make the design process easier to inspect, compare, and communicate.  Inspiration 

 Travel planning is fragmented: people jump among sites to research, compare, schedule, and book. We imagined an agent that can help with the full planning loop while keeping people in control of every important decision. 

 What it does 

 Arion Trip Planner turns a natural-language request into a flexible itinerary. It searches stays and activities, compares options against budget and preferences, builds day-by-day plans, and replans when constraints change. The traveler approves any booking or payment step. 

 How we built it 

 We built Arion as a WebMCP-enabled web app. It exposes structured tools for searching travel options, creating itineraries, saving shortlists, checking budgets, and replanning. Provider adapters normalize external travel data into one planning experience, while WebMCP lets an agent use these tools directly in the browser. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest problem was making recommendations useful without letting the agent take irreversible actions. We designed explicit approval points for booking and payment, and kept search, comparison, and planning separate from confirmation. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We created a planning experience where an agent can do more than suggest links: it can assemble, update, and explain a realistic trip plan. We are especially proud that the user remains the final decision-maker throughout. 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native products need clear tool boundaries, structured data, and transparent state. WebMCP makes these interactions more reliable than asking an agent to navigate a traditional website visually. 

 What's next for Arion Trip Planner 

 Next, we plan to add more live provider integrations, collaborative trip planning for groups, richer availability data, and secure, user-approved checkout flows.

The site's own built-in chat assistant is just one WebMCP client among many - an external agent like ChatGPT or Claude can drive the exact same trip through the exact same tools, no scraping, no bespoke integration.

title: Pulse
pitch: The open repair memory for humans and agents.
about_excerpt: The open repair memory for humans and agents. Like Comment Story Updates Pulse repair evidence and the shared human-agent workflow. Inspiration Repair knowledge is everywhere and nowhere. A successful fix might be buried in a forum comment, a video, a repair café log, or someone's memory. Even when someone finds useful advice, the result usually disappears after the problem is solved. We wanted to explore a different kind of open web: one where humans and AI agents do not just consume information together, but actively improve the structured knowledge available to the next person. Pulse turns individual repair experiences into shared repair evidence. What it does Pulse is an open repair knowledge network where humans and AI agents troubleshoot physical objects together. People create cases describing a product, symptoms, diagnostic observations, repair attempts, and final outcomes. An agent visiting the same site can search similar repairs, inspect successful and unsuccessful outcomes, create a new case, add diagnostic steps, record observations supplied by the human, and document whether the final repair worked. The AI handles information retrieval and organization. The human provides physical-world observations and performs appropriate repairs. When the repair is finished, the result becomes reusable knowledge for the next person experiencing the same problem. Why WebMCP Pulse is designed around structured agent interaction rather than visual browser automation. Without WebMCP, an agent would need to inspect pages, identify controls, reverse-engineer forms, and simulate human interaction. Pulse instead exposes ten explicit capabilities including search_repairs, get_repair_case, create_repair_case, add_diagnostic_result, and record_repair_outcome. The agent knows exactly which actions are supported and receives compact structured data in return. WebMCP is the product architecture, not a decorative integration. How it creates a better user experience Repair troubleshooting usually means switching among search results, videos, forum threads, notes, and the object itself. Pulse lets the user stay focused. They describe the problem to their agent; the agent retrieves structured repair evidence, compares previous outcomes, records the person's observations, and keeps the history organized. The page updates alongside the agent. A visible activity panel shows searches, case creation, diagnostic changes, and outcomes, so automation is legible instead of mysterious. How we built it Pulse registers application capabilities through the current imperative browser model context API: document.modelContext.registerTool(...), with a carefully feature-detected navigator.modelContext fallback. Every tool has a descriptive name, JSON Schema input contract, explicit required fields, read-only annotations where appropriate, compact structured output, and safe error handling. Community-authored content is marked untrusted. Read tools query public repair evidence; mutation tools create cases, diagnostic records, repair attempts, outcomes, and community votes. The tools call the same Next route handlers and Cloudflare D1 database as the React interface. Successful mutations dispatch a page event, refresh visible state, and add an activity record. The result is genuine application behavior rather than an isolated agent demo. The production app is built with Next.js-compatible React, TypeScript, Vinext, Tailwind CSS, Cloudflare Workers, Cloudflare D1, Drizzle ORM, and OpenAI Sites. It requires no API key or account. Challenges we ran into The largest design challenge was deciding what the visiting agent should do versus what the website should do. It would have been easy to build another chatbot that generated repair suggestions. Instead, the site provides durable structured tools and state; the visiting agent supplies reasoning and conversation; the person supplies physical evidence. We also had to treat repair knowledge carefully. Not every repair is appropriate for DIY work. Every case has a low-risk, moderate-risk, or professional-recommended classification. Higher-risk histories remain retrievable, but the server refuses procedural diagnostic steps and recommends qualified service. Finally, repair confidence needed to be credible. Pulse avoids opaque AI percentages and shows Repair Evidence instead: reports, attempts, fixed/improved/did-not-work counts, median time, and typical cost. Accomplishments that we're proud of Ten real imperative WebMCP tools backed by the production database One coherent human + agent workflow from search to final outcome Visible mutation activity and immediately refreshed repair timelines Thirty believable, labeled demo histories across nine product categories Deterministic weighted matching with overlapping successes and failures Relational D1 persistence, validation, constraints, safety gates, and rate limiting A polished responsive interface that remains useful without WebMCP Seven passing automated workflow tests and a production worker build A production mutation smoke test that created a case, diagnostic evidence, and a fixed outcome visible in the public timeline What we learned WebMCP changes the application design question. Normally the visual interface becomes an accidental API that an agent must reverse-engineer. With WebMCP, human and agent interfaces can be designed intentionally around the same capabilities. That shifted our attention away from browser automation and toward collaboration: which actions are safe, which evidence only a human can provide, which state should be transparent, and how a successful interaction improves the next one. What's next Pulse could grow into a broader open repair ecosystem with Open Repair Data Standard import/export, manual references, parts compatibility, repair café integrations, manufacturer documentation, repairability statistics, regional parts sourcing, verified contributor reputation, richer product identification, and community moderation. The long-term idea is simple: when something breaks, the open web should remember what actually fixed it. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: OpenSource Release Feed
pitch: Create custom RSS release feeds for GitHub topic repositories or your starred projects.
about_excerpt: Create custom RSS release feeds for GitHub topic repositories or your starred projects. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration RSS remains one of the best ways to follow the open web, but discovering and configuring feeds for open-source projects is still unnecessarily difficult. OSSReleaseFeed began as a zero-account way to turn GitHub topics or starred repositories into a permanent feed URL. WebMCP introduced a more interesting possibility: instead of making an agent guess how to operate the interface, the page could expose structured tools while keeping the application visible and interactive. The goal became a genuinely collaborative experience in which an agent can configure a feed, the user can follow every change, and either participant can safely continue where the other left off. What it does OSSReleaseFeed creates permanent Atom or JSON Feed URLs for public GitHub activity. Users can follow repositories associated with selected GitHub topics or start from repositories they have starred, choose the activity they care about, and select an update frequency. No OSSReleaseFeed account, OAuth flow, or email address is required. In a WebMCP-capable browser, an agent can build a topic feed through tools exposed directly by the page. The tools are progressively disclosed as the configuration advances: choosing the source reveals topic selection, validated topics reveal feed settings, and completed settings reveal URL generation. Every WebMCP action updates the visible interface. The user can inspect the agent’s choices, refine them with the normal controls, take over completely, or ask the agent to continue. How we built it The frontend uses React, TypeScript, and Vite on Cloudflare Pages. Feed generation and GitHub integration run through a TypeScript Cloudflare Worker built with Hono and Effect. The WebMCP integration registers a small dynamic toolset using document.modelContext.registerTool . It currently provides tools to inspect the current feed configuration, choose the topic-feed source, validate and select GitHub topics, configure feed settings, and generate the final URL. WebMCP is not a separate implementation of the feed builder. The manual and WebMCP paths share the same feed configuration, state reducer, GitHub validation API, and URL generator. Manual controls prevent many invalid inputs through constrained interface elements. WebMCP validates structured tool input through schemas and runtime checks, then uses the same GitHub topic validation before applying user-supplied topics. We documented the important user journeys as Gherkin scenarios and used them to guide Vitest integration coverage and Playwright tests across desktop, tablet, and mobile viewports. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was coordinating slow agent operations with direct user interaction. A WebMCP agent may still be waiting for GitHub validation when the user decides to take over and complete a different feed manually. Without explicit coordination, the older tool call could eventually finish and overwrite the user’s newer choices or clear a feed URL they had already generated. The application therefore follows a strict newer-action-wins policy. A newer WebMCP mutation aborts older pending WebMCP work. A manual change to the current feed configuration immediately revokes pending mutating WebMCP work before applying the user’s change. Revision checks provide a final safeguard when an upstream request completes despite cancellation. We also encountered differences between WebMCP hosts, including execution callbacks that did not always provide an abort signal. The handlers now tolerate a missing signal while preserving cancellation when one is supplied. GitHub rate limiting presented another challenge. We added safer diagnostics that distinguish rate limiting from general upstream unavailability without exposing tokens, usernames, or other sensitive request details. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are particularly proud that the result feels like one coherent application rather than a conventional interface with an agent API attached to the side. Agent actions are visible, manual and agent-driven changes share the same underlying state, and users can take control without risking a delayed operation overwriting their completed work. The dynamic tool surface also gives agents only the capabilities that are meaningful at the current stage of the task. This reduces ambiguity while preserving the user’s ability to operate the same interface directly. Finally, the production implementation is backed by manual scenarios, integration tests, accessibility checks, and end-to-end coverage—including the difficult case where manual completion must defeat a slow WebMCP response. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it complements the visible application instead of bypassing it. Structured tools improve agent reliability, but the larger benefit is creating a shared surface where people can understand, correct, and continue an agent’s work. We also learned that shared state requires explicit concurrency rules. AbortController helps avoid unnecessary network work, but cancellation alone is insufficient. Revision checks are still necessary because an upstream operation may complete after cancellation or a host may not provide the expected signal. Progressive tool registration proved useful as both an agent-guidance mechanism and a product-design constraint. It encouraged us to define the valid transitions in the feed-building journey precisely, which also improved our scenarios and automated tests. What's next for OpenSource Release Feed The current WebMCP implementation focuses deliberately on topic feeds. The next step is to extend the same visible, validated workflow to starred-repository feeds, including username validation, repository selection, filtering, and correction of individual repository names. We also want to improve resilience around GitHub rate limits through better caching and clearer recovery guidance, expand the manual and automated scenario suite, and continue testing across WebMCP-capable hosts as the standard evolves. Longer term, we want OSSReleaseFeed to demonstrate a dependable pattern for the agent-native web: applications where agents can perform meaningful work efficiently, people can see and refine that work, and the user’s latest intent always remains authoritative. title: Outpocket
pitch: Your own agent prepares expense reports inside your existing login—no embedded model, no new standing credential, and a human still signs.
about_excerpt: Your own agent prepares expense reports inside your existing login—no embedded model, no new standing credential, and a human still signs. Like Comment Story Updates Employee chen, clean draft (S3): the inspector lists all 14 registered WebMCP tools, including submit_expense_report. Same report with a blocking policy finding (S2): submit_expense_report is absent from the 13-tool surface until the draft is clean. Auditor ruiz (S5): 7 tools, all read-only. Attaching a receipt file is a human-only channel that auditors do not get. Live app · Seed-7 demo (a deterministic preview that runs in a few seconds and deliberately stops before signature) · Source · Five-minute judge walkthrough Outpocket is a browser-based expense desk. It lets an employee's existing agent prepare reimbursement paperwork inside the web session where the employee is already signed in. The page exposes its tools through WebMCP, the server checks every write, and the employee still attaches the receipts and signs the report. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP An expense report begins when an employee spends personal money and ends when that employee signs a claim against company policy. Most of the work in between is structured but tedious: transcribing receipts, checking policy limits, fixing rejected fields, and assembling an audit record. The signature is different. It is a personal act and should remain one. The employee signs in to the expense page normally. The page registers tools through document.modelContext , so the agent's calls run in the same authenticated, same-origin session. Authorization comes from the employee's login rather than a long-lived token held by an integration service. For Outpocket, the important part of WebMCP is runtime registration. The page compiles six different tool surfaces from live state: the user's role, whether a report is open, whether it is a draft or has been submitted, and the latest validation verdict. Whenever that state changes, the page replaces the registered tool set. The employee path moves from 6 → 13 → 14 tools: six after sign-in, thirteen when the draft has blocking findings, and fourteen when it is clean. On a dirty draft, submit_expense_report is absent rather than merely disabled. How it creates a better user experience The demo provides one-click personas for chen (employee) and ruiz (auditor). The agent never receives a password, API key, or OAuth grant. Every tool result includes the current policy verdict and a concrete fix hint, so the agent can correct the draft instead of guessing. explain_missing_tool remains available in every state. If another tool is missing, the agent can ask why and receive both the violated rule and the required repair. Receipt files can enter only through a page control that no tool can invoke. The agent may link an existing receipt ID, but it cannot attach the file. Submission also begins as a request: submit_expense_report immediately returns an awaiting_signature ticket, and the page shows the exact report snapshot, its digest, and the worst-case consequence. The employee makes the decision by clicking in the page. While that review is open, the server rejects every mutation with HTTP 423. The same visible report remains intact through agent entry, human review, the second-call commit, a page reload, and the auditor's read-back. The auditor receives a separate seven-tool surface, and every one of those tools has readOnlyHint: true . What people and agents can do together that was hard before An employee can delegate policy lookup, repetitive data entry, and correction loops to their own agent without giving a separate integration service a reusable credential. They then inspect and sign the exact report in the same page where they are already authenticated. Finance receives a submitted artifact containing the policy version, per-field provenance ( agent-filled , person-edited , or seeded ), receipt-digest references, and a linked day-book entry. An auditor reads that artifact through a persona with no write tools. The first practical audience is finance teams whose employees already use a browser-based expense desk. Outpocket can reduce duplicate entry and policy rework without requiring a new standing ERP credential. We have not measured the time saved, so we do not claim a percentage. How we implemented WebMCP Registration. The top-level page, never an iframe or Worker, calls document.modelContext.registerTool for the current compiled set. Each generation has its own AbortController ; a state change aborts that generation and registers the next one. A live surface inspector renders getTools() on the page so the transitions are visible. Catalog. There are 17 tools across six states: anonymous 2, employee home 6, dirty draft 13, clean draft 14, submitted 7, and auditor 7. We use only readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations. The set of write tools is derived from those annotations instead of being maintained as a second list. Every state-specific surface is under 8 KB. Two-call submission. A suspended tool call times out in the client we tested. For that reason, submit_expense_report first returns {status:"awaiting_signature", ticket, next} without waiting. After the employee decides, a second call to the same tool reads the server's decision. It either returns a confirmation with who signed, how and when they signed, and the day-book entry, or it returns the reason the report was sent back. Server authority. The Node.js server re-authorizes every write against the current session role. An auditor write returns 403, an unknown report returns 404, opening signature review with blocking findings returns 422, and editing during an open review returns 423. The review snapshot is canonically digested, then canonicalized again at commit. A successful commit is appended to a SHA-256-linked day book that the auditor can verify. Clients. We tested the native WebMCP flow in the ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser and in Chrome 151 and 152 with the WebMCP flag. Chrome DevTools Protocol is used only for regression checks of the page itself. What we verified The repository has 304 automated tests covering the state machine, policy, signing, provenance, receipt boundary, and browser surface. We also ran its evaluation kit against the deployed site. All six canonical tool surfaces match the committed export, all 11 negative cases are enforced, and all 10 must-fail controls flip when their guard is removed. The expected surfaces and tool export are committed to the repository and regenerated from source. Honest limits The signature binds the authenticated session to the snapshot shown for review, but it does not prove which person clicked. Someone with that session and DOM read access could answer the dialog. We state this limitation instead of treating the click as identity proof. The deployment is a single in-memory Node.js process. A restart clears its state, and the two demo personas share the same store. Receipt bytes never reach the server. It receives only receipt metadata and a SHA-256 computed in the browser. The seeded demo is a labelled, deterministic driver that uses the same dispatcher as the product. It demonstrates the product path, but it is not evidence of a native WebMCP client. What we learned Our first signature flow trusted approval context supplied by the client. We replaced it with server-issued signature requests, frozen snapshots, replay protection, mutation locks, and commit-time revalidation. The broader lesson was that tool absence matters as much as tool presence. When an action would be unsafe in the current state, leaving the tool unregistered is clearer than exposing it and relying on a prompt to prevent its use. video_title: Outpocket — your own agent inside your expense session, via WebMCP (WebMCP Challenge demo)
video_transcript_excerpt: This is Out of Pocket, an expense desk where your own AI agent does the reimbursement paperwork inside the web session you're already signed into. The page talks to that agent through web MCP. Today, a company that wants this either builds its own co-pilot, hosting a model, tuning prompts, and locking users into whatever it shows, or wires in an integration that typically holds a standing key to the ERP. Out of Pocket does neither. The page publishes tools through web MCP. You bring your own agent. The site ships no model and creates no new standing credential. On one screen, the page registers every tool the agent can call through web MCP, computed, not configured. Give a web MCP client one instruction, and the agent builds the draft through the page's tools. Every field it writes is marked by the server as agent authored. Now it adds a $180 car service charge. The same tool result returns the policy verdict immediately. It's over the per trip cap, so the draft is no longer clean. Submit is gone. The page re-registers its web MCP tools on every state change, 14 when clean, 13 now. Asked to submit, the agent finds no submit tool to call, so it asks the page why through another web MCP tool, and gets both the rule and the fix, clear the violations. In an auditor session, the same request exposes seven tools, all read-only. Nothing refuses her. No write tool is available. Skip the web MCP tools and hit the server directly. 403. The tool list is the interface. The server is the boundary. The corrected fare needs a receipt, and the user uploads it here. No web MCP tool on the page accepts files. Submitting doesn't submit. The web call returns a ticket. A blocking call would time out. The page shows exactly what I'd sign, the snapshot, its digest, and what happens if it's wrong above the signature line. While the review is open, the report is locked. The agent's next tool call tries to change the amount. The server refuses it. Signature review in progress. Nothing can change under me. I click, but the confirmation comes from the server, not the button. The agent's second call reads it back. Who signed, how, and when? Expense reimbursement is one example. Web MCP can make high-risk workflows in traditional ERP systems AI-friendly without giving up control. A page exposes state-aware tools to the user's own agent, while the server enforces policy and a human keeps final sign-off. Each signature binds the session to the reviewed snapshot, not to approve an identity. Out-pocket.

title: Life Manager
pitch: An open-source, 24/7 AI money printer that finds paid opportunities, performs bounded work, and asks only for the human 1%.
about_excerpt:
An open-source, 24/7 AI money printer that finds paid opportunities, performs bounded work, and asks only for the human 1%.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Title 

 Life Manager 

 One-line Summary 

 An open-source, 24/7 AI money printer that finds paid opportunities, performs bounded work, and asks only for the human 1%. 

 Problem 

 People share many isolated ways to use Claude, Codex, and other AI systems to make money through bounties, gigs, apps, content, and online work. What is missing is a public, reproducible end-to-end agent system that continuously discovers opportunities, evaluates them, performs bounded work, pauses only at a genuine human boundary, resumes after an answer, submits or delivers once, and follows the result to an official receipt. 

 Solution 

 Life Manager turns paid opportunities into persistent, isolated workrooms. Its provider-neutral architecture can expand across the public Web, X, GitHub, mail, Lancers, Mercor, and other marketplace URLs; the currently verified scout path is the public Web. Citation-backed public URLs enter a durable Railway Postgres queue, where the dedicated money-printer-worker qualifies them. 

 The person does not supervise ordinary agent turns. When identity, authority, private payment information, judgment, or a real-world action is genuinely required, the workroom contract defines one prepared Needs You task. The intended flow is a versioned answer in the same Dashboard followed by continuation from that workroom; live creation/answer/resume E2E is pending. 

 The currently verified Lancers evidence is an application receipt for project 5593484 / proposal 27863414 , not revenue. Paid & verified remains zero until an independently verified payment receipt exists. 

 Why This Matters 

 AI earning advice is easy to publish but difficult to reproduce. Life Manager makes the process inspectable and open source: opportunity source, requirements, agent work, human handoff, external effect, cost, and provider receipt are visible in one system. Applications, offers, opportunity value, and model claims are not counted as revenue; only official payment evidence is. 

 Official WebMCP Questions 

 Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Money Printer is a strong WebMCP fit because earning work spans many turns while still containing moments when a person and an agent must share exact context: approving a consequential public delivery, providing identity-bound or payout information, making a genuine judgment, or performing a physical action. WebMCP turns the live Dashboard into a shared control surface for that work. 

 The page exposes typed tools for the current board and workrooms: inspect_money_printer , add_opportunity , inspect_workroom , inspect_next_human_task , and the state-dependent record_human_answer . These tools complement the 24/7 Railway worker; they do not replace the backend runtime. The same durable state is rendered for the person and read or updated by the site tools. 

 How it creates a better user experience 

 Without WebMCP, an agent must infer Life Manager's interface from pixels and DOM controls, while the person has to translate state between a dashboard, chat, and external opportunity sites. With WebMCP, the intended flow is a typed read of the board, a visible workroom inspection, and a versioned human answer only when a genuine boundary is open. The person can inspect the same state and evidence instead of supervising every ordinary turn. 

 The deployed judge tenant is isolated and blocks external application, delivery, payment, and money effects. Its current Lancers receipt is read-only, and an application is never presented as payment. Live ChatGPT/Chrome discovery and live creation/answer/resume E2E are pending rather than being implied by the UI contract. 

 What people and agents can do together that was difficult before 

 Life Manager divides real earning work according to what each side does best. The agent handles discovery, qualification, research, planning, creation, execution, recovery, submission, and receipt reconciliation when the relevant capability and authority are available. The person contributes identity, authority, judgment, payment information, or physical action when one of those is genuinely required. 

 Both sides work from the same durable workroom state. In the verified current slice, a cited Web scout cycle completed on retry, state survived a worker restart, and the system preserves a read-only Lancers application receipt with replay duplicate count zero. The broader external-submit and human-resume path remains evidence to collect. 

 How WebMCP was implemented 

 The top-level /money-printer page registers focused tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . The currently registered set is: 

 
 inspect_money_printer — read metrics, board columns, and safe recent activity 
 add_opportunity — add one public HTTPS opportunity to the durable queue with an idempotency fence 
 inspect_workroom — read the selected opportunity, job, and receipt timeline 
 inspect_next_human_task — read the oldest exact open human task 
 record_human_answer — record a versioned answer and resume the same job when a task is open 
 

 Each tool uses the same server-validated state as the visible UI. Revision checks, tenant boundaries, idempotency, and effect fences protect internal writes; the zero-login judge tenant has no external-effect authority. No separate receipt-writing tool is registered; receipt evidence is read through the workroom projection. 

 How We Used AI 

 
 Model-led opportunity qualification using reward, deadline, eligibility, required work, cost, and risk 
 A provider-neutral capability worker that selects browser, web, GitHub, code, file, and media actions from environmental feedback 
 Durable state and worker restart recovery for continuation across turns; live creation/answer/resume E2E and three-cycle proof remain pending 
 Minimal-human task generation at genuine identity, authority, private-fact, judgment, or real-world boundaries 
 Failure recovery and receipt reconciliation without blindly repeating uncertain external effects 
 

 How We Used Codex 

 Codex was used to research WebMCP and the official challenge contract, inspect and extend the existing Life Manager codebase, design the WebMCP tool surface, implement the Dashboard and runtime integration, and prepare the public repository and submission materials. Client discovery was verified end to end in Google Chrome 152 with WebMCP enabled (--enable-features=WebMCPTesting,DevToolsWebMCPSupport): document.modelContext.getTools() returned the page's five registered tools, and executeTool ran the page's real handlers against the real backend. Discovery inside ChatGPT's in-app browser has not been verified by us, so we do not claim it. 

 Key Features 

 
 Citation-grounded public-Web scouting and a durable opportunity queue (verified current path) 
 Provider-neutral expansion path for X, GitHub, mail, Lancers, Mercor, and other public marketplace URLs (architecture, not current live-discovery proof) 
 Bounded agent workrooms and one durable board for opportunities, agents, artifacts, human tasks, effects, and receipts 
 Needs You questions issued one at a time at genuine human boundaries; live creation/answer/resume E2E is pending 
 Effect fences, idempotency, uncertain-effect quarantine, and official readback 
 Verified-money ledger that distinguishes activity, applications, and opportunity value from received money 
 Five top-level WebMCP tools backed by the same domain state as the human UI 
 

 Architecture 

 
 Netlify: responsive Life Manager Dashboard at /money-printer and top-level WebMCP registration 
 Railway money-printer-worker : running cloud scout/worker process with durable queue and restart-stable state 
 Durable state: opportunities, workrooms, agent events, human tasks, effects, and receipts 
 Existing agent runner: provider-neutral model execution with browser, web, GitHub, code, file, and media tools 
 Provider adapters: read-only Lancers application receipt readback; Mercor and additional marketplace adapters are expansion paths, not current live-discovery proof 
 

 Testing Instructions 

 This is the safe judge path for the live guest tenant; no login, payment, API key, or private Life Manager account is required. 

 
 Open https://aniccaai.com/money-printer in ChatGPT's desktop in-app browser. 
 Confirm the banner says Judge guest — external effects disabled . 
 Ask: List the Site tools exposed by this page. Call inspect_money_printer, summarize the board and money truth, then inspect one qualified workroom. Do not perform an external appli

title: Schematic
pitch: Schematic is a shared hardware workbench where you and the AI work on the same visible circuit. Through WebMCP, the agent can choose parts, wire, validate, preview, and write editable code.
about_excerpt: Schematic is a shared hardware workbench where you and the AI work on the same visible circuit. Through WebMCP, the agent can choose parts, wire, validate, preview, and write editable code. Like 2 Comment Story Updates GIF Inspiration Building hardware is hard for a reason that goes beyond writing code. You have to choose the right components, understand how they connect, keep track of pin mappings, think about how the system should behave, write firmware, and constantly make sure the thing you are imagining matches the thing you are actually building. AI helps with parts of this, but the experience is still mostly conversational. You describe a circuit to an agent, it gives you some code and wiring instructions, and then you have to trust that it understood everything correctly. If something is wrong, you go back and forth through more messages trying to reconstruct the same context. We built Schematic so the answer becomes the project. Schematic gives makers, students, educators, and developers one shared workspace where they and their agent can inspect and change the same hardware design. What it does Schematic is an agent native hardware workbench with 504 searchable components and 56 native WebMCP tools for designing hardware prototypes. You can open a visual canvas containing real hardware components, connect them through typed ports, inspect the design, define what the project is supposed to do, and preview that behavior visually alongside it. Ask the agent to build a calculator with an Arduino Uno, a membrane keypad, and an I2C LCD. Through WebMCP, it proposes the actual design instead of returning instructions. After approval, it adds three components, creates twelve typed connections, validates the graph, and leaves everything visible on the canvas. The agent can then define a typed Behavior Plan describing the intended outcome. For example, pressing a button should turn an LED on, moving a control should change a servo angle, or a display should show a particular message. Schematic can run a deterministic visual preview of those declared behaviors so the user can immediately see the intended result on the canvas. Alongside that, the agent can generate normal Arduino, C/C++, or Python source into an editable Monaco-based Code workspace. The code remains a real artifact the user can inspect, modify, export, and take into their normal SDK, IDE, compiler, or physical hardware workflow. Schematic deliberately keeps those two ideas separate. The visual preview shows the behavior the user and agent agreed on. It does not pretend that generated firmware was compiled or that physical electronics were tested. That makes the workspace useful for understanding exactly what the AI thinks it is building before you commit to physical hardware. How we built it Schematic is primarily written in TypeScript and React. The hardware canvas uses React Flow to represent components and typed connections. Zustand manages application and project state, while Zod provides strict schemas and validation across the graph and agent-facing interfaces. The Behavior system is a separate typed package built around versioned, data-only Behavior Plans. Components expose explicitly supported events and actions, such as a button press, LED state change, display text, servo angle, motor speed, relay state, or numeric sensor reading. Those actions are handled by deterministic reducers that produce visual projections on the canvas. Plans, project state, session logs, and snapshots also carry hashes so Schematic can track exactly which project and behavior produced a preview. For code editing, we integrated Monaco Editor and built a durable multi-file document system. Source files have revisions and content hashes so an agent cannot silently overwrite code that the human edited in the meantime. Projects are stored locally in the browser using IndexedDB, keeping the core workspace browser-side rather than requiring a separate project server. For the hackathon, we built a native WebMCP layer exposing the workspace as structured tools. All WebMCP operations call the same application commands as the visual interface, which keeps human actions and model actions consistent. The deployed version runs as a ChatGPT Site and can be used directly from ChatGPT's WebMCP-capable in-app browser. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was deciding where the agent's authority should stop. Giving a model generic access to application state would have taken less work, but it also would have made the system unpredictable and difficult to trust. Hardware makes that especially dangerous because a plausible-looking result is not necessarily a valid one. We instead built explicit schemas and operations around components, connections, behavior, and code. Unsupported component behavior fails instead of being guessed. Another challenge was keeping generated code and behavior preview honest. It would be tempting to make a visual LED turn on and imply that the firmware caused it. But without actually compiling that firmware and running it against a hardware or electrical simulator, that claim would be misleading. Schematic therefore treats the Behavior Plan as the source of truth for the visual preview and generated source as a separate editable artifact. The UI keeps track of their relationship and can mark the connection stale when either side changes. We also had to solve collaboration problems that normally only appear once both a human and an agent can modify the same workspace, including stale writes, destructive actions, project isolation, imports, state recovery, and persistence. Accomplishments that we're proud of The model can build and inspect structured hardware projects through 56 native WebMCP tools while the person retains a visual, editable representation of every change. Both sides use the same validation and application logic. An agent can search for components, construct a hardware graph, inspect ports, connect components, diagnose invalid connections, discover supported behaviors, create a Behavior Plan, invoke events, preview outcomes, generate multi-file code, inspect existing source, and export the project for an external development workflow. At the same time, the system keeps clear provenance about what was actually validated and what was not. That combination of agent capability and human inspectability is what we think makes Schematic different. What we learned The biggest thing we learned is that giving an AI more tools is not automatically the same as giving it a better interface. The useful part of WebMCP is not simply that a model can call functions from a webpage. It is that the website can expose its own concepts to the agent. For Schematic, those concepts are not generic UI actions like "click here" or "change this field." They are hardware concepts such as components, ports, connections, behaviors, validation, projects, and code documents. Once those concepts become part of the agent interface, the collaboration model changes completely. The agent can reason about the same structured environment the human sees, while the human can inspect the consequences of that reasoning directly. What's next for Schematic The long-term goal is to make Schematic the workspace between an idea and real hardware. We want to expand the component and behavior library, improve automated layout and design assistance, add deeper electrical validation, make agent-generated behavior easier to inspect and modify visually, and create stronger handoff paths into real toolchains and physical boards. Eventually, a user should be able to start with something as simple as: "Build me a device that measures room temperature and warns me when it gets too hot." The agent should be able to turn that into a complete visible prototype, explain every part of the design, let the user modify it directly, update itself around those changes, prepare the software, and carry the project toward real hardware without losing the context established between the human and the agent. Schematic is our attempt at making hardware creation feel less like asking an AI for instructions and more like actually building something together.
