title: Lockstep
pitch: A co-op puzzle you play with WebMCP
about_excerpt: A co-op puzzle you play with WebMCP Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every agentic web demo I'd seen was an agent doing a chore for someone. You hand over the wheel, look away, and hope. That framing treats the human as an obstacle to route around. Co-op games already solve this. In Portal 2 's co-op campaign, the level design makes you need the other player. You can't brute-force past a partner — you have to talk to them. So I built that, with an AI agent as player two. Not an assistant. A teammate who is genuinely stuck without you. What it does You control the human. An AI agent controls the robot. Coloured pressure plates hold coloured doors open. Step off the plate and the door slams. The plate that opens your door is only reachable by the robot — and vice versa. That's not decorative. A solver verifies it: on every level, the human cannot reach their goal if the robot never moves. The agent gets six WebMCP tools — read the board, move the robot, hint, reset, change level, and speak to you . What it cannot do is move your character. There is no tool for that. I never wrote one. So when it needs you on a plate, it has no mechanism except to ask and wait. That missing tool is the whole design. It's what turns "watch an AI solve a puzzle" into "solve a puzzle with an AI." Three levels, ending with one where you must walk into the robot's lane, hold its door with your body, then clear out before it can pass. How we built it Vanilla JavaScript. No framework, no build step, no dependencies. Five static files on Vercel. levels.js — level data, movement rules, and a breadth-first solver over the joint state space: every combination of (human position, robot position) . It runs unmodified in Node, so before designing a single pixel I could ask each candidate level two questions — is it solvable , and is it solvable with the robot frozen . I needed a yes and a no. Anything solvable single-handed got thrown out. game.js — engine, renderer, input, and a built-in agent that drives the same public API the tools call. It recomputes the joint solution after every move, then executes only the robot's half. When the next optimal move is yours, it stops, marks your tile, and asks. webmcp.js — six tools with schemas and descriptions written for a model, not a developer. Registration is defensive across five API shapes with a 10-second retry, since the surface is still moving between browsers. The decision I'd defend hardest: the tool descriptions carry the game rules. get_game_state returns an ASCII board, a legend, and a plain-English rule string. An agent that's never seen this game plays it correctly first try, because the page taught it how. Challenges we ran into Making the agent a partner, not a cutscene. My first version computed the joint solution and executed all of it — moving both characters, finishing the level while I watched. Technically impressive, completely pointless. The fix: compute the joint plan, execute only your half. That's the difference between a demo and a game. One CSS line that silently broke everything. I had .intro { position:fixed; inset:0; z-index:400; display:grid; } and closed the overlay with element.hidden = true . But display:grid overrides the hidden attribute. The overlay never went away — it sat at z-index:400 swallowing every click. The game underneath ran perfectly the whole time. Nothing reached it. I lost hours debugging game logic that had nothing wrong with it. No way to test any of it. That bug got through because I was verifying code by reading it. No Puppeteer, no Playwright, not even jsdom available. So I wrote a minimal DOM shim from scratch — enough createElement , getElementById , classList and event dispatch to load the real files and click things programmatically. It caught a second bug in minutes: the restart button threw LS is not defined from an implicit global. Two real bugs in the first five minutes of having tests, in code I'd convinced myself was correct. Accomplishments that we're proud of The missing tool. The most important decision in this project is a function I never wrote. Restraint in a tool surface turned out more expressive than another capability. Provable co-dependency. "You need each other" is easy to claim, hard to guarantee. The test suite searches from the human's start with the robot frozen and asserts the goal is unreachable — on every level. Design intent, verified by machine. 41 passing assertions on a hackathon project , using a DOM shim I had to write myself. It degrades gracefully. Built-in agent, hands-free auto-solve, or a real WebMCP agent. The first two need no special browser — whatever a judge is running, it works. What we learned Semantic tools beat pixel-guessing by more than I expected. A screenshot agent would have to infer that an amber tile is a door, that an outlined square is a plate, and that they're causally linked. get_game_state just says so. Watching an agent play correctly first try made the WebMCP argument concrete in a way reading the spec hadn't. Write tool descriptions for the model, not yourself. Rewriting them as instructions to a collaborator — "you control ONLY the robot, never the human" — measurably improved behaviour. Test the wiring, not just the logic. Both bugs that cost me time lived in the seam between JavaScript and the DOM. The pure functions were fine. It was the glue that broke. What's next for Lockstep Asymmetric information — tiles only one of you can read, so the conversation carries real information instead of just coordination. Latency as a mechanic — timed levels where the agent's thinking time becomes part of the puzzle. A level editor with the solver attached , rejecting any level solvable alone at design time. Community levels with a machine-checked co-op guarantee. Two-agent mode — the tool surface doesn't care who's holding it. Beyond the game. Agent handles reach and speed, human holds the actions that need a person, both negotiating in the same view. That's the shape of any high-stakes agentic workflow. Lockstep is the smallest legible version of it. title: Unspoiled
pitch: Read Wikipedia without learning the ending.
about_excerpt: Read Wikipedia without learning the ending. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Wikipedia does not use spoiler warnings. That is a deliberate policy, settled in 2007 after a long debate, and it is not going to change: the plot section of every film, series and novel article states the ending as plainly as it states the release date. So looking up one fact about a show you are halfway through means reading around the ending and hoping. The obvious answer — ask a model to summarise the article carefully — throws away the article. You get one paraphrase, mediated and unverifiable, and you have lost the thing you came for. We wanted the real page, still navigable, with the parts you have not earned yet held back. What it does Unspoiled is a Wikipedia reader whose masking is driven by your agent. The agent reads the article on your behalf, decides which sentences would spoil it for you , and the page enforces that decision sentence by sentence — with every decision, and its reason, printed on your screen where you can overrule it. On the Breaking Bad article, the page's own presets withhold 203 of 738 sentences before an agent says anything. Tell your agent you finished season three and it opens exactly those seasons — 49 sentences in one call — and leaves season four closed. Why WebMCP is the right fit The division of labour is the whole idea: The page knows the article. Which sentences exist, which section they sit in, which of them read like a giveaway. The agent knows the reader. Which seasons they finished, whether they read the source manga, how much they want to know before watching. "What counts as a spoiler" is the intersection of those two, and neither party holds both halves. And because the agent can leave rules behind in the page, that intersection is not consumed by one answer: it keeps applying to the next article you open, with or without the agent present. To be straight about the boundary: a bespoke backend plus a frontend could reproduce this behaviour. What WebMCP contributes is that the live page exposes semantic operations over its own local state — no server integration to build, no screen-coordinate automation to break, and the article never leaves the reader's machine except as the Wikipedia request itself. What people and agents do together here The agent decides; the page enforces and shows its work. apply_mask takes sections, paragraphs or individual sentence ids to show or hide, and one thing it cannot omit: a reason. Every call is announced the moment it happens — "Your agent showed 6 sentences and hid 20", with the reason on the line below — and kept in "Agent activity" at the foot of the article, newest first, timestamped. A call that matched nothing is still a row, reading "0 shown · 0 hidden": an agent cannot quietly decide nothing. You can overrule any of it, on the page. Tap an opened sentence and it closes again. Click a withheld band and it opens. Your action writes the same shown/hidden sets the agent writes, and it is the last word — the reader's hand is above the agent's, which is above the page's own heuristics. What the agent read is visible too. read_article_content is ungated on purpose: your agent reads the whole article, because that is what it takes to judge what would spoil it for you. So the page says so, in a banner across the top: "Your agent has read: Episodes, Season 1 (2008), Season 2 (2009) and 9 more — in this conversation your agent knows what those sections say, even where the page still withholds them." The honest shape of this app is not "the agent is kept ignorant" — for a famous work the model likely knows the ending from training anyway. It is that the asymmetry runs the other way: your agent knows the article, you do not yet, and what reaches your eyes is a decision you can inspect and reverse. What the agent writes outlives the conversation. This is the part a chat cannot do at all. With add_rules the agent turns what it learned about you into standing rules for the page: literal phrases that come off the page wherever they appear, in this article and in every article you open after it. Each rule needs a label and a reason, and the label must not contain its own phrases — the call is rejected if it does, because the label is what you will see. The phrases themselves sit behind a "Show phrases" button you may never press, so a rule can be audited, and removed, without the audit spoiling you. In the demo one rule takes Breaking Bad from 154 withheld sentences to 184; following a link to Jesse Pinkman , with no agent involved, it is still withholding 54 there. And it works with no agent at all. Five named presets — Show everything, Ending only, Major spoilers, Spoiler-safe, Maximum protection — run the page's own wording heuristics, grouped into categories (death, identity, outcome, relationship, ending, return). On Breaking Bad that is 38 / 161 / 203 / 508 of 738 sentences. The agent raises the ceiling; it is not the floor. How we built it A static Vite + React + TypeScript app on Vercel. No backend: article text is fetched straight from the MediaWiki action=parse API in the browser, which allows CORS. The page parses an article into sections, paragraphs and sentences, then applies a two-level risk ladder: narrative and analysis sections (Plot, Episodes, Themes, Series overview, あらすじ) are withheld wholesale, while everything else is judged sentence by sentence against reveal wording. Withheld text is never in the DOM — a withheld paragraph is drawn as a band whose height scales with how much is hidden ("3 sentences withheld · 251 chars · reveal"), never as real text behind a blur. Opening sentences animates as a single stream of words, and tapping one closes it again. Five tools are registered on document.modelContext : open_article — the outline with per-section ids, risk and withheld counts read_article_content — full text with paragraph and sentence ids and a shown flag apply_mask — show/hide by section, paragraph or sentence id, with a required reason add_rules — labelled phrase rules that persist across articles and sessions, never echoing the phrases get_masking_report — counts, decisions, rules by label, sections read — and no article text English and Japanese Wikipedia are both supported, internal links open inside Unspoiled and the browser's back button walks the articles you came through, light/dark/system themes are respected, and the reader works on a phone. 508 tests cover the risk scoring, the tool surface and the reader's precedence over the agent. Challenges we ran into Everything returned to the agent is a leak surface. The first version happily put a withheld heading in a tool result's reason field — "hidden because 'Series finale' gives away the ending" — which hands over the spoiler while claiming to protect it. Reasons became fixed phrases that never interpolate article text, and no tool returns a withheld heading by default. Calibrating the ladder took real articles. An early version withheld the entire lead and Plot sections of everything; a later one hid the Sales and Manga sections of Attack on Titan , which spoil nothing. Wording heuristics also miss what has no giveaway words — "his mother is eaten by a Titan" — which is exactly the gap apply_mask exists to fill. Section headings are not enough on their own. Lost calls its plot "Series overview", so its per-season summaries scored as safe and stayed readable. The fix keys narrative sections off the whole heading path, so Series overview > Season 1 is plot while Reception > Critical reception > Season 1 stays readable. WebMCP as shipped has sharp edges. The API is document.modelContext , not navigator.modelContext . Tool arguments arrive as a JSON string and results are JSON-stringified. There is no image content type — a tool surface is text in, text out. There is no unregisterTool , and re-registering a name rejects with InvalidStateError , so registration has to be idempotent to survive React's double mount in development. And a page cannot initiate anything: there is no way to prompt the agent or even detect that one is attached, so tool descriptions are the only steering a page gets, and each of ours names the call that should come next. What we learned The claim we started with — "the agent can never learn the ending" — was not true, and building the thing is what showed us. For a famous work the model knows the ending from pretraining, and any sentence the reader opens becomes visible to the next tool call. What a page can actually promise is narrower and more useful: it controls what it transmits, it shows every decision and its reason, and it puts the reader's hand above the agent's. Writing the honest version of the claim made the product better, because it moved the value from a guarantee we could not keep to an audit trail we could. The second thing: the artifact matters. A summary is consumed once. A rule written into the page keeps working tomorrow, on the next article, with no

video_transcript_excerpt: This is Wikipedia. It has no spoiler warnings. That has been the policy since 2007. The plot section states the ending as plainly as the release date. Unspoiled is the same article, read through a page that holds things back. On its own, one slider does it. Now I bring an agent. It opens the article and reads it. All of it, and my page tells me so. Then it decides what I get to see, and that decision lands in the page, sentence by sentence. Nothing here is blurred. A withheld sentence is simply not in the page. I see how much is missing, and how long it is, but never the text. Here is the half only an agent has. It knows I stopped after season three, so it opens those seasons, and leaves season four closed. Forty-nine sentences, opened in a single call, because the agent knew which seasons I had already watched. Every decision comes with a reason it was made to give, kept in order for the whole session. And I am above it. Anything it hid, I can open with a tap. This is the part a summary cannot do. My agent writes the rule into the page. Labelled, with a reason, and without ever printing the words back at me. The phrases themselves stay behind a button I may never press. What I see is the label, and how much it takes off the page. And it stays. I open a linked article, no agent involved, and it is still protecting me. The page knows the article. The agent knows me. Neither could decide what counts as a spoiler alone.

title: Fantasy Premier League (FPL) WebMCP
pitch: Build, compare, and refine hypothetical FPL transfer plans with an AI agent on the same live squad workspace, without changing your real team and full access to all FPL data
about_excerpt: Build, compare, and refine hypothetical FPL transfer plans with an AI agent on the same live squad workspace, without changing your real team and full access to all FPL data Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Fantasy Premier League decisions involve constant trade-offs between form, fixtures, budget, and risk. We wanted to make that process collaborative, so a manager and an AI agent can inspect the same squad, make competing plans, and refine them together without touching the user’s real FPL team. What it does FPL Planner is a read-only transfer-planning workspace. Users load a public FPL team ID, create hypothetical transfer drafts, compare budgets and points hits, and change their starting XI, bench order, captain, and vice-captain. The agent uses WebMCP tools to inspect squads and drafts, search players, create transfer scenarios, edit lineups, and query local Premier League history. Every transfer remains hypothetical. How we built it We built the app with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and the public FPL API. The app fetches live player, squad, fixture, and entry data, then checks FPL rules locally, including budget, position quotas, club limits, transfer costs, and legal formations. We added a local dataset of four Premier League seasons so historical results can be queried without web search. WebMCP exposes structured tools for draft reading, player queries, transfer scenarios, lineup changes, and historical match analysis. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was modelling FPL transfers accurately while keeping the interface simple. Every change can affect budget, free transfers, points hits, squad validity, captaincy, bench order, and draft history. We also had to make human and agent changes work together. A draft should remain editable regardless of whether the user or agent created it. Finally, we adapted the caching strategy for deployment. Local in-memory caching works during development, but a serverless deployment needs shared caching and explicit refresh behaviour. Accomplishments that we're proud of We created a genuinely collaborative planning experience rather than a chatbot that only gives recommendations. The agent can work on the exact draft the user is viewing, while the user can inspect every decision, restore original players, make their own changes, and compare versions. The app also uses structured WebMCP tools instead of relying on UI scraping or ambiguous browser actions. What we learned We learned that the best agent experience is shared control, not full automation. Clear, narrow tools with validation make agent actions more reliable and understandable. We also learned that live-data apps need thoughtful caching, refresh behaviour, and transparent constraints to build user trust. What's next for Fantasy Premier League (FPL) WebMCP We want to improve draft comparison, add richer transfer explanations, and give the agent more ways to evaluate fixture runs and long-term squad plans. We would also expand historical analysis, support more advanced planning strategies, and make the app easier to use across more devices while preserving the same transparent, read-only workflow. title: λ-SPEC WebMCP
pitch: Resilience you can delegate. Evidence you can audit.
about_excerpt: Resilience you can delegate. Evidence you can audit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Rich analytical web apps are easy for humans to use but brittle for agents. A browser agent normally has to infer intent from forms, synthesize clicks, and scrape charts back out of the DOM. λ-SPEC explores a better contract: a scientific web application that exposes its real domain capabilities directly to an agent while keeping the human in the same visible workspace. What it does λ-SPEC measures observed system–environment coupling and asks what remains when environmental support is progressively withdrawn. It computes coupling λ, complementary fragility Φ, rolling λ and dλ/dt, an environmental-withdrawal stress envelope, ranked measured environmental drivers, confidence, limitations and exportable evidence. For the WebMCP Challenge, λ-SPEC was extended with eight typed WebMCP tools. An agent can discover datasets, load and configure a demo, run the resilience analysis, inspect the current evidence, inspect the withdrawal envelope, ask an evidence-bounded interpreter and run an end-to-end collaboration workflow. Why WebMCP is essential The agent is not clicking buttons or scraping charts. document.modelContext.registerTool(...) exposes the underlying analysis contract with constrained JSON schemas, read-only annotations and explicit validation. Tool calls update the same in-page state the human sees. A person can manually change the method, rolling window or column roles and then ask the agent to continue from that exact revised state. That human→agent handoff is the core improvement: both sides operate on one visible scientific state instead of maintaining separate hidden automation contexts. How we built it Challenge-specific implementation lives in lambda_spec/static/webmcp.js . The registered tools are: list_resilience_demos load_resilience_demo configure_resilience_analysis run_resilience_analysis get_resilience_state inspect_environmental_withdrawal ask_resilience_evidence run_resilience_collaboration Inputs are bounded with enums, limits, uniqueness constraints and validation against the active dataset. WebMCP progressively enhances the app: if document.modelContext is unavailable, λ-SPEC still works normally for a human. Existing project vs. challenge work λ-SPEC v1.2 existed before the challenge with its analysis engine, demos, charts, CSV workflow, exports and evidence interpreter. The WebMCP layer was added during the challenge period beginning at commit b40ec1f6ff4d2ff2f506b08331f69fe678754499 . Subsequent challenge commits add tool registration, shared human/agent state, tests, deployment configuration and judge materials. How to test Open the live app in a WebMCP-capable browser/runtime and ask: Analyze the orbital telemetry demo. Tell me whether measured coupling is strengthening or weakening, inspect the environmental-withdrawal envelope, identify the strongest measured environmental drivers, and tell me what to investigate next. Stay within the measured evidence. Then manually change the coupling method or rolling window and ask: Inspect the current resilience state again and continue from the state I changed. The floating WebMCP · human + agent workspace panel reports agent activity visibly. Scope and limitations λ-SPEC measures observed coupling. It does not establish causality, provide clinical diagnosis, certify engineering safety, make financial suitability determinations, or guarantee forecasts. The withdrawal curve is a controlled signal-removal stress envelope, not a literal simulation of every real-world intervention. My contribution covered system architecture, AI workflow design, WebMCP integration, UX/product design, implementation, testing, and demonstration. I designed the human-agent interaction model so AI agents can understand available web capabilities, execute structured actions, and return useful results while preserving human oversight. I focused the platform on health and education use cases, translating complex workflows into accessible, explainable, agent-ready experiences. I also coordinated the project positioning, technical narrative, public demo, and final Devpost submission. title: ReStock
pitch: Wholesale buyers order in messy plain language. Restock gives distributor sites a WebMCP tool layer that resolves those requests to real SKUs — and knows when to ask instead of guess.
about_excerpt: Wholesale buyers order in messy plain language. Restock gives distributor sites a WebMCP tool layer that resolves those requests to real SKUs — and knows when to ask instead of guess. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration My brother has a phone accessories store. Every time he restocks, he sends his supplier a message like: 2 cases of 6ft usb c braided black, 10 tempered glass for the 14 pro, 3 chargers And then somebody on the other end sits down and turns that into SKUs by hand. In a wholesale catalog that last line might be listed as WL CHGR 65W SINGLE USB PRT BLK REMAX . It takes twenty minutes and usually a phone call to confirm. Every order, every week. I assumed for a long time that this was a search problem. It isn't. Software that tries to solve it by matching ends up guessing, the buyer receives the wrong charger, and after that happens once nobody trusts the automation again. What the person on the other end is actually good at is knowing which lines they can fill and which ones they have to ask about . What it does Restock makes a distributor's ordering portal something an AI agent can operate directly. The demo storefront, Harbor Wireless Supply , has 243 SKUs named the way wholesale catalogs actually name things: abbreviations, inconsistent casing, pack units that don't match how buyers talk. An agent passes the buyer's raw sentence to resolve_order and gets back a decision for each line. Resolved, with the reason stated. "2 cases of 6ft usb c braided black" comes back as SKU 10009 , Cable Usb-c 6ft Braided Black Premium , matched on cable, braided, USB-C, 6ft and black . The buyer said "cases" and the catalog sells EA, so Restock records both instead of quietly converting one into the other. Needs clarification. "3 chargers" really is ambiguous in this catalog, so instead of picking one Restock returns what separates the candidates (product type) and the three actual options: charger, car charger, wall charger. The agent asks the buyer and calls choose_option with the answer. Not found, said plainly. It never substitutes something close. submit_order refuses while any line is still unresolved , the same way the portal's own Confirm button stays disabled. Why WebMCP fits this problem Catalog resolution can't live in the agent. The distributor is the one who knows the catalog, the pricing, the pack units, what's in stock, and what counts as ambiguous in their own inventory. An agent scraping the page would have to reconstruct all of that from rendered HTML, and it would guess in exactly the places where the distributor would have asked. With WebMCP the site can publish that judgment as a tool contract instead. The agent handles the language, the site handles the catalog and decides what needs a question. What people and agents can now do together The part I find interesting isn't the matching, it's the question . When Restock returns NEEDS_CLARIFICATION it's telling the agent: this one is mine to ask, here's what to ask, here are the options to offer. That's backwards from how this normally works. Usually the agent decides when to bother the human. Here the website decides, because it's the one that knows where its own catalog is ambiguous, and the agent just carries the question to the buyer in whatever language the buyer speaks. The buyer answers once and the order closes. How I built it Next.js on Vercel. Five tools registered natively with document.modelContext.registerTool — no extension, no polyfill — and annotated so an agent knows which four only read and which one writes. Behind the tools there's lexical search over the catalog, an LLM pass that splits a sentence into order lines with quantities and units, and a decision layer that compares the surviving candidates for each line and works out what actually distinguishes them. If they differ on exactly one attribute, that attribute becomes the question . I validated it against a set of real buyer phrasings before wiring up any of the WebMCP part. The tools drive the same order draft the human UI does , so the application can't tell a tool call from a click. The order fills in on screen while the agent works. Challenges I ran into Getting the tools to work was easier than getting them to be honest. My first version threw exceptions with genuinely useful messages, like "1 line still needs clarification" . Agents never saw any of them — a thrown error arrives as a generic failure and the reason is gone. I also rendered a WebMCP status line server-side for my own debugging. Agents that read the served HTML saw it say the tools weren't ready yet, believed it , and stopped before ever trying to call anything. That one cost me most of an afternoon. And submit_order shipped with no annotations, so it wasn't classified as an action at all. Everything else was marked read-only, and the one tool that actually places the order was invisible as a thing an agent could do . None of these were visible from inside the app. They only showed up when I started calling my own tools the way an agent would . What's next Restock is meant to be infrastructure rather than a storefront : a hosted tool layer a distributor can point at their own catalog. The one in the demo is synthetic. Ingesting a real catalog is the next piece. title: Proust's Reader
pitch: Untangle the sentence, preserve the prose.
about_excerpt: Untangle the sentence, preserve the prose. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration “...savour in a momentary glimmer of consciousness the sleep into which were plunged the furniture, the room, that whole of which I was only a small part and whose insensibility I would soon return to share.” I stared at this sentence for three minutes. I understood every single word. I still did not understand the sentence. Damn it, Proust. While reading In Search of Lost Time , I realized that vocabulary was not my problem. Syntax was. My workaround was to leave the reading app, paste the sentence into ChatGPT, and read a long explanation. After doing this a few times, the interruption became exhausting. And I did not want a summary. I wanted Proust. Reading literature is not just about extracting meaning. It is also about rhythm, structure, metaphor, punctuation, and the way a sentence unfolds. I wanted just enough help to see how a difficult sentence works, without replacing it with AI-generated summaries. That is why I built Proust’s Reader . What it does Proust’s Reader is an EPUB reader. It helps you understand a difficult sentence by untangling its structure inside the original text. Highlight a confusing sentence, ask your agent for help, and it can use WebMCP tools to: Mark the spine — reveal the main subject, verb, and core structure. Unfold nested structure — show buried clauses and phrases, what they modify, and what they mean in context. Reorder the syntax — temporarily show the sentence in a more familiar word order. Show the plain meaning — only if you are still completely lost. The idea is to give progressively stronger hints instead of immediately flattening the sentence into a paraphrase. The original sentence always stays at the center. No separate AI explanation to mentally map back onto the book. No summaries. No turning Proust into bullet points. Just enough scaffolding to understand the sentence. And get back to reading. How I implemented WebMCP I exposed four WebMCP tools from the reader: mark_spine , unfold_nested_structure , reorder_syntax , and show_plain_meaning . When the reader highlights a sentence, the agent can discover these tools and invoke the one that matches the user’s request. The tool receives the selected sentence and nearby context, and the result is rendered back into the reader so the original sentence can be annotated, unfolded, reordered, or paraphrased directly on the page. I intentionally exposed several focused tools rather than one generic “explain this sentence” action, so the agent can choose how much assistance to provide. Why WebMCP fits in Prost's Reader For my case, WebMCP is especially useful because it helps preserve an immersive reading experience , even when I run into a sentence with a monstrous grammatical structure. (Damn it, Proust!) Instead of copying the sentence, leaving the book, and asking an AI to explain it somewhere else, I can ask for help and let the agent operate directly on the sentence I am already reading. More importantly, WebMCP makes the explanation interactive and visual . The agent can mark the grammatical spine, unfold nested phrases and clauses, or temporarily reorder the syntax. All happen inside the original text. That makes it much easier to see how the sentence is constructed, instead of reading another explanation and trying to map it back onto the book in my head. WebMCP makes this simple goal possible: get unstuck without leaving the reading experience. How people and agent collaborate in Prost's Reader People still do the reading. They decide when a sentence feels difficult, what kind of help they want, and when they are ready to return to the original text. The agent provides the scaffolding. It can use the reader’s WebMCP tools to reveal the sentence spine, unfold nested structures, reorder difficult syntax, or show a plain-English meaning when needed. Together, the reader and agent can work through a difficult sentence step by step without turning the experience into a separate AI conversation. The reader keeps control of the interpretation. The agent simply makes the structure easier to see. Instead of replacing difficult literature, they can now work through it together inside the text. title: GhostLayer — Agent Speed, Human Authority
pitch: GhostLayer gives agents fast, typed WebMCP tools while keeping consequential actions behind a visible human decision.
about_excerpt: GhostLayer gives agents fast, typed WebMCP tools while keeping consequential actions behind a visible human decision. Like Comment Story Updates A consequential call waits with zero drafts until human approval. Approval creates one tab-local fictional invoice; replay stays at one row. Two page-owned WebMCP tools are live and discoverable. Pause removes both tools from the agent surface; resume restores them. Inspiration Browser agents usually have to infer intent from interfaces designed for people: find the right control, interpret changing DOM structure, and guess whether an action is harmless or consequential. WebMCP changes that relationship. A website can publish an explicit capability with a typed contract instead of making an agent reverse-engineer the screen. We wanted to explore the product-design consequence of that shift, not only the reliability benefit. If an agent can act faster through declared tools, the application should become equally explicit about where human authority begins. GhostLayer asks a simple question: what if the agent could discover and prepare structured work immediately, while the website retained validation, effect preview, approval, rejection, lifecycle, and recovery at the point of consequence? What it does GhostLayer is a human-authority layer for product and platform teams exposing commerce, finance, support, and administrative actions through WebMCP. It keeps consequential work behind a human-owned commit boundary instead of giving an agent unchecked authority. The public Challenge Edition proves that product pattern in a fictional, client-only CRM sandbox with two page-owned WebMCP tools: find_customer performs an exact read-only lookup over three clearly fictional customer records and returns structured output. create_invoice_draft accepts a returned customer ID, a 1–160 character description, and a fictional amount from $0.01 to $5,000. It validates the input, then keeps the tool call pending while the site shows the exact effect for human review. Nothing is created while approval is pending. Rejecting, cancelling, expiring the two-minute window, pausing the agent surface, or resetting the sandbox creates no draft. Approval creates one tab-local demo draft. Repeating the same normalized approved request returns the existing invoice with replayed: true instead of adding another row. The human can pause the entire agent surface, which disposes both WebMCP registrations, and resume it to publish the same bounded contract again. Reset clears all fictional state in the current tab. Visible forms provide a transparent manual path through the same lookup, validation, approval, rejection, replay, pause, and reset behavior when native WebMCP is unavailable. The public challenge build intentionally contains no real customer data, login, application credentials, application API, D1 database, R2 bucket, external CRM, payment flow, or durable persistence. Reloading, closing, resetting, or opening a new tab starts clean. It demonstrates a governed interaction pattern; it does not claim durable or globally exactly-once execution. From sandbox to a production app A production team keeps its existing identity, policy, database, and business API. The request path becomes: agent request → typed WebMCP contract → GhostLayer review → authenticated, policy-checked backend commit → durable receipt returned to the agent. The public app proves the complete visible decision loop; production adopters connect server-side RBAC, durable idempotency, and audit storage at the same boundary. How we built it The challenge Site is a TypeScript application built with React 19 and Next.js 16 through Vinext/Vite for the OpenAI Sites runtime. The bounded adapter schema and WebMCP bridge began in the earlier GhostLayer 0.5 private prototype and are reused transparently here. The new challenge-period work is the standalone public native WebMCP experience: its judge sandbox, page-owned registration, visible approval, rejection and expiry semantics, replay protection, Pause/Resume lifecycle, Reset behavior, deployment isolation, and verification. The private owner application, extension, control plane, and credentials are not part of this submission. The tool contract in app/challenge-contract.ts defines the fictional records, exact-origin adapter, typed input and output schemas, and separate read and confirm risk levels. A shared WebMCP bridge feature-detects secure document.modelContext , registers the page-owned tools, validates adapter configuration and exact-origin availability, validates provider inputs and outputs, limits serialized tool results to 1,536 bytes, and uses an AbortController to dispose registrations with page or human-controlled lifecycle changes. The React application owns the consequential boundary. create_invoice_draft returns a promise that stays unresolved while the approval panel is visible. The panel shows the customer, description, amount, and two-minute decision window. Approval resolves the call after creating one in-memory draft; rejection, cancellation, expiry, pause, reset, or teardown rejects it without a write. A stable replay key is derived from the normalized customer ID, trimmed description, and amount in cents. State and a short eight-entry activity log remain in React memory, with an eight-draft-per-tab cap. Vitest uses deterministic fake timers to verify the exact two-minute expiry and tests schema validation, normalization, and replay-key stability. Playwright covers route isolation, absence of application API calls, tab isolation, zero-write rejection, approval, and the native WebMCP discovery/execution/replay/pause/resume chain in a compatible Chromium build. GhostLayer had an earlier private adapter/extension prototype. This standalone public Challenge Edition was created during the submission period as a new directly testable WebMCP application. The challenge-period work comprises the client-only judge sandbox, direct page-owned native tool registration, governed approval/rejection/expiry, same-tab replay, Pause/Resume and Reset controls, deployment isolation, and the accompanying automated verification. The dated public commit history records this package; the earlier owner-only prototype is not included or required to run the submission. Challenges we ran into An evolving API surface. WebMCP is experimental, and the current draft and available Chromium implementation can expose slightly different provider callback shapes. The bridge supports both without weakening validation or lifecycle cancellation. Waiting safely for a person. A consequential tool had to remain pending across visible review without silently committing, leaking an unresolved invocation, or writing after cancellation, expiry, pause, reset, or teardown. Replay without overclaiming. The demo needed to prevent duplicate rows for the same normalized request while staying honest that this is tab-local behavior, not durable cross-device idempotency. A genuinely safe public judge target. The experience had to be fully interactive without credentials, private routes, production data, persistent storage, or application API calls. Progressive availability. Native WebMCP is not available in every browser, so the manual forms needed to explain and exercise the same application-owned behavior without pretending to be an agent call. Accomplishments we are proud of A real WebMCP tool invocation remains pending until the person approves or rejects the exact effect. The visible invoice count stays at zero during review, and rejection or expiry creates nothing. An approved replay returns the same tab-local invoice rather than adding a duplicate row. One human control removes both tools from agent availability and can restore the bounded contract. Input and output validation, exact-origin checks, bounded provider output, and cancellation are enforced inside the provider path. The judge sandbox is useful without collecting or persisting user data and includes a manual fallback for incompatible browsers. Browser tests exercise both the visible safety behavior and the native WebMCP chain. What we learned Typed tools remove UI ambiguity, but the schema is only the beginning of a trustworthy WebMCP product. The application still needs to own validation, effect previews, approval semantics, cancellation, lifecycle disposal, replay behavior, and recovery. We also learned that human control is most convincing when it changes the capability surface itself. Pausing GhostLayer does not merely disable a button; it removes both registered tools. Finally, safe replay semantics must be described at their real scope. The current sandbox can prove same-tab duplicate prevention, while durable idempotency, authorization, and multi-tenant isolation belong in a separately reviewed server-backed system. What's next Test the provider bridge against additional browser implementations as the WebMCP draft evolves. Extract the visible governed-approval bound

title: Tourbrick
pitch: Tourbrick is a voice OS for tour operators to create tours using voice commands
about_excerpt: Tourbrick is a voice OS for tour operators to create tours using voice commands Like Comment Story Updates Torubrick: The AI operating system for tourism professionals Tourbrick — About the project Tagline A shared WebMCP workplace where tour operators, travellers, and their AI agents co-create trips together. Inspiration I am a tour guide and tour operator. A good private trip depends on hundreds of details that do not fit neatly into a booking form: relationships with suppliers, scenic roads, seasonal nuances, great meals, rooms with a view, and my professional experience. Much of this knowledge still lives in documents, messages, and people’s heads. Traditional back-office software can store records, but it struggles to create interesting, inspiring trips with local specifics. General AI can suggest a generic itinerary, but it does not know what the tour company can actually provide, and it should not make silent changes to operational records. That's why we create Tourbrick — a space where professional tour operators and AI agents can work together. What it does Our demonstration begins with a real kind of request that is difficult to serve from a catalogue: a couple wants to spend five days travelling around Estonia and experience the sauna culture. The company has no pre-designed tour for that. First, ChatGPT uses Tourbrick’s WebMCP tools to read the original message and turn it into a structured brief. Then, ChatGPT can search Tourbrick’s inventory: individual experiences, suppliers, accommodation options, transfers, etc. From those records, it can assemble a custom trip around four sauna experiences grounded in the real-world services that we work with. Tourbrick turns the selected records into a five-day itinerary with a stored road route and a timetable for every day. The manager can open day three and see breakfast, the drive south, lunch, the Mooska smoke-sauna experience, the hotel, and dinner in chronological order. Each item remains connected to its supplier record, rate, duration, and conditions. Costs are grouped into accommodation, experiences, transportation, and meals, with every line behind the total. Nothing is silently committed. Tourbrick first creates a no-write preview. The manager can inspect, edit, or reject it; accepting saves exactly the reviewed version. It does not book a supplier, send a message, or take payment. Once reviewed, the same trip becomes a customer presentation. For this prototype, we created a sauna-led presentation to give it a personal feeling instead of the fixed website template. The customer page is also WebMCP-enabled. Travellers can open it with their own ChatGPT, focus a specific day, and prepare feedback such as: “Could we replace day two’s spa with a quieter countryside sauna?” Why WebMCP A conventional MCP server can expose a database or service even when no webpage is open. That is useful, but it is not the experience we wanted to create. With WebMCP, the webpage itself becomes the integration and the shared workspace. ChatGPT discovers the tools offered by the page the person is currently viewing and works in the same live context. The manager and the agent can look at the same request, map, timetable, and cost review. When the traveller opens the public proposal, their ChatGPT discovers a separate, customer-safe set of tools without requiring access to the operator’s workspace or a separately configured Tourbrick MCP connection. Before this, an operator had to manually reconcile records across spreadsheets and back-office screens, or copy incomplete context into a chat. Customer feedback arrived separately and then had to be matched back to the right trip and day. With Tourbrick, both agents work against the relevant structured version while people see and control the decisions on the page. What we built during the hackathon Tourbrick builds on an existing tour-operations product direction and domain model. During the WebMCP Challenge, we created the agent collaboration layer and the complete end-to-end experience demonstrated in the video: Tour operator tools for reading customer requests, publishing grounded briefs, searching inventory, previewing and creating custom trips, inspecting saved versions, and opening exact itinerary days. A visible operator journey from an ordinary customer message to a mapped, costed, day-by-day and hour-by-hour private trip. Preview-before-write controls, explicit approval, content hashes, immutable versions, idempotency protection, and loud rejection of stale data. Persisted Mapbox routes that are calculated when a new connection is needed and then reused rather than recalculated on every view. A separate customer presentation with three public, customer-safe WebMCP tools for reading the shared proposal, focusing a day, and drafting an unsent change request. Live deployments for both operator and customer experiences, plus the public source repository, setup instructions, and automated tests. How we built it The operator and customer interfaces use React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. Each top-level page registers typed tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , including a clear name, description, JSON input schema, execution handler, and read/write annotations. The application API is built with FastAPI and Pydantic, with PostgreSQL storing inventory, requests, immutable trip versions, customer presentations, and reusable route geometry. Mapbox provides road routing. The customer presentation runs against a separate public-only backend that does not expose manager routes, API documentation, or the operator MCP surface. The most difficult part was making agent work operationally trustworthy. A proposal can combine many records and prices, so approval is bound to the exact preview the manager saw. We also had to keep route legs connected to real timetable transfers so the map and itinerary describe the same journey. The finished workflow was tested end to end using ChatGPT’s in-app browser. The public repository’s 209 frontend tests and 203 backend tests cover tool registration, validation, approvals, versioning, routing, customer isolation, and the visible workflows. What we learned The important change about WebMCP is that the human interface and the agent interface no longer need to be separate products. The page can expose precise actions while still giving the person a map, itinerary, evidence, costs, and a clear approval boundary. We also learned that different people should not receive the same tools. The operator can search inventory and create a trip; the traveller can read the shared proposal and prepare feedback. Both collaborate with AI around the same journey, but Tourbrick preserves the responsibilities and access of each participant. What’s next The sauna presentation demonstrates a larger direction: customer proposals do not have to be forced into one fixed website template. An agent could compose the presentation around what matters to that particular traveller — saunas for this trip, wildlife, food, architecture, or accessibility for another — while the underlying itinerary remains structured and reviewable. The next product steps are live supplier availability, contracted rates, richer operator permissions, and turning confirmed customer feedback into a manager-reviewed itinerary revision. For my business — and for more than a million tour operators like me — WebMCP moves AI out of a separate chat window and into the work itself. Built With codex python typescript Try it out webmcp.tourbrick.com trips.tourbrick.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Alex Farlander Karit Jaakson Like Share this project: Updates Alex Farlander started this project — Sep 03, 2026 04:40 PM EDT

title: AutoWebMCP: Teach an Agent to Fish
pitch: Turn human workflows into agent-ready WebMCP tools. AutoWebMCP learns what a user means, not just where they click, and publishes verified, typed semantic capabilities with guardrails.
about_excerpt: Turn human workflows into agent-ready WebMCP tools. AutoWebMCP learns what a user means, not just where they click, and publishes verified, typed semantic capabilities with guardrails. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a semantic interface for agents. But what about the enormous number of applications that were never built to expose one? Most browser automation approaches teach agents where to click or how to reproduce a sequence of UI actions. That makes the agent depend on interface mechanics rather than application meaning. We asked a different question: What if a user could teach an application a capability simply by demonstrating how they already perform the task? AutoWebMCP turns those demonstrations into agent-ready WebMCP tools. Teach → Semanticize → Validate → Publish → Agent The key idea is simple: the demonstration is evidence, not the automation. What it does A user performs a normal workflow while the AutoWebMCP Teach Mode extension observes the interaction. AutoWebMCP analyzes that evidence and proposes a typed semantic capability representing what the user intended, rather than exposing individual clicks as agent actions. For example, a human editing several controls in Salesforce can become: update_opportunity_details(opportunity_id, stage, close_date, main_sponsor) The user reviews and confirms the semantic contract. AutoWebMCP then establishes an execution binding, validates it against the live application, and publishes the capability as a WebMCP tool. The resulting pipeline is: Human demonstration → Semantic capability → Execution binding → WebMCP tool → Agent We tested this with two very different applications. SignalBase is a cooperative application. AutoWebMCP can bind a learned capability to an action supplied by the application itself. Salesforce Lightning is the harder case. It was not built for AutoWebMCP, so learned capabilities execute against the application's existing interface through the AutoWebMCP runtime. To an agent, both appear as semantic WebMCP tools with names, descriptions, typed schemas, identity requirements, and safety semantics. In our demo, one natural-language instruction composes three independently taught capabilities: Find a VP-level contact in SignalBase. Search Salesforce for the relevant Opportunity and obtain its exact record identity. Update that Opportunity. The sequence is not hardcoded. The model chooses among the live WebMCP tools using their published descriptions, schemas, and results. How we built it AutoWebMCP has three main parts. Teach Mode is a Chrome extension that captures evidence while a user performs a workflow. It observes the interaction without treating the resulting event sequence as a replay script. Training Studio turns that evidence into a semantic capability. A model proposes the business intent, capability name, description, and typed inputs. The user reviews and confirms that contract before publication. The demonstration alone is not enough to safely execute the capability. AutoWebMCP combines observed evidence with platform, application, and tenant intelligence to help ground concepts such as business meaning, valid value domains, entity identity, tenant-specific vocabulary, execution semantics, and verification behavior. Critically, the semantic contract remains separate from the execution binding . An agent operates on concepts such as stage , close_date , and opportunity_id , while the runtime resolves how those concepts map to the application when the capability executes. We do not persist CSS selectors, XPath expressions, or screen coordinates as the semantic contract. Finally, WebMCP is the publication surface . Confirmed capabilities are compiled into tools with descriptions, typed input schemas, required fields, value domains where known, and supported annotations. For the cross-application demonstration, we also built a small page-side agent harness over the actual WebMCP API. On every step it: reads the current tools from document.modelContext.getTools() gives those descriptions and schemas to the model validates the selected tool and arguments against the live tool set invokes the tool through document.modelContext.executeTool() feeds the structured result back to the model for its next decision There is no separately hardcoded SignalBase-to-Salesforce workflow. The model has to infer the composition from the semantic tools it is given. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem turned out not to be recording browser interactions. It was deciding when an inferred capability is trustworthy enough for an agent to use. A demonstration contains incomplete and sometimes ambiguous evidence. A field label may be tenant-specific. A choice may have a constrained value domain. Two records can have similar names. A successful request does not necessarily mean the intended state was persisted. That pushed AutoWebMCP toward a stronger principle: Search may be fuzzy. Mutation must be exact. Writes therefore require an exact target identity, and execution verifies both the target and the requested outcome. If the runtime cannot establish what happened, it reports uncertainty instead of manufacturing success or blindly repeating a potentially committed mutation. Testing against a live Salesforce org exposed failure modes we would not have found in a controlled demo. Navigation can destroy the browser context waiting for an execution result. Browser extension service workers can disappear between captured events. A mutation can succeed even when its caller never receives the result. Those failures shaped the runtime's guardrails, retry semantics, target-identity checks, and distinction between requested state and verified state. Cross-application composition created another challenge. WebMCP tools belong to documents, while our demo combines a capability taught from SignalBase with capabilities backed by Salesforce. We therefore made publication location explicit and created a control surface where selected capabilities can coexist while still being invoked through the WebMCP API. Accomplishments that we're proud of The biggest accomplishment is that the original idea survived contact with a real enterprise application. We demonstrated the full loop: demonstrate → semanticize → human confirm → bind → live validate → publish → discover → compose → execute → verify The same learning pipeline supports two very different execution strategies: a cooperative application-provided binding in SignalBase and a learned browser execution binding against Salesforce Lightning. We are particularly proud that the agent-facing abstraction is semantic rather than mechanical. The agent sees: update_opportunity_details(...) not: click_button(...) → fill_input(...) → choose_option(...) → click_save(...) We also demonstrated model-driven composition across independently taught capabilities. From one business instruction, the agent selected a SignalBase contact capability, a Salesforce Opportunity search capability, and a Salesforce update capability based on the published WebMCP metadata and prior tool results. The safety behavior became an accomplishment of its own. AutoWebMCP can refuse to mutate an entity it cannot identify, distinguish an attempted change from a verified outcome, stop when a write may already have persisted, and preserve ambiguity rather than silently choosing among multiple candidate records. Those are not theoretical safeguards. Several were added after the corresponding failure happened during live testing. What we learned Our biggest learning is that turning a demonstration into an agent capability is fundamentally different from recording a macro . The interaction trace tells us what happened. It does not, by itself, tell us what the action means. The difficult work lies in extracting a durable semantic contract from imperfect evidence, grounding that contract in the application's concepts and environment, and then resolving it safely when an agent invokes the capability later. We also learned that semantic understanding and execution should remain separate. A stable concept such as close_date should not become synonymous with whatever DOM element happened to represent Close Date during the demonstration. And we learned that verification is part of the capability, not an afterthought. For autonomous systems, "I attempted the action" and "I established that the intended state now exists" are materially different outcomes. This changed how we think about AutoWebMCP. What began as an experiment in automatically generating WebMCP tools increasingly looks like a semantic capability compiler . What's next for AutoWebMCP: Teach an Agent to Fish WebMCP is the first publication target, but the learned semantic capability does not inherently belong to WebMCP. The same architecture could eventually publish a confirmed capability through WebMCP, an external MCP server, an API, or another agent runtime while preserving the semantic
video_transcript_excerpt: What if you could teach existing web applications to become agent ready without programming every tool by hand? For this demo, AutoWebMCP has learned three capabilities across two applications. Signal base can find right contact, Salesforce can search and update opportunity. These are published as typed WebMCP tools, so I can give an agent one business level instruction. With these WebMCPs in place, I can in natural language ask my agent to perform a series of tasks. It first finds the VP in Signal base. It then realizes Salesforce update requires an exact opportunity identity, so it searches for the opportunity before attempting the update. Notice the guardrails. If Salesforce is not in the required state, the tool changes context but reports nothing was updated. A mutation only proceeds against the exact requested record. Finally, the system verifies both the resulting values and the target identity. The agent is working with semantic capabilities, not browser clicks. So, where do these tools come from? A user teaches AutoWebMCP simply by doing the work they already know. I start teach mode and perform the workflow normally. But AutoWebMCP is not recording just a macro. The interaction trace is evidence, not the automation. The interesting part happens next, where all these traces are sent to the studio. AutoWebMCP takes the evidence and tries to understand user's intent. Instead of exposing individual clicks, it proposes one business capability with a semantic description and typed inputs. Application and tenant intelligence help ground that capability in what the application means, what values are valid, and how it can safely execute. The semantic contract remains separate from the execution binding. The user reviews what AutoWebMCP understood, confirms it, and tests the binding against a live application. Only after the save is confirmed is the capability published as a WebMCP tool that an agent can discover and compose with other tools, as you saw in the first act. The user teaches by doing. AutoWebMCP semanticizes the intent. WebMCP makes the resulting capability available to agents. AutoWebMCP, teach an agent to fish.

title: Asympta World
pitch: Asympta World is a living AI world where people, businesses, and agents coordinate, trade, communicate, and complete real-world tasks together.\n
about_excerpt:
Asympta World is a living AI world where people, businesses, and agents coordinate, trade, communicate, and complete real-world tasks together.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but most of them still live inside isolated chat windows. 

 They can reason, search, plan, and use tools, yet the real world is not a single tool. A simple goal such as “prepare dinner for tonight” can involve understanding a person's preferences, finding nearby businesses, checking availability, purchasing goods, coordinating delivery, and adapting when something changes. 

 At the same time, businesses have their own agents, resources, schedules, inventory, and constraints. 

 We imagined a different interface for this future: 

 What if AI agents existed inside a shared world where people, businesses, services, and other agents could coordinate directly? 

 That became Asympta World . 

 Instead of showing AI as a sequence of hidden API calls, Asympta World turns agent activity into a visible, spatial, living system. You can watch agents move through the world, communicate, discover services, coordinate tasks, exchange information, and complete real-world workflows. 

 The inspiration is simple: 

 
 AI should not only answer. It should be able to participate. 
 

 

 What it does 

 Asympta World is a living AI world where people, businesses, and autonomous agents coordinate, communicate, trade, and complete real-world tasks together. 

 The interface is built around an explorable world map. 

 A person can give an agent a goal. The agent then begins moving through the world and interacting with the entities required to complete it. 

 For example, a task may involve: 

 
 understanding the user's intent, 
 discovering relevant businesses or services, 
 communicating requirements, 
 checking resources or availability, 
 coordinating multiple participants, 
 performing actions, 
 adapting when conditions change, 
 and returning the completed result to the user. 
 

 The important difference is that Asympta World models both sides of an interaction . 

 A restaurant is not simply an API endpoint. Its side of the world may have its own agent coordinating orders, ingredients, preparation, scheduling, communication, and delivery. 

 A supplier may interact with the restaurant. 

 A delivery service may interact with both. 

 The user's agent coordinates across all of them. 

 This creates something closer to a miniature digital economy than a traditional chatbot. 

 Asympta World also makes autonomous activity understandable: 

 
 agents visibly move toward relevant locations, 
 task progress reflects estimated completion time, 
 the camera can automatically follow active work, 
 agent status and communication can be observed, 
 scheduled tasks can exist inside the same world, 
 Auto Explore allows agents to discover useful next actions, 
 active parts of the map react visually when work is happening, 
 and the interface supports multiple languages across both UI and agent context. 
 

 The goal is to make autonomous systems feel observable, understandable, and alive instead of invisible. 

 

 How we built it 

 Asympta World is built as an interactive web application with a simulation and coordination layer underneath the visual world. 

 The world 

 The map acts as the primary interface rather than a traditional dashboard. 

 It is designed as a large, zoomable environment where agents, businesses, resources, and activity can exist spatially. 

 We developed a lightweight visual system that can display many active entities while keeping movement smooth and the interface readable. 

 The simulation engine 

 Underneath the map is a world simulation representing: 

 
 agents, 
 people, 
 businesses, 
 resources, 
 tasks, 
 workflows, 
 locations, 
 events, 
 and relationships. 
 

 Rather than hard-coding every interaction as an animation, the simulation maintains world state and lets the interface reflect what is actually happening. 

 This allows agents to move, exchange information, react to events, and participate in multi-step processes. 

 Agent workflows 

 Tasks are represented as sequences of coordinated actions. 

 An agent can transition through states such as discovery, travel, communication, negotiation, execution, waiting, and completion. 

 The visual world reflects those states. 

 We also built estimated workflow timing so that progress follows the expected duration of the underlying task rather than an arbitrary animation percentage. 

 Business-side simulation 

 One of the most important architectural decisions was to simulate more than the user's agent. 

 Businesses and services can participate as active entities in a workflow. 

 This lets us demonstrate agent-to-business, business-to-supplier, and multi-party coordination rather than treating every external service as a passive database lookup. 

 WebMCP and tool interaction 

 Asympta World is designed around the idea that agents should interact with capabilities exposed by the web instead of requiring every website to be manually rewritten into a custom integration. 

 WebMCP provides an important building block for this model: websites can expose structured capabilities that agents can discover and use. 

 Asympta World explores what happens when those capabilities exist inside a shared spatial coordination layer. 

 Instead of thinking: 

 User → Agent → Website 

 we started thinking in terms of: 

 Person ↔ Agent ↔ Business Agent ↔ Services ↔ Other Agents 

 with the world itself providing the context connecting them. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Making an agent feel like it actually exists in the world 

 It is easy to place an agent icon on a map. It is much harder to make the agent's movement correspond meaningfully to what the system is actually doing. 

 We had to connect task state, destination selection, animation, camera movement, and progress so that they behave as one system. 

 Showing complex activity without overwhelming the user 

 A real workflow can involve many simultaneous actions. 

 Displaying everything creates visual noise. Hiding everything makes the world feel fake. 

 We experimented with temporary activity indicators, contextual agent status, dialogue bubbles, fading map activity, automatic camera following, and progressive disclosure to find a better balance. 

 Modeling the supply side 

 Many agent demonstrations stop once an order is sent. 

 But the interesting part often begins after that. 

 A business may need to confirm inventory, prepare materials, coordinate staff, request something from a supplier, schedule fulfillment, and arrange delivery. 

 Representing these processes forced us to think about the world as a network of interacting systems instead of a single user's workflow. 

 Performance 

 A living world means many moving objects, effects, state transitions, and UI updates. 

 We repeatedly had to reduce unnecessary rendering work, control how much context was displayed at once, and make activity effects temporary rather than permanently accumulating. 

 The principle became: 

 
 The world can become more complex without rendering cost growing at the same rate. 
 

 Localization 

 Another unexpected challenge was keeping language changes consistent across a live simulation. 

 Static interface text is straightforward to translate. Dynamic agent statuses, workflow messages, task descriptions, and rapidly changing state are more difficult. 

 We had to treat language as part of the world state rather than merely translating the surrounding UI. 

 Designing something that feels like a product 

 It was easy for an agent simulation to start looking like a debugging dashboard. 

 We deliberately kept returning to the question: 

 Would somebody actually want to explore and use this? 

 That pushed us toward a calmer map interface, fewer permanent controls, contextual information, smoother motion, and a visual language closer to a real product than a developer demo. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The biggest accomplishment is that Asympta World became more than an animation of an AI agent. 

 It became a working model of a different way to think about agent interfaces. 

 We are particularly proud that: 

 
 agents visibly move through the environment as tasks pro

pitch: An agent-native local C2C marketplace enabling humans and AI agents to discover nearby secondhand deals, filter urgent BU (Butuh Uang) fast sales, and bargain via WebMCP.

An agent-native local C2C marketplace enabling humans and AI agents to discover nearby secondhand deals, filter urgent BU (Butuh Uang) fast sales, and bargain via WebMCP.

 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration & Problem Statement 

 Buying pre-owned goods on local peer-to-peer (C2C) platforms like Facebook Marketplace or OLX is notoriously tedious. Buyers spend hours manually filtering locations, calculating physical distances for COD (Cash On Delivery) meetups, and checking whether sellers are willing to negotiate or urgently selling ("BU / Butuh Uang"). 

 LocalMarket AI bridges this gap using WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) . By exposing structured tools directly to AI agents inside browser contexts (such as ChatGPT in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled), an AI agent can instantly assist users in finding nearby pre-owned items, filtering urgent deals, and negotiating prices. 

 What It Does 

 
 Distance Radius Filtering : Filters pre-owned items by physical COD distance (e.g. < 1 km , < 3 km , < 5 km ). 
 ⚡ BU (Butuh Uang) Deals Discovery : Instantly isolates urgent secondhand sales sold below standard market value. 
 WebMCP Price Bargaining : Exposes native make_offer tools allowing AI agents to negotiate prices and propose COD meetups automatically. 
 Interactive WebMCP Inspector : Built-in visual overlay displaying real-time tool registrations and executions. 
 

 WebMCP Implementation 

 LocalMarket AI implements window.document.modelContext.registerTool({...}) for 5 core tools: 

 
 search_nearby_deals : Filter listings by query, location radius (km), budget, and category. 
 filter_urgent_bu : Extract top urgent "BU (Butuh Uang)" bargains. 
 get_item_details : Retrieve seller verification score, item condition rating, and meetup locations. 
 make_offer : Submit custom price bargain offers and COD requests to sellers. 
 view_my_offers : Retrieve active user/agent offer shortlists. 
 

 How We Built It 

 
 Frontend : Clean, responsive dark-themed UI built with HTML5, Tailwind CSS, and Vanilla ES6 JavaScript. 
 Protocol Integration : Pure client-side WebMCP implementation with graceful degradation for standard browsers. 
 Dataset : Pre-owned item catalog enriched with geolocation metadata, seller verification ratings, and COD safety scores. 
 Testing : Fully tested with a 17-point automated blackbox and functional test suite ( test_runner.js ). 
 

 What's Next for LocalMarket AI 

 We plan to expand LocalMarket AI by integrating real-time geolocation APIs, web push notifications for accepted bargain offers, and multi-agent automated price negotiations.

about_excerpt:
Adversarial AI council (Tech, Finance, Risk, Strategy) debating your problems with live web citations, human-in-the-loop steering, and WebMCP native support.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 We’ve all been there: you ask an AI for advice, and it instantly agrees with everything you say, echoing your thoughts back to you. That feels nice, but it's dangerous for serious decisions. We realized that what builders and founders actually need is friction, rigorous cross-examination, and diverse perspectives—not a digital yes-man. That’s why we built SynthCouncil. 

 What it does 

 SynthCouncil is an adversarial multi-agent AI council designed to stress-test your toughest problems. Four distinct virtual experts—Tech, Finance, Risk, and Strategy—simultanéously analyze your query, scrape live web evidence to back up their claims, and brutally challenge each other's assumptions in structured debate rounds. 

 The best part? It operates under your complete supervision using a human-in-the-loop architecture. No agent moves forward or makes arbitrary decisions without your explicit direction. Once you have enough insights, you can wrap up the debate early and receive a clean, Zod-validated verdict complete with actionable owners and clickable sources. Plus, it's fully WebMCP-native, meaning an AI-enabled browser can drive the entire council autonomously. 

 How we built it 

 We designed SynthCouncil as a modern monorepo to keep things modular and clean: 

 
 Frontend: Built with Astro and React for a lightning-fast, sleek, minimal UI supporting both dark and light modes. 
 Backend: Powered by Node.js, Express, and GenKit, orchestrating asynchronous agent loops and Supabase (PostgreSQL) for persistence. 
 AI & Evidence: Powered by OpenRouter (using GPT-4o-mini for speed and intelligence) coupled with a robust live-search web fallback mechanism. 
 Deployment: The API lives on Render via an infrastructure-as-code Blueprint ( render.yaml ), while the static frontend is distributed globally via Netlify. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was orchestrating the delicate balance between autonomous multi-agent friction and human control. Managing asynchronous state streams without breaking the UI, synchronizing environment variables safely across Render and Netlify, and preventing LLMs from generating placeholder URLs when search context gets tight tested our patience. We solved it by enforcing strict Zod validation schemas and building graceful error-handling fallbacks. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are genuinely proud of building a fully functional, production-ready adversarial architecture from scratch in record time. Going from a conceptual multi-agent debate to a live, deployed app complete with a WebMCP bridge and a clean human-in-the-loop workflow feels amazing. 

 What we learned 

 Building SynthCouncil taught us that multi-agent systems are only as good as their orchestration layer. Giving humans the power to inject context and steer debates midway transforms an AI from a simple novelty into a truly powerful decision-making utility. 

 What's next for SynthCouncil 

 We want to expand the roster of expert personas, integrate deeper custom tool-calling capabilities, and refine the WebMCP browser extension to make autonomous agent collaboration even more seamless.
