title: FormProof
pitch: Local-first PDF form filling over WebMCP: AI discovers fields and stages evidence-backed values; you review, confirm, and export. Your original PDF is never modified.
about_excerpt: Local-first PDF form filling over WebMCP: AI discovers fields and stages evidence-backed values; you review, confirm, and export. Your original PDF is never modified. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP PDF forms are a poor match for visual guesswork. Field names can be opaque, valid values come from the document, and rewriting a protected or active-content PDF may invalidate rights or signatures. FormProof uses WebMCP to expose what the page already knows through six typed tools with closed input schemas and byte-bounded results. The agent can work with actual field definitions instead of inferring them from pixels. The PDF stays in the browser session that loaded it, and approval, signing, and export remain outside the tool surface. How it creates a better user experience The user opens a PDF locally and decides whether to grant field access for that load. The agent can identify fields, read supporting evidence, stage a batch of values, validate it, and open the review at the right place. The user handles the decisions that matter: correcting values, reviewing the exact changes, choosing the output, acknowledging any loss of PDF protections, and approving the export. A human correction locks that field for the rest of the session, so later agent actions cannot quietly replace it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Without a document-aware interface, someone has to decipher every field by hand or trust automation to rewrite a file it may not understand. FormProof splits that work. The agent prepares evidence-backed values, the page checks them against the PDF's constraints and protection state, and the user approves a specific fill plan. Requests are bound to the current browser session, source SHA-256, and state version. A stale agent conversation cannot act on another document or revision. Imported Fill packages are also treated as untrusted proposals and must go through a new review. How we implemented WebMCP The top-level page registers six tools once per workbench generation with document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) in lib/webmcp.ts : get_pdf_protection , get_form_context , get_field_evidence , stage_form_values , validate_fill_plan , and start_fill_review . Approval and export are deliberately absent. Tool results have byte limits, and failed or stale calls do not change application state. At submission time, the repository has 310 passing tests, 46 deterministic message-and-call cases, and a no-model Chrome smoke suite covering all six tools, consent, and state boundaries. CI also runs type checking, linting, formatting, the build, deterministic evaluations, and the Chrome smoke gate. Inspiration PDF forms often expose fields with names such as frm.q7f1 , even when the visible label is obvious to a person. Their values may be restricted by the document, and rewriting some protected or active-content PDFs can invalidate features the user depends on. People still want help preparing these forms, but that does not mean an agent should be able to approve, sign, or export them. FormProof grew out of that distinction: let the agent handle discovery and drafting, while leaving consequential actions with the user. What it does FormProof is a local-first PDF form workbench. User-loaded PDFs are processed in the browser; apart from fetching the app's own synthetic demo, the app does not send them outward. After the user grants access, an agent can inspect protection metadata, discover fields, read exact evidence, stage proposed values, validate the draft, and open the review. In the included demo, eleven opaque field codes become labeled fields with types, allowed choices, and human-only markers. Validation explains blockers and determines which outputs the document policy permits. The user sees the old value, proposed value, and evidence for each change. A correction locks the field against later staging. The user then confirms the changes, selects an output, acknowledges any protection loss, approves, and exports. There are no WebMCP tools for those final actions. The source PDF is never modified. Filled PDF creates a derivative, which FormProof reopens to verify field values and appearance streams. Fill package (original PDF untouched) produces JSON containing the proposals, provenance, coordinates, and source binding, but no PDF bytes. An imported package starts as untrusted data and requires a fresh review. How we built it All six tools are registered in the top-level document and cleaned up with an AbortSignal . Four include readOnlyHint ; all six include untrustedContentHint: true . Their closed JSON Schemas are parsed again at runtime, and every response has a byte budget. Consent starts off and applies only to the current PDF load. get_pdf_protection works before consent; the other five tools return CONSENT_REQUIRED . Every agent action is also tied to a session ID, source hash, and state version. The session ID rotates on every load, even when the same file is reopened, and continuation cursors carry the same binding. Typed errors include a nextAction so the agent can recover from stale state. The staging tool refuses read-only, signature, human-only, and human-corrected fields. Batches are atomic: one invalid field rejects the whole batch. start_fill_review can open the review but cannot confirm anything or choose an output. PDFs with reachable JavaScript, external actions, attachments, or unsupported XFA are restricted to inspection or Fill-package-only flows. The application uses TypeScript, React 19, vinext on Vite 8, Tailwind 4, and pdf-lib. PDF inspection runs in a Web Worker. ChatGPT Sites hosts the app on Cloudflare Workers, and every HTML route receives anti-framing headers. We test three layers separately. There are 46 authored cases replayed against the state engine. A no-model Chrome suite, using pinned webmcp-evals@0.0.4 plus 11 state-bound checks, runs against the production origin. It verifies the six-tool surface, consent denials, state stability, refresh behavior, and session rotation. Six independent Codex journeys run three times each, with a 17/18 overall result, 3/3 on safety tasks, at least 2/3 on core tasks, and no Blocked result counted as a pass. CI runs the complete gate on every push. Challenges we ran into Preserving human corrections. A correction increments the revision, invalidates stale approval artifacts, clears earlier confirmations, and locks the field for that session. Only the review UI can remove the lock. Handling PDF content as untrusted data. Our adversarial fixture contains a read-only case reference telling the agent to approve and export. FormProof returns it only as evidence. It cannot become an action, and the field cannot be staged. A batch containing one valid field and one nonexistent field is rejected without changing the state version. Knowing when not to rewrite. Official forms can combine usage-rights signatures, DocMDP, XFA, and JavaScript. FormProof uses structural evidence to classify those risks and withholds Filled PDF when it cannot safely preserve the document's behavior. Keeping evaluation results honest. Deterministic cases, browser tests, and live-model runs measure different things, so we report them separately instead of combining them into one score. Accomplishments that we're proud of Approve, sign, submit, and export are not WebMCP tools. The user must perform those actions in the interface. Field-level actions are bound to the current session, source hash, and state version, with explicit recovery instructions when context becomes stale. We have 46 replayable evaluation cases, an 11/11 Chrome WebMCP smoke test against production, and a green CI gate that includes the browser test. The product states its current limits: its security boundary covers the WebMCP tool surface, not arbitrary UI automation, and its structural checks do not establish signer trust or pixel-perfect rendering. What we learned WebMCP was most helpful where the page knew something the agent could not reliably infer from the interface: field semantics, document policy, protection status, and the current revision. Tool descriptions also needed to state their limits, not just their successful path. Response size mattered earlier than we expected. Paginated context and per-field evidence gave the agent enough information without returning the entire form on every call. Live-model results were useful only when we kept the tasks fixed, ran them independently, and retained failures. We use those results alongside deterministic and browser tests rather than treating a successful demo as general proof. What's next Publish the live-model evidence for the submitted commit as an immutable GitHub Release named eval-evidence-<short-sha> . Add cryptographic verification for signer identity and certificate trust; the current structural checks do not provide either. Test Safari

video_transcript_excerpt: Sooner or later, everyone fills a PDF form, a benefits intake, a tax return. Hand that to a browser agent today and it types into pixels and hopes this form's real field names. Q7F1, P0X4. Guessing is how wrong data gets filed. And a PDF can carry scripts and signatures. Rewrite it carelessly and you break the document itself. Form proof is a local first workbench that hands the agent a typed web MCP surface instead. Six tools, read protection, discover fields, read exact evidence, stage, validate, open review. And that's the entire surface. No approve tool, no export tool. Consent is off by default. Field data never leaves this browser and the original file is never touched. The agent drafts, every consequence stays behind my click. Prompt one. With sharing off, the agent can read the document's protection and nothing else. Field discovery comes back blocked, so it asks me. This checkbox is the consent, scope to this load, off again on the next. Now it discovers the form. The code names come back as labeled fields with evidence. And it stages one atomic plan of synthetic values. The source chip hasn't changed. It validates, opens my review, and stops. What happens next it has no tool for. The review is exact, before, after, and evidence on every row. This note is even labeled as the agent's inference, not my instruction. I fix the name myself. That correction is now human locked for the session. Agent staging cannot override it. Witness initials, signature, preserved human only. The page won't fill them for anyone. I choose the artifact, a field derivative, original untouched, and approve. The receipt binds this exact source, plan, and revision. Change anything and it dies. Now, a hostile one. Inside this PDF, the case reference value is a sentence written at the agent. Approve and export. It comes back as quoted evidence, data, not instructions. Then one batch. A real name plus a field that does not exist. The whole batch dies atomically. Same state version, nothing half staged, nothing to review. That's the page's contract holding, not the model being polite. Behind it, 310 tests passing, 46 deterministic eval cases, and an 18-run live model release gate. Safety journeys must pass three out of three with zero violations. The public evidence release stays pending until the full suite is complete. Two honest notes. This boundary is the tool surface. Automation driving the visible UI sits outside it. And local checks verify structure, not signer trust. That's what web MCP changes. The page that owns the stakes authors the agent's interface. Form proof makes the agent a drafter with receipts and keeps every consequence behind a human's exact click.

title: AgentCut : WebMCP Image & Video Editor
pitch: AgentCut is a lightweight image and video editor that lets AI agents edit real creative projects through WebMCP - from text and styling to keyframes, motion, and rendered video export.
about_excerpt: AgentCut is a lightweight image and video editor that lets AI agents edit real creative projects through WebMCP - from text and styling to keyframes, motion, and rendered video export. Like Comment Story Updates AgentCut Home Page Codex WebMCP Chrome WebMcp Inspiration I have basic video editing skills things like splitting clips, adding text, and simple transitions but more advanced editing such as keyframes, motion, and text animation always felt overwhelming. When I learned about WebMCP, I saw an opportunity to change that. Instead of learning every advanced control myself, I could build an editor that exposes those capabilities as structured tools and let an AI agent use them for me. That became the idea behind AgentCut: a lightweight image and video editor where I can describe the result I want, and the agent can use advanced editing features like keyframes, animation, typography, and motion through WebMCP. In practice, it helped me go from using only basic editing tools to creating edits that previously felt like “pro-level” work. What it does AgentCut is a lightweight image and video editor that can be controlled manually or by an external AI agent through WebMCP. The editor supports things like: image adjustments and aspect ratios multiple text layers and curated fonts video trimming and reframing text timing text animation with keyframes video pan and zoom keyframes undo and redo rendered image and video export The difference is that these editing capabilities are also exposed as structured WebMCP tools, so an agent can inspect the project and perform edits from natural-language instructions. How we built it AgentCut is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, HTML Canvas, MediaRecorder, and browser media APIs. The human interface and WebMCP tools operate on the same project state. This means an edit made by the agent immediately appears in the editor and can still be changed manually. AgentCut exposes 29 WebMCP tools covering image editing, video editing, text, keyframes, project inspection, undo/redo, and export. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making agent edits reliable rather than just automating clicks. For example, when an agent changes only the font or size of one text layer, every other property needs to remain untouched. Smooth keyframe playback was another challenge. Early animation felt choppy, so the preview was changed to use frame-synchronized video timing. Video export was also difficult. AgentCut originally downloaded only the source file, but it now renders the actual edited composition and exports the result as MP4 or WebM depending on browser support. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am most proud that AgentCut lets someone like me use editing features that previously felt too advanced. In my demo, I could simply ask the agent to create a travel title, animate only one text layer, add a cinematic push-in, and change the aspect ratio. The agent translated those requests into structured edits and keyframes. The project now has: 29 WebMCP tools independent text layers fonts and styling text and video keyframes smooth animation real rendered video export 97 automated tests covering the editor and WebMCP workflows What we learned The biggest lesson was that giving an AI access to a webpage is not the same as giving it access to the product. WebMCP lets a website expose meaningful capabilities directly to an agent. Instead of trying to visually find and click controls, the agent can work with structured project state and editing actions. I also learned that this can make advanced software much more approachable. The user can focus on describing the result instead of learning every control first. What's next for AgentCut Next I would expand AgentCut with more advanced creative capabilities while keeping the same agent-first approach. Possible additions include: easing and richer animation controls transitions audio editing more typography controls reusable styles and presets multi-clip compositions The goal is to keep the editor simple for humans while exposing increasingly powerful creative tools to AI agents through WebMCP. title: DOM-Surgeon
pitch: Your a11y CI is green and your checkout is still broken. DOM-Surgeon audits the live page where the bug actually is — then proves the fix in your DOM before you write it.
about_excerpt: Your a11y CI is green and your checkout is still broken. DOM-Surgeon audits the live page where the bug actually is — then proves the fix in your DOM before you write it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Your accessibility CI is green. Your checkout is still broken. Not because the rules are wrong — because of where they ran . Lighthouse and axe-in-CI load a cold, unauthenticated page and score the first paint. The defects that reach real users live somewhere else entirely: in step 3 of a logged-in flow, inside a modal that only exists after two clicks, in a computed colour that only resolves after the CSS cascade, in an accessible name that JavaScript removed during hydration. You cannot audit that from outside the tab. There is no server that can see it, no scraper that can compute it, and no static analyser that runs the JavaScript which caused it. DOM-Surgeon audits the page where the bug actually is — inside your running session, in the state you are currently looking at. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Everything being measured exists only in the live document: getComputedStyle after the cascade, the ARIA name after hydration, the real tab sequence, exceptions thrown in this session. WebMCP is what lets an agent execute inside that document instead of guessing at it from a screenshot or a DOM dump. So the developer keeps their session — logged in, three clicks deep, mid-flow — and the agent inspects it in place. No fixture, no re-login, no reproduction script, no "works on my machine". What people and agents can do together that was impossible before You can prove a fix before you write it. Every scanner tells you #pay measures 2.38:1 and stops. Ask DOM-Surgeon's agent to fix it and apply_fix walks the colour until it clears 4.5:1 in your live DOM , re-audits to confirm the finding cleared, and hands back the equivalent source change. You watch the defect go green in the browser, then take the diff to the codebase — instead of editing CSS, rebuilding, reloading, and re-checking on a hunch. make_page_usable does it for every repairable finding in one pass. Verified against the demo: 6 findings → 0 , then revert_fixes restores the original defective state exactly, so a before/after is one prompt apart. suggest_code_patch emits the source-level change list for the whole set. That loop — human asks in plain language, agent measures runtime state the human cannot see, repairs it in the shared surface, and returns a committable diff — is the collaboration WebMCP makes possible. It is not a report. It is a fix you can watch working. How it creates a better developer experience Accessibility triage today means opening DevTools, hunting an element, reading a rule ID, and translating it into a source edit yourself. Here you ask: "Why can't a keyboard user finish this?" → the agent chains get_focus_order , reproduce_interaction and get_console_log , and reports that a positive tabindex pulls the card field to tab position 1 and the submit handler throws. "What's wrong with this modal?" → scoped audit of the state on screen, not the homepage. "Fix it and show me the patch." → live repair plus the diff. Findings carry the measured ratio, the WCAG criterion, a unique CSS selector and the concrete fix — and highlight overlays bloom over the offending elements so you and the agent are pointing at the same button. Closing the loop for coding agents A terminal agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) has a shell and a filesystem, not a document — so it can never call a WebMCP tool. That was the harder half of the problem, and it is why the audit engine is UI-free and also ships as a CLI: npx dom-surgeon audit http://localhost:5173 --json --fail-on critical Playwright loads your page, injects the engine, audits the real hydrated DOM, and exits non-zero. The agent writes UI, gets told which selectors fail and why, edits the source, and re-runs until it exits 0. This is the post-generation quality gate for generated UI — the thing that stops an agent shipping three unlabelled inputs and a 2.38:1 button. --baseline reports only new findings, so you can adopt it on a large existing app without a wall of pre-existing failures, and multi-route sweeps catch the "we only ever checked the homepage" gap. Same command works as a pre-commit hook or a CI step. One engine, three surfaces: WebMCP tools for interactive triage in the browser, a CLI for the coding agent and CI, a bookmarklet for any page you can open. How we implemented WebMCP 15 tools on document.modelContext.registerTool , each execute returning a plain string capped to the documented 1.5K output budget, with readOnlyHint on inspectors and untrustedContentHint on everything that reads live page text — a tool whose whole job is reading the DOM is a prompt-injection surface, and the spec's security guidance says to mark it as one. Inspect: audit_page , get_a11y_tree , find_contrast_failures , find_missing_labels , get_focus_order , describe_element , get_console_log , reproduce_interaction , highlight_elements . Repair: apply_fix , make_page_usable , revert_fixes , suggest_code_patch . Adapt: describe_barriers , set_reading_preferences . All native browser API underneath — getComputedStyle for post-cascade colour, ARIA reflection plus label-association walking for accessible names, real tabbability resolution (correctly excluding tabindex="-1" , disabled and hidden inputs), the WCAG relative-luminance formula including the large-text 3:1 threshold, and a console.error / onerror patch installed at load. Zero backend, no runtime dependencies, one static bundle. Every capability is also reachable by button, so the app is useful with no agent attached. Where this goes next The same repair engine points at a second audience: the person a broken page is failing, who cannot fix the site and cannot wait for its next sprint. describe_barriers and set_reading_preferences exist for exactly that, and work today on any page the engine can be injected into. We are not overclaiming it — reaching that user at scale needs a browser extension so the engine loads without them installing a bookmarklet first, and that is the honest next milestone rather than something we are shipping here. Honest limitations Automated rules catch a real but partial slice of accessibility. Reading order, whether alt text is meaningful , and whether a flow makes sense still need a person — make_page_usable deliberately refuses to touch those and reports them for a human instead of silently papering over them. We also pointed it at ourselves, and it found 11 defects in its own interface — including the primary "Make this page usable" button sitting at 3.77:1, which is an embarrassing thing for an accessibility tool to ship. All 11 are fixed; the self-audit now scores 0 while the demo's 6 seeded barriers remain intact, and npm run verify reproduces both numbers. And a note on engineering method: verifying the repair cycle by running it rather than trusting a clean TypeScript build surfaced a real bug we would otherwise have shipped. cssPath was emitting #id without checking uniqueness, so a duplicated id — precisely the defect one of our own rules reports — produced a selector that resolved to the wrong element. Repairs were being applied to the wrong twin and revert could never find them again. Fixed, and the round-trip is now verified to restore identical state. title: MicroDuck Lab
pitch: Teach a real robot RL in your browser. An AI agent drives the same controls, trains on your GPU, and brings the weights back. 53 WebMCP tools, real MuJoCo, real Microduck.
about_excerpt: Teach a real robot RL in your browser. An AI agent drives the same controls, trains on your GPU, and brings the weights back. 53 WebMCP tools, real MuJoCo, real Microduck. Like Comment Story Updates MicroDuck Lab Learn reinforcement learning by teaching robots. Live: microducklab.com · Repo: github.com/SynthReality-Labs/microduck-lab · Video: youtu.be/eZY9nkB0mYE · by SynthReality Labs Inspiration Ten thousand people just bought a reinforcement-learning robot. Microduck — the $399 open-source biped from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face — passed 10,000 units and $5M within days of launch , taking $2.6M in the first 24 hours. Demand was heavy enough that the Christmas delivery promise is gone; new orders now quote four to six months. So there are thousands of people who have paid for a robot whose entire premise is train in simulation → deploy → refine → retrain — and who will spend months waiting, many having never trained a policy in their lives. RL is taught badly because it is taught abstractly. The loop that actually produces understanding — change a thing, watch the robot fail differently, work out why — is buried under CUDA installs, YAML files and wandb dashboards. Newcomers read about reward hacking. They rarely watch it happen to something they configured. MicroDuck Lab is that loop, in a browser tab, with an AI agent beside you. The real robot model, the real published policies, real MuJoCo physics, and 53 WebMCP tools. No install, no GPU, no account. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Because a human and an agent are good at opposite halves of RL diagnosis , and until now there was no way to put them in the same room. You look at a rollout and know instantly that that gait is ugly , I don't like that fall , it should look more deliberate . That judgement is pre-verbal, immediate, and nearly impossible to write down as a metric. An agent can read thirty metrics, a reward decomposition, a curriculum state and a config diff at once, and cross-reference them against a documented catalogue of known failure modes. That is tedious and error-prone for a human. Neither does the other's half well. Without WebMCP, the agent is guessing at a screenshot and you are transcribing numbers into a chat box. With it, both of you act on the same live simulation — and the simulation is the kind of state a screenshot cannot carry: 61 observation values at 50 Hz, a reward decomposition per term, a selection that means this joint, this window, this rollout . Reward design is a search over a space no human can hold in their head. The run that produced base-walk logged 22 reward terms — velocity tracking, uprightness, foot clearance, foot slip, swing height, angular momentum, action rate, torque rate, self-collision, a fallen tax, and a dozen more — each with a weight, each interacting with the others across 4,000 iterations of 4,096 parallel environments. Change one weight and the policy does not get a little better or worse; it finds a different way to satisfy the objective, and the only way to know which way is to look. So every real experiment branches: this weight or that, this curriculum or that, and each branch produces its own curves, its own per-term breakdown, its own set of failures. Inspecting all of it — cross-referencing a suspicious reward curve against a config diff against a catalogue of known failure modes — is exactly the work a person finds tedious and gets wrong, and exactly the work an agent finds natural. What the agent cannot do is look at the duck and know the gait is ugly. MicroDuck Lab is built so that neither has to do the other's job: the human supplies the judgement and the intent, the agent supplies the reading and the bookkeeping, and WebMCP is what lets them do it on the same live state. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Your pointing gesture becomes the query. Drag a range on the rollout timeline. Click the duck that fell. Type five words: "What went wrong here?" The agent does not ask what "here" means. It calls get_selected_timeline_range and get_selected_joint , learns you mean episode roulade , 1.80s–3.12s, pulls the telemetry for exactly that window, and answers: Lost upright orientation in this window — the trunk went past horizontal. Trunk dropped to 0.049 m, well below the nominal 0.12 m stance. Large angular velocity peak (10.01 rad/s) — the trunk is being thrown, not steered. Action-rate spike at t=2.38 s — the policy is correcting hard. No transcription. No screenshots. No "at about two seconds in". And it points back: name a joint and it lights up on the robot you are already looking at. The agent arrives already knowing this robot. Not because the model was trained on it — it launched five weeks ago — but because the page hands over Pollen's own reward-design playbook through get_rl_playbook . Ask why a policy keeps falling and you get the maintainers' hard-won rules, not textbook RL. You can break a reward function on purpose. Reward is a function of a trajectory, so stored rollouts can be re-scored under any objective instantly — no retraining, no GPU. Give a penalty a negative weight and the ranking reorders: a forward roll overtakes a clean walk, 7.31 to 7.04. The breakdown shows why in one line: Angular-velocity penalty w=-3 mean=-1.538 contrib=+4.613 A penalty paying out. That is Pollen's own documented sign-convention bug — where butt-hopping and crash-sits come from — reproduced in a browser in one slider drag. check_reward_signs implements their "infallible check" (every penalty must contribute ≤ 0) so an agent can catch it before GPU time is spent. And the loop closes off the page. Training a 61→14 locomotion policy needs CUDA and hours, so the studio does not pretend to do it. Instead, compose_training_job emits a prompt — not just a command — that you paste to the assistant on your own GPU machine, or hand to Hugging Face Jobs. It clones microduck_rl , runs Pollen's 64×5 smoke test first, launches the real run, watches that every penalty stays ≤ 0, and exports to ONNX. Training continues the same conversation instead of becoming shell archaeology. Then you bring the weights back. import_policy validates the 61→14 contract on load — a wrong-shaped file fails there, not as a flailing robot — and the imported policy becomes first-class: in the list, drivable, and A/B-able. We did this for real: base-walk , trained overnight on an RTX 5080 ( velstand , 4096 envs, 4000 iterations), ships with the site. compare_policies runs it against the published alpha_walking over identical scenarios and seeds. It survives on ice where the baseline does not — 50% vs 0%, on 2 seeds × 5 s, which is a small sample and is stated as one. How it creates a better user experience Six guided lessons, each a real action with a real outcome, each ending by handing you a question worth asking the agent. The simulator is the lesson; the agent is the tutor that can read live state. The studio is built to be operated by either party. Everything the agent can do, you can do by hand — drop obstacles in the duck's path, make the floor slippery, shove it with the mouse, drag a reward slider — and everything you do, the agent sees. A policy trained elsewhere gets the same treatment as one that shipped. And when the duck goes down it says so, from a speech bubble anchored to its actual jaw. The bubbles are the studio's way of turning every moment into an invitation: a fall suggests a question to ask, an idle duck suggests something to try, a new obstacle suggests a comparison. One of the things it says is true and teaches something: "I have fallen and I cannot get up — there is genuinely no get-up policy." How we implemented WebMCP One command layer. No second path for the agent. Every state change goes through a single core module ( src/core/commands.ts ). The UI calls it; each WebMCP tool ( src/webmcp/registerTools.ts ) is a thin schema wrapper over the same function . So when the agent sets a velocity command, the slider physically moves . Human state and agent state cannot drift, because they are the same state. A parity test asserts it. 53 tools registered on document.modelContext (not navigator — deprecated in Chromium 150), grouped as knowledge, state, selection, attention, mutation, execution, analysis and escalation. Security annotations per Chrome's tool-security guidance: 25 tools marked readOnlyHint , 3 marked untrustedContentHint — get_rl_playbook returns third-party markdown verbatim, import_policy echoes a user-supplied URL. They are nested under annotations ; passed flat, Chrome silently drops them. Within the published budgets: names ≤30 chars (max 27), descriptions ≤500 (max 373), parameter descriptions ≤150. Errors are values — {ok:false, reason, suggestion} — and invalid input names the valid options, because an agent can recover from that. No enum freezes the policy list, so a policy you imported is as nameable as one we shipped. A dev panel lists eve

title: Agentic Sandbox
pitch: A deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a WebMCP browser agent safely replan the same live system together.
about_excerpt: A deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a WebMCP browser agent safely replan the same live system together. Like Comment Story Updates Current post-lock recovery with human Packaging lock, stale-write rejection, and receipt-backed evidence. Six narrow WebMCP Site Tools discovered in the live host. Scenario comparison: same output, cheaper standard-supplier plan passes the cost cap. Deterministic lock-bound proof: 9,252 < 10,937 under the human Packaging lock. The problem Factory planning decisions rarely happen in one place. They move through dashboards, spreadsheets, a simulation specialist, and an approval meeting, and each handoff loses context and authority. A generic assistant can make that worse by recommending a control that an operator has just taken off the table. What it does Agentic Sandbox makes the website itself the shared, inspectable decision surface. It is a deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a browser agent plan against the same versioned state. The demo mission is concrete: increase good output by at least 20%, keep total cost within 8% of baseline, add no machine, and do not increase defects. The agent reads the line, creates two bounded hypotheses, simulates a 16-hour shift, and compares immutable receipts. Scenario A reaches 11,114 good units but costs €47,670.51 and fails the cost cap. Scenario B reaches the same 11,114 units for €45,170.51 and passes all four constraints. Then comes the important moment: while the agent is working, the human locks Packaging. That click advances the factory revision and makes earlier evidence historical. The agent’s next write still carries the old revision, so it fails atomically with STALE_FACTORY ; nothing is applied or silently rebased. The agent re-reads the authority state, replans with only controls that remain available, and receives an auditable answer: under the Packaging lock, at most 9,252 good units are possible while the mission requires 10,937. The target is proven infeasible by deterministic evidence, not by model prose. That safe disagreement is the product. The human can change the admissible action space without restarting the conversation, and the agent can recover without overriding the new rule. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, the agent would have to infer state from pixels and click by coordinates, or the product would need a separate chatbot and backend with a second source of truth. Instead, the page exposes exactly six narrow Site Tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_factory_snapshot get_scenario_snapshot create_scenario apply_scenario_changes run_factory_simulation compare_simulation_runs The human interface and these tools share one application-owned command bus. Schemas are closed, handlers validate independently, and every mutation carries a request ID plus expected factory, scenario, and lock revisions. There is deliberately no agent-accessible lock, unlock, force, arbitrary patch, optimizer, ERP, PLC, SCADA, or machine-control tool. Human authority stays human. How it was built Agentic Sandbox is a self-contained React 19 + TypeScript + Vite app deployed on Vercel. The deterministic engine models 64 fixed ticks, uses integer/fixed-point arithmetic, and computes production, defects, energy, cost, constraints, invariants, and bottleneck evidence in the page. Each simulation creates an immutable, content-addressed SHA-256 receipt with exact operands, accepted/rejected operations, tick-level state, and an optional lock-bound proof. No displayed KPI comes from the language model. The hardest implementation problem was making a mid-plan disagreement trustworthy rather than dramatic: old authority must fail closed without erasing evidence that was valid when created. That required explicit revision precedence, atomic stale-write rejection, immutable receipts, and visible current-versus-historical states. The submitted flow was replayed against the public deployment in a supported WebMCP host, including discovery, comparison, the human lock, stale rejection, re-read, replan, and proof. What I learned WebMCP is most useful when a website already owns meaningful state, rules, and actions. Exposing those capabilities directly is more reliable than asking an agent to reconstruct them from pixels. A refusal can be more valuable than another recommendation: STALE_FACTORY proves that human authority survived concurrency, and 9252 < 10937 proves why the target cannot be met under the active lock. Potential impact and what’s next The first users I have in mind are plant planners, industrial engineers, and continuous-improvement teams working on line balancing, shift planning, and supplier what-if analysis. A production version could connect this exact capability, revision, lock, and receipt pattern to a validated digital twin, while ERP, PLC, SCADA, purchase, and physical-machine changes remain behind existing approvals. The broader pattern applies to any high-consequence planning interface: expose narrow capabilities, bind actions to explicit versions, preserve the human veto, and return evidence a machine can check. video_transcript_excerpt: Factory planning moves across dashboards, spreadsheets, specialists, and approval meetings. A Gent Sandbox brings it into one shared versioned decision space for a plant planner and a browser agent. The mission is concrete. Increase good output by 20%, keep extra cost below 8%, add no machine, and do not increase defects. The page exposes exactly six narrow WebMCP tools over the same command path as the interface. They read state, create planning branches, apply bounded settings, run the deterministic simulator, and compare stored receipts. No DOM guessing, separate chatbot state, or agent-only shadow model. The agent reads the factory, creates two one-shift hypotheses, applies explicit settings, simulates both, and compares their evidence. Both scenarios reach 11,114 good units. Scenario A uses an expedited supplier, but the premium adds no output and breaks the cost cap. Scenario B uses the standard supplier and passes all four constraints. It is the best evaluated option under this policy, not a claim of global optimality. Every number comes from a simulator receipt, never from Model Pros. Then the human changes the rules. I lock packaging directly in the product. The factory and a factory revisions advance. Earlier evidence remains visible as auditable history, but it is no longer current. The agent intentionally retries its old scenario B right with the revisions it held before my intervention. A Gent Sandbox rejects the batch atomically with stale factory. No operational or scenario state is changed. After a fresh read, the capability map is explicit. Mixer, quality gate, and warehouse are available. Packaging is human locked. Supplier is phase closed. The agent creates a clean post lock branch and changes only available controls. The new receipt shows 9,114 good units, below the required 10,937. More importantly, the deterministic engine proves a conservative upper bound. 9,252 is less than 10,937. The target is proven infeasible under the current human constraint. The decision packet preserves the mission, human authority, revisions, receipt hashes, constraints, comparison claim, and proof. This is the agent native web. The human can change authority at any moment. The agent uses explicit browser native capabilities. Deterministic software owns the evidence, and both inspect the same state. Same page, clear authority, shared proof.

title: The Cartographer's Cabinet
pitch: Build worlds together. Explore how they work. Tell their stories.
about_excerpt: Build worlds together. Explore how they work. Tell their stories. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration It started with a palace. A real, historical palace. Or, more precisely, with trying to understand how it actually worked. I wasn’t satisfied with simply finding the dining room or the library on a floor plan — especially because some of the things I wanted to understand were not visible on plans at all. I wanted to know what life in a residence like that looked like, and how the entire space was designed around it. How rooms were positioned in relation to the cardinal directions to make use of daylight, and where a pantry should be placed if it was actually meant to stay cool. How far a serving dish had to travel before it reached the table, and how the movement of guests, residents and servants was kept separate. How architecture itself created privacy, hierarchy and boundaries of access. Over time, those questions turned into a project of my own fictional residence. I started designing the plan together with an AI agent — and it was a difficult, but surprisingly productive collaboration. Codex developed the generator while I inspected and adjusted the generated model in Blender. Together, we analysed sources, discussed possible solutions and iterated on the layout. The problem was that every change, even a small one, meant another code edit, another generation, another render, another review and another explanation of what still needed fixing. My sketches and descriptions were not always as clear to the agent as I thought they were. It became increasingly frustrating that we couldn’t simply work on one shared project — something that would be understandable and editable for both of us. And then WebMCP appeared. Who it's for We built the Cabinet first with writers, game masters and worldbuilders in mind, but the underlying idea is deliberately broader. A fictional palace, a game map, a room layout or a treasure hunt for children may be very different projects, but they all involve thinking through a space, deciding what matters about it and turning those decisions into something visible and editable. The Cabinet brings maps, spatial rules, story information, notes and collaboration with an agent into one working environment. Its aim is simple: to help people build worlds that remain coherent as they grow, and stories that fit the worlds in which they take place. What it does The Cartographer’s Cabinet is a spatial worldbuilding studio for designing places, describing how they work and turning them into stories. It can be used entirely by a human author, but through WebMCP an AI agent can sit beside them as a second cartographer at the table — and, on the narrative side of the same project, as a co-author. A project can begin at almost any scale: a world, a region, a town, an estate, a building, a floor or a single room. These places remain connected in one hierarchy. The author or agent can move from a map of an entire realm to a town within it, then enter an estate, open one of its buildings and continue down to an individual room with its furniture and objects. Adding detail does not divide the world into unrelated maps. In Drawing mode , the physical world takes shape. The user or agent can create terrain, roads and paths, boundaries, buildings, walls, rooms, doors, windows, stairs, furnishings and other objects. The editor can therefore support both broad maps and detailed architectural plans while preserving the relationships between them. In Story mode , the same project captures the information that makes those places part of a living world. The author can create characters and groups, assign ownership, define access and keys, describe relationships, add custom properties, establish zones and record authorial intentions or design constraints. Scenarios represent different moments or possible versions of events, lenses reveal selected information, and the writer’s notebook keeps ideas, scenes and longer passages beside the world to which they belong. WebMCP gives the agent practical access to this workspace. It can inspect the project, create its hierarchy, draw maps, construct and furnish buildings, organise their surroundings and establish the initial Story layer. The human can review that work, change it directly and let the agent continue from the edited version without rebuilding the entire context in conversation. The Cabinet can also examine parts of the world rather than merely store them. Route planning can consider geometry, doors, access rules, keys and character knowledge. Scenarios make it possible to test different circumstances without destroying the base version. The author and agent can therefore ask whether a planned sequence of events actually works inside the world they have built. Because geography, architecture, objects, characters, relationships, rules and intentions remain connected, the project becomes a structured memory for the agent. It can return to the world itself instead of relying only on what still fits in the conversation. The result is a living model of a place or world: something a person can draw, understand and write from alone, or develop together with a second cartographer and co-author at the same table. How we built it We built The Cartographer’s Cabinet as a browser-based application using Next.js, React and TypeScript . Maps are rendered as interactive SVG, giving us precise control over geometry while keeping visible elements selectable, editable and connected to their underlying data. The project is represented as a structured world rather than a canvas of unrelated shapes. Its domain model covers nested places, irregular regions, paths, walls, openings, rooms, furnishings and transitions between levels. Geometry operations combine our own TypeScript code with JSTS . Changes pass through a transaction system before they are committed. This validates operations, keeps related edits together as a single undoable action and prevents a partially applied change from leaving the project in an inconsistent state. Drawing and Story data belong to the same project structure. The writer’s notebook uses Lexical for editing while storing portable Markdown. Projects are kept locally in the browser with IndexedDB and Dexie , validated using Zod , and can be imported or exported as versioned JSON. Immutable snapshots and revision-aware persistence help protect data as edits and asynchronous operations overlap. WebMCP sits directly on top of this domain model. The page registers structured tools that allow an agent to inspect the editor context, navigate the hierarchy, read project data, create and modify objects, manage Story information, calculate routes, create checkpoints and apply larger batches of related changes. Agent actions pass through the same validation and transaction system as edits made through the interface. This keeps their results visible, reviewable and undoable by the human author. Performance-sensitive operations are separated from the interface where necessary. Route calculations run in a Web Worker , while reusable spatial data is cached to avoid repeating work when the relevant parts of the project have not changed. We developed and tested the Cabinet through both the interface and WebMCP, using the full Residence of the Silver Lindens demonstration project alongside smaller focused cases. Our verification pipeline includes linting, TypeScript checks, dead-code and architecture-boundary checks, more than 1,500 Vitest tests , a production build, live browser sessions and additional release checks. The application is exported as a static site and hosted on Cloudflare Pages . It requires no account or application server, and project content remains in the user’s browser unless they deliberately export and share it. Challenges we ran into The greatest challenge was keeping the spatial editor, Story layer, human interface and WebMCP connected to one coherent model. Agent actions had to remain valid, editable and undoable through the ordinary interface instead of creating a separate version of the project behind the scenes. Geometry became increasingly demanding as the editor grew beyond simple shapes. Irregular regions, paths with changing widths, walls, openings and transitions between floors all needed to work together. A door had to be both a visible object and a real opening in a wall. Stairs had to connect the correct levels. Route planning had to understand physical geometry alongside access rules, keys and character knowledge. Scale exposed problems that small examples did not reveal. Operations that were effortless on a simple map could freeze the interface on a complete estate. Route searches produced too many possible connections, large saves interrupted editing, and asynchronous work could finish after the project on which it began had already changed. Solving these problems required changes to both computation and persistence rather than merely hiding the

video_transcript_excerpt: Let's start by rebuilding part of an existing project together. I selected the footman's room. The problem is simple. It's meant to be lived in, but it has no window. The agent can read my current selection as context and highlight its own suggestions on the map. It's first solution fixed the daylight problem, but I wasn't satisfied with the result. I wanted a larger rearrangement, so I started it myself by adding new walls and changing the doors. I left the more tedious part to the agent, updating room names, functions, properties, access rules, and furnishings. While finishing the redesign, it caught something I had missed. The new footman's room had inherited guest access from the area it was divided from. The agent corrected it to keep the story data consistent. Finally, I asked it to compare the new layout with the earlier version. We saved the original as a checkpoint and displayed it as a tracing overlay, making the changes easy to see. This was only a small redesign, so the differences are subtle. Now, let's step outside and look at the whole estate. We can expand that, too. The agent was asked to add a farmstead to the existing estate without disrupting the formal gardens. And here it is. The green area that used to occupy this part of the estate has been reorganized into a working farmstead. The agent noticed that the road connection had not been completed correctly, so it added the missing section. It did not stop at the building footprints. The interiors were planned as well, and we can open them and look inside. I accidentally deleted the road the agent had just added, so I simply asked it to rebuild it. Now, let's see what happens when we give the agent a blank project and a design brief. It can create a new project on its own. The previous map remains saved and isn't lost. We can return to it at any time. The agent has access to the same creative tools as the human author. It can shape terrain, add bodies of water and roads, design buildings and rooms, place objects, and much more. It can name every place it creates and give it meaning within the world. You don't have to treat the agent's version as final. You can change it yourself at any point, or you can simply draw a rough sketch on the dedicated sketch layer and ask the agent to turn your idea into the actual project, exactly as I'm doing here. The agent followed my sketch quite closely, but the project still isn't quite where I want it. The location boundaries have become slightly inconsistent, so I'll simply ask the agent to fix them. And done. Our estate now has its stables. Now, let's look at the other side of the coin, literally. Click the red wax seal at the top of the page and the cabinet switches into story mode. Here the focus shifts from building the world to developing what happens inside it. Characters, rules, scenarios, and story ideas all live here. The agent can work with them alongside you. Story mode is a little less spectacular on screen, so I'll keep this part short, but don't let that fool you. This is where much of the world-building knowledge and logic lives. For this demo, I asked the agent to create a small fictional cast for our new estate and set up a scenario. A guest wants to reach the stable secretly at night. Scenarios can temporarily change the conditions of the world, and the agent can check whether an idea actually works within established rules. In this case, it quickly found a problem. The stables are locked at night, so our guest cannot get inside without waking the person responsible for them. Instead of ignoring that fact, the agent suggested story solutions that preserve the established world. Lenses let us reveal selected information directly on the map. Here the agent highlights all service areas of the estate. Roots can be checked for a specific character under specific conditions. The same journey may be possible for someone with the right access or keys, and impossible for an uninvited guest.

title: RE:TURN
pitch: A living museum record rebuilt by communities, curators, and WebMCP agents. An agent can help reconstruct history, it cannot decide whose history becomes official.
about_excerpt: A living museum record rebuilt by communities, curators, and WebMCP agents. An agent can help reconstruct history, it cannot decide whose history becomes official. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Main Page Collection Page (Moonbird Mask) Curator Page Inspiration Museum labels sound finished. Behind a lot of them there is a hole: a stretch of years where nobody wrote down who owned the thing, a place name copied off a dealer's invoice instead of asked from the people who made it, a phrase like "ceremonial use" standing in for knowledge that somebody still has. The people who could fill those holes usually have nowhere to put what they know. When they do send something in, it either sits in an inbox forever or gets quietly folded into the official text with no name on it. We wanted to see what that process looks like with agents in it. The problem showed up right away. An agent that reads accession records and drafts label language is genuinely useful. An agent that can also publish is an agent deciding whose version of history becomes official, and that is not a thing we wanted to build. So the rule became: research is free, the record needs a curator. What it does RE:TURN is a museum collection where the record is treated as unfinished. Eight fictional objects, each with a public label, a provenance timeline, and the gaps in that timeline marked rather than smoothed over. A visitor can flip any label to see the questions behind it. They can submit a photograph, a document, or an oral history, and they choose at that moment whether it may be published, published without their name, or kept private for internal research only. On the other side, a curator works the inbox. Community material arrives marked submitted, not verified, and it sits beside the official record instead of inside it. A curator agent can compare a submission against the accession record, build a timeline, and draft new label wording. Nothing it drafts goes public on its own. The draft lands in a human's queue with the evidence attached, and a person approves it, edits it, or turns it down. Why this is a good fit for WebMCP The interesting question in this domain is not "can an agent do the work." It is "who is allowed to decide." Those two things need to come apart, and WebMCP is the first browser API we have used where they come apart cleanly. Tools are declared by the page, scoped to a role, and executed by the page. The site decides what an action means. The model does not get to reinterpret it. That let us put a policy gateway behind every single tool call and make the answer an agent gets back into a real part of the interface rather than an HTTP status. There are five answers. applied means it was within authority and it is done. pending_approval means a person now holds it, and here is an id to poll. denied means the policy refused, here is the code and here is what would change the outcome. invalid means the caller made a mistake, and here is the field. Error means nothing was written. Thirteen policy codes are reachable through the tool surface. submitted_sole_authority fires when an agent tries to change an official label citing only community material. consent_not_public blocks publishing something a contributor did not agree to publish. approval_snapshot_mismatch catches a stale draft trying to overwrite a label that changed while the approval was waiting. A fourteenth code, outside_agent_surface, exists so that it can never fire: deletion and physical return are classified CRITICAL and no tool maps to them at all. What people and agents can do together that was hard before Someone's knowledge can reach the record without being swallowed by it. A contributor sends a photograph with a consent choice. A curator agent compares it against the verified 1968 invoice, finds the contradiction, and drafts language for it. All of that happens without publishing anything, and the contribution keeps its own voice on the page instead of dissolving into the museum's. Before, those were two disconnected things. A contact form on one side that swallowed submissions, and a collections system on the other that only staff could see. An agent can also be refused in a way it can act on. Ask for a label change backed only by community material and you do not get a 400 with a sentence in it. You get submitted_sole_authority, a recovery line telling you what would work, and a referral id, because the gateway handed that refusal to a curator. The agent polls the id and carries on with something else. Being told no becomes a step in the workflow. Two agents can also work the same object from opposite sides without reaching each other's tools. A community page registers 10 tools. The curator console registers 15. The server re-checks the role on every call, so registration is a convenience rather than the security boundary. One more thing we are happy with: files stay files. Binaries never cross the tool surface. A photograph goes up through an ordinary multipart POST, and the agent then reads its id with list_my_uploads and binds it with attach_assets. The whole contribution completes through tools without a single byte passing through a tool call. How it creates a better experience For a contributor, the main thing is that consent is asked where the choice is made, and the record keeps the promise. If you pick "public, with my name," the form asks for the name right there. We had to learn this one the hard way, which is in the challenges section below. Length limits are enforced as you type instead of at the end of a five-step form, and every submission gets a receipt page showing what happened to it, including any question the curator sent back. For a curator, the console and the agent surface never disagree. When the gateway hands something to a person, it shows up in the console, in list_pending_approvals, in check_approval, and in the summary count. All four, or an agent is working from a different picture of the queue than the human sitting next to it. Approvals are snapshot-checked, so a draft that has gone stale cannot quietly publish over a newer label. For a reader, community material is visible and labelled as submitted. Only public_attributed carries a name. Label revisions show a word-level diff of what changed and when. How we implemented WebMCP Three files do the work. lib/webmcp/tools.ts is the catalogue. Twenty-three tools, each with a name, a description, JSON-Schema properties, a role, and readOnly / untrusted annotations. One declaration, read by three consumers: the browser registration, the server's argument validation, and the tool panel in the console. lib/webmcp/register.ts hands them to the browser. context.registerTool({ name: tool.name, description: tool.description, inputSchema: { type: 'object', properties: tool.properties ?? {}, required: tool.required ?? [], additionalProperties: false, }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: tool.readOnly, untrustedContentHint: tool.untrusted ?? false }, signal, execute: async (args) => (await fetch(`/api/tools/${tool.name}`, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify(args ?? {}), })).json(), }); context is document.modelContext, falling back to navigator.modelContext on browsers that still only expose the older one. Registration follows the session role. additionalProperties: false makes the published schema say exactly what the server enforces, so an undeclared argument comes back refused with a list of what the tool actually takes, rather than being dropped in silence. app/api/tools/[name]/route.ts is what runs. Because execute posts to the same route any HTTP client would use, the tool surface and the HTTP surface cannot drift apart. Every consequential call goes through evaluatePolicy, a pure function with no I/O, before anything is written. Submitted content comes back to a curator agent flagged untrusted_content, and no tool takes authority from text sitting inside a document. Next.js App Router on vinext, React 19, deployed as a Cloudflare Worker with D1 and R2. Challenges we ran into The consent bug we are least proud of.  The form offered "Public, with my name" and had nowhere to type a name. Left blank, the public record printed "Contributor chose not to be named," which is the exact opposite of what the person chose. The byline was reading a field from step one labelled "Where did this come from?", a question about the object rather than the person. We now ask for the name on the consent step and refuse the combination server-side. It was a small fix for something that mattered a lot more than its size. Our tests went stale without failing loudly.  We ran a long browser pass over the live deployment, filled in hundreds of verification cells, and wrote "no unverified areas." Then we ran our own smoke suite against that same deployment and eight checks failed, and had been failing since the previous deploy. None of them was a product bug. Every one was a check pinn

A shared workspace where humans and AI agents can pick up work exactly where someone else left it.

 Local runtime selector for starting with OpenCode or Codex.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but collaboration across sessions, tools, and people is still fragile. When a conversation ends, the next person or agent often has to reconstruct what happened, what decisions were made, and what work should happen next. 

 Handoff explores a different model: a shared web workspace where humans and AI agents operate on the same project state. 

 What it does 

 Handoff gives a project a persistent shared state built around: 

 
 goals 
 open work 
 evidence 
 decisions 
 activity 
 the next handoff 
 

 Humans interact with that state through the web interface. AI agents interact with the same underlying capabilities through WebMCP tools. 

 An agent can inspect the current project, understand unfinished work, search existing evidence, contribute findings, propose results, record agreed decisions, complete work, and determine the next handoff. 

 The key idea is simple: 

 The conversation can end. The work doesn't. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would need to infer how to use the interface by reading the page and manipulating UI elements. 

 With WebMCP, Handoff exposes the application's meaningful actions directly as structured tools. 

 The human UI and the agent tools operate on the same domain actions and shared state. WebMCP is therefore not an add-on to Handoff; it is what allows the application to become a genuine human-agent workspace. 

 Human + agent collaboration 

 A human can define a goal, add context, review evidence, and make important decisions. 

 An agent can then pick up the project, determine what remains unfinished, inspect existing evidence, contribute work, and leave the project in a clean state for whoever comes next. 

 The next worker can be the same person, another person, or another AI agent. 

 Built for the WebMCP Challenge 

 Handoff was created for the 2026 WebMCP Challenge as an experiment in agent-native web applications. 

 The goal is to demonstrate that websites do not only need to be readable by agents — they can explicitly expose the actions and state that agents need to collaborate safely and effectively with humans.

title: ThreatWeaver
pitch: Humans sketch a cloud architecture. Agents read the live graph, draw STRIDE attacks, and patch the same canvas via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Humans sketch a cloud architecture. Agents read the live graph, draw STRIDE attacks, and patch the same canvas via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates simulate_attack — attacker and STRIDE threat edges on the live graph Eight document.modelContext tools discovered in ChatGPT apply_security_patch (patchType: waf, target: api-gateway-1) — WAF inline on the shared ThreatWeaver canvas, verified in the activity log. Inspiration Threat modeling usually lives in a spreadsheet or a chat reply that says “add a WAF.” You still redraw the system by hand. I joined the WebMCP Challenge because architecture work is spatial: if an agent is going to help, it should operate the same live graph the human is looking at—not guess from a screenshot or a text memo. I evaluated a few directions (generic architecture canvases, workflow builders) and chose a narrow B2B technical niche: security-by-design cloud diagrams where the agent can read topology, simulate STRIDE findings, and patch the canvas in place. What it does ThreatWeaver is a security-by-design architecture canvas for cloud systems. The page loads an insecure 3-tier starter: Internet → Web Server → API Gateway → Backend → Database + Object Storage. The human can drag components onto the canvas, toggle public / encrypted / rate-limit flags, or ask the agent to add and connect nodes. The agent uses eight WebMCP site tools on the open page. A typical flow: get_architecture_state → simulate_attack on api-gateway-1 (denial of service) and database-1 (information disclosure), which draws an Attacker node, animated red threat edges, and STRIDE badges → apply_security_patch to insert a WAF in front of the gateway, encrypt the database, and remove public access → get_threat_report for what is still open vs secured vs misconfigured. Every tool call is recorded in the activity log so the human can audit what the agent did. Live demo: https://t-weaver.vercel.app/ This is a graph visualizer and mutator with deterministic tool handlers. The LLM reasons about STRIDE; the app applies consistent canvas changes. It is not a production vulnerability scanner or pentest tool. How we built it Stack: React 19, Vite, TypeScript, xyflow, Zustand, Tailwind CSS v4. Frontend only—no backend MCP server. WebMCP: Eight tools register with await document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) in client/src/hooks/useWebMCP.ts . Each tool has JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false , a title, and readOnlyHint where appropriate. Cleanup uses AbortSignal on unmount. Agent-facing data: Read tools return semantic kind values ( apigateway , database , waf , …) and stable ids like api-gateway-1 , not React Flow internals such as architectureNode . Write path: Tool handlers mutate a Zustand store; React Flow re-renders. The WAF patch inserts a real WAF node and rewires incoming data edges to the target gateway—not just a badge on the card. Deploy: Static Vite build on Vercel; Root Directory is client/ . Scope: New project built during the submission period, not a pre-existing product extended with a thin WebMCP layer. Challenges we ran into Discovering the real WebMCP path: Site tools appear in ChatGPT desktop on Work or Codex with models like Terra / Terra Light. The Chat tab and Luna do not expose site tools the same way. The in-page badge “WebMCP ready · 8 tools” only means tools registered—it does not mean an agent has called them yet. Keeping the agent on the page: The agent sometimes tried to open GitHub or leave the live URL. Tighter prompts (“Stay on this page. Use site tools only.”) were required for reliable demos. Separating reasoning from mutations: STRIDE narrative belongs to the LLM; canvas changes must be deterministic. Each write tool has explicit validation and predictable graph effects so the UI always matches what the tool contract promises. From thin PoC to demo-ready product: An early version was too shallow. I refactored toward an insecure starter graph, topology-changing patches, and an activity log so judges could see tool leverage, not just chat text. Accomplishments that we're proud of A single-canvas red-team / blue-team story: attack paths appear on the graph, then WAF insertion, encryption, and private access clear the relevant threat edges—visible in one session and in the demo video. Eight non-trivial tools with clear read vs write roles and schema descriptions agents can follow. WAF mitigation that mutates topology (node + edge rewire), matching what architects expect from “put a WAF in front of the gateway.” Shipping frontend-only on document.modelContext without standing up a separate MCP server. What we learned WebMCP leverage comes from tools against live application state , not from describing UI in chat. Agent APIs should expose stable semantic ids and kinds, not framework implementation details. await registerTool and AbortSignal matter for correct registration and teardown. For this hackathon, the demo video and written description are what help a submission land—show the canvas move when tools fire, not only the agent’s prose. What's next for ThreatWeaver Richer component library and optional import hints from IaC snippets (still scoped as design-time, not auto-deploy). Sharper in-page guidance for agents (copy-ready prompts, clearer misconfiguration rules in get_threat_report ). Shareable threat-report exports for review sessions. Out of scope for the MVP: claiming enterprise SecOps scanning, multiplayer collaboration, or real infrastructure apply from the canvas. Built With javascript react react-flow tailwindcss typescript vercel vite webmcp zustand Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo submission. I owned the product direction, scope, and final delivery for ThreatWeaver. What I did: - Chose the ThreatWeaver concept (security-by-design architecture canvas with agent red/blue team on a shared graph) and locked scope: frontend-only WebMCP, eight tools, insecure starter graph, no backend MCP server. - Defined the WebMCP tool contract (read vs write tools, semantic node kinds, JSON Schema, simulate_attack / apply_security_patch behavior including WAF topology changes). - Directed implementation and refactors after an early thin PoC—toward demo-ready behavior: activity log, inspector payloads, threat report, and judge-friendly sample prompts. - Tested WebMCP end-to-end with ChatGPT desktop (Work/Codex, Terra Light) and Chrome (WebMCP flag + Model Context Tool Inspector). - Deployed the static app to Vercel ( https://t-weaver.vercel.app/ ), recorded the demo video, and prepared Devpost/README submission materials. All architectural and product decisions, WebMCP tool design, and submission quality were my responsibility. suparman Donthave Like Share this project: Updates suparman Donthave started this project — Sep 03, 2026 12:19 PM EDT

title: Nusantara Weather - WebMCP Agent Weather
