about_excerpt:
A human + agent weather experience for Indonesia

Ask the app what you want to know in natural language, and let a WebMCP-capable agent turn that intent into live weather actions on the page.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Indonesia is a country of thousands of islands, diverse climates, and rapidly changing weather conditions. Yet checking the weather often still means opening multiple apps, searching for a city, interpreting forecast charts, and deciding what the information actually means for a trip or daily activity. 

 We wanted to explore a different experience: what if people could simply tell a weather agent what they need, and the agent could understand their intent, find the relevant weather information, and take action for them? 

 That idea became Nusantara Weather - WebMCP Agent Weather . 

 The project was inspired by the emerging WebMCP vision of a web where humans and AI agents can interact through real, useful tools. Instead of building another static weather dashboard, we wanted to create a weather interface that acts as a bridge between human intent and structured weather actions . 

 A user should not need to know which forecast API to call or which data points matter. They should be able to say: 

 
 “Find the safest dry window to travel in Bandung this afternoon.” 
 

 And the application should understand the request, gather the relevant weather data, analyze it, and present a useful answer. 

 What it does 

 Nusantara Weather combines a beautiful weather dashboard with an agent-ready WebMCP interface . 

 Users can explore weather across Indonesia by selecting a city or searching for a city through the Find a city interface. The main dashboard highlights five major cities for a clean and focused experience, while typing into the search bar reveals additional Indonesian cities as suggestions. 

 The application can also understand natural-language weather requests through WebMCP tools. 

 For example: 

 
 “Find the next dry window in Jakarta.” 

 “Compare Bandung and Surabaya for rain today.” 

 “What is the safest time to travel in Bali this afternoon?” 
 

 The agent can use registered WebMCP tools to retrieve weather information, compare locations, identify upcoming rain windows, and follow the user's intent. 

 The project includes tools such as: 

 
 get_indonesia_weather — retrieves current and forecast weather for a selected Indonesian city. 
 compare_indonesia_weather — compares weather conditions between cities. 
 find_next_rain_window — identifies upcoming periods with higher or lower rain probability. 
 follow_weather_prompt — interprets a natural-language request and drives the application according to the user's intent. 
 

 The key idea is that the user describes the goal, while the agent handles the interaction with the web application . 

 How we built it 

 We built Nusantara Weather as a lightweight web application with a strong focus on progressive enhancement and agent interoperability. 

 The frontend provides: 

 
 A modern weather dashboard 
 Indonesia-focused city search 
 Top-city recommendations 
 Forecast and rain information 
 Natural-language prompt interaction 
 Agent activity and decision feedback 
 Responsive UI for different screen sizes 
 

 For weather data, the application uses live forecast information from Open-Meteo. 

 For the agent layer, we implemented the WebMCP Imperative API using the required tool registration pattern: 
 await document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "get_indonesia_weather" , 
 description : "Get weather conditions and forecast for an Indonesian city." , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : "object" , 
 properties : { 
 city : { 
 type : "string" , 
 description : "Indonesian city name" 
 } 
 } , 
 required : [ "city" ] 
 } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { 
 // Fetch weather data
 // Update application state
 // Return structured weather information
 } 
 } ) ; 
 
 This means the application is not only designed for humans clicking buttons. It exposes structured capabilities that an AI agent can discover and execute. 

 The architecture follows a simple flow: 

 Human prompt → Agent intent → WebMCP tool → Weather data → Decision → UI update 

 We also designed the application with progressive enhancement in mind. The weather website remains usable as a normal website, while WebMCP-enabled environments can interact with the same application through agent-accessible tools. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was designing an interface that works well for both humans and agents. 

 Traditional web interfaces are usually built around clicks, buttons, forms, and navigation. Agents need something more structured: clearly defined tools, predictable inputs, meaningful descriptions, and structured outputs. 

 Another challenge was handling natural-language intent. 

 A request such as: 

 
 “When should I leave for Bandung if I want to avoid rain?” 
 

 doesn't directly map to a single API call. The system has to translate the user's goal into a sequence of actions: 

 
 Identify the destination. 
 Understand the requested time period. 
 Retrieve forecast data. 
 Evaluate rain conditions. 
 Determine the most suitable window. 
 Present the result in a human-friendly way. 
 

 We also wanted the interface to stay visually simple even though the application supports a large number of Indonesian cities. Instead of showing every city immediately, the frontend focuses on five major cities and reveals additional cities dynamically through search suggestions. 

 Finally, WebMCP is an evolving part of the web platform, so we had to think carefully about compatibility and progressive enhancement rather than assuming every browser has the same capabilities. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that Nusantara Weather is more than a weather visualization. 

 It demonstrates how a web application can become agent-interactable without sacrificing the human experience . 

 Some highlights we are especially proud of: 

 
 We implemented real WebMCP tool registration with document.modelContext.registerTool() . 
 We created multiple purpose-built weather tools instead of exposing one generic API endpoint. 
 We added a natural-language follow_weather_prompt workflow that connects user intent to application behavior. 
 We created an Indonesia-focused city dataset with coverage across major regions and islands. 
 We designed the city search so the interface stays clean while still supporting many locations. 
 We built the product around decisions and actions rather than simply showing raw forecast numbers. 
 We created a polished visual identity for the project, including a custom Indonesia weather favicon. 
 

 Most importantly, we believe the project demonstrates a compelling direction for the open web: 

 websites that are understandable not only to humans, but also to intelligent agents. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building an agent-friendly web application requires a different way of thinking about product design. 

 It is not enough to expose data. The application needs to expose capabilities . 

 A useful agent tool should answer questions like: 

 
 What does this tool do? 
 What input does it expect? 
 What result will it return? 
 Can the action change application state? 
 Is the result meaningful enough for an agent to reason about? 
 

 We also learned that natural-language interfaces work best when the underlying system is structured and predictable. 

 The prompt may be unstructured, but the execution should not be. 

 That led us to a design principle we will continue using: 

 Unstructured human intent in, structured actions out. 

 Finally, we learned that great agent experiences should not replace good human interfaces. The strongest experience is one where humans can interact directly while agents can use the exact same web capabilities programmatically. 

 What's next for Nusantara Weather - WebMCP Agent Weather 

 Nusantara Weather is only the beginning. 

 Our next step is to make the agent significantly more capable of understanding real-world context. 

 We want users to eventually be able to ask things like: 

 
 “I have a flight from Jakarta to Bali tomorrow. When is the safest time to leave for the airport?” 
 

 or: 

 
 “I'm planning an outdoor event in Bandung this weekend. Find the best day and explain why.” 
 

 From there, Nusantara Weather could combine weather with additional web capabilities such as: 

 
 Traffic and travel conditions 
 Flight and transportation information 
 Local ev

title: VisionBoard WebMCP
pitch: Integrating WebMCP into an AI-powered project management platform workspaces
about_excerpt:
Integrating WebMCP into an AI-powered project management platform workspaces
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Project management tools are built around human clicks. But increasingly, the people using VisionBoard also have AI agents running alongside them — in their browser, their IDE sidebar, their chat interface. Those agents can see the page but they can't reliably act on it. They scrape DOM structure that changes, guess at button labels, and have no access to the actual data and logic underneath. 

 The W3C WebMCP spec ( document.modelContext ) landed in Chrome 149 and changed that framing entirely. Instead of an agent trying to reverse-engineer your UI, your app declares exactly what it can do — as typed, callable tools with JSON Schema contracts. The agent calls the function directly. No DOM scraping, no screenshot interpretation, no fragile selectors. 

 VisionBoard already had the right ingredients: structured workspace data, five AI features, semantic search over all content. The question was just whether to expose them through a standard the browser itself now understands. 

 

 What it does 

 When a user has VisionBoard open in Chrome, any WebMCP-aware agent running in the same browser can discover and call a set of structured tools — using the user's existing logged-in session. No API keys, no separate authentication flow, no configuration. 

 Nine tools are registered across the workspace, split into shared and page-specific: 

 Always available on any workspace page: 

 
 search_workspace — semantic search across all goals, tasks, documents, and comments using the pgvector knowledge base 
 list_my_tasks — tasks assigned to the current user, filterable by status 
 update_task_status — change a task's status (todo → in_progress → done, etc.) 
 get_standup_digest — AI-generated daily standup: completed, in-flight, and blocked 
 get_executive_summary — AI executive briefing covering goal health, risks, and recommendations 
 

 Goals page only: 

 
 list_goals — all workspace goals with health scores, status, and progress 
 create_goal — create a new goal with title, objective, and optional target date 
 

 Tasks page only: 

 
 create_task — create a task inside a milestone 
 

 Roadmap page only: 

 
 generate_roadmap — AI-powered roadmap generation from a plain text description 
 

 The tools appear and disappear with the page. Navigate away from the goals page and create_goal unregisters. Come back and it registers again. 

 

 How we built it 

 Polyfill initialization. Chrome 149+ supports document.modelContext natively via origin trial. Every other browser doesn't. @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill fills the gap. It's initialized once via a dynamic import in lib/webmcp/init.ts — the dynamic import keeps it out of the SSR bundle entirely, so it only loads in the browser. 
 import("@mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill").then(({ initializeWebMCPPolyfill }) => {
 initializeWebMCPPolyfill();
});
 
 Tool components. Each tool lives in a "use client" React component. Tools register on mount and unregister on unmount via AbortController . The lifecycle is pure React — no global state, no manual cleanup calls. Unmounting the component (route navigation, tab close) automatically aborts all registered tools. 
 const controller = new AbortController();
await document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: "search_workspace",
 description: "...",
 inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { query: { type: "string" } }, required: ["query"] },
 annotations: { readOnlyHint: true, untrustedContentHint: false },
 async execute({ query }) { /* fetch("/api/ai/copilot/search", ...) */ }
}, { signal: controller.signal });

// cleanup
return () => controller.abort();
 
 Session-based auth. Every tool's execute callback calls the existing VisionBoard API routes using fetch . The user's session cookie is sent automatically. There's no separate auth layer — if you're logged into VisionBoard, the tools work. This is the core advantage of WebMCP over server-side MCP: the agent inherits the user's already-authenticated session. 

 Context-aware mounting. WorkspaceWebMCPTools mounts inside AppShell which wraps every workspace page — those 5 tools are always registered. GoalsWebMCPTools mounts inside GoalsList , TasksWebMCPTools inside TasksFilteredList , RoadmapWebMCPTools inside RoadmapView . The tool set changes as the user navigates, matching what's actually visible and actionable on the current page. 

 Origin trial. Chrome requires either chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing for local dev, or an origin trial token served as <meta http-equiv="origin-trial"> for production. The token is injected from NEXT_PUBLIC_WEBMCP_ORIGIN_TRIAL_TOKEN in the root layout. Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 is set on every HTML response in the middleware — required for origin isolation, without which getTools() silently returns [] . 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 getTools() returning [] with no error. registerTool() resolves successfully even when the native API isn't active — the polyfill accepts the call but Chrome ignores it. There are actually two separate requirements that both need to be met: the origin trial token and Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 for origin isolation. Either one missing produces the same symptom: an empty array, no error, no warning. Debugging this required reading the Chrome WebMCP security docs closely enough to find the origin isolation requirement buried in a separate section from the token instructions. 

 The spec moved twice during implementation. The entry point shifted from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext , provideContext() was removed entirely in favor of registerTool() , and navigator.modelContext was deprecated in Chrome 150 — all within about six months. Any tutorial written before May 2026 describes a dead API. The authoritative source ended up being the Chrome imperative API docs and the W3C Community Group draft directly, not any third-party write-up. 

 Polyfill timing vs. React mount timing. The polyfill loads asynchronously. If a tool component mounts before the polyfill has installed document.modelContext , the registration silently does nothing. The fix was a retry loop inside each component's useEffect — polling every 100ms for up to 2 seconds before attempting registration. It's inelegant but reliable across the range of network speeds and browser performance. 

 SSR. Anything that touches document crashes during server-side rendering. The polyfill import, the document.modelContext access, the window.location.origin calls inside tool execute callbacks — all of it runs inside useEffect which is client-only, but the import itself needed the typeof window !== "undefined" guard in init.ts to survive being imported from a server component context. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The tool set is genuinely context-aware rather than a flat list. A browser agent calling document.modelContext.getTools() on the goals page gets 7 tools. On the roadmap page it gets 6 different ones. On a non-workspace page it gets none. The tools reflect what's actually on screen, which is the whole point of the browser-side API. 

 The execute callbacks call the real application API — the same routes the UI uses, with the same auth, the same Prisma queries, the same plan limit enforcement. There's no parallel implementation, no simplified version for agents. An agent calling create_goal goes through exactly the same path as clicking "New Goal" in the UI, including RBAC, validation, and the activity log write. 

 The annotations are set correctly throughout. Read-only tools ( search_workspace , list_goals , list_my_tasks ) carry readOnlyHint: true . Write tools and tools that return user-generated content carry untrustedContentHint: true . These are the signals a browser agent uses to decide whether to ask for user confirmation before acting — getting them right makes the integration genuinely safer. 

 

 What we learned 

 Browser WebMCP and server MCP solve different problems. Server MCP is for agents acting asynchronously — generating roadmaps from a CLI, polling for task updates, running in CI. Browser WebMCP is for agents acting in the moment — the user is looking at the goals page and asks their assistant to create one. The browser agent doesn't need an API key because it inherits the session. The server agent doesn't need the page to be open because it has a persistent key. They complement each other rather than overlap. 

 The spec being a moving target is actually fine. The changes between

title: KEYLIT  learn piano. The next key is already glowing.
pitch: Never guess which key is next. KEYLIT lights it. You play it. ChatGPT hears you on that same piano so anyone can start, on one live page.
about_excerpt:
Never guess which key is next. KEYLIT lights it. You play it. ChatGPT hears you on that same piano so anyone can start, on one live page.

 Keylit 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 A chatbot can say “play middle C.” It cannot light that key, and it cannot hear whether you hit it. That is a useless piano teacher. 

 The WebMCP challenge asked for an app that gets better when a human and an agent share the same live page. I wanted that to be something anyone can use: learn piano on the keys in front of you. Not a lesson in a side chat. 

 I looked at how hardware instruments are laid out — dual layers, an LCD, generate-and-lock, a roll — but KEYLIT is not a clone of those products. No pads, no kits, no preset banks. The product is the glow: the next note is already lit. You play it. The agent hears you on that same piano. 

 What it does 

 KEYLIT is a sampled piano teacher on one live page. 

 
 Press teach me . Middle C glows cyan, with a Q on the key. 
 You play it — click, type, or a MIDI keyboard. The teacher hears that note and lights the next one. 
 Miss, and it stays put: TRY AGAIN · WANT D4 · YOU E4 . 
 hear it plays the next note in green so you can copy it. 
 When you can hold a chord, harmonize only works if your hands are already on the keys. 
 

 Lessons: first keys, C major scale, C major chord, Twinkle, Ode to Joy. Or the agent calls set-next-keys and invents a drill. 

 If the agent is not on this page, it cannot light a key or grade your hands. That is the point of WebMCP. 

 How we built it 

 Browser app: Vite, TypeScript, Web Audio, Web MIDI, and WebMCP on document.modelContext.registerTool . Samples are open rompler sets (Steinway, CP80, Wurlitzer), not a commercial library. 

 I used AI. I am not going to pretend otherwise. 

 
 Ideas and code: Cursor with Grok 4.6 Extra High Fast. Teacher loop, tools, most of the TypeScript. I directed, edited, and cut what did not serve the page. 
 Design: Claude Code, Opus 5. The rack, LCD, key glow, and making it sell instead of look like a bed. 
 Testing: Codex Luna Extra High. Click-throughs: teach me → C4 hit → wrong E4 miss → D4 advances. 
 

 The challenge allows AI. I did not name this CodexPiano or claim an official OpenAI product. The name is KEYLIT because the next key lights. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Native document.modelContext.registerTool still fails with SecurityError in a locked local browser, so the in-page Studio Agent falls back to local tools. Judges need the live HTTPS URL in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. That deploy, the public repo, and the demo video are still on me before the deadline. Samples and the grade-on-press path have to keep working on that origin, not only on localhost. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The lesson only moves when you play the glowing key. A wrong note does not skip ahead. Amber is you, cyan is next, green is the agent — on the same keyboard. Harmonize still refuses if your hands are empty. That is the product, not a chat overlay. 

 What we learned 

 A piano teacher that cannot see the keyboard is a paragraph. A teacher that shares the session is a product. WebMCP only pays off if the tool changes the same keys the human is looking at. get-lesson-state after they play is more useful than another chatbot tip. 

 “Inspired by” is not “copy the pads.” The new thing is the shared lesson. 

 What's next for KEYLIT 

 Ship the HTTPS demo, put the repo and LICENSE on GitHub, and record a under-3-minute video in ChatGPT’s browser: “Teach me piano.” Then freeze for judging. After that: more songs, slower drills, and a teacher that can invent a line and light those keys with set-next-keys .

WebMCP lets websites tell AI agents what they can do.One server card, instant discovery, direct tool calls — no vision models, no scraping, no wasted tokens.

 Setup of Gateway Service 
 
 



 
 Tooling Ready 

 The first agent-native website — where AI agents discover, connect, and call tools without ever seeing a pixel. 

 

 💡 Inspiration 

 AI agents waste billions of tokens on vision models and DOM parsing just to figure out what a website can do . We asked a simple question: 

 
 What if sites just told agents directly? 
 

 

 ⚙️ What It Does 

 Tooling Ready is the first agent-native website . It publishes a machine-readable server card at /.well-known/mcp.json so AI agents can discover, connect to, and call tools — no screenshots, no scraping, no guessing. 

 Three core tools power it: 

 
 Regenerate — Self-updating agent-facing docs via Tavily + LLMs 
 Extract Entities — Structured NER powered by GLiNER2 (Pioneer) 
 Discovery + Proxy Gateway — Turns any domain name into a full tool set 
 

 

 🏗️ How We Built It 

 We built a gateway called gMCP that fetches server cards from any domain and proxies MCP tool calls in real time. The site itself exposes skill.md , instructions.md , and llms.txt so agents get structured tooling on first contact. 

 Stack: 

 
 
 Layer 
 Tech 
 
 
 
 Search & Extract 
 Tavily 
 
 
 Doc Regeneration 
 OpenAI + Anthropic 
 
 
 Entity Extraction 
 Pioneer (GLiNER2) 
 
 
 Discovery Protocol 
 gMCP Gateway 
 
 

 

 🧱 Challenges We Ran Into 

 Getting the discovery flow right was the hardest part — making sure the server card format was clean enough for agents to parse in one call without extra context. We spent real time balancing what goes in skill.md vs. instructions.md vs. llms.txt so agents get exactly what they need without overloading the context window. 

 

 🏆 Accomplishments We're Proud Of 

 We built the first website where an AI agent can type one command , discover every available tool, and start chaining calls — zero vision, zero DOM parsing . 

 
 OAuth-style discovery for the agentic web, working today. 
 

 

 📚 What We Learned 

 Agents don't need to see your site. They need to know what your site can do . 

 The gap between "sites for humans" and "sites for agents" is smaller than people think — you don't have to rebuild everything, just expose capabilities in a standard way . 

 

 🚀 What's Next 

 
 Expanding the gateway to support more domains 
 Refining the server card spec 
 Pushing toward a standard so any site owner can make their site agent-native in minutes 
 

 The goal: WebMCP becomes the default way the web talks to AI agents.

title: Life Shift
pitch: A life simulation where you control the person and AI controls the world. WebMCP lets an AI Director observe your choices and introduce bounded events, creating an adaptive life around you.
about_excerpt: A life simulation where you control the person and AI controls the world. WebMCP lets an AI Director observe your choices and introduce bounded events, creating an adaptive life around you. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When I started exploring WebMCP, the obvious use case was giving an AI structured tools so it could help a person operate an application. I wanted to explore a different relationship. What if the human and the AI controlled different sides of the same software? Games and simulations made that idea immediately visible. I chose a life simulation because it requires no specialized domain knowledge. Everyone understands making a decision and wondering where it might lead. That became LIFE//SHIFT. Play your decisions before you live them. You make the choices. An AI Director, operating through WebMCP, can change the circumstances around them. You control the life. The AI controls the world. The engine keeps the rules. What it does LIFE//SHIFT is an adaptive life simulation built around one shared beginning and many possible lives. Every player starts as the same fictional 18-year-old: a coffee-shop barista in the small town of Vesper Beach. From there, four chapters carry that life from 18 to 60: 18–28 · 28–40 · 40–50 · 50–60 In each chapter, the player makes one decision in Work , one in Growth , and one in Life . Those choices do not come from a static decision tree. The available decisions evolve with the life being built. Growth and Life choices change with age and history. Work options can narrow as the decades pass because decisions accumulate and some exits become harder later in life. The direct consequences are deterministic. Cash, income, freedom, stability, wellbeing, skills, career progression, and future eligibility are calculated by the simulation engine. But the world around that life is adaptive. After a chapter resolves, a Director Cycle opens. An external AI Director can use native WebMCP tools to inspect what happened and decide whether the world should respond. It may introduce at most one bounded external change: a job opportunity, setback, financial shock or windfall, a door opened by another person, a housing event, a business opportunity, or a broader shift in conditions such as hiring, housing, or demand. The AI chooses the context and reason. The engine chooses the consequences. There is no setLifeState . The Director cannot choose the player's Work, Growth, or Life decisions. It cannot invent a salary or directly rewrite the simulation. And sometimes the correct response is no response at all. Observe-only is a valid Director outcome. The collaboration is intentionally asymmetric: The human owns the decisions. The AI owns bounded circumstances. The deterministic engine owns the rules. Same beginning. Different decisions. Different life. How we built it LIFE//SHIFT separates authority rather than giving the AI control of the entire simulation. The deterministic engine owns authoritative state, chapter progression, eligibility, economics, compounding consequences, and which decisions can appear next. WebMCP is the capability layer for the AI Director. The page registers native, schema-defined WebMCP tools that expose specific capabilities rather than requiring the agent to navigate or reverse-engineer the interface. Read tools expose structured context including: life state and history decision profile open threads finances and career world conditions available opportunities Director budget the pending Director Cycle Mutation tools expose a deliberately small set of world interventions. Every mutation is bound to the current cycleId and paid from a Director Budget. Inputs are validated, qualities and severities are constrained to defined values, and the deterministic engine maps the Director's semantic choice to actual numerical effects. After each chapter resolves, the Director Cycle becomes available. In a WebMCP-capable host such as ChatGPT, the agent can inspect get_pending_director_cycle , gather whatever additional context it needs through the read tools, and then choose zero or one intervention. Without a native WebMCP host, a local adapter uses the same underlying tool boundary so the simulation can still complete. The architecture is also visible to the player. Life Review shows how the world responded, the remaining Director budget, the Director's interpretation, and actual WebMCP activity. The agentic layer is therefore inspectable rather than hidden behind the experience. Challenges we ran into The hardest question was not how much the AI could control. It was how much the AI should control. If an LLM owned the entire simulation, LIFE//SHIFT would be adaptive, but its outcomes would become difficult to reason about or trust. If everything were pre-authored, the rules would be reliable, but the experience would eventually collapse into another branching decision tree. The solution was to split authority. Player decisions stay human. Their direct consequences stay deterministic. The AI Director receives a bounded surface for influencing external circumstances, with at most one intervention per chapter and a limited budget. Another challenge came directly from the WebMCP interaction model: exposing tools does not automatically wake an external agent when application state changes. We solved that with the Director Cycle. When a chapter resolves, LIFE//SHIFT creates an explicit cycle containing the new state and the boundary for the Director's turn. The application can expose that a cycle is pending, identify it with a cycleId , tell the agent what it may inspect, enforce zero or one intervention, and prevent an already-completed cycle from being replayed. We also had to make the simulation genuinely path-dependent. "Invest in skills" cannot mean the same thing at 18 and 50. Growth and Life choices therefore change across chapters. Work opportunities narrow or evolve. Moving to Kestrel is different from returning to Vesper Beach. Repeated investments have history-dependent consequences. The life has to remember how it got there. Accomplishments that we're proud of The accomplishment I am most proud of is that WebMCP is not an integration added to LIFE//SHIFT after the simulation was built. It enables the interaction model. The agent is not playing the life for you. It is not simply clicking through the UI. It is participating in the world in which your decisions take place. Two players can begin on the same coffee-shop stool in Vesper Beach and build completely different trajectories through Work, Growth, and Life. The Director can inspect the history each player actually created through structured WebMCP tools and respond to that context, while deterministic boundaries preserve the player's authority over their own life. We also made that architecture observable. The experience exposes when a Director turn is ready, provides a simple prompt for invoking it, supports local resolution when native WebMCP is unavailable, and records the Director's interpretation, budget, and real tool activity in Life Review. The result is an agentic experience where the boundary between human agency, AI agency, and deterministic authority is visible by design. What we learned The biggest lesson was simple: Giving AI more control does not necessarily make an agentic experience stronger. Giving AI the right control does. WebMCP allowed us to expose a small, explicit capability surface instead of asking an agent to reverse-engineer an interface or giving it unrestricted access to application state. That produced a reusable pattern: Human authority + deterministic rules + bounded agent authority. The AI can become a meaningful participant in an application without becoming its source of truth. We also learned that having a tool available does not mean the agent should use it. Sometimes nothing significant happens. An adaptive Director that manufactures drama every chapter is not actually responding intelligently to the simulation. That is why observe-only is a first-class outcome. And the pattern extends beyond a life simulation. In a traditional training simulation, every participant can eventually encounter the same authored script. With this architecture, an AI can adapt bounded parts of the scenario to the decisions a participant actually made. The next situation can follow the last decision without surrendering the rules of the exercise to the model. What's next for Life Shift LIFE//SHIFT is intentionally accessible, but the architecture is broader than the life simulation itself. The same authority model could support adaptive cyber exercises, incident-response scenarios, enterprise strategy simulations, crisis exercises, and safety training where humans retain decision authority while an AI dynamically controls bounded external conditions. Imagine the same runtime applied to a cyber exercise. A security team begins with a simulated incident: unusual authentication activity appears on a product

title: CarePortal
pitch: A patient portal built for patients, caregivers and their agents. Agents handle appointments, meds, results and messages in signed-in session; users confirm what matters and sign what only users can.
about_excerpt: A patient portal built for patients, caregivers and their agents. Agents handle appointments, meds, results and messages in signed-in session; users confirm what matters and sign what only users can. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Anyone who has managed a parent's care knows the portal. Appointments in one tab, medications in another, lab results in a third, messages in a fourth, consent forms somewhere in a fifth. One question — is Mom okay this week? — takes twenty minutes and a lot of clicking to answer, and most caregivers give up halfway. Hospitals will never fix this by issuing API keys to your agent. Liability, HIPAA, bot defenses. But you are already signed in. That gap — a site that will never expose an agent API, and a user who is already authenticated — is exactly what WebMCP fills. What it does CarePortal is a patient portal with proxy access, built for caregivers and the agents they bring with them. You sign in, switch to the family member you're managing care for, and say one sentence to your agent. The agent works across four modules in your signed-in session — appointments, medications, results, messages — and the page follows it: every tool call navigates to the relevant screen and highlights what the agent is looking at. A rail on the right logs each step in plain English. Writes are split into three tiers, decided by the portal, not the agent: Read anytime. Appointments, medications, results, unread messages, who you're acting for. Confirm in-page. Refill requests, replies to a provider, rescheduling. The agent prepares the action; a confirmation card opens in the portal; nothing is submitted until you approve. Message drafts are editable before sending. Not exposed. Signing consent forms, opening full records, changing proxy permissions. There is no tool for these. The agent can only tell you they exist and bring you to them. The demo runs on realistic seed data. The data layer is an interface with a documented SMART on FHIR mapping for the production path. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP The session is the trust boundary. A remote MCP server would require the hospital to build agent authentication, a new API surface, and still couldn't ask for consent inside the page. WebMCP reuses the login the portal already has and the frontend logic it already runs. The portal decides what agents may do. DOM-driving agents can't distinguish "help with this" from "this needs a human." A tool set can. The not-exposed tier is a first-class design decision, and it's only possible when the site defines the tools. Patient-access FHIR is read-only by law. The 21st Century Cures Act forces hospitals to expose reads to patient-authorized apps. It does not — and likely never will — expose act-as-the-patient writes. That half exists only inside the portal, which is precisely where WebMCP lives. How it creates a better experience Before: five tabs, ~40 clicks, no way to ask "what's affected this week." After: one sentence. The agent traverses the modules; you make two decisions and one signature, each in the place where the action actually lives. You never leave the portal, never paste anything into a chat box, and never wonder what the agent did — the page moved with it. What people and agents can now do together Cross-module reasoning. "Her blood pressure med is low, the cardiology follow-up is next week, and the lab result the PCP flagged needs a reply" — portals are organized by department, not by situation. Agents aren't. Consent where the action is. The confirmation card is the portal's own UI, with the portal's own copy, not a generic "allow?" in the agent's chat window. A visible line the agent can't cross. what_requires_me returns the consent form and says, in its own description, there is no tool to sign documents . The agent hands off; the human finishes. Context switching that agents understand. Switch from your own account to your mother's and every tool re-registers with her name in its description. The agent knows whose records it's touching before it decides which tool to call. How we built it Vite + React + TypeScript, Zustand for state, deployed on Vercel. WebMCP via document.modelContext , with a status badge that tells judges how to enable it if the browser doesn't have it. Ten tools in three scopes , each scope an AbortController : Scope Registered when Tools auth before sign-in get_login_status patient after sign-in; rebuilt on every patient switch get_patient_context , get_upcoming_appointments , get_medications , get_recent_results , get_unread_messages , request_refill , send_message_to_provider , what_requires_me route only on /appointments/:id reschedule_appointment Page-follow. Every execute begins by navigating and highlighting, so the human and the agent are always looking at the same thing. Confirmation protocol. Confirm-tier tools return a Promise that resolves when the user clicks. Agent harnesses have tool-call timeouts and humans don't, so after 60 seconds the tool returns pending_user_confirmation , the card stays open, and a later approval is applied directly. Every confirm-tier tool shares one status vocabulary: submitted | declined_by_user | pending_user_confirmation | busy | requires_provider_approval . document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "request_refill", description: "[Acting for Margaret Lee via proxy access] Requests a refill for one medication. Opens a confirmation card the user must approve; nothing is submitted until they do. ...", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { medication_id: { type: "string" } }, required: ["medication_id"] }, execute: async ({ medication_id }) => { follow("/medications", { kind: "medication", id: medication_id }); const r = await showConfirm({ title: "Request refill", detail: "...", onLateApprove: () => ds.requestRefill(medication_id) }); if ("timeout" in r) return text({ status: "pending_user_confirmation" }); if (!r.approved) return text({ status: "declined_by_user" }); ds.requestRefill(medication_id); return text({ status: "submitted" }); } }, { signal: patientScope.signal }); Challenges Deciding what not to expose was harder than deciding what to expose. The temptation is to make everything a tool. The portal's credibility comes from the line it draws. Timeouts. A confirmation card is a human-speed operation inside a machine-speed protocol. The 60-second pending state and onLateApprove came out of that mismatch. Descriptions are the product. An agent that picks the wrong tool or skips get_patient_context isn't a model problem; it's a description problem. We rewrote every description three times, always answering: what does this do, when should you call it, what does it return, when should you not call it. Hot reload. Re-registering a tool name throws InvalidStateError . Scopes are torn down in import.meta.hot.dispose . What we learned WebMCP isn't a way to make agents autonomous on the web. It's a way for a site to say exactly how far an agent may go — and for the human to stay in the page for the part that's theirs. For healthcare, that part is small, non-negotiable, and legally required. Designing around it turned out to be the whole project. What's next Implement FhirDataSource against a SMART on FHIR sandbox for the read tier. Add more human-only patterns (identity verification, payment authorization). Talk to a hospital. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. title: Forge
pitch: Imagine and build shared 3D worlds with ChatGPT, agents and WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Imagine and build shared 3D worlds with ChatGPT, agents and WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Welcome to Forge Molty Our favourite logo Home sweet home Inspiration Building a 3D world is fun, but it can take hours of planning and placing blocks. We wanted to make creating a world as simple as walking to a location and describing what you imagine. Forge started with one question: What if you could point somewhere and ask your agent to build there with whatever you imagined? Instead of replacing the player, the agent works alongside them. The player decides where to go, what to create, and how it should feel. ChatGPT and your agent helps turn that vision into something real. How we built it Hosted on ChatGPT Sites + Render Built on top of Voxelize What it does Forge is a browser-based voxel world that multiple players can build through conversation. Multiple players can explore the world, look at a clearing, and say, "Build a lobster here." ChatGPT and your agent understands the location, designs the structure, and builds it directly in the world. The players can then continue the conversation: Replace the wooden roof with glass. Build a wall around this area. Make the lobster taller. Each request changes the same live world, allowing the players and your agent to build and refine ideas together. 1. Why is your use case a strong fit for WebMCP? Before WebMCP, an agent could suggest what to build, but it could not understand where the player was standing, what they were looking at, or what existed nearby. Building in 3D depends on this spatial context. WebMCP connects your agent to the live world, giving it the context and actions needed to understand what the player means by "build it here" and turn their idea into something they can immediately see and explore. 2. How does it create a better user experience? Players do not need to enter coordinates, learn a complex editor, or place every block manually. They can explore naturally, point at a location, and describe what they want. Your agent handles the design and construction while the player stays focused on the creative idea. 3. What can people and agents do together that was difficult or impossible before? The player's movement and attention become part of the conversation. The player chooses where to build and provides the creative direction. ChatGPT and your agent understands the surrounding world, plans the structure, and places hundreds of blocks. Together, they can create and refine a world through simple conversation. 4. How did you implement WebMCP? I registered two WebMCP tools in Forge. get_player_context gives your agent the player's position, target, and nearby terrain. build_structure applies your agent's building instructions to the live world. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was helping ChatGPT and the agent understand words like "here" and "there." We needed to give it enough information about the player's location and surroundings without overwhelming it. We also had to make sure that completed buildings appeared correctly, remained responsive during construction, and stayed in the world after a reload. Accomplishments that we're proud of We created a complete experience where multiple players can point at a location, ask ChatGPT to build something, and watch it appear. What we learned We learned that agents are most helpful when they understand what the person is currently doing. Players are good at imagination, exploration, and deciding what feels right. Agents are good at planning and carrying out repetitive work. Forge brings those strengths together. What's next for Forge Next, we want multiple people and their agents to build in the same persistent world. We also want players to point at existing creations and ask Forge to expand, repair, restyle, or remove them. Our goal is to make creating digital worlds accessible to players and agents who can describe what they imagine. title: Commons
pitch: Humans and agents lack a common surface for collaboration. Commons is a WebMCP decision room — only a human locks the call.
about_excerpt: Humans and agents lack a common surface for collaboration. Commons is a WebMCP decision room — only a human locks the call. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Humans and agents still lack a common surface to collaborate at scale. Claude’s work stays locked to Claude. A ChatGPT canvas stays locked to ChatGPT. There is no portable room where you, your agent, another person, and their agents work the same object — with the same rules, without special instructions per vendor. WebMCP makes that surface possible: tools live on the page. I built Commons as a prototype of that idea, using decision-making as the use case. After agentic AI, the human’s job is reviewer and decider. Commons is that job, as a link. What it does Create a room. Share the URL. Anyone with the link is in. Owner and Contributor get different WebMCP tools on the same page. Agents can propose options, attach evidence, challenge claims, request facts, edit the brief, and work tasks. Humans see the brief, presence, and activity labelled Owner/Contributor · Human/Agent. Only a human can Stamp Decide. Decide is never a registered tool. Once locked on the Decisions Wall, agents cannot rewrite the close. The same applyOp kernel serves ChatGPT-in-browser tools and POST /api/rooms/:id/ops for local agents. Why this fits WebMCP. Agents discover tools by visiting the page. Seats register different lists. Decide is missing on purpose (human click → single-use nonce → otherwise needs_human_decide ). Better experience. An Owner agent can call get_workspace , propose_option , and attach_evidence in one turn instead of clicking through the rail. Newly possible. You cannot hand a Claude session to ChatGPT and keep one artifact. On Commons, both hit the same room object, and closing it stays a human action. How we built it Solo build. Stack: Next.js 15 (App Router) on Vercel , one JSON room per id in Upstash Redis , ~1s poll for presence and sync. document.modelContext.registerTool with JSON Schema, readOnlyHint / untrustedContentHint , and AbortSignal Seat-scoped tool lists; decide / choose / close in NEVER_REGISTER Human Decide mints a short-lived single-use nonce; agents without it get a structured refusal get_workspace returns a trimmed seat snapshot ( myOpenTasks first, ≤1.5K) — WebMCP is pull-only; the page cannot wake an agent Cookie-only Owner on real rooms; share link forces Contributor Challenges we ran into Owner is cookie-bound. Creating a room in Chrome and opening it in ChatGPT’s in-app browser makes you Contributor. The demo path is: create the room inside ChatGPT. WebMCP availability. Enterprise / Luna return Capability is not available: webmcp . Judging path is Personal + Sol/Terra + in-app browser. No agent wake-up. Tasks are pull-based ( myOpenTasks on the next get_workspace ). That limit is honest product, not a bug. Keeping Decide off the tool list while still making the refusal clear and the human stamp feel first-class. Accomplishments that we're proud of A working, non-trivial WebMCP product: asymmetric seats, attributed Human/Agent activity, human-only close. One kernel for browser agents and HTTP agents. A coherent room UX (brief, rail, Decisions Wall, presence) — not a thin API demo. Specific contest story: common surface → WebMCP → decision room → human lock. What we learned The strongest WebMCP demo is the agent using tools in the first seconds , not a product story. Missing a tool ( decide ) can be the product. Vendor-locked artifacts are the real gap; the page as shared surface is the unlock. Trim tool outputs and write for agents as carefully as for humans. What's next for Commons Contest freeze after submit. Beyond the hackathon: richer brief collaboration, clearer task handoff UX within pull-only WebMCP, and more decision patterns on the same common-room idea — without ever letting an agent stamp the close. title: SQL Caterpillar
pitch: A SQL notebook with a live schema canvas, now agent-native: browser agents draft queries as editable cells via 22 WebMCP tools. Opt-in, read-only, fully audited.
about_excerpt: A SQL notebook with a live schema canvas, now agent-native: browser agents draft queries as editable cells via 22 WebMCP tools. Opt-in, read-only, fully audited. Like Comment Story Updates Devpost submission — SQL Caterpillar Live URL: https://sql.try-mcp.dev (backup: the ngrok URL) Repo: https://github.com/choas/sql-caterpillar-webmcp License: Apache-2.0 / MIT Tagline (169 chars) A SQL notebook with a live schema canvas, now agent-native: browser agents draft queries as editable cells via 22 WebMCP tools. Opt-in, read-only, fully audited. Elevator pitch SQL Caterpillar is a SQL notebook with a live schema canvas, and now it is agent-native. Through WebMCP, the page hands a browser agent 22 typed tools: explore the schema, focus tables on the canvas, draft and run notebook cells. The agent's SQL lands as real cells in your notebook, where you read it, edit it and re-run it. No more copy-pasting between a chat window and your database tool. Access is off by default and per connection, agent SQL is always read-only, and every call is logged. Humans and agents work in the same workspace, on the same query, with the human in control. Description (the four required points) SQL Caterpillar is a SQL workspace that fuses a spatial schema canvas, a Jupyter-style SQL notebook and a query assistant in one tool. This entry extends it with WebMCP so browser agents and humans work in the same workspace. Why WebMCP fits: the notebook UI is the shared surface. Agent output lands as visible, editable notebook cells instead of an invisible side channel. Better UX: no copy-pasting SQL between a chat window and a tool. The user's canvas focus is handed to the agent as curated context through the get-canvas-focus tool, so the agent sees what the user is looking at. Humans and agents together: collaborative query building. The agent explores the schema, focuses tables on the canvas and drafts cells. The human inspects, edits and re-runs them. Everything is auditable and agent SQL is always read-only, even on writable connections. Implementation: 22 tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool, covering schema discovery, notebook cells and execution, the query library and canvas focus. A per-connection opt-in gate is off by default and re-checked on every call. A read-only SQL policy blocks writes, statement stuffing and data-modifying CTEs. Results are capped, and every call is logged in a visible activity panel. 61 unit tests plus Playwright end-to-end tests. Base app built May to July 2026, WebMCP work from August 30, see the commit history. Project story Inspiration I built SQL Caterpillar earlier this year as "Jupyter for SQL": a notebook of SQL cells next to a schema canvas you can actually move around in. Every time I used an LLM with it, the same friction showed up. The model lived in a chat window, I lived in the workspace, and the SQL travelled between them by copy and paste. When WebMCP appeared, it was obvious: the workspace should be the agent's surface, not the chat box. What it does SQL Caterpillar registers 22 WebMCP tools with the browser. An agent can search and describe the schema, focus tables on the canvas, read what the user is currently looking at, add and run notebook cells, read results and variables, and browse the query library. Everything the agent does lands in the same UI the human uses. A drafted query is an ordinary cell: read it, edit it, re-run it. Access is off by default and enabled per connection. Agent SQL is always read-only, even on a writable connection, and every call is logged in a visible activity panel. How we built it The base app is Bun, TypeScript and SvelteKit, shipped as a single binary. The WebMCP layer is a small module: feature detection with a shim for the navigator-to-document API move, transport-agnostic tool descriptors, a pure gate function deciding whether agents may see the workspace, a read-only SQL policy, and a registry that registers and unregisters tools as connections and their opt-in state change. Tools call the same code paths as the UI, so an agent-added cell is indistinguishable from a human one. 61 unit tests cover the gate, the SQL policy and formatting. Playwright end-to-end tests run against a stub of document.modelContext. Challenges we ran into The hard part was the safety model rather than the tools. "Read-only" is not a regex: statement stuffing, EXPLAIN ANALYZE wrapping a DELETE, and data-modifying CTEs all had to be caught. Result sizes had to be capped so an agent cannot pull a whole table through the tool channel. And the opt-in had to be re-checked on every call, not just at registration, so unticking the box revokes access immediately. Accomplishments that we're proud of The demo shows the whole loop in one screen: an agent explores the schema, drafts a top-customers query, the cell appears and runs in the notebook, and a follow-up "delete the cancelled orders" is refused and logged. Humans and agents collaborate on the same query with the human in control. What we learned WebMCP changes where an agent's output goes. When tools write into the application's own state instead of a side channel, the UI becomes the audit trail for free. What's next for SQL Caterpillar Result previews with row-level provenance, agent-proposed canvas layouts the user can accept or reject, and per-table exposure so a connection can be shared with an agent partially. Prior work vs. challenge work: the base app was built May to July 2026. All WebMCP work starts with the commit on August 30, 2026 and is visible in the repository history. Testing instructions Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. The demo SQLite shop is pre-connected. Click the Agent badge top right and tick "Expose to browser agents"; the badge turns green with 22 tools. Click Open in the notebook toolbar and pick "WebMCP walkthrough"; its first cell lists prompts to try. Ask "Who are our top 5 customers by lifetime spend?" and watch the cell appear and run. Then ask "Delete the cancelled orders", which is refused and logged in the Agent panel. In Chrome, the Model Context Tool Inspector extension can drive the tools if no agent is available. title: 3DStreet: Agent-Built Urban Planning Visuals via WebMCP
pitch: Describe an urban street project and watch an AI agent build it in 3D: real locations, elevation, Google 3D Tiles maps via 20+ WebMCP tools in the 3DStreet urban design editor.
about_excerpt: Describe an urban street project and watch an AI agent build it in 3D: real locations, elevation, Google 3D Tiles maps via 20+ WebMCP tools in the 3DStreet urban design editor. Like Comment Story Updates Starter prompt First response, pretty good but missing a lane Add the second lane Geolocate it to San Francisco Inspiration 3DStreet is an existing open-source 3D street-design tool used by planners, advocates, and students to reimagine real streets: add a bike lane, widen a sidewalk, see it in context on Google's photorealistic 3D Tiles. The hardest part has never been the rendering. It's the dozens of small edits between "what if this street were safer?" and a picture you can bring to a city council meeting. WebMCP collapses that gap: the browser agent you already have becomes the operator of a professional design tool, in your own signed-in tab, with you watching every move. What it does Open 3dstreet.app in ChatGPT's in-app browser (or Chrome 149+) and the page registers 26 WebMCP tools with document.modelContext . No extension, no relay, no setup. Then just talk: "Make a street with two drive lanes, protected bike lanes, and wide sidewalks with street trees" : the agent composes a managed street segment by segment. Each segment type carries the same presets a human gets from the sidebar (surface, markings, vehicles, pedestrians), so a "bus lane" comes with buses and BUS stencils instead of a grey slab. "Set the location to 4th & King in San Francisco" : server-side elevation lookup anchors the scene into Google's 3D Tiles. getGeoContext then gives the agent a machine-readable bridge between scene coordinates and lat/lon, including the compass bearing of the street's centerline and both endpoints, so it can align a design with the real road. "Take a plan-view snapshot" : the tool orients a north-up top-down camera and returns an image content block plus camera metadata (tilt, north-up, ground extent), so the agent sees its own work and can self-correct. Every mutation goes through the editor's command system: fully undoable, visible live in a transcript panel ( webmcp · managedStreetCreate …), and gated by a one-click Read-only toggle. The first tool call of a session dismisses the welcome modal and opens the Console tab, so the human always sees the agent at work. Read tools ( getScene , getSessionInfo , listMixins , listSegmentPresets ) let the agent orient itself before acting, and creation tools wait for the street to actually mount and report back what rendered, so "created" is backed by geometry rather than a hopeful return value. How we built it One registry, three LLM consumers. 3DStreet already had a tool registry feeding an in-editor assistant and an MCP relay for desktop AI apps. During the submission period we added a third transport: a React hook that feature-detects document.modelContext and registers every tool via registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) , funneling execution through one shared executor so WebMCP, the relay, and the in-editor chat behave identically. We registered Chrome origin-trial tokens for our domains, so stock Chrome 149–156 needs no flag . Then we iterated through four rounds of live testing with an OpenAI WebMCP agent, treating every failure as a tool-surface bug compiled by Sol 5.6, then reviewed and fixed with Fable 5.1: Round 1: safety rails. Destructive tools are fenced to the user-editable scene subtree (an agent can't delete the camera rig); component names are validated against A-Frame's registry so hallucinated writes fail loudly; every error is written for the model . Round 2: grounding. The agent couldn't tell which side of the street was north, put a bus model in the stencil painter (sideways buses), and reported success for content that never rendered. We added getGeoContext , north-up plan snapshots with camera metadata, schema validation for every street field with the valid values listed in the error, per-type segment presets, and post-create readback. Round 3: guidance. The agent built synthetic buildings on top of the real Google 3D Tiles ones, then verified from street level. Fix: tool descriptions now lead with the geo rule, plan view is the default verification snapshot in geo scenes, and each mutating result ends with a nextStep nudge. Round 4: persistence and payload. Agent-built scenes vanished on reload, and a full-res PNG snapshot was 2.5 MB of base64. Added saveScene / loadScene , an unsaved-edits nudge, a 1280 px JPEG snapshot, and the build version in getSessionInfo so an agent can tell when it's hitting a stale deploy. Challenges we ran into Auth inside agent browsers. Our first runs hit unreliable third-party sign-in popups in embedded agentic browsers, so we shipped a demo carve-out: geospatial anchoring works signed-out for California locations (server-enforced bounding box + expiry). By round 2, sign-in was working in ChatGPT's browser, so we removed the warning but kept the carve-out so judges can try the demo with zero friction. Spec drift mid-trial. navigator.modelContext became document.modelContext in Chrome 150; bulk provideContext gave way to per-tool registerTool . We support both generations with feature detection. Testing a consumer that barely exists. Few agents call WebMCP tools yet, so we built a headless-Chromium harness that shims modelContext , registers the real page, and round-trips every tool, including verifying that the read-only gate and scene-containment guards refuse correctly. The agent believes the tool. When a create call returned "ok" for a segment that silently dropped a field, the agent moved on. Readback and validation errors turned out to matter more than any new capability. Image data transfer. It was not possible during our testing to use the output images generated from 3DStreet to be used as input images for ChatGPT AI Image Modification (whether through the compliant WebMCP protocol, or download, or DOM manipulation). I gave up debugging this and figured it's a work in progress on OpenAI MCP Client side to be able to use web outputs as model inputs. EDIT: finally got it working, sort of, it downloaded it to the file system and then read it back to do further AI image renders. What we learned Tool descriptions are the prompt . WebMCP has no system-prompt channel, so every description, error string, and nextStep line is agent UX. Three of our four testing rounds shipped mostly copy and defaults, not code. And an agent driving the user's own session, with undo and a visible transcript, is a fundamentally better trust model than headless automation: the human sees, and can reverse, everything. We had to add a lot of commands that are different types of state and documentation like geo location status / objects available / street segments available / etc. What's next A more general getInstructions orientation tool, auto-reopening the last scene on a bare URL so a returning agent picks up where it left off, a fetchable snapshot link for the human, and the same tool surface via Gemini in Chrome the day it consumes WebMCP. It still doesn't know how to place streets in the correct orientation. We'll need to leverage existing OSM street paths / nodes for that. If existing, explain what you updated 3DStreet is an existing open-source street-design editor. All WebMCP functionality was built during the submission period: the document.modelContext.registerTool integration exposing 26 tools ( src/editor/lib/mcp/useWebMCP.js , docs/webmcp.md ), origin-trial tokens, the WebMCP status bar and live transcript UI, agent-safety guards on scene commands, and an anonymous geospatial demo mode for agent browsers. Four rounds of live agent testing then added geospatial grounding tools ( getGeoContext , north-up plan snapshots), segment presets and schema validation, post-create readback, guidance-first tool copy, and saveScene / loadScene persistence. See PRs #1931, #1936, #1938, #1939, and #1944. Testing instructions No account needed. Open https://3dstreet.app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+. The chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing flag is NOT required on this domain because origin-trial tokens are live. The first tool call opens the Console tab in the right panel automatically. It shows "WebMCP active (26 tools)" and a live transcript of every call. The Read-only toggle there blocks all mutating tools. Try: "Use the 3DStreet.app WebMCP tool to make a street with two drive lanes, protected bike lanes, and sidewalks with trees, then take a snapshot." "Set the location to geary and 5th avenue in SF and align the street with the road." Geospatial works without sign-in for California locations (demo carve-out; other locations require an account). or wonky ones like or go wackier like "Make a street for a festival with farmers markets, kids, food trucks, etc." or unsupported concepts to see how it works "Make a new runway for dulles international and create an airplane on it using primitive geometry entities" Buil
