title: Wilofox Deck Studio
pitch: Create and present visual lessons with an AI agent by your side—on the web, during live streams, and across multiple screens, powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Create and present visual lessons with an AI agent by your side—on the web, during live streams, and across multiple screens, powered by WebMCP. Like 10 Comment 8 Story Updates Wilofox Deck Studio: a human-and-AI workspace for creating and presenting visual lessons with WebMCP. Organize, search, create, and import presentation decks from one visual library. WebMCP connects people and AI agents through shared state and four structured presentation tools. Build structured presentations with sections, content, speaker notes, diagrams, and live previews. Control the live session with timers, speaker notes, quick navigation, and a separate audience view. Presenter control panel with slide navigation, speaker notes, timer, and blackout controls. Present lessons progressively with visual diagrams, navigation shortcuts, and annotation tools. Audience presentation mode with progressive navigation, visual diagrams, and annotation tools. Build complete lessons with structured content, live previews, diagrams, and presentation settings. Two-screen workflow: presenter controls and audience view stay synchronized in real time. Inspiration Wilofox Deck Studio began with a problem I experienced personally—and one that many educators, trainers, content creators, consultants, and live-stream presenters likely share. Existing tools allowed me to design slides, but I could not find one workspace that supported the complete reality of presenting: organizing a lesson, preparing visual content, writing speaker notes, controlling time, managing multiple screens, seeing what comes next, and annotating ideas live without interrupting the flow. I wanted the creative flexibility of a visual design tool, but shaped around how people actually teach and communicate. I needed to prepare everything in the browser, operate the presentation from a separate control screen, keep the audience view clean, and use pointers, highlights, drawings, and shapes while explaining. That personal need became Wilofox Deck Studio. When I discovered WebMCP, I saw a natural extension of the original vision: the workspace could become a shared environment where a person and an AI agent collaborate on the same presentation—not through a disconnected chatbot, but through structured actions connected to the real product. What it does Wilofox Deck Studio is a browser-based workspace for creating and delivering structured, interactive presentations. It is designed for educators, content creators, trainers, professionals, and live-stream presenters who need more than a traditional sequence of static slides. Users can: Create presentations from scratch, start from built-in examples, or import structured JSON. Organize content into sections and progressively ordered slides. Search, filter, categorize, duplicate, and manage presentations from a visual library. Combine written content with diagrams, images, videos, code, and embedded web resources. Add speaker notes and estimated presentation time. Configure formats, categories, series, production status, themes, typography, and colors. Preview content and visual resources while editing. Present using a single screen or a separate presenter-control window. See the current slide, upcoming slide, speaker notes, reference clocks, timer, and timing status. Navigate progressively or jump directly to a specific part of the presentation. Use a laser pointer, pen, highlighter, colors, arrows, rectangles, and other shapes during a live explanation. Zoom, pan, isolate the content or diagram, undo annotations, and temporarily black out the audience screen. Reserve an interface area for a camera or chat in an OBS composition. Export and reuse presentation content in formats such as JSON, HTML, PDF, and PowerPoint. The result is a workflow that connects preparation, editing, rehearsal, presentation, and live interaction within one coherent experience. How WebMCP is used WebMCP adds a structured agent layer to the existing presentation workflow. Wilofox exposes four tools: create_deck creates a complete, editable presentation from structured input. get_deck_context reads the current presentation state, including changes made manually by the user. update_slide updates one targeted slide while preserving the rest of the deck. navigate_to_slide moves the shared interface to a requested slide for review or presentation. These tools allow a compatible AI agent to understand and operate Wilofox without guessing where to click or attempting to interpret a complex editor only through pixels. The agent works with the same presentation state that the person can see and edit. There is no hidden agent-only copy. When a tool changes a slide or creates a deck, the result is validated, stored, rendered in the interface, and immediately available for human review. The user remains in control: every result can be inspected, edited manually, presented, exported, or replaced. Why WebMCP is a strong fit A presentation editor contains many controls, panels, fields, and possible actions. Asking an agent to operate that environment through visual guessing would be fragile and imprecise. WebMCP gives Wilofox a small, explicit set of meaningful capabilities with structured and bounded inputs. This makes agent behavior easier to understand, safer to execute, and more closely aligned with the user’s intention. A practical workflow can look like this: The agent creates a structured lesson. The educator reviews it and manually adjusts the content. The agent reads the latest shared state. The educator asks it to improve only one specific slide. The updated result appears inside the same editor. The person makes the final teaching and design decisions. This kind of collaboration would otherwise require copying content repeatedly between a chatbot and a presentation tool, manually reconstructing context, and risking the loss of previous edits. Human and agent collaboration Wilofox is designed around a simple principle: the agent contributes speed and structured assistance, while the person contributes judgment, subject knowledge, creativity, and final control. The shared presentation is the source of truth. Manual edits and agent actions use the same state, rendering, validation, and persistence flow. This prevents the agent experience from becoming a parallel prototype disconnected from the real application. For educators and presenters, this means less time transferring information between tools and more time reviewing, refining, and communicating ideas effectively. How I built it Wilofox Deck Studio is built with HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript using a portable single-file application architecture. It runs directly in the browser without requiring a traditional backend. Presentation data and configuration are stored locally using IndexedDB, supporting a local-first workflow. The application includes: A presentation library and filtering system. A structured slide editor. Visual diagram generators. A presentation runtime. Live annotation tools. Multi-window presenter controls. Import and export workflows. Local state and persistence management. WebMCP was implemented through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool includes: A clear name and description. An explicit JSON Schema. Bounded and validated inputs. Targeted execution behavior. Reuse of the application’s existing state and persistence functions. Visible results rendered through the normal interface. WebMCP support is implemented as a progressive enhancement. Browsers without WebMCP can still use the complete manual presentation experience. What was added during the WebMCP Challenge Wilofox Deck Studio existed before the challenge as a human-operated presentation workspace. During the challenge, I meaningfully extended it with an agent-accessible collaboration layer by: Registering four structured WebMCP tools. Defining explicit schemas and bounded tool inputs. Connecting agent actions to the application’s real state. Preserving manual changes during targeted agent updates. Reusing the existing rendering and persistence workflow. Maintaining compatibility with browsers that do not support WebMCP. Adding documentation, testing instructions, examples, and visual explanations of the human-agent workflow. The WebMCP implementation is therefore not a separate demonstration attached to the product. It extends the way the existing application can be operated. Challenges The main technical challenge was maintaining one reliable source of truth across multiple experiences: The editor. The presentation window. The presenter-control window. IndexedDB persistence. Manual user actions. WebMCP agent actions. An agent update had to preserve work already completed by the user. Improving one slide should not replace the entire presentation, remove unrelated content, or create a disconnected version. title: RelayRoom
pitch: Resolve one disruption across three companies—without copying data between three portals
about_excerpt: Resolve one disruption across three companies—without copying data between three portals Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Supply-chain exceptions are rarely owned by one company. A delayed shipment may require a buyer to change an order, a supplier to reserve replacement inventory, and a carrier to select a new route. Today, operations coordinators manage these multi-party recoveries through email chains, spreadsheets, phone calls, and manual copy-pasting between incompatible portals. This process is slow, error-prone, and lacks audit trails. We built RelayRoom to demonstrate how WebMCP can enable secure, coordinated cross-organizational workflows without requiring every company to integrate with a central backend or surrender control of their systems. What it does RelayRoom is a neutral coordination room that orchestrates supply-chain recovery across three simulated partner portals (buyer, supplier, carrier) using browser-native WebMCP. Each partner exposes a minimal, explicitly allowlisted set of tools that the coordination room can discover and execute. The system: Discovers tools from three distinct origins with exact trust boundaries Queries constraints from all partners (deadlines, inventory, routes, costs) Simulates feasible recovery candidates using a deterministic solver Presents a coordinated plan with cost deltas, timing, and rollback options Requires explicit user approval before any partner actions execute Stages all partner actions first, then commits in a deterministic order Automatically runs compensating rollbacks if any step fails Generates signed audit receipts showing tool, origin, inputs, results, and timestamps The hero scenario resolves CASE-1047: 480 sensor modules needed by Friday, with original supplier short 170 units, backup supplier requiring minimum reservations, and carrier route running 36 hours late—all while keeping added logistics cost under 10%. How we built it Architecture: Monorepo with separate apps for the coordination room and three partner portals, plus shared packages for contracts, operations logic, simulator, and UI components. Tech Stack: TypeScript, React, Vite for all surfaces Express.js for backend APIs SQLite for operational databases (buyer, supplier, carrier, workspace) WebMCP draft implementation for cross-origin tool discovery and execution Zod for schema validation Zustand for state management Vitest for unit tests, Playwright for E2E tests Docker Compose for containerized deployment Key Implementation Details: Each partner portal runs on a distinct origin with its own branding and state WebMCP tools are registered with exact exposedTo allowlists containing only the RelayRoom origin The room discovers tools using getTools({ fromOrigins: [...] }) and executes them with origin-scoped permissions SQLite transactions prevent overlapping reservations from overbooking resources Idempotency keys are tied to transaction, partner, and phase for safe retries Approval is written before any partner action; changed plans are rejected before execution Compensation restores previous order contents with new revisions and releases staged/committed allocations Challenges we ran into Cross-origin WebMCP implementation: The WebMCP draft is still evolving. We had to implement the protocol correctly while providing a compatibility bridge fallback for browsers that don't support native WebMCP yet. Transaction safety across distributed systems: Designing a staged commit pattern with proper compensating rollback that works even when network timeouts or partial failures occur. Origin isolation vs. coordination: Keeping each partner's state truly isolated while still enabling the coordination room to discover and call their tools without importing their stores directly. Deterministic simulation: Building a solver that produces feasible candidates from normalized partner evidence without relying on AI hallucinations. Permission granularity: Designing tool schemas that expose exactly the capabilities needed for coordination without giving away unnecessary access to partner systems. Accomplishments that we're proud of Real cross-origin WebMCP implementation: The deployed demo makes the cross-origin architecture obvious with three distinct origins and proper allow="tools" permissions. Complete transaction safety: Staged commit with automatic compensating rollback, idempotency keys, and SQLite transaction guarantees. Deterministic solver: The system computes feasible candidates without requiring AI, though it can optionally use OpenAI/Gemini for selection and explanation. Full audit trail: Every tool execution is logged with origin, inputs, results, and timestamp—providing clear attribution for every action. Comprehensive testing: Unit tests cover expiry, duplicate import rollback, idempotency, changed approval rejection, exact allocation, and failed compensation. E2E tests verify the hero flow and failure-plus-rollback scenarios. Production-ready deployment: Docker Compose support, environment variable configuration, and proper security headers for HTTPS deployment. What we learned WebMCP's potential: Browser-native tool sharing is a powerful primitive for cross-organizational interoperability that doesn't require every company to build to the same central API. The importance of staged commits: In distributed systems, staging all actions first and validating feasibility before commit is essential for safety. Origin boundaries matter: Keeping each partner's state isolated while enabling coordination is not just a security concern—it's fundamental to the interoperability story. Deterministic > AI for core logic: AI is valuable for selection and explanation, but the core solver should be deterministic to ensure reliability. Audit trails build trust: When coordinating across company boundaries, being able to show exactly who authorized which action is critical. What's next for it Multi-leg route optimization: Extend the solver to support multi-leg and split-shipment networks beyond the current single-route constraint. Real provider integrations: Complete certification and live-testing with actual ERPNext, Shippo, and other provider adapters. SSO and account management: Add single sign-on, password reset, and account revocation UI for production deployment. Tenant isolation: Transform from single-organization deployment to multi-tenant SaaS with proper data isolation. Additional exception scenarios: Support more than one polished exception scenario beyond the CASE-1047 hero case. Native WebMCP browser support: Full validation in a supporting browser build once native WebMCP is widely available. title: Autonomous Procurement & Supply Chain Negotiator
pitch: A procurement dashboard where 8 WebMCP tools let an AI agent crunch supply chain data in parallel while humans retain exclusive control over purchase orders via an unforgeable approval system.
about_excerpt:
A procurement dashboard where 8 WebMCP tools let an AI agent crunch supply chain data in parallel while humans retain exclusive control over purchase orders via an unforgeable approval system.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Supply chain disruptions cost manufacturers 15-20% of EBITDA . When a port closes or commodity prices spike, procurement teams scramble across 5+ separate systems—checking inventory, calling freight forwarders, reviewing supplier health, and manually calculating landed costs in Excel. By the time they respond, they've lost hours and thousands of dollars. 

 We built The Autonomous Procurement & Supply Chain Negotiator to solve this. We wanted to show that WebMCP isn't just for chatbots—it's for serious enterprise tools where humans and AI work together safely . 

 The "aha" moment came when we realized WebMCP lets an AI agent orchestrate data from multiple sources in parallel , triggered by a single human gesture—something that was impossible before. 

 

 What It Does 

 The Autonomous Procurement & Supply Chain Negotiator is a real-time dashboard where: 

 
 A global heatmap shows port congestion, supplier health, and active shipping lanes 
 A priority slider lets the human express "Cost vs Speed" preferences 
 A WebMCP agent fires 8 tools in parallel to analyze commodities, inventory, shipping routes, supplier health, and bulk discounts 
 3 alternative sourcing routes appear as clickable cards 
 A PO draft is generated and placed in an approval queue 
 Human approval (with cryptographic token verification) executes the final purchase order 
 

 The agent does 99% of the work —data aggregation, scenario modeling, and drafting. The human does the 1% that matters —deciding to spend money. 

 

 How We Built It 

 Tech Stack 

 
 Frontend: Next.js 15 + React Server Components + Tailwind CSS + shadcn/ui 
 State Management: Zustand + React Query 
 Charts & Maps: Recharts + Mapbox GL 
 Deployment: Vercel (with Cloudflare edge caching) 
 WebMCP: 8 tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() 
 

 The 8 WebMCP Tools 

 We registered strict input schemas for every tool: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "fetch_commodity_prices" , 
 description : "Fetches real-time spot prices for copper, lithium, crude oil, gold, and silver." , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : "object" , 
 properties : { 
 commodities : { 
 type : "array" , 
 items : { type : "string" , enum : [ "copper" , "lithium" , "crude_oil" , "natural_gas" , "gold" , "silver" ] } 
 } , 
 currency : { type : "string" , enum : [ "USD" , "EUR" , "GBP" ] , default : "USD" } 
 } , 
 required : [ "commodities" ] 
 } , 
 execute : async ( { commodities , currency } ) = > { 
 // Parallel fetch from CommodityPriceAPI + Live-Rates.com
 // Return { commodity: { price, change_24h, change_7d, volume } }
 } , 
 annotations : { readOnlyHint : true } 
 } ) ; 

 // Plus 7 more tools:
 // - calculate_landed_cost
 // - analyze_supplier_health
 // - simulate_bulk_discount
 // - get_inventory_status
 // - assess_port_risk
 // - generate_po_draft (requires human approval)
 // - execute_approved_po (human-only)
 Critical Safety Pattern : Human - in - the - Loop ( HITL ) 
The agent cannot execute purchase orders . We implemented an unforgeable approval system : 

generate_po_draft creates a draft but does not send it

When the human clicks "Approve," we generate a cryptographic token ( SHA -256 hash of draft ID + user ID + timestamp + nonce ) 

execute_approved_po verifies the token before executing

All approvals are logged in an audit trail with timestamps and user IDs

javascript
 // Token verification in execute_approved_po
 const isValid = verifyToken ( po_draft_id , human_approval_token ) ; 
 if ( ! isValid ) throw new Error ( "Invalid or expired approval token" ) ; 
 // ... execute PO
 Parallel Orchestration
When the human drags the priority slider , the agent orchestrates all tools in parallel : 

javascript
 const [ prices , inventory , landedCosts , portRisks , supplierHealth , discounts ] = 
 await Promise . allSettled ( [ 
 fetch_commodity_prices ( { commodities : [ "copper" , "lithium" ] } ) , 
 get_inventory_status ( { skus : [ "SKU-1001" ] } ) , 
 calculate_landed_cost ( { supplier_id , origin , destination } ) , 
 assess_port_risk ( { port_code : "NLRTM" } ) , 
 analyze_supplier_health ( { supplier_id } ) , 
 simulate_bulk_discount ( { supplier_id , sku , min_qty : 1000 , max_qty : 10000 } ) 
 ] ) ; 
Agent Reasoning Sidebar
We display a live log of agent tool calls to build trust : 

text
🔄 fetch_commodity_prices → Copper up 4.2 % in last hour
🔄 get_inventory_status → Safety stock : 2 , 300 units ( above threshold ) 
🔄 calculate_landed_cost → Route via Rotterdam : $ 42.50 / unit
🔄 assess_port_risk → Rotterdam congestion : HIGH ( 72hr delay ) 
🔄 analyze_supplier_health → Elbe Metalworks : 92 / 100 ( APPROVED ) 
🔄 simulate_bulk_discount → Optimal qty : 5 , 000 units ( savings : 8.5 % ) 
Challenges We Faced
 1 . WebMCP Flag Only in Chrome Canary
Early development was tricky because WebMCP requires Chrome 146 + with the #enable - webmcp - testing flag . We worked around this by building a graceful fallback— if WebMCP isn't available , the app runs in simulation mode with mocked tool calls so the UI still works for local development . 

 2 . Balancing AI Autonomy vs . Safety
We debated how much autonomy the agent should have . Too little → useless . Too much → dangerous . The two - tool split ( generate_po_draft + execute_approved_po ) was the perfect compromise—the agent does all the work but cannot spend money without human approval . 

 3 . Real - Time Data Integration
Commodity APIs have rate limits and some require paid keys . We built a 5 - minute Cloudflare KV cache and used Promise . allSettled ( ) so one failing API doesn't break the entire orchestration . 

 4 . State Management
Coordinating UI state ( slider value , selected route , tool outputs ) across React components required a robust Zustand store with distinct slices for UI , tool results , and agent reasoning logs . 

Accomplishments We're Proud Of
✅ Sub - 800ms orchestration — 6 parallel tool calls , UI updates in under a second
✅ Unforgeable approval system — Agents cannot bypass human approval
✅ Full Next . js production app — Not a prototype , deployed on Vercel
✅ Agent reasoning sidebar — Builds transparency and trust
✅ Global heatmap — Real - time port congestion and supplier health visualization
✅ 9 hours to deadline — Submitted on time ! 

What We Learned
WebMCP is a Game - Changer
Before WebMCP , building this would have required a complex backend orchestrator , custom API routes , and WebSocket connections . WebMCP lets the browser handle orchestration natively , eliminating hundreds of lines of backend code . 

The Browser is the New Orchestrator 
With WebMCP , the browser isn 't just rendering UI—it' s coordinating data fetching , tool execution , and state updates . This shifts the architecture dramatically toward thin servers and intelligent clients . 

Human - in - the - Loop is Essential
Enterprise AI isn 't about replacing humans—it' s about augmenting them . The two - tool split with cryptographic approval tokens is a pattern we'll use in future WebMCP projects . 

What's Next
🔹 Real API Integration — Replace mock data with CommodityPriceAPI , CerebroChain , and D & B APIs
🔹 Multi - User Teams — Add team workspaces with role - based permissions
🔹 Slack / Teams Integration — Notify procurement teams when critical alerts fire
🔹 Predictive Analytics — Use historical data to forecast future disruptions
🔹 Mobile App — Build a React Native companion for on - the - go approvals

Why This Wins the WebMCP Challenge
Criterion How We Score
WebMCP Leverage 8 tools with strict schemas , parallel orchestration , secure HITL pattern , AbortSignal cleanup
Execution Full Next . js production app with real - time UI , deployed on Vercel , working live demo
Potential Impact Solves a billion - dollar problem — supply chain disruptions cost 15 - 20 % of EBITDA
Creativity & Ambition Slider - driven agent orchestration + global heatmap + unforgeable approval tokens

title: Streaming Lens — streaming market data, agent-native
pitch: Market research on streaming — micro-drama, African OTT, piracy, sports rights. Free WebMCP tools tell an agent what the paid data covers and how fresh it is, without returning a value.
about_excerpt: Market research on streaming — micro-drama, African OTT, piracy, sports rights. Free WebMCP tools tell an agent what the paid data covers and how fresh it is, without returning a value. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We already sell streaming-market research: 17,470 sourced datapoints on micro-drama, African OTT, piracy, the creator economy and sports rights, behind a paid MCP server with 194 tools. So the WebMCP question was never "what demo could we build" — it was sharper and more uncomfortable: what does a paywalled B2B product do when the visitor is an agent? Today, agents scrape sites like ours. They read the marketing pages, miss the data entirely, and invent the numbers. Blocking them is not an answer either: an agent that leaves with nothing never comes back, and never buys. Giving the data away ends the business. WebMCP allows a fourth option, and that is the whole submission: describe the asset precisely, withhold its substance, and always say where the substance lives. What it does Every page of lens.streaming-radar.com — 49 of them — registers tools on document.modelContext . Seven, all free, no key, no account, and no flag for the visitor to enable: we serve a first-party Chrome origin-trial token in <head> . ask_site — returns the page sections that answer a question, with canonical URLs. search_intelligence_archive — searches the published newsletter editions and analyses. check_data_coverage — the one that carries the idea. Ask about any company, country or topic and it returns how many sourced datapoints we hold, which report silos they sit in, which countries and years they cover, the confidence mix, when the most recent one was updated, and one sample datapoint — metric name, unit, source, confidence — with its value withheld . Asked about ReelShort: 408 datapoints, across five silos, 2022 to 2028, the most recent updated this week. get_market_signals — the live monitoring feed; it also re-renders the visible feed on the page. estimate_streaming_pnl — drives the on-page P&L calculator and returns the model output. Registered on /calculator only: a tool with no valid target is a broken contract. request_report_teaser — the conversion step. Requires an explicit consent argument and fills the page's own email gate, so the human sees what the agent did. browse_reports — the catalogue. Then the boundary itself. Until this week, a paid tool called without entitlement answered Authentication required — three words, a dead end. Now the JSON-RPC error carries error.data : what the silo holds (5,306 datapoints, 51 countries, 2004 to 2033 on our vertical-drama silo), one sample with its value withheld, the URLs to buy or authenticate, and the exact instruction to replay the call with a key. The refusal proves possession instead of ending the conversation. The same computation answers the free tool and the refusal, because they answer the same question and must answer identically. How we built it The site is static HTML with no bundler and no package.json , so the SDK is vendored as a pinned ESM asset and the module graph is injected by the site's page producer , never edited page by page. Tools are side-effect-free ES modules, registered once per document, unregistered on pagehide . The tools never reimplement the page. request_report_teaser calls the site's own email-gate API through a small public seam; estimate_streaming_pnl moves the calculator's real controls and lets the page compute; get_market_signals reads the same endpoint the visible feed reads. One behaviour, one implementation, whether a human or an agent triggers it. Agent traffic is measured server-side with a cookieless beacon — no cookie, no identifier, nothing to consent to — because GA4 only loads after a cookie banner and an agent never clicks Accept. Without it, agent traffic would be strictly invisible. Challenges we ran into A cache header that silently ate a release. Two new tools worked on the origin and reached no browser. Cloudflare Pages does not let a more specific _headers rule override a broader one — it concatenates them: max-age=31536000, immutable, public, max-age=300, must-revalidate . Browsers keep the first directive, so the modules stayed immutable for a year. The fix was to move the whole graph out of the /js/ prefix; there is no negation and no override. Short acronyms matching inside words. Our coverage counter used ILIKE '%ott%' and returned 109 rows; word-bounded, 78. Twenty-eight percent phantom matches in a number we use as a commercial argument. The same bug in our signal matcher had been filing Ridley Scott stories into the sports silo — ott inside Scott , mma inside summary . Both are bounded now, with regression tests. Bilingual pages. Our HTML carries French and English in the same DOM, hidden by CSS. In a detached document no CSS applies, so the first version of ask_site handed agents both languages glued together: "En brefTL;DR". A surface that switches off in silence. Without a valid origin-trial token, document.modelContext simply does not exist and the SDK no-ops — no error anywhere. Our pipeline health check now reads the token off the deployed page, decodes its expiry, and goes red fourteen days before. Accomplishments that we're proud of It is not a demo. It is a production B2B product, the surface is measured, and the independent webmcp.com directory grades the implementation A . 1,404 tests green, including three whose only job is to prove no datapoint value can escape through the free surface. What we learned An agent-native paywall is not a wall with an API. It is a boundary that explains itself. Publish the shape, withhold the substance, always say where the substance lives — everything else follows. What's next for Streaming Lens An agent-reachable checkout, so the handoff completes without a human copying a key. And per-call payment at the edge: our MCP already runs on Cloudflare, and a 402 with a machine-readable price is the same envelope we just built, with an amount attached. pitch: The User and ChatGPT share one live cart and the agent proposes a gift, the user approves, review, and then confirm. Therefore nothing is placed without the user
about_excerpt:
The User and ChatGPT share one live cart and the agent proposes a gift, the user approves, review, and then confirm. Therefore nothing is placed without the user
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Asked Agent to recommend a gift under 40 pounds for someone who cooks 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Website page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Use the site tools to call g et_account,get_saved_customer, get_shop_state. Quote the exact JSON, call apply_saved_profile. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Asked Agent to recommend a gift under 40 pounds for someone who cooks 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Website page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Use the site tools to call g et_account,get_saved_customer, get_shop_state. Quote the exact JSON, call apply_saved_profile. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Asked Agent to recommend a gift under 40 pounds for someone who cooks 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every "AI shopping" demo I'd seen had the same problem: the agent clicks buttons it's guessing at, or it shops in a parallel page you can't even see. I wanted the opposite. One real shop, one cart, where ChatGPT and I are looking at the exact same thing and I get the final say. 

 That's what Hearth is, a small home goods shop for the table and kitchen. You browse and click like you would anywhere else. The agent, meanwhile, calls real site tools and nothing gets bought until you approve it, review it, and confirm it. 

 What it does 

 I and the agent share the same tab and the same cart. 

 The agent calls recommend_gift instead of silently adding something to your bag. A tradeoff card shows up: here's the pick, here's why, here's what it costs and that makes the cart stay empty. 

 You hit Approve on the page only then does the item land in your cart. 

 explain_cart and prepare_order build a review of everything while ordering stays locked. 

 If the agent tries place_order without confirm: true , it gets blocked and Undo Last restores your last cart snapshot if anything goes sideways. 

 Privacy was a deliberate part of the demo. Once you sign in, get_account and get_saved_customer only return a profileStatus flag, like hasShipping: true . Your street address and phone number never leave this browser; they sit in a local demo vault. Checkout keeps those fields hidden too, until you personally choose Use saved details or Show saved address which makes the agent unable to see them. 

 Why this is a fit for WebMCP 

 A shop is a terrible scraping target. Filters, quantities, promo codes, checkout, and a yes/no question about how much you're willing to spend, and an agent guessing at all of that through the DOM is fragile and blind. WebMCP lets the page declare those actions up front. The agent doesn't just click or hunt for buttons, it calls search_products , recommend_gift and prepare_order . Since it's the same page, you watch the DOM update live, right next to you. 

 The hard part was always the trust gap: how do you let an agent "help" while you're still the one who sees everything, approves everything, and can undo everything without handing it your address? Structured tools let the site describe the action, its inputs, and its guardrails directly. That's what solved it. 

 What I learned 

 The biggest lesson is learned is that agent usefulness is not the same thing as agent autonomy. The moments where the agent actually felt useful weren't when it acted on its own, they were when it made a clear proposal, showed its reasoning, and waited one step for my approval. 

 How I built it 

 Static HTML and ES modules on Netlify, No backend, Auth and the customer vault are plain localStorage. 

 mcp-boot.js looks for document.modelContext / navigator.modelContext early. webmcp.js builds each tool (name, description, inputSchema, execute) and registers it with registerTool, including search_products: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "search_products" , 
 description : "Search the shop by words such as mug, skillet, linen, gift, or wool." , 
 inputSchema : { type : "object" , properties : { query : { type : "string" } } , required : [ "query" ] } , 
 execute : async ( { query } ) = > shop . searchProducts ( query , "agent" ) 
 } ) ;

title: Shopfront Copilot
pitch: Shop together with your AI agent, but only you can hit "buy."
about_excerpt: Shop together with your AI agent, but only you can hit "buy." Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The WebMCP spec's own authors flagged the sharpest risk in agentic commerce in their own draft. Section 6.3.2.3 walks through an ambiguously named tool, finalizeCart , that an agent could call and silently complete a real purchase. An agent shopping "on your behalf" today has two bad options: screen-scrape the UI (brittle, no ground truth), or call a private backend API directly (bypasses whatever safety rails the storefront's own UI enforces). WebMCP offered a third path: let the agent call the exact tool the UI itself uses, on the exact same page state a human is looking at. We wanted to build a storefront that took the spec's own warning seriously enough to actually engineer around it, not just write a paragraph about "responsible AI" in a README. What it does Shopfront Copilot is a storefront where a shopper and their AI agent browse, compare, and buy together. The agent can: Search & filter the catalog by price, category, and other bounded fields Compare 2-4 products side by side in a real on-page comparison table Check return policy for a product Add / remove cart items , reversible either direction Watch a product for price drops All of it runs through the same WebMCP tools registered on document.modelContext that the storefront's own UI calls. A shopper also controls an Autonomy Dial (read-only vs. browse-and-cart) and an optional spending cap , both enforced with machine-readable refusal codes the agent can act on. The checkout gate: the headline feature Action Exposed to the agent? Can it complete a purchase? checkout (WebMCP tool) Yes No. Always returns { status: "confirmation_required", cart_summary } . Never mutates the cart. Confirm-purchase click Not a registered tool at all. Yes, this is the only thing that finalizes an order, and it's gated behind WebAuthn on a plain onClick handler an agent can't reach. There is no tool an agent can call, no matter how it's worded, that completes a purchase. How we built it Stack: Next.js (App Router), TypeScript, React, Tailwind State: client-side React context persisted to localStorage , no backend database Tools: defined once in lib/webmcp/tools/ , registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() , so a human's click and an agent's tool call run through the identical code path into the identical shared cart The safety layer is factored out into its own framework-agnostic package, webmcp-guardrails : Autonomy tiers & spending caps that gate mutating calls Structural-absence check that proves confirm_purchase was never registered, rather than just asserting it in prose Flight recorder that logs every tool call as structured, timestamped data Intent-snapshot diffing that freezes what an agent saw when it called checkout and flags anything that changed by the time a human confirms To prove the pattern holds against a real model, not just scripted scenarios, we added a live agent mode backed by Groq , driving the exact same tool registry and guardrails a simulated harness uses. Checkout confirmation is server-verified through WebAuthn with zero database, and everything degrades gracefully in browsers without document.modelContext support, which today is most of them. Challenges we ran into Making the checkout gate airtight meant resisting the temptation to "just add a permission check" to a confirm_purchase tool, since a runtime check is something an agent, or a future refactor, could route around. We made the property structural instead of declarative : the function that finalizes an order simply is never wired into the tool registry. We also hit five places where the WebMCP spec doesn't yet define an answer: No standard classification for irreversible actions No agent identity to key a per-agent rate limit or trust tier on No way for a shopper's consent decision to persist and reach the agent before it fails once No push channel for telling an idle agent a watched price actually dropped No standard primitive for an agent to pause and ask a human a question We wrote up each gap and our workaround as an RFC rather than silently papering over them. Keeping the demo honest against a real model was its own challenge: a live Groq-backed agent will happily try creative phrasings to get a tool to do more than its contract allows, which made for a good adversarial test of whether our guardrails actually held. Accomplishments that we're proud of confirm_purchase cannot be reached by an agent under any circumstance, and we can prove it structurally , not just document it webmcp-guardrails is genuinely reusable: pure TypeScript, no dependency on React or this app's domain Live agent mode means the checkout gate is tested against a real model actively trying to complete a purchase, not just scripted scenarios What we learned The safest thing you can do with a dangerous capability isn't a well-worded permission check, it's not exposing the capability's implementation to the caller at all . We also came away convinced that several of the gaps we hit (agent identity, a standard human-question primitive) sit upstream of a lot of other trust problems in agentic web tooling, and are worth pushing at the spec level rather than solving per-site forever. What's next for Shopfront Copilot Publish webmcp-guardrails to npm so other WebMCP sites can adopt the structural-absence pattern without rebuilding it Prototype an irreversibleHint annotation as a concrete proposal back to the WebMCP spec Prototype a standard ask_human -shaped primitive for the same reason Built With next react typescript webmcp Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Yanfunmi Jeje Like Share this project: Updates Yanfunmi Jeje started this project — Sep 03, 2026 04:47 AM EDT

title: Handback - Universal Agent Handoff
pitch: One encrypted link that moves an AI session to a different agent. The one you're already talking to packages the work; the next one picks it up. No account, nothing to install.
about_excerpt: One encrypted link that moves an AI session to a different agent. The one you're already talking to packages the work; the next one picks it up. No account, nothing to install. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration You finish an hour with one agent and open a different one. Everything you settled is still in the first window: the decisions, the constraints, the things you ruled out and why. The second agent has never seen any of it. The workaround everyone uses is to paste the transcript. That makes the next agent re-derive conclusions you already reached, and it leaves another copy of your conversation in another tool. I wanted the state itself to move, not a recording of the conversation that produced it. What it does You say one sentence to the agent you're already using: save this to handback.link . One tool call later you have a link. Nothing was copied, pasted or re-explained. Whoever you send it to points any agent at that link, and that agent reads fields instead of prose: the objective, the decisions and the reasoning behind them, the constraints, the open tasks, the questions nobody has answered. It doesn't have to work out what was already settled, because the settled things are fields. The same link accumulates versions as it travels. Each one is sealed with a hash tied to its own version and its parent, so anything edited outside the approval path stops matching and the page says so. Nothing is overwritten: click any version in the History list to read it, and an agent can ask for one by number and walk back through how the work changed. No account, no sign-up, no email address, nothing to install; the product is one URL. Why this needs WebMCP The agent has to be the one doing the packaging, and that's what makes this a WebMCP problem instead of an API problem. If a person has to copy the conversation into a form, I've rebuilt the work I'm trying to delete. The conversation is already sitting in a browser tab, so the tools have to run in that tab. No server-to-server integration, no OAuth, no API key, no connector per vendor. There's a second reason, and it's the one I'd defend hardest: Handback can't read what it stores. The browser encrypts with AES-256-GCM and puts the key in the URL fragment, which browsers never send to a server. A server-side MCP integration can't work this way, because the server would need the plaintext to be useful. Page-local tools are what let the encryption sit in front of the service instead of behind it. Nearly every WebMCP build I've seen points the same way: a site exposes its own features so an agent can operate it. Search the catalogue, book the appointment, fill the form. Handback points sideways. The page isn't the destination, it's a transfer point between two agents that will never talk to each other directly. What people and agents can do together now Work that crosses from one vendor's agent to another, with nobody retyping it, through a service that can't read it. The part I haven't seen elsewhere is the approval gate, and it only works because the tools live in the page. Auto-approval is on by default, because making someone click between an agent and its own work is friction nobody wants. But handback_settings is one-way. An agent can call it with requireApproval: true and put a human back in the loop. requireApproval: false comes back refused, with reason: "human_only" . There's no approve tool and no commit tool. So an agent that's been prompt-injected by the handoff it just read can raise the bar, and has nothing in its tool list that lowers it. A remote MCP server can't offer that. It hands an agent a settings endpoint, and it has no way to make "off" unreachable. One limit worth stating plainly: this covers the tools, not the browser. Anything driving the page through browser automation clicks the control the way a person would, and no website can stop that. What the one-way gate buys is that the WebMCP path, which is the route a prompt injection travels, contains no move that reduces human oversight. How I built it Five tools on document.modelContext , and they make one loop around a single link. stage_handoff does the packaging and saves the result. Its input schema is the whole handoff state and it returns the URL in the same call. The description tells the agent to reply with the url field verbatim, because an agent that summarises what it just saved buries the one thing the person needs to copy. get_handoff_receipt answers "did that save, and what was the link?" It returns created with the URL and version, pending while a draft waits for a human click, or none when this page holds no handoff. read_handoff is what the receiving agent calls. It takes a sections array, an optional character offset for paging through one long section, and an optional version . Every version is kept, so an agent can walk back through how the work changed rather than only seeing where it landed, and the reply carries currentVersion so it knows how far back it is looking. This tool and both writers are annotated untrustedContentHint: true , and the description says the content came from other people and other agents and is information to consider, never instructions to follow. A handoff is exactly the shape a prompt injection would arrive in. stage_contribution writes back. Every proposal names the baseVersion it was built on, and a stale one is refused with the current version handed back, so the agent can re-read and re-propose without a person stepping in. handback_settings governs the other four: retention, and the one-way approval gate above. All five declare an outputSchema alongside the inputSchema , so every result is a typed value an agent can branch on. readOnlyHint marks the two readers. Registration happens once per document and tears down through an AbortController . One JSON Schema in shared/schema.ts drives the tool surface and the server-side validation together, so the two can't drift. React and Vite on the front end, Cloudflare Workers and D1 behind it, and the site runs Chrome's WebMCP origin trial so visitors never touch a flag. Challenges I ran into Building against a spec that moved under me turned up five things, all written up in docs/WEBMCP-COMPATIBILITY.md : The entry point migrated window.agent → navigator.modelContext → document.modelContext , so I probe document then navigator. Thrown errors are discarded by design. The spec flattens any rejection to a bare UnknownError , so every refusal here is a returned value carrying a reason the agent can read. Output budgets are real. A ChatGPT session gave up on an oversized response and scraped the page instead, so read_handoff pages long sections. Extensions inject late, so the API needs polling after mount. A <form id="modelContext"> clobbers the property into a truthy Element, so the check is typeof registerTool === "function" . The one that taught me most came from a stranger. Someone found the site, handed off from a real ChatGPT session, and their tab got reclaimed while it waited for a confirmation. On the reopened page, get_handoff_receipt answered pending , which its own description defines as waiting for a human click. Nobody was waiting. That single status was carrying three unrelated meanings, so it became three: created , pending and none . What I learned More of my time went into the sentences an agent reads than into the functions behind them. Most of the bugs I fixed were an agent doing something reasonable with a description I had left ambiguous. Returning a refusal as a value beats throwing it. Give the agent a reason it can read and the current state, and it corrects itself in one more call without the person ever seeing it. What's next This gets better as WebMCP spreads, in the direction that matters. Every new site registering tools makes that one site callable. A handoff layer works the other way round: every new agent that speaks WebMCP can read and write a Handback link with no work from me and no integration on their side, because the contract is a page and a JSON Schema instead of a partnership. Two agents that have never heard of each other pass work through one URL. That's the same trade the web made the first time, a common surface instead of an integration per pair. A handoff layer is close to worthless with one agent and hard to replace once there are twenty. Nearer term: a DELETE route so a never-expiring handoff can be withdrawn, and richer fields in the manual create form to match what the agent path already produces. Built With cloudflare-d1 cloudflare-workers json-schema playwright react three.js typescript vite vitest web-crypto-api webmcp Try it out handback.link github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Building Handback helped me understand WebMCP by actually using it. I learned a lot about tool design, agent workflows, and where the standard still feels early. I think WebMCP has real potential to become a simple way for websites to work directly with AI agent

title: Persistent Web Skills Runtime
pitch: A WebMCP-first runtime that learns browser workflows once, reuses them reliably, and repairs them when the web changes.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-first runtime that learns browser workflows once, reuses them reliably, and repairs them when the web changes. Like Comment Story Updates Persistent Web Skills Runtime Persistent Web Skills Runtime (PWS) is a WebMCP-first Chrome runtime that lets agents learn a browser workflow once, reuse it as a versioned skill, and repair it when the web changes. The problem Agentic browser tasks are commonly rediscovered through fragile clicks on every run. Small UI changes can break a workflow, while useful structured WebMCP tools may be ignored or forgotten. Repeated exploration is slow, brittle, token-intensive, and hard to trust. The solution PWS routes each task through a clear priority ladder: Native WebMCP → Cached Web Skill → Browser/DOM learning fallback It discovers the page's current WebMCP tools first. If there is no suitable native tool, it learns a successful semantic browser workflow, stores it in IndexedDB with immutable version history, validates the outcome on reuse, and repairs only the failed step when a dependency changes. The live taskboard demo shows an 11-action Learn → Reuse → Repair flow: it learns a create-task workflow, reuses it, survives a Create Task → Add Task UI change with a validated v1 → v2 skill repair, and demonstrates live native tool registration through toolchange . Key features Native-first WebMCP routing via document.modelContext.getTools() , live toolchange synchronization, and current-tool rebinding. Safe capability snapshots that persist metadata, not executable tool handlers. Semantic locators based on role, name, labels, stable attributes, and meaningful text instead of brittle structural selectors. Dependency-only DOM fingerprints, explicit result validation, and targeted step repair. An inspectable Runtime Inspector, execution log, timings, validation status, and skill versions. Built with React, TypeScript, Vite, a Chrome Manifest V3 extension, IndexedDB, Node.js, and an optional OpenAI Responses API service. API keys remain server-side; the interactive demo runs without a key through deterministic local learning and repair adapters. Career value I work as an agent engineer and repeatedly test browser automation over many fresh pages. I wanted a way for agents to achieve stronger results with fewer tokens. Building PWS made the practical value of WebMCP clear: expose structured tools, preserve proven workflows as reusable skills, and give agents a safe answer to reuse instead of forcing them to rediscover the UI. This can make agent browser work faster, more reliable, and easier to trust. title: Werkstern Podcast
pitch: A local podcast recorder where ChatGPT suggests the cuts and you approve each one. It works from the markers you set while recording, with a preview, a full undo, and untouched originals.
about_excerpt: A local podcast recorder where ChatGPT suggests the cuts and you approve each one. It works from the markers you set while recording, with a preview, a full undo, and untouched originals. Like Comment Story Updates Product Picture apply edit Inspiration My girlfriend is a medical student. I'm training as an alternative practitioner, the regulated German profession called Heilpraktiker . We spend a lot of our time on opposite sides of the same questions, and we kept ending up in long kitchen-table conversations about what the evidence actually says, where it's thin, and where people are being handed something more confident than anyone can honestly claim. At some point we figured those conversations would make a decent podcast. Then we looked at our calendars. We both work full time and we're both still studying. Finding two hours to record was doable. The rest of it was the problem. An hour of the two of us talking turns into a long evening of cleanup: the false starts, the "hold on, let me say that again", the twenty seconds where one of us is looking up a paper. Every podcast we know that quietly stopped after four episodes stopped for that reason. So the podcast went on hold and we built the tool first. A slightly ridiculous order of operations, but here we are. What it does Werkstern records each person's voice locally and uncompressed. While you're talking, you tag things with a single keypress: retake, error, good point, chapter, source. Those tags are the whole idea. The tedious part of editing gets done while you're still in the conversation, by the person who just heard what went wrong. Afterwards, ChatGPT reads the finished take through WebMCP and suggests specific regions to remove, in seconds. The app lists them for you, you keep or drop each one, and only then does anything get cut. You get an audible preview before you commit and an undo that puts everything back. The original recordings stay untouched, which we verify byte for byte in the test suite. Why we used MCP We started from a constraint. We're recording medical conversations, including half-formed thoughts and things one of us says and then takes back. That audio stays on the machine, so any design that began with uploading the file was ruled out early. The second thing that shaped it was accuracy. In a conversation about medicine the qualifier is often the load-bearing part of the sentence. "This helps in a narrow group of patients" and "this helps" are two different claims, and only one of them is true. We needed to see every proposed cut before it happened. WebMCP fit both of those. The model never receives audio. It receives a deliberately thin description of the take: markers, director signals and pause windows, all in seconds. No names, no device labels, no file paths, no tokens. It reasons over that and hands back numbers, and the app does the actual cutting locally with FFmpeg, sample-accurately. That division of labour is what made the project feel workable. The model handles the part it's good at, which is reading a conversation and having an opinion about what to trim. The app handles the part it's good at, which is being exact and reversible. The approval step in between is where most of our care went. How we built it The recorder came first and took most of the time. Capture. An AudioWorklet per station at 48 kHz, 24-bit mono, with echo cancellation, noise suppression and automatic gain deliberately switched off. Two-second chunks, each carrying a CRC32, buffered in IndexedDB so a Wi-Fi dropout costs you nothing. Node, Fastify and ws on the host machine; the browser side is plain ES modules with no framework. Clock drift. Two laptops have two crystals, and over an hour they disagree. This was the hardest audio problem here. Werkstern writes a 1 kHz stripe digitally into every raw track just after the start and again just before the stop, then locates both afterwards by cross-correlation. For each guest track the correction factor is $$f = \frac{n_{\text{end}} - n_{\text{start}}}{N_{\text{end}} - N_{\text{start}}}$$ where $n$ are the guest's stripe positions and $N$ the host's, in samples. We report it as $(f - 1) \times 10^{6}$ ppm and correct it with asetrate plus SOXR resampling at 28-bit precision. A take is accepted only when the residual offset stays under 240 samples, which at 48 kHz works out to $$\frac{240}{48\,000} = 5\ \text{ms}.$$ Rendering. The soundboard stays out of the microphone signal. Every pad press is stored as an event, and the final stereo mix is rebuilt afterwards from that log plus a content-addressed copy of each sound file. Replace a sound six months later and the old episode still renders exactly as it did. The agent layer sits on top and touches none of that. Eight tools registered in the top-level document through document.modelContext.registerTool : four read-only ones, preview_edit_batch which validates and displays without saving anything, and three writing tools behind the approval dialog. Every schema is closed with additionalProperties: false and bounded lengths, and each tool carries an honest readOnlyHint so the host can tell reading from writing. Cuts are stored as batches of source-time regions with a revision number that only ever goes up. Every write has to state the revision it believes is current, so a command built on stale information gets rejected instead of landing on a take that has moved on. The preview you hear is the complement of what was removed: for regions $R = {[s_i, e_i)}$ over a take of length $T$, it plays $[0, T) \setminus \bigcup_i [s_i, e_i)$, concatenated. Challenges we ran into Approval turned out to be a concurrency problem. Our worst bug had nothing to do with audio. Two approval requests could share the same dialog element: the second one overwrote the text of the first while it was still open, and one click then resolved both promises. You would have read "render a preview?" and, with that same click, authorized a permanent edit. Approvals are serialized now, and a second request arriving while one is open gets refused. Cancelling, losing the connection, leaving the dialog unanswered, and a dialog that fails to open all count as a no. Undo had a hole in it. If you queued a preview render and then hit undo, the render was still holding the old region list and would cheerfully write the audio you had just discarded back to disk. A render now re-reads the take before it starts and gives up if the batch is gone. We reviewed our own work adversarially, and it was uncomfortable. Before calling it finished we ran an independent audit against our own commit. It came back with one critical finding and a handful of serious ones. Then, while fixing those, I introduced a new one: my approval guard could get stuck and silently refuse every write for the rest of the session. It only surfaced because a browser test behaved oddly and I chased it instead of writing it off as flakiness. I'm glad I did. Testing a modal dialog under browser automation was miserable. The automation pane we used never dispatches the <dialog> close event. showModal() opens it, close() sets the return value, and the listener simply never runs. Instead of calling it working on a harness we couldn't trust, we proved the flow two other ways: unit tests with a DOM stub where the event does fire, and an end-to-end test that drives the real FFmpeg binary over a synthetic take, checks the output is exactly 48 kHz stereo 16-bit at the expected length, and confirms the source file's SHA-256 is identical before and after. Being straight about filler words. The first feature everyone asks for is automatic removal of "um" and "äh". We have no transcript and no speech recognition, so we can't do it. get_edit_capabilities says so directly in its output, to the model, in the tool response itself. Leaving that vague would have taken one sentence. and honestly we didnt had time to make a video, so we simply asked ChatGPT to generate one :D What we learned The question that mattered shifted over the project. It started as how much the model could do on its own and ended up as how precisely we could stop it. One approval covers exactly one write. Anything ambiguous resolves to no. The recordings come out identical to how they went in, and we can show that rather than claim it. We also learned how much of this rests on the unglamorous half. Nobody will ever notice the sync stripes or the checksum on every two-second chunk. Without them there'd be no trustworthy take for a model to reason about in the first place. What's next Local transcription with faster-whisper, running on the same machine so nothing has to leave it. That's what would unlock filler words and picking highlights by what was actually said. We left it out of this round because we wanted the smaller claim to be accurate. After that, a preview that spans several edit batches at once. And, eventually, the podcast. Built With ai-agents audio-processing audioworklet chatgpt c

title: FluencyLab
pitch: A WebMCP-powered communication simulator for practicing clearer writing and speaking under pressure.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered communication simulator for practicing clearer writing and speaking under pressure.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 FluencyLab started from a simple problem: knowing what you want to say and being able to communicate it clearly under pressure are two different things. 

 This comes up in interviews, meetings, presentations, and everyday workplace conversations. Someone may understand their work well but still struggle to organize their thoughts quickly, explain an idea concisely, or respond confidently when put on the spot. 

 I wanted to explore what a focused practice environment for those moments could look like. So, I designed FluencyLab as a communication training simulator where users can practice responding to realistic prompts, receive structured feedback, and try again. 

 For this prototype, I focused on interview and workplace communication practice. 

 What I Built 

 FluencyLab is a web-based communication training simulator for practicing clearer writing and speaking-style responses under time pressure. 

 The prototype uses a structured prompt bank with different practice scenarios. A user can receive a prompt, write a response, and get feedback across areas such as: 

 
 Clarity 
 Structure 
 Vocabulary 
 Confidence 
 

 FluencyLab also provides an improved sample response so the user can compare it with their first attempt and then try the exercise again. 

 The core practice loop is: 

 Choose a drill → Respond → Get feedback → Retry 

 I exposed this workflow through WebMCP tools so an AI agent can work with FluencyLab without having to guess how the app works or what actions are available. 

 For example, a user can tell an agent: 

 
 "I have an interview tomorrow. Help me practice explaining my experience clearly and concisely." 
 

 From that goal, the agent can use FluencyLab's WebMCP tools to choose a relevant practice prompt, let the user respond, analyze the response, and help them try again. 

 How I Built It 

 FluencyLab is currently a lightweight web prototype built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. 

 The application uses client-side routing for the different sections and practice flows, and a structured prompt bank provides the scenarios used during practice. 

 For the WebMCP integration, I exposed parts of the FluencyLab practice flow as tools an agent can use. The tools allow the agent to generate a practice prompt, analyze a user's response, and retry the same exercise. 

 One of the things I had to think carefully about was what should actually become a WebMCP tool. I wanted each tool to map to something useful that already happens within FluencyLab. 

 The app can still be used normally through its interface, but WebMCP gives an agent a structured way to understand what FluencyLab can do and guide the user through the same practice experience. 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges was deciding what should become a WebMCP tool. 

 It would have been easy to expose many small UI actions, but I didn't think that would necessarily make the agent experience useful. Instead, I had to think about the user's actual goal. What is the user trying to accomplish, and what does the agent need from FluencyLab to help them do it? 

 Another challenge was deciding how much to build for the prototype. FluencyLab does not yet have a large dynamically generated library of scenarios, so I used a structured prompt bank and made it possible for the agent to choose the right practice flow based on what the user wants to work on. 

 This gave me a practical way to demonstrate the WebMCP experience without building functionality that wasn't necessary for the prototype. 

 What I Learned 

 Building FluencyLab with WebMCP made me think differently about how a website can work with an AI agent. 

 When building for the web, I normally think about what a person sees and interacts with: pages, buttons, forms, navigation, and the steps they take to complete something. With WebMCP, I also had to think about how an agent knows what the application can do. 

 Instead of having the agent look at the page and try to figure out which buttons to click, FluencyLab can expose specific actions as tools. The agent knows those actions are available and can use the ones that make sense for what the user is trying to accomplish. 

 I also learned that deciding how those tools should work is as much a product-design question as it is a technical one. What you call a tool, what it does, what information it needs, and what it returns all affect how well an agent can use it. 

 What's Next 

 There is still a lot I would like to explore with FluencyLab. 

 I would like to expand the prompt library with more interview scenarios, meetings, presentations, difficult workplace conversations, and writing exercises. I would also like to add actual voice-based practice so users can respond verbally instead of typing a response to simulate speaking. 

 Longer term, I would like FluencyLab to recognize areas a user repeatedly struggles with and use that to suggest what they should practice next or gradually introduce more challenging scenarios. 

 I would also like to explore what more of the FluencyLab experience could be exposed through WebMCP as the product grows, while keeping the main idea simple: helping people practice expressing what they already know more clearly and confidently.

title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation.
